Uniform Title: Tattvacintāmaṇi, Chapters 16 through End Author: Pūrṇānanda Commentator: Bhuvanamohana Śaṅkhyatīrtha
Description: Critically edited from original manuscripts with the original commentary by Bhuvanamohana Saṅkhyātīrtha and with notes by Cintāmaṇi Bhaṭṭācārya.
Notes: Transcribed by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 1: December 11, 2007.
Publication year: 1936 Publication city: Calcutta Publication country: India
The Sixteenth Chapter: [The Promise to Describe the Inner Sacrifice] Now I shall describe the inner sacrifice, which bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life.
[The Supreme Self’s engagement in creation despite being devoid of qualities:
There was the one supreme Brahman, subtle, eternal, and beyond the senses; when the watery portion had passed away, the desire to create arose. (2)

1. Thus, having explained the procedure for ritual placement (*nyāsa*) up to its conclusion through fifteen chapters, and since the sequence of worship (*pūjākrama*) must now be discussed according to the logic of the occasion:
"Those who abandon the deity residing within themselves and search for the deity externally..."
Having abandoned the Kaustubha gem held in his hand, he wanders about out of a craving for glass.
Having visualized Śivā within one's heart as if she were standing outside, one should worship her;
and for whichever deity, according to their respective ornaments and vehicles.
"O Supreme Goddess, one should contemplate that very [deity] during his worship," according to such statements from the sixth chapter of the *Śāktānandatarangiṇī*; and:
"Having performed the procedure for the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), one should perform the external sacrifice (*bahiryāga*)."
One who is devoid of internal sacrifice has no authority in external sacrifice.
The fruit of external sacrifice never exists without internal sacrifice;
therefore, O Hero, one should diligently undertake internal sacrifice.

And because it is heard in the third chapter of the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya* that the external sacrifice (*bāhyayāga*) is preceded by the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), [the author] sets forth the sequence of the internal sacrifice in this exposition, beginning with the words "Now" (*atha*).
The word "now" means immediately after the description of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) which is an ancillary of worship.
2. Having thus proposed the determination of the sequence of the internal sacrifice (antaryāga), [the author states]:

"One should also contemplate the principles (tattvas) of all beings within the Cause (kāraṇa), which are merged in the state of seeds (bījabhāva) within the Supreme Self (paramātman) in reverse order."
[The Process of Emanation in Brief] Immediately following the dissolution, the supreme creation is manifested in the form of a bubble;
within that are the worlds, and that egg (aṇḍa) becomes twofold. (3)
Having reflected thus, O Goddess of the gods, one should contemplate the portion of earth that has entered into water,
and the water as the form of fire, and that form of fire [as the form of the Self].
Following the direction stated in the eleventh chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra* regarding the dissolution of the other principles (*tattva*) in sequence into *prakṛti*, which is their cause,

and the subsequent dissolution of *prakṛti* into the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), [the author] describes the state characterized by the manifestation of the nature of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) with the words beginning "There was one" (*ekamāsīt*). Thus, having set forth the previously mentioned order of dissolution:
O Supreme Goddess, one should contemplate the Great One as dissolved in Prakṛti;
the seeker of liberation should contemplate Prakṛti as dissolved in the Supreme Self.
Having thus described the dissolution of all things up to primordial nature (prakṛti) into the Supreme Self, [it continues]:
"There was neither day nor night, neither twilight, nor sun, nor even moon;
this entire universe was composed of darkness and devoid of worlds."
Having contemplated that which is unknown and unperceivable, as if entirely asleep,
O Great Goddess, one should not conceptualize anything at all.
"In the beginning, there was the one Supreme Brahman— eternal, subtle, beyond the senses,

consisting of eternal bliss, the abode, whose form is light, and who is the ancient. By such passages, the state consisting of the mere manifestation of the Supreme Self at that time is described in that very [text] by the Blessed Lord.
Manu also says:
"This was then enveloped in darkness, unperceived, without distinguishing marks, beyond the reach of reasoning, unknowable, as if entirely asleep."

By these and other such statements, the state of the great dissolution (mahāpralaya) has been described in this very manner. He states the cause for the desire to create (sisṛkṣā): "the watery portion. The meaning is that without water, neither creation nor the maintenance of the created living beings would be possible. This desire to create occurs merely through such declarations as "Let waters be born; let earth be born," and "It [the Self] thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate.'"
[This is] from the Chāndogya Śruti (3.4). Now, he demonstrates the sequence of creation with the words "of the dissolution," etc. By this, it is stated that the creation of water occurs first.
Also, in the eleventh chapter of the Gandharva-tantra:
Within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) there is water, and therein the imperishable frog;
on its back, which is the locus for the worship of Kālāgni and others as described in the Nirukta, the practitioner of mantra should worship the form of Kālāgnirudra.
[The Nature of the Support-Power and Others, and the Instruction for Worship] Therein, one should contemplate the Support-Power (Ādhāra-śakti), who is the very form of the Root-Nature (Mūla-prakṛti),
the Goddess resembling the autumnal moon, holding two lotuses. || 5 ||

One should worship the Tortoise, who has the luster of a sapphire and is mounted upon a stone in the shape of a tortoise, supporting the Tortoise on his head; and one should worship Ananta, who resembles a jasmine flower.
The best of practitioners should worship Brahmā seated above.
From the union of those two, there arose a rain consisting of supreme nectar;
O Goddess, it floods this entire universe in its fullness.
There, in that water, the supreme practitioner should contemplate his own self;
he should contemplate a bubble there, and therein he should contemplate the Supreme Nature (Prakṛti).
This very same point has been stated by such passages as these. Regarding the phrase "within that," the *Gandharva Tantra* clearly states in its eleventh chapter:
"From primordial nature (prakṛti) indeed arises the Great One (mahat), and from the Great One likewise arises the I-maker (ahaṃkāra);
from the I-maker arises the mind (manas), and from the mind the ether (kha) has arisen."
Having drawn the wind from space, one should contemplate fire arising from that wind;
having reached water from fire, one should then contemplate earth from water.

Thus, "of two kinds" means it is divided into two parts; and this division is to be performed with the *praṇava*. As it is said in that very same place: "Having divided [it] into two with the *praṇava*, one should fill it completely with streams of water."
Upon his head stands the white deity in the form of a boar, dark as the *tāla* tree, holding the earth upon his tusk. (8)
One should worship Vasumatī, who holds a blue lotus in her hand, who is adorned with necklaces and armlets, and whose girdle is the shimmering ocean.
The divine nectar of red rice is like the essence of pure lac. || 10 ||
With both hands, one should worship an island in the waters that resembles coral,
strewn with the nine jewels and endowed with the eight supernatural powers.
[The Worship of the Four Seats] One should worship Uḍḍīyāna between the navel and the sexual organ;
likewise, Jālandhara in the mouth, and Kāmarūpaka in the anus. 12.
One should worship Pūrṇagiri in the center of the heart and Śrīhaṭṭa above the palate;
at Pūrṇagiri, a person should worship the Svarṇagiri-pīṭha. (13)
One should worship the Kalpodyāna (the garden of the wish-fulfilling tree) all around it with perfumes and flowers.
[The nature of the Kalpavṛkṣa and the instruction for its worship.]
In the center, the practitioner of mantra should place the Kalpavṛkṣa tree, which fulfills all desires.
The supreme tree, the eternal abode of all beings, consists of the [five] letters;
it has the five exhilarating seed-syllables as its trunk and the Bindu and Nāda as its great roots.
12. "Between the *śakti* and the *nābhika*" means between the *anāhata* and the *maṇipūra* [cakras].
14. "Fulfilling all desires" means pervading all directions with its branches and sub-branches. (p.
546) It has expanded in all directions through the branches of the syllables of the earth.
The three worlds were completely covered by his own water, syllables, and leaves.
Blazing with sprouts the color of fire, resembling coral shoots,
and illuminating the beauty of his body with flowers radiant as the color of wind.
Bowing low with fruits as numerous as the syllables of the sky, that supreme refuge of all beings sprinkles the Supreme Goddess with the honey known as the highest nectar.

It is fashioned by the Vedas, Agamas, and other scriptures; it is highly exalted and captivating; it is composed of Śiva and Śakti; and it is the very foundation upon which the three worlds rest. (19)
[Contemplation of the Pārijāta and other trees: In the midst of that, the mantra-practitioner should visualize a beautiful Pārijāta tree;
he should also contemplate Kadamba, Nāga, Punnāga, Campaka, and other such trees. (20)
At the root of the Kalpa tree is a jeweled ground with sands of golden luster;
[the nature of the wish-fulfilling gem house and so forth, and the instruction on its visualization:
in the center is the unsurpassed wish-fulfilling gem house, having the form of light. (21)
Resembling the rising sun, it pervaded the entire sphere of the universe;
it was a hundred yojanas in extent and adorned with various jewels.
It was provided with four gates, adorned with golden walls,
beautifully embellished with arrangements of jewels, and graced with eight door-panels.
It was constructed with the nine precious gems, adorned with lofty archways,
and embellished by rows of banners hanging from the tips of golden staffs.
The pillar situated in the central corner is endowed with the nine jewels and adorned with great rubies, lapis lazuli, and jeweled chowries. || 25 ||
It was enriched with canopies of pearl necklaces, resplendent with golden pillars,
filled with gentle breezes, and adorned with fragrant flowers.
Adorned with many jewels, conchs, bells, and various articles, it was beautified by the humming of tall bees wandering about, intoxicated by honey. || 27 ||
Adorned with pavilions featuring panels attached to the walls of the palace,
its surrounding quarters were bowed down by hosts of gods led by Indra.
A parasol fashioned from gold and jewels [is placed] above the mandala;
in its center is a circle of gems of supreme brilliance. (29)
[The nature of the jeweled altar and so forth situated in the midst of the Nandana garden, and the instruction for its visualization:
the altar fashioned of jewels.
One should contemplate her situated there, red in color and adorned with four squares.
In that space was a lion-throne adorned with various jewels;
in its center was a great wheel filled with a flood of nectar.
In the midst of that, one should meditate upon the triple-peaked mountain, which is radiant and composed of light.
One should perform protection with the weapon-mantra (astra) and protect [the space] with the cow-seal (dhenumudrā).
[The Yonimudrā:
I shall now describe the yonimudrā, both external and internal. One should contemplate it by contracting the anus and likewise the other, the brahmasūtra. (33)
Having agitated the circle of nectar, which has the form of a blazing lamp-flame, it returns once more as a stream of nectar to the root lotus. (34)
And thus one should perform it in seven ways for the sake of bringing about the presence of the Goddess.
[The Sequence of Meditation:
Having recollected the supreme [Goddess], who consists of Brahman, through the yoga of meditation by means of the root mantra, (35)
Having filled [the breath] by means of *pūraka* and having retained it by means of *kumbhaka*,
one should worship that Sundarī, who is surrounded by a host of Yoginīs.
[He meditated on] Mahātripurasundarī, who is joined with flowing nectar within the lotus-like body of the Goddess, and who is worthy of being saluted by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
[Instruction on the Meditation on the Door-keepers with their Powers:
Thereafter, one should meditate upon the door-keepers, each with his respective power, at every door. || 38 ||
[The Installation of the Goddess in the Thousand-Petaled Lotus] One should install the supreme Sundarī in the center of the thousand-petaled lotus;
within that, the liṅga of Bhairavānanda is situated in the womb (yoni). 39.
[The Contemplation of Their Unity]: Having brought about the unification of those two, the wise one should cause the nectar to be heard;
through the union of tongue and mouth, he should always drink that nectar. (40)
[The Worship of the Goddess, the Mental Sacrifice, and the Prohibition of Invocation:
Having brought the Beautiful One into one's heart, one should then worship her;
for in this mental worship within the heart, there is no invocation. (41)
34. Regarding "at the root": the meaning is "in the lotus situated at the *mūlādhāra*.

40. Regarding "into a state of oneness": this refers to those two, the *liṅga* of Bhairava and the bliss of Sundarī. "Nectar" means the supreme nectar produced from their state of aesthetic fusion (*sāmarasya*).
One should worship with the nectars and joys of both [the male and female principles] through the secret transmission.
[The determination of the number of vessels for the ritual services such as water for the feet:
One should prepare three vessels for the water for the feet (pādya), and likewise three vessels for the respectful offering (arghya). (42)
Then, one should have six vessels for sipping water (ācamana), three vessels for honey (madhu),
and one vessel for excellent enjoyments (subhoga) prepared upon the sixteenth petal.

[The Sequence of Mental Worship] One should offer the supreme nectar-water dripping from the stalk of the hanging ewer with its thousand petals, along with the well-perfumed flower of meditative visualization (bhāva). || 44 ||
Having placed [the vessel] in the hand according to the prescribed rule, one should fill a golden bowl;
the supreme substance is offered with mental services (mānasopacāras).
Thinking "I am imagining," one should mentally construct the ritual offerings.
[In this regard, the rule for the offering of water for the feet and so forth:
One should offer water for the feet at the lotus-feet, arghya-water upon the head, and water for sipping (ācamana) in the mouth;
one should offer the honey-mixture (madhuparka) three times into the mouth, and then pour out the honey-water.
Having again offered water for sipping (ācamana), the wise one [should offer] perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
[The distinction regarding the mantras for the ritual offerings:
In the mantras for the preliminary offerings, one should sequentially apply the heart-mantra, the fire-love-mantra (vauṣaṭ), and the water-mantra for the foot-water and so forth;
for the incense and flowers, one should offer them with "namaḥ" and "vauṣaṭ," ending with the heart-mantra for the others. 49.

44 | *Bhāvayati*: The "flowers of mental cultivation" (*bhāvapuṣpa*) will be explained further on. 49 | Now he states the specific [mantras] for the offering of services (*upacāra*): *Hṛt* means *namaḥ*; *vahnivallabhā* means *svāhā*.

The mantra for water is *svadhā*. And thus, the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) is offered with the word *namaḥ* at the end, the respectful offering (*arghya*) with *svāhā* at the end, and the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*)...

The practical meaning is that one should offer the incense with a mantra ending in *svadhā*, the flowers with a mantra ending in *namaḥ*, and the other ritual services (*upacāra*) with a mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*. (p.
550) [Herein is a variation in sequence according to another scripture.]
According to the Kuloḍḍīśa system as well, another method is now stated. || 50 ||
One should employ "svadhā" for incense and lamps, "svāhā" for the food offering and the water for sipping, and "namaḥ" in all other services, joined with the name ending in the nominative case.
[In this very regard, the opinion of the authors of the Kalpasūtras:
Furthermore, according to the view of the Kalpasūtras, in all ritual services (upacāras), the mantra "I offer" (kalpayāmi namaḥ) should be applied as prescribed. || 52 ||
[Special offerings for worship, such as *svayambhū* flowers, etc.
With *svayambhū* flowers, or even those produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, the practitioner should diligently worship the Supreme Goddess with flowers of intention (*bhāvapuṣpa*). 53.

[In that regard, there are fifteen flowers of existence: freedom from deceit, freedom from egoism, freedom from passion, freedom from pride, likewise freedom from delusion, freedom from hypocrisy, freedom from hatred, and being devoid of agitation. || 54 ||
The wise know that non-miserliness and non-greed are two flowers;
non-violence is the supreme flower, and the restraint of the senses is a flower. (55)
The flower of compassion, the flower of patience, and the flower of knowledge as the fifth—thus fifteen flowers of disposition are prescribed for worship. (56)
[Other offerings: One should present an ocean of nectar, a mountain of flesh, and a heap of fish.
[The worship of the six limbs, etc.]
Then, having performed the six ancillary rites, one should worship Rati together with the Guru and the Nityās.
[The Rubbing as an Auxiliary to the Bathing] Having drawn a mandala on his left and led the Mistress of the Gods there,
the wise one should perform the rubbing with clarified butter according to the prescribed rule. (58)
[The Bathing of the Goddess:
With fragrant divine oils, by thousands of celestial maidens, and with thousands of golden jars filled with fragrant water. (59)
With a spirit of devotion, one should sprinkle Bhavānī, who is affectionate toward her devotees,
with the pure waters of various holy fords using thousands of royal elephants.
By thousands of Naga maidens, by Kinnaras, and by hosts of Apsarases,
[he was honored] with the five nectars, the five products of the cow, milk, and even the curds of cows.
With coconut water, sugarcane juice, and cool water, as well as with cool water mixed with the seven types of earth; || 62 ||
With pure cold and warm water, as well as with water containing jewels, with water from all medicinal herbs, and even with highly fragrant water; || 63 ||
With a concentrated mind, one should perform the bathing of the Goddess using the *Sahasraśīrṣa* mantra and the *Pāvamānī* hymns, with eight jars and golden pitchers.
63. "With the waters of all medicinal herbs" (*jalaiḥ sarvauṣadhīnām*). Regarding the group of all medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadhigaṇa*), the *Dīpikā* states in its third chapter:
"Sura, māṃsī, vacā, kuṣṭha, śaileya, the two types of *rajanī*, *śaṭhī*, campaka, and *musta*—this is remembered as the group of all medicinal herbs."
64. "With the *sahasra*," and so forth; this means with the mantras of the *Puruṣasūkta*, beginning with "The Puruṣa has a thousand heads.
"With the *pāvamānī*" means with the *Pāvamānī-sūkta*, beginning with "The *pāvamānī*s are auspicious, yielding milk easily, dripping with clarified butter.
(p. 552) [The sequence for adorning the body of the Goddess.]
Having cleansed his body with unguents, one should have him dressed in fine linen garments;
likewise, one should perform the grooming of the hair with a comb and its binding according to the prescribed rite.
One should apply a tilaka on the forehead and vermilion in the parting of the hair;
likewise, one should provide red garments, garlands, and red ornaments.
One should apply a red ointment made of fragrant sandalwood and sihlaka;
one should provide all ornaments wherever and with whatever they may shine.
65. "Binding according to rule" means hair that has been consecrated (*saṃskṛta*) through the sequence of etymological definitions (*nirukta*).

67. Regarding "with *sihlaka*": the suffix *-ika* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*). *Sihlaka* is a specific fragrant substance. Amara states: "Turaṣka, piṇḍaka, sihlaka, and yāvana are synonyms. Regarding "all ornaments," the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya* clearly explains this in its third chapter:
One should offer a captivating conch adorned with a necklace of lordly serpents;
likewise, one should give bracelets, armlets, rings, and bangles,
as well as a toe-ring, all embellished with various gems.
One should place anklets on the feet and small bells on the waist;
one should also give a crest-jewel fashioned from gems,
as well as well-adorned earrings and ear-ornaments.
One should apply collyrium to the eyes, a pearl from an elephant’s tusk to the tip of the nose,
a leaf-pattern ornament to the neck, and a necklace adorned with pearls and gems; likewise,
one should wear a third necklace of bliss and a jeweled ring upon the finger.
By such statements as these, the various types of ornaments are also demonstrated in works such as the *Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī* and the *Gandharvatantra*.

The meaning is that regarding the principle "that by which something shines," whichever particular ornament brings about a specific beauty in whichever particular limbs, that ornament should be applied to those respective parts.

(553) [Instruction on Prostration Following the Offering of the Final Service to the Auspicious Sandals: Having offered the precious auspicious sandals marked with the staff-sign of coral, and having brought [the deity] into the center of the yantra, one should prostrate with a concentrated mind. || 68 ||
[The Mantra of Salutation] I bow to the illustrious Tripurasundarī, who has arrived;
she who generates all auspicious fortune and whose very nature is that of all the gods. 69.
[Furthermore, the instruction on worship and its sequence:
Having again offered water for the feet and so forth, one should worship the Supreme Goddess.
One should indeed offer fragrance to the Goddess through the nostril by means of the Tattva. (70)
Having worshipped with flowers of pure intention, one should offer incense that wafts like the wind;
one should present the supreme light of a lamp and offer various food offerings.
Likewise, from the earth element and from the wind element, he fashioned an auspicious chowrie;
the solar disc became a mirror, and the full moon became a parasol. (72)
A lotus, a girdle, a garland, a radiant necklace of joy,
and various divine flowers produced from the seven continents.
70–72 | Now, he teaches the worship of the Goddess once again as she is mounted upon the yantra, beginning with the words "again" (*punaḥ*) and so forth.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "water for the feet and so forth" (*pādyādikam*), the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) and the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) are to be understood. He describes the ritual services (*upacāra*) such as perfume and the rest with the words beginning "through the nose" (*nāsā*) and so forth.

"By means of the principles" (*tattvena*) means by means of the twenty-four principles (*caturviṃśatitattva*). As it is said: "The wise one should offer perfume by means of the twenty-four principles."

This is in accordance with the statement in the third chapter of the *Kaulāvalī*: "with the flowers of the emotional states" (*bhāvapuṣpaiḥ*). The eighteen flowers of the emotional states have been previously demonstrated in this very same *Prakāśa* by the passage beginning with "without deceit, without egoism," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "as food offerings" (*naivedyāni*):
the connection is that one should present the food offerings consisting of the earth element (*pṛthvītattva*).
73. It should be understood that "various kinds of flowers" is prescribed for the worship of Śakti. Specifically, it is stated in the third chapter of the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*:
"Karavīra, Javā, Droṇa, Campaka, and Nāgakeśara."
From the base up to the aperture of Brahmā, one should offer this bell, which consists of the sound of the unstruck resonance (*anāhatadhvani*), by means of the nectar-wind within the *suṣumṇā*. (74)
Having performed worship with lamps and having offered them, one should awaken [the deity]. || 75 ||
Among the mudrās to be demonstrated, the Sundarī-mudrā consists of directing the wind rising from the base through the *suṣumnā* to the end of the sixteen [finger-breadths],
while the eyes are fixed on the tip of the nose, free from blinking or opening. || 76 ||
Drawing [the breath] into the middle of the eyebrows,
the wielder of the sword of knowledge should not touch tooth with tooth, lip with lip, nor palate with the tongue.
If one is capable, one should perform the *lakṣa* outside, free from the blinking and opening of the eyes;
this is that *Sundarī Mudrā*, which brings delight to Bhairava. (78)
The right fist is closed with the index finger placed against the nose;
this is the mudrā known as Vismaya (Astonishment), which causes one to be possessed by wonder. || 79 ||
"Furthermore, one should diligently offer to the Goddess garlands made of *kadamba*, *pārijāta*, and other such flowers, combined with fragrances.
(74) Now, he describes the procedure for the offering of the bell, beginning with the words "from the root" (*ā mūlāt*): from the *mūlādhāra*...
The channel named Suṣumṇā exists, extending as far as the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). As it is said in the fifth chapter of the Gāndharva [Tantra]:
"That which is situated in the middle of Meru, extending from the root to the aperture of Brahmā, is the Suṣumṇā; it consists entirely of splendor and has the form of fire."

By means of this very *suṣumṇā*, the vital air (*vāyu*) circulates from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *brahmarandhra*. Due to the impact of that very air, a certain uninterrupted sound arises within the heart-lotus (*hṛtpuṇḍarīka*), which consists of the *śabdabrahman* and is known as the *anāhata*.
That very sound is designated here by the term *anāhatadhvani*. One should present that very resonance as the sound of a bell.
This is the realized meaning.
79. Regarding the phrase "the joined fist," the reading in the *Tantrasāra* is "the firm fist.
(p. 555) [Nādamudrā]
The right fist with the thumb raised is the Nāda-mudrā;
that same mudrā, through the joining of the index finger and the thumb, is celebrated as the Bindu-mudrā. (80)
[The Knowledge Seal (Jñānamudrā):
When the Knowledge Seal (jñānamudrā) is not positioned directly in front [of the practitioner],
[it is the Yoga Seal (Yogamudrā)].
When joined at the region of the heart, it is called the yoga-mudrā. || 81 ||
[Regarding the outer and inner *yonimudrā*: One should then perform the *yonimudrā*, for that very same [mudrā] may also be internal.
Being heedful in the tasting of its flesh and blood is for the sake of liberation. 82.
This is that supreme liberation, permeated by the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa);
its own will has become the Supreme Bliss Bhairava himself. 83.
The power of the vital wind (vāyuśakti), situated in the bulb (kanda) and entering the gateway of the Suṣumṇā,
is slender like the awn of a grain of wild rice (nīvāraśūka) and more subtle than a spider's thread (viṣatantu).
Resembling ten million flashes of lightning and possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
she is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the entire world.
80. Regarding "muṣṭi": the meaning is that the right hand is the "Nāda-mudrā" when its thumb is held in a fist.
The practical implication here is that one should hold the thumb of the right hand restrained by the other four fingers.
81. If the aforementioned Bindu-mudrā, which consists of the joining of the index finger and the thumb, is instead positioned facing [the practitioner], then...

The meaning is that it is called the "Knowledge Seal" (*jñānamudrā*). Thus, it is stated in the seventh chapter of the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*: "One should worship the Supreme Goddess with the seal known as Knowledge;
this is declared to be the Knowledge Seal by means of the thumb and forefinger."
Regarding "in the heart" (*hṛditi*): the meaning is that this very *bindumudrā*, when joined at the heart, is called *yogamudrā*.
(82) Regarding "the womb" (*yonīti*): *yonimudrā* is of two kinds, distinguished by being external or internal. Among these, the external *yonimudrā* is well known.
He describes the internal *yonimudrā* with the words beginning with "that very [mudrā]" (*saiva*).

Agitated by the bursting open of the knots of the heart, the knots of the palate, and the door-panels [of the channels], one should lead [the breath] into the Śāmbhava triangle situated between the *bindu* and the uvula. (86)
Having entered, she delights intensely and incessantly with the Puruṣa;
one whose mind is steady should always meditate so that the mind may become stable. 87.
[The twofold nature of samādhi according to the distinction between self-awareness and non-awareness:
Therein, samādhi arises, adorned with two designations;
one is indeed named "self-aware" (svayaṃprajñāta), while the other bears the name "non-aware" (asaṃprajñāta). (88)
[Therein, the state of] self-cognition arises through the preponderance of the notion of Śiva;
[it is] the state of non-cognition.
But that which is called "non-cognition" (asaṃprajñāta) indeed becomes the Śiva-principle. || 86 ||
Regarding the distinctions of self-awareness (*svayaṃprajñāta*):
the distinction of self-awareness may be intense or even more intense.
Regarding the distinctions of non-awareness (*asaṃprajñāta*): [the same applies].
The variety of non-discerning [samādhi] is dull, and likewise, it is even more dull. || 90 ||
[Regarding the nature of the first two divisions:
It is characterized by laughter, weeping, horripilation, trembling, perspiration, and so forth;
and it is observed as concentration (*samādhi*) that is intense and even more intense. (91)
[The nature of the two divisions of the second stage:
The eyes are closed as if blinking, the body remains with its characteristic posture, and concentration is observed to be slow and even slower. (92)
88. Regarding "samādhi": there is a twofold division of samādhi based on the distinction between *samprajñāta* (cognitive) and *asamprajñāta* (non-cognitive).

Furthermore, various sub-divisions of these two types, according to their degrees of intensity—such as intense (*tīvra*) or more intense (*tīvratara*)—are specifically demonstrated in the *Vyāsabhāṣya* on the *Pātañjala-sūtra*.
(p. 557) May one become perpetually happy through the yoga of Śambhu.
Having summoned the union of those two, [he attained] the supreme nectar of Gokula.
Having mentally offered water, rebirth no longer exists;
then the beautiful woman becomes delighted by that knowledge consisting of bliss. 94.
[The placement of the Goddess upon a bed of flowers for the sake of rest, and the conversation of affection:
Then, having prepared a bed of flowers, he led the Sovereign of the Gods there;
with rhythmic claps that made the mind dance and which gave rise to the erotic and other aesthetic sentiments. (95)
One should please the Supreme Goddess with dances, songs, and instrumental music;
therefore, the Mother Kāmeśvarī is pleased, as is Kāmeśvara. (96)
[The Fruit of Mental Sacrifice] Having performed a single great mental worship, the supreme internal adoration,
one attains perfection and is not bound by bondage. 97.
[The commencement of the exposition on the fire-oblation of knowledge (jñānahoma): I shall proclaim the fire-oblation of knowledge by which one becomes composed of Brahman.
[In that regard, the square sacrificial pit (caturasrakuṇḍa):]
Having meditated upon the fire-pit known as the quadrangular one by means of his knowledge, the knower of mantras [should proceed]. (98)

98. Having thus described the intermediate worship (*antarārcana*), he begins to explain its constituent part, the knowledge-oblation (*jñānahoma*), with the words beginning "the knowledge-oblation" (*jñānahomam*). The knowledge-oblation is indeed a mental oblation (*mānasahoma*). It is termed a "knowledge-oblation" because the procedure of the oblation to be described hereafter is accomplished by means of knowledge alone. He states its fruit with the words beginning "by which" (*yenetyādinā*).
"By knowledge" (jñānena) means by knowledge alone, that is, by the mere activity of the mind, by mere contemplation. "Called square" (caturasrākhyam):

this sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is to be conceived as being like the square pit described in the seventh chapter [of the *Jñānārṇava*]. With this very intention, it is stated in the twenty-second chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*:
"Having meditated upon the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) called 'quadrangular' by means of knowledge, as previously described"—thus it is said.
[The fourfold nature of the selves. (p. 558)
Indeed, the number of the Ātman-s according to the Vedas must be known by the best of practitioners. [The fruit of knowing the explained Ātman:
By the mere knowledge of these, rebirth no longer exists. (99)
The essential nature of the self exists in all living beings through its common aspect;
yet that self, whose form is vital breath, is the Supreme Self within the heart. (100)

[The Self’s Pervasiveness of Moving and Non-Moving Bodies] Pervading the entire body, whether moving or non-moving, one should know the Self to be the nature of the *haṃsa*, manifesting as the play of inhalation and exhalation. (101)
[Due to the power of delusion, this very thing receives the designation "living being"]:
"Living being" (jīva) would be merely a name for that same thing, characterized by breath through delusion;
inhalation and exhalation are states of the body, which is nothing but delusion—of this there is no doubt. (102)

99. Regarding "the selves" (*ātmānaḥ*): the meaning is that the Vedas are fourfold in number, categorized by the distinctions of the self (*ātman*), the inner self (*antarātman*), the supreme self (*paramātman*), and the self of knowledge (*jñānātman*).

From this point until the end of the section on "light" (*prakāśa*), almost everything corresponds with the twenty-second chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*. Prior to the two quarters beginning with "the selves" (*tatrā'tmāna*):
"O Goddess worshipped by heroes, that [maṇḍala] should be known as square by means of the *ātman*s.
Thus two quarters [of a verse] are seen. Here, it appears that these two quarters beginning with "by means of the *ātman*s" have been omitted due to the scribe's negligence;
otherwise, the description of the four *ātman*s would result in an inconsistency. And thus:
By reflecting upon the words of the *Niruktajñānārṇava*, it follows that a square sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be prepared by means of the fourfold self of the *Nirukta*;
and he himself will state:
"The Self, the Inner Self, the Supreme Self, and the Knowledge-Self are proclaimed [as the four]."
"One should meditate upon this form as a square fire-pit of consciousness.

(100–102). Having thus described the fourfold nature of the Self, he defines its essential nature—characterized by its conjunction with all embodied forms and so forth—with the passage beginning "by the common [nature]" and ending with "it is indeed an error, there is no doubt. By this, the individual self (jīvātman)—

Just as the space within a jar appears divided due to the breaking of the potter's wheel [and the subsequent shattering] of the jar, the jar itself becomes divided; yet there can be no division in space itself. (103)
Likewise, when the body perishes, the individual soul residing within the body remains pervading the entire world by itself; therefore, the state of the Self is great.
The non-difference between the individual self and the supreme self has been established. He is the form of all vital breaths, pervading the bodies of all moving and unmoving beings;

he is the nature of the *haṃsa*, consisting of both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. Therein, it is the very Self—who possesses all the manifestations such as inhalation and exhalation and is situated within every body—that is designated as the "individual soul" (*jīvātman*) due to delusion. In ultimate reality, however, there is nothing other than the supreme self.

The individual self (jīvātman) has no existence; the perception of breath, exhalation, and so forth as attributes of the body occurs solely through the power of delusion. For this very reason, it is said in the fifth chapter of the Gandharva Tantra:
"The Self is indeed eternal, omnipresent, immutable, and free from defects."
The One is divided through delusion and illusion, not by its own nature;
therefore, for me there is no duality, no phenomenal world, and no cycle of existence.
By these and other [verses], the eternality, unity, omnipresence (*vyāpakatva*), and so forth of the Self (*ātman*) have been established. (vv.

103–104) Now, one might raise the objection: "Since the difference of the Self according to the delimitation of this or that body is established by experience, how can its unity and other such qualities be proven?
He dispels this doubt by means of an illustration, beginning with the words "the potter" (*kulāla*). Just as...
Even though space is one, when jars are produced by means of different potter's wheels, the space delimited by each respective jar appears as if it were distinct;

however, in reality, it is the jar itself that possesses distinctness or difference, whereas in space there can be no such distinctness. Space is indeed one; its conventional usage as being divided occurs solely due to the difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). For this very reason, Viśvanātha [states] "one..."

It has been stated that [the Self] exists even though it is conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Having thus presented the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), he demonstrates the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words beginning "In the same way" (*tathā*).
Just like the space delimited by a jar and so forth previously shown, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) residing within the body and delimited by the body is called the individual soul (*jīva*);
however, upon the destruction of the body, being free from limiting adjuncts, this very Self pervades the universe and remains everywhere—in all worlds, this [Self].
The ellipsis is "having pervaded the entire collection of objects," or rather, this is how the connection [of the sentence] is to be understood.

Just as upon the destruction of various individual jars, the space delimited by those respective jars is nothing other than the Great Space (mahākāśa), so too upon the destruction of various bodies, the Self delimited by those respective bodies is nothing other than the Supreme Self (paramātman).
The essential meaning is that there is no independent existence of the Self as a separate individual soul (jīva).
With this very intention, it is stated in the fifth chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*:
"Just as space is said to be the space within a jar and the great space,
so too delusion is declared to be twofold, by way of the self as the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)."
Listen also to the knowledge of the Self as taught by Śiva. (105)
[The Nature of the Inner Self:
By the word "inner" (antaḥ), all secrets and subtle forms are indicated;
pervading everything by way of the nature of the Supreme Self, it unfolds. 106.
Because it pervades everything—whether moving or unmoving—by virtue of its intrinsic nature as the internal organ, it is therefore celebrated as the "Inner Self" (antarātman). || 107 ||
[The Nature of the Supreme Self:
Indeed, when that very self, the *haṃsa*, becomes accessible to the yogi, only then does he become truly "sighted," possessing the wings of the Vedas and Agamas. (108)
He is the pair of feet of Śiva and Śakti, whose eyes are the three *bindus*;
he who is the supreme swan (*paramahaṃsa*), for he indeed exists everywhere.
Then the elements are born; hear now of them in their proper order:
ether, wind, fire, water, and earth, in succession. (110)
The first seed of these five elements is said to be in the middle of the lake called ignorance, which is filled with the mud of delusion. (111)
In the lotus of conceptual proliferation, which has blossomed from the lotus-stalk of reality, the dwelling of this very delusion becomes illusory upon being seen. (112)
When this very Mahākāla becomes free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca), then Haṃsa, in the form of withdrawal, reveals his own self. || 113 ||
108 | He describes the nature of the Supreme Self (paramātman) with the words beginning "He alone," and so forth. By the words beginning "To that extent," the assumption of form is indicated.
(p. 561) "He has no state of being a bird at all; I am that Self established [therein]. Know Him as the Supreme Self—thus has this been declared. (114)
[The nature of the self consisting of knowledge:
That by which all this is known at all times and with equanimity. (115)
Just as the moon and the sun are constantly seen within water and milk, so too is the equality of milk perceived through the distinction between water and milk. 116.
In mud and sandalwood paste there is no difference between an outcaste and a twice-born;
however, the witness of all beings is proclaimed to be the Self of Knowledge. (117)
[Conclusion of the Description of the Fourfold Self] The self, the inner self, the supreme self, and the knowledge-self have been proclaimed.
[The previously promised four-cornered sacrificial pit consists of these four selves.]
One should visualize this very form as a square fire-pit of consciousness. || 118 ||
[The nature of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa):
It is beautiful with the girdle of bliss, endowed with the point and the three circles;
it has the form of the womb of the half-measure, and is eternally composed of the bliss of Brahman. 119.

[In that sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa)]: In the fire which consists of the Supreme Deity, which is expanded by the lamp of all-knowledge, and which resembles [the deity], one should offer the intense oblation of phenomenal existence (prapañca-āhuti). || 120 ||
The form known as sound, consisting of the alphabet and adorned with the letters of the syllables—
when these syllables are offered here, the soundless Brahman is born.
115 | "By which this is known"—this refers to what will be stated later: "that is proclaimed to be the nature of knowledge.
120 | Regarding the term *sannibha*: it means that in which there is a *nibhā*, or radiance, that is real (*satī*); the sense is that it is illuminated. (p.
562) [The conceptualization of the oblation therein.]
Regarding what is to be done and what is not to be done, as well as sin and merit, intention and conceptualization—
the lord of practitioners should prepare the sacrificial offering by means of both dharma and adharma.
[The instruction for the oblation with that sacrificial offering:
The officiating priest should offer oblations with mantras into the fire whose nature is consciousness;
having meditated upon the supreme Root-Vidyā, which is of the nature of Brahman and consists of pure consciousness. (123)
[Therein, the first mantra:
"In the fire of the Self, kindled by the oblation of dharma and adharma, I perpetually offer the functions of the senses with the ladle of the mind, by way of the path of the *suṣumṇā*."
The mantra, accompanied by the wife of Agni (Svāhā), has been revealed at the end of the root [mantra]. || 124 ||
[The second mantra:
In the fire whose nature is consciousness at the navel,
kindled by knowledge, I perpetually offer the activities of the senses as oblation with the ladle of the mind.
The mantra, ending with the root [mantra] and joined with the wife of Vahni (Svāhā), has thus been declared. || 125 ||
[The third mantra:
Grasping with the hands of light and space, I offer into the fire, using the ladle of *unmanī*, that which is filled with the oil of the portions of merit and demerit.
The mantra, accompanied by the wife of Agni (svāhā), was [uttered] at the end of the root-mantra by the Great-Souled One. || 126 ||

123. "One should offer oblations" means with the mantras to be described hereafter, beginning with *dharma-adharma*. By this, it is meant that one should offer the previously prepared sacrificial oblation (*havis*). The rest is clear. 124. He states the first mantra for the *jñāna-homa*: "Dharma... and so forth. And thus, first the root [mantra], and then...

The meaning is that one should offer the first oblation into the fire of the nature of the Self by reciting from "dharma-adharma" up to "juhomy aham," and then uttering "svāhā. The "functions of the senses" (akṣavṛttīḥ) refers to the operations of the sense organs. 125. He states the second [oblation] with the words "nābhau" (in the navel); here too, as before, the root [mantra] is used, followed by the portion from "nābhau" up to "juhomy aham."
Then, with the utterance "svāhā," one should offer the second oblation into the fire in the form of consciousness located at the navel; this is the meaning.
(126) Regarding the word "prakāśa": here too, the sequence of the oblation is as before.
(The fourth mantra, p. 563)
In the fire of consciousness— which blazes with uninterrupted fuellessness at its very limit, which is the adversary of the darkness of illusion,
and which is the ground for the unfolding of certain wondrous rays—
I offer the entire universe, beginning with the earth and ending with Śiva.
And at the end of the root mantra, the practitioner should offer oblations for the sake of attaining Brahman. || 128 ||
[The nature of the fire as Brahman]:

When, at that time, the man who knows Brahman becomes free from phenomenal proliferation (niṣprapañca), then he is manifestly composed of pure consciousness and is solely of the form of Brahman. || 129 ||
[Conclusion] This mantra for the internal oblation has been declared as the destroyer of all sins. || 130 ||
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Pūrṇānanda Paramahaṃsa. || 16 ||
127 | "Within" means within the interior of the body. It blazes—that is, it flares up—without fuel, meaning without any material substance to be consumed as fuel.

Likewise, it is the adversary of the darkness of *māyā*, the obstructer of the gloom that is the nature of *māyā*, the ground for the unfolding of wondrous rays, and the source of the radiance of a multitude of extraordinary beams; in that certain ineffable essence, consciousness (*saṃvit-caitanya*) exists as fire in the form of that [flame].

The meaning is: "I offer as an oblation the entire universe, which consists of the principles beginning with Earth (pṛthvī-tattva) and ending with Śiva (śiva-tattva), starting from the element Earth and concluding with the principle of Śiva.

Here, this should be noted: in the Śaiva Āgamas, thirty-six principles (tattvas) beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth are expounded. These have been specifically detailed in the commentary on verses 113–114 of the fifth chapter (*Pañcamaprakāśa*), in the context of defining the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*).

These have been demonstrated. Therein, the determination of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth was made according to the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*). Here, however, for the purpose of the dissolution of the universe during the performance of the fire-oblation of knowledge (*jñānahoma*), there is the instruction on the thirty-six principles beginning with Earth and ending with Śiva according to the order of reabsorption (*layakrama*). It is precisely with this intention that it is said, "beginning with the earth and ending with Śiva. The sequence of the oblation, however, remains as before.

The Seventeenth Illumination: [The nature of the Śrīcakra; the nature of the mudrās; the determination of the materials and implements for constructing the yantra; the prohibition against constructing the yantra at night; the regulation regarding this matter; the extraction of the Śrīcakra; the specific details therein; the ninefold divisions of the cakra.]
The Secret of the Wheel: The Worship of the Sacred Seats.
[The Promise to Describe the Yantra: I shall proclaim the extraction of the yantra, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments. (1)

1. Having thus explained the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*) in the previous chapter, the author undertakes in this chapter to describe the worship diagram (*pūjāyantra*) of the goddess Śrī Tripurasundarī, beginning with the words "the extraction of the diagram" (*yantrōddhāram*). Here, it should be noted that for the venerable Tripurā, there are three types of conventions (*saṅketa*): the convention of the diagram (*yantra-saṅketa*), the convention of the mantra (*mantra-saṅketa*), and the convention of the worship (*pūjā-saṅketa*).
As it is stated in the first chapter of the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
"The convention of the wheel, the convention of the mantra, and likewise the convention of worship—
these three types of convention are proclaimed for the Goddess Tripurā."
As long as one does not know these three supreme conventions,
so long shall one not become a bearer of the supreme command within the wheel of Tripurā.

Thus, the words *cakra* and *yantra* have the same meaning. Among these, the convention regarding mantras has already been stated, and the convention regarding worship will be explained in the eighteenth chapter (*prakāśa*). This chapter is begun for the purpose of defining the convention regarding the *yantra*. Furthermore, the meaning of the term "convention" (*saṅketa*) has been explained.

In the *Yoginīhṛdayaṭīkā*, Amṛtānandanātha states: "The term *saṅketaka* is like a convention (*saṅketa*); just as a woman and a man who have made an appointment dwell together anywhere, so too do Śiva and Śivā reside here. And thus, from this word "convention," it is understood that the Blessed Goddess, the venerable Tripurā, whose essence is the *Kāmakalā*, dwells here in the wheel (*cakra*) with the Blessed Kāmeśvara.
[The Etymology of the Term *Yantra*] It restrains all evil and protects the practitioner from great fear through worship and meditation; therefore, it is proclaimed as a *yantra*. (2)
Therefore, the body is the machine, and the mantra is the unbroken knowledge.

[The threefold nature of the body: They declare the body to be of three kinds: the elemental (bhautika), the mental (manomaya), and the supreme (para) which consists of knowledge, eternal, indestructible, and uninterrupted. || 4 ||

2 | He explains the etymology of the term *yantra* with the words "it restrains" (*yamayati*), and so forth. By this, its designation as a *yantra* is established because it restrains transgressions and because it acts as a protector from fear. In the *Tantrasāra*, however, it is stated: "Because it restrains all suffering arising from defects such as desire, anger, and the like."
They call it a *yantra* because the deity, when worshipped therein, is pleased;
likewise, those who know the Tantras say it is called a *yantra* because it restrains suffering (*duḥkha-niyantṛṇāt*).
Thus, the etymological derivation of the word *yantra* has been demonstrated.
[Verse 3] He declares that the *yantra* is of the nature of the body of the Goddess with the words beginning "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).
"Therefore" means that because it possesses qualities such as being the restrainer of all previously mentioned sins, the *yantra* is the body of the Goddess. Now, [one might ask], what is a *yantra*?
If one asks, "If it is the body of the Goddess, what knowledge (*jñāna*) is there in that?", he says: "Mantra is knowledge.

To exclude produced (*janya*) knowledge, he adds "unbroken" (*akhaṇḍita*), which means eternal (*nitya*). For this very reason, after describing the sequence for the construction of the Śrīcakra in the fourth chapter of the *Gandharvatantra*, [it is said]:
Thus, this great wheel, consisting of the Great Śrī Tripurā, is called the body; it is the yantra, the mantra, and the indivisible knowledge.

By this, this very meaning has been clearly stated. (4) He demonstrates the threefold nature of the Goddess’s body with the words beginning "the body" (*śarīram*). The meaning is that the body is threefold: composed of the elements (*bhautika*), composed of mind (*manomaya*), and composed of knowledge (*jñānamaya*). Among these, he states the distinction of the body composed of knowledge with the word "supreme" (*param*).

Among bodies defined by etymological derivation (*nirukta*), the body consisting of knowledge (*jñānamaya*) is supreme; that is to say, it is the most excellent. He states the reason for its excellence with the words beginning "eternal" (*nityam*). It is eternal, meaning devoid of origination, and indestructible, meaning devoid of dissolution. By the term "eternal" itself, its nature as being free from origination and destruction is indicated.
They say that *mudrā* is material; know that *yantra* consists of mind;
they say that *mantra* consists of knowledge—thus the body becomes threefold.
In this case as well, when the mental [perception] is destroyed, the material [object] is certainly not present;
therefore, both would be perishable, and thus it is established that the one [the mental] is real. (6)
Because it is empty in the beginning, middle, and end, one perceives nothing therein;
this is not produced by anything, since the progenitor consists of pure knowledge.
Nothing has been seen or heard; therefore, entities indeed do not exist. Yet there, various and diverse bodies are seen, just as they are here.
Below each [level] they exist in gross forms, and increasingly subtle as one goes higher;
distinguished by various colors and shapes, and taking refuge in various classes of beings, they all, having established their objects, dissolve there in every way.
[The nature of the mudrās as previously promised:
Now, I shall describe the body of the mudrās, which is most wonderful. (10)
The Mahāmudrā in the form of the source (yonirūpā) is proclaimed as the body;
the nine limbs are proclaimed as beginning with Saṃkṣobhaṇī and ending with Trikhaṇḍā. || 11 ||

Even though the meaning of "absence" (*rāhitya*) could be understood [from the previous term], because the word "indestructible" (*avināśī*) is used again, it should be understood that here the word "eternal" (*nitya*) intends merely the state of being devoid of origination. He states the conclusion: "uninterrupted" (*nirantaram*). This means existing as delimited by the three periods of time.
(5) He defines their essential nature (*svarūpa*) in sequence, beginning with the word "mudrā": thus, *mudrā* is the physical body.
The meaning is that there are three kinds of bodies: the *yantra* as the mind-made body (*manomaya-śarīra*), and the *mantra* as the knowledge-made body (*jñānamaya-śarīra*).
(10) With the words beginning with "Now" (*atha*), he promises to describe the body of the *mudrās* among those previously mentioned.

(11) While defining the body of the *mudrās*, he demonstrates the relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅga-aṅgibhāva*) among the *mudrās* by means of the passage beginning with "in the form of the womb" (*yonirūpa*).
[The Etymology of the Term *Mudrā*] Because she delights herself in the fluid state consisting of peaceful bliss,
and because she indeed generates a body composed of the elements, she is called *mudrā*. (12)

[The determination of the construction of the yantra, its substratum, and its implements: On a delightful patch of ground smeared with cow dung, or with red lead powder (sindūra), or with the dust of saffron; 13.

In this context, because the *yonimudrā* is predominant as the form of the *mātṛkā* that gives birth to the three worlds, it possesses the status of the principal member (*aṅgin*); for this very reason, it is called the *mahāmudrā*. The term "body" (*śarīra*) means the principal member. Next, he enumerates the mudrās that constitute its members, beginning with "the agitator" (*saṃkṣobhaṇī*) and so forth. These are:

the Agitator of All (*sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇī*), the Enchanter of All (*sarvavidrāviṇī*), the Attractor of All (*sarvākarṣiṇī*), the Subjugator of All (*sarvavaśyakarī*), the Intoxicator of All (*sarvonmādinī*), and the Great Goad (*mahāṅkuśā*).

The *khecarī*, the *bīja*, and those called the *trikhaṇḍā*—these are the nine. Thus, the intention of the speaker is that the body of the mudrās consists precisely of this tenfold set of mudrās, which exist in the relationship of limbs (*aṅga*) and the possessor of limbs (*aṅgin*). The essential forms of these mudrās, however, will be explained in the eighteenth chapter.
12. Regarding the word "himself" (*ātmānam*): because it gladdens the self—that self which consists of peaceful bliss—one [makes] that self fluid (*dravam*).
Therefore, the connection is that it generates a body composed of the elements (bhūta), and thus it is called a *mudrā*. However, in the *Tantrasāra* it is said:
"Because it gladdens (*modana*) all the gods and because it dissolves (*drāvaṇa*) the succession of sins, it is therefore celebrated as *mudrā* by the sages who know the Tantras."
Thus, the sequence of derivation has been stated otherwise [in a different manner].

13. Now, he explains the materials for the substratum and the construction of the Śrīcakra, beginning with the words "with cow dung" and ending with "one should draw the King of Yantras. Furthermore, he says in the fourth chapter of the Gandharva Tantra:
Then, seated facing the east, he should begin the process of drawing the wheel upon a very beautiful plate made of gold, silver, copper, or other metals.
O Goddess, it is taught here that the cloth should be square, even, pure, adorned with a raised center,

The meaning is that the first [wheel] has a single unit of height, the second has twice the height of the former, and the third has three times the height of the former; thus, by this sequence, the machine (yantra) brings about prosperity and fame through the progressive elevation of the fourth wheel and those following. "In the region of the tip of the previous *śakti*. By the word *śakti*, a triangle is meant. Consequently, [it refers to] the region of the tip of the previous *śakti*.
At the apex of the middle triangle, one should draw a single straight line extending from south to north, like a measuring-stick or a measuring-rod. Regarding the term "junction" (*sandhi*):

thereafter, following the construction of the straight line at the apex of the middle triangle between the two aforementioned triangles, the Guru [should act] from the two corners of those two *śaktis*.

By this, the eastern tip...

The interior of the triangle has been reached. All accomplishments (sarvasiddhi).

Then, one should draw the form of the Yoni using the syllables *Pūrva*, *Śakti*, *Īśa*, and *Vahni*.
The wise practitioner should draw a line in the form of a hexagon from the southeast corner of Śrīkaṇṭha, extending toward the east, the Śakti, the Īśa, and the fire (southeast) corners.
Having drawn the upper line so that it kisses the tip of Śrīkaṇṭha,
one should extract [the letters] from the right and left corners of Śrīkaṇṭha as before.
There should be a ten-cornered figure; likewise, one should draw another ten-spoked [figure] outside it.

That [triangle] is called *pradā* (bestowing), and the eight-petaled lotus outside it is called *sarvarogahara* (remover of all diseases). With this very intention, it is stated in the root text that a nine-cornered figure (*navakoṇa*) is produced. Furthermore, in the fifth chapter of the *Gandharvatantra*:
"One should draw a single triangle with its apex pointing west, and then above that..."
One should draw another triangle, with its middle and apex pointing toward the center of the previous triangle.

thus there shall be an eight-cornered wheel situated in the middle of a triangle.

By the statement "in the middle of the triangle" as a qualification of the term "eight-cornered," it is clearly understood that there is a triangle in the center and an eight-cornered figure outside of it.

Regarding another triangle, he says: "by the south," etc.; that is, also by means of the southwest and northwest corners of Śrīkaṇṭha.

From the fire of the eastern Śaktīśa, starting from the eastern Śakti of the eastern triangle, one proceeds by dividing the joints of the two upper lines from the northeast and southeast corners [forming the fourteen-spoked wheel].

On the left and right of the ten spokes, however, there are four central corners.

This is clearly stated in the fifth chapter of the *Gandharvatantra*:
Then listen, O Pārvatī, to the construction of the ten-spoked wheel.
Among the three lines running north to south that are there,
one should extend two of those lines, excluding the middle line.
"By that [method], having made a hexagon, and having made four divisions at the joints, one should draw two lines so that it becomes a ten-cornered [figure].
Now, he describes the outer ten-spoked wheel, which accomplishes all aims, beginning with the word "tathā" (likewise). Likewise:

One should construct this outer ten-spoked [lotus] by means of the very same sequence of the ten spokes previously described; there is no difference whatsoever here. This is clearly stated in the fifth chapter of the Gandharva Tantra:
"In the same way, the construction of another ten-cornered [figure] is proclaimed."
In this manner, there are five lines running from south to north.
O Goddess, having left a space between two (or three) lines in their middle,
one should extend the two outer lines from east to west as before.
"By that [method], having made a hexagon and having made the four divisions of the joints,
one should draw two lines so that a decagon comes into being.
(33–35) Now, he describes the fourteen-spoked wheel (*cakra*) which bestows all prosperity, beginning with the words "In the decagon," and so forth.

One should draw a hexagon according to the sequence for dividing the junctions mentioned previously. This is the meaning: having expanded [the lines] according to the sequence previously described, one should then draw a hexagon by means of the sequence for dividing the junctions mentioned before.

The "lines situated in the middle of the flanks" means the four lines constituting the left and right corners of the aforementioned hexagon; one should extend these in the form of corners. When this is done, a group of eight corners arises. Regarding the word "remainder": it refers to the remaining six corners.

One should extend [the lines] according to the method previously described for the ten-cornered [figure]. Having extended the two straight lines between the east and west as before, one should draw one straight line each extending north-south from the west and east of the ten-cornered figure, and thus extend six corners in the sequence of the ten-cornered figure; this is precisely what is meant by the phrase "by the rule of the ten-cornered [figure]. "Just as" (yathā) means "in that manner."
The connection is that one should cause it to increase so that the supreme fourteen-spoked wheel is produced. This is clearly stated in the fifth chapter of the *Gandharvatantra*:
"Now the construction of the fourteen-spoked wheel is described."
In this manner, there are seven lines running from south to north.
Leaving aside two lines among them,
the practitioner of mantra should extend two long lines on the outside from east to west, as before.
Having formed a hexagon with that [line], and having created four junction-divisions,
one should then form ten spokes from those very same four junction-divisions.
One should draw two lines on the outside; thus, there shall be nine and five lines.
Then, one should fashion the other four corners with its tips.
"Thus, it shall have fourteen spokes and be enchanting to the eye.

Here, at the base of the eight-petalled and sixteen-petalled [lotuses], the circle is intended solely for the purpose of demarcating the boundary. Even the three circles outside the sixteen-petalled [lotus] are not for the purpose of worship— O Great Goddess, it is said that the triad of circles is not used in worship.
[Here is the distinction: According to the Kuloḍḍīśa-mata, the root-mantra (mūla) should be placed in the directions starting from the east.
[The location of the Binducakra: It resides in the center of all the cakras.
The wise one should draw the bindu-cakra within the triangle in the very center of everything.
Thus, from the statement in the fifth chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*. This wheel is described concisely in the *Yāmala* as held in the *Tantrasāra*:
"The [wheel] consisting of a point, a triangle, an eight-cornered figure, two sets of ten spokes, an eight-petaled lotus, an eight-coraered figure, and sixteen petals joined together."
The three circles and the three abodes of the earth constitute the Śrī Cakrarāja, which has arisen from the Supreme Deity.
Thus it is said. Regarding the prohibition against imagining filaments (*kesara*) within the lotus that constitutes this yantra, the *Bhūtabhairava*, as cited in the *Tantrasāra*, states:

(38) Thus, having described the sequence for the construction of the Śrīcakra through the *Cūḍāmaṇi-saṃvāda*, he now divides the nine cakras according to the *Kuloḍḍīśa-saṃvāda* with the words beginning "In the Kula... The nine cakras and their names are found in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*.
As they were shown in sequence in the first chapter:
"O beloved, I shall tell you of the ninefold nature of the wheel:
the first consists of three earths, and the second has sixteen spokes."
Next, the eight-petalled [lotus] is proclaimed;
immediately after that, the fifth is ten-cornered, and the sixth is also ten-spoked.
The seventh should be a lotus with seven petals, the eighth a central triangle, and the ninth a triangle in the center; hear now their names from me.

The wheel that deludes the three worlds, which fulfills all hopes; O Goddess, the wheel that agitates all, which bestows all good fortune; the wheel that accomplishes all aims, the supreme granter of all protection.
O Goddess, it removes all diseases and likewise consists of all perfections;
it is also composed of all bliss—listen, O beautiful one, to this ninth [chapter].
[The Wheel that Enchants the Three Worlds] The wheel named Trailokyamohana is square and bestows happiness;
the practitioner of mantra should contemplate it as having the luster of pearls, adorned with the letters of the Mātṛkā. (39)
The Wheel that Fulfills All Aspirations:
Resembling the autumn moon, beautiful with sixteen spokes, it is named "Fulfiller of All Aspirations" and is conjoined with the sixteen vowels. (40)

Thus, by the statement "In this way, here the ninth [wheel] shall be in the middle of the triangle," that very wheel consisting of universal bliss (*sarvānandamaya*) which was mentioned is indicated in the root text by the words "in the center of all" (*sarvamadhya*) and so forth:
"Here the Great Goddess Mahātripurasundarī is to be worshipped."

Thus, because of its preeminence, it is mentioned first according to the statement in the first chapter of the *Yoginīhṛdaya*; however, its specific details will be explained later. "The Bindu-cakra" means the central bindu whose nature is Śiva.
"Consisting of universal bliss" refers to the station of the central bindu, which is of the nature of Śiva; this is according to the statement in the fifth chapter of the *Tantrarāja*.

39. Now, he explains the nine wheels beginning with the Trailokyamohana in sequence, starting with the words "trailokya" and so forth. The square is the outer enclosure (*bhūpura*), and it consists of three lines on all sides; for it has been stated previously that "the triad of earth-disks (*bhūbimba*) should be made," and this triad of earth-disks is the resting place of the three Mothers, Paśyantī and the others.

And because it is stated in the *Kāmakalāvilāsa*: "The powers of Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī, manifested from the central triangle, shine forth as far as the three aforementioned cities. "Resembling pearls" means white in color.
One should worship the Buddha in the Trailokyamohana-cakra.
Those three lines, resembling them [in color], are known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.

By this statement from the fourth chapter of the *Gandharvatantra*, it is declared that the lines possess, in their respective order, the colors of their presiding deities—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. Consequently, from the aforementioned statement of the *Gandharvatantra*, it is understood that these [lines] have the colors red, black, and white respectively. The phrase "by the letters of the Mātṛkā" means by the letters of the Mātṛkā beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa'.
As it is said in the tenth chapter of the Jñānārṇava:
"For the sake of attaining success, [one should construct] a square adorned with the letters of the Mātṛkā,
fashioned with pearls and rubies, and shining with level ground."
"It is named Trailokyamohana, which bestows the fruits of the wish-fulfilling tree.
(40) Now, he describes the Sarvāśāparipūraka-cakra, which consists of sixteen petals, beginning with the words "śaradindu" and so forth.
It is "resembling the autumnal moon," meaning it is characterized by a color like that of the moon during the autumn season. This has been stated in the Jñānārṇava:
In the tenth chapter (p. 577):
[The Wheel that Agitates All] It resembles the hibiscus flower, has eight petals, and is most beautiful.
It is named Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa (the All-Agitating), and it is endowed with the eight groups of letters beginning with 'ka'.
This beautiful wheel, consisting of the threefold etymology, is the supreme creator of emanation. (42)
The wheel that bestows all good fortune has fourteen spokes and corners, possessing a radiance equal to the newly risen sun;
it is named "Bestower of All Good Fortune" and is adorned with the letters from *ka* to *ḍha*. (43)
O auspicious lady, it has the form of a moon-mandala with sixteen spokes, the abode of all things,
the fulfiller of all desires, and raining down a shower of nectar.

Thus: "sixteen-spoked" means sixteen-petalled; "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*). Here, the word "mind" is indicative of the five elements, the ten sense organs, and the mind—the sixteen transformations of the Goddess.
These aforementioned sixteen transformations reside upon the sixteen petals in the form of the sixteen powers (*śakti*), beginning with Kāmākarṣiṇī.
The essential meaning is as clearly stated in the *Kāmakalāvilāsa*:
"The elements, the ten senses, and the mind— these sixteen transformations of the Goddess—
reside within the center of the sixteen-spoked [cakra] in the form of Kāmākarṣiṇī and the others."
Thus [it is said]. "Endowed with the sixteen vowels" means distinguished by the sixteen vowels beginning with *a*; the meaning is that the sixteen vowels reside in the sixteen petals in sequence.
(41) Now, he describes the wheel of universal agitation (*sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇacakra*), which consists of eight petals, beginning with the word *javā*. It resembles the *javā* flower.

It is red in color like a hibiscus flower (*javākusuma*). It has eight petals and eight segments. It is joined with the eight groups of consonants beginning with *ka*; on the five petals are the five groups beginning with *ka*. On the sixth petal are *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*. On the seventh petal are *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha*. On the eighth petal are *la* and *kṣa*: such is the sequence for the arrangement of the eight groups.

The meaning is that this wheel consists of the triad of wheels known as Trailokyamohana, Sarvāśāparipūraka, and Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa. This is also stated in the tenth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*:
"O Maheśānī, these three constitute the wheel of emanation (*sṛṣṭicakra*) which bestows happiness.

(43) Having thus described the triad of wheels consisting of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), that which consists of maintenance (*sthiti*) must now be discussed; and so, in accordance with the sequence, [the following is stated]:
[The Wheel for Accomplishing All Aims] (p.
578): Resembling molten gold and vermilion, it has ten corners;

[The Wheel of Stability consisting of the three etymologies:
This wheel of stability, which consists of these three, bestows great wisdom. || 46 ||
He describes the wheel that bestows all good fortune with the words beginning "fourteen-spoked," etc. "Fourteen-spoked and cornered" is clear.

(44) Now, he explains the wheel that accomplishes all aims (*sarvārthasādhakacakra*) with the verse beginning with "taptā... and so forth. It is red in color, resembling molten gold and vermilion. As it is said in the tenth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*:

accomplishes all aims and always grants whatever the mind desires.

(45) He describes the wheel consisting of a second ten-cornered [figure], which effects all protection, beginning with the words "taruṇa... and so on: "Resembling the hue of the young morning sun..."
