(46) He states that this triad constitutes the wheel of maintenance (*sthiticakra*) with the words beginning "sthitī" (maintenance). The connection is as follows: this triad—known as the Bestower of All Prosperity (*sarvasaubhāgyadāyaka*), the Accomplisher of All Aims (*sarvārthasādhaka*), and the Protector of All (*sarvarakṣākara*)—is the wheel of maintenance which bestows great gnosis (*mahājñāna*).

Also, in the tenth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*, after describing the aforementioned three wheels: (p. 579) [The Wheel that Removes All Diseases] "Resembling a ruby (*padmarāga*), eight-cornered, and bestowing success (*siddhi*)."
It is named "The Remover of All Diseases" and is adorned with eight groups [of verses].
[The Wheel that Bestows All Siddhis]:
Resembling a pomegranate flower, triangular, and bestowing all prosperity;
this wheel that grants all siddhis consists of three lines beginning with the letter *a*.
[The Wheel Consisting of All Bliss:
Situated between the syllables *ha* and *kṣa*, it brings about the accomplishment of all;
the supreme state is the wheel of the bindu named "Consisting of All Bliss. (49)
"O Great Goddess, these three constitute the wheel of maintenance (*sthiti-cakra*), which bestows happiness.
Thus it was said.
(47) Having thus described the triad of wheels consisting of maintenance, the triad of wheels consisting of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) is now to be discussed; and so, that which follows in sequence—
He describes the wheel that removes all diseases with the words beginning with *padmarāga*: "having the color of a ruby," meaning red-colored;
"adorned with the eight groups of letters" means that, according to the method stated for the wheel that agitates all, the eight groups of letters beginning with *ka* reside within the eight spokes.
This is stated in the tenth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*:
"O lady of excellent hips, it is an eight-cornered [cakra], as red as the rays of the rising sun, resembling a ruby in appearance, and always a remover of all diseases.
(48) He describes the cakra that bestows all siddhis with the words beginning "dāḍimī": "resembling the pomegranate flower..."

It is red in color like the flower of the pomegranate (*dāḍima*). It bestows all prosperity, meaning it brings about the attainment of every kind of wealth and power. It consists of three lines beginning with *a*, *ka*, and *tha*.

This means that the sixteen vowels beginning with *a*, as well as the consonants from *ka* to *ta* and from *tha* to *sa*, exist respectively in the form of each individual line. As stated in the tenth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*:

"O Goddess, the Cakra, which has the luster of a thousand rising suns and the brilliance of the Bandhūka flower, bestows all accomplishments; it is the abode of all and the eternal source of prosperity, a triangle that is the cause of the manifestation of everything. Thus [it is said].

49. Now, he describes the final dwelling place of the Bhagavatī, the wheel consisting of all bliss called *bindu*, beginning with the words "ha-kṣa": [the wheel of withdrawal (*saṃhāracakra*) consisting of the aforementioned triad], the supreme state of her who dwells upon the lap of Kāmeśvara and is unconditioned by space, time, form, and so forth. (p. 580)
And this triad, consisting of Sadāśiva, is the cause of dissolution. || 50 ||
[Instruction on the offering of a handful of flowers at the Wheel of Etymology:
One should scatter a handful of flowers there with the root mantra of the Yoginī.
[Instruction on accomplishing the non-emptiness of the wheel:]
Or with pearls, gems, and corals, using the vidyā-mantra in reverse order. || 51 ||
The ritual action should never be performed when it is not empty, for in an empty state, obstacles will always arise.
[Conclusion of the Nine Wheels:
The wheel consisting of the nine wheels is adorned by the goddess Bālā. || 52 ||
[The names of the Cakreśvarīs:
The first is the goddess Tripurā; the second is Tripureśvarī;
the third is named Sundarī; and the fourth is Tripuravāsinī. (53)

The meaning is that it is the supreme state, the most excellent abode of the illustrious Tripurasundarī. For this very reason, having described the Sarvānanda-cakra in the first chapter of the *Yoginīhṛdaya*, it says:
"Here the Great Goddess Mahātripurasundarī is to be worshipped."
Thus it has been said. It is stated clearly in the *Kāmakalāvilāsa*:
"Seated upon the wheel consisting of the *bindu*, that Goddess Tripurasundarī rests upon the lap of Kāmeśvara, her crest-jewel fashioned from a digit of the moon."
Her own hands are adorned with a noose, a goad, a sugarcane bow, and five flower-arrows;
her body is as red as the rising sun, and she possesses three eyes in the form of the moon, the sun, and fire.
Thus [it is said]. Here, by the expression "her body is as red as the morning sun," the redness of the *bindu* is also stated.
Regarding the phrase "situated between the letters *ha* and *kṣa*," the analysis of the compound is: that which has the two letters *ha* and *kṣa* situated in its middle.
(51–52) Regarding the word "liberated" (*muktā*): having worshipped the *yantra*, one should place therein—using the root mantra in reverse order—one of the items beginning with pearls.
The meaning is that one should never leave it empty. He concludes with "na" (not). The rest is clear.

53–54. Having thus taught the nine wheels beginning with Trailokyamohana and ending with Sarvānandamaya, [he states] regarding them: "In the fifth [wheel] is Tripurāśrī, and in the sixth is Tripuramālinī."
In the seventh [pīṭha] is Tripurāsiddhā, and in the eighth is Tripurāmbikā.

In the ninth [cakra], the illustrious Mahādevī Mahātripurabhairavī is worshipped; all the deities, whether manifest, secret, or residing in the most secret [places], are to be worshipped in their respective locations within the cakra. || 55 ||

The traditions (sampradāyas), the Kulas, the Kaulas, and those dwelling in the Nigarbha; those dwelling in the secret (rahasya), the secret of the higher and lower (parāpara-rahasya), and those dwelling in the supreme secret (parama-atirahasya). || 56 ||
Rājarājeśvarī, Pūrṇā, and Mahātripurasundarī—all these reside within the wheels; having ascertained their locations, one should worship them. (57)
[The Sovereign Power of Knowledge regarding the Conventions of the Wheel of Etymology] That practitioner who knows the ninefold convention of the wheel is a true adept;
how could one who does not know it in its ninefold form worship the Goddess? (58)
[The Praise of the Knowledge of the Auspicious Cakra] This sovereign Śrīcakra, consisting of all scripts, worthy of worship by all the gods,
whose nature is eternal bliss, which brings the worlds under its control, and which is the sole cause of both worldly enjoyment and liberation—
He sets forth the names of the nine Mistress of the Wheels (*cakreśvarī*) who are to be worshipped in sequence, beginning with the words "The first," and so on.

Even in the first chapter of the *Yoginīhṛdaya*, having stated the names according to the aforementioned sequence, it says: "And one should worship these nine wheels in the order previously mentioned."

Thus it has been stated [verses 55–57]. Regarding the phrase "the ninth": in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*, where the name *Mahātripurabhairavī* occurs, it is *Mahātripurasundarī*. Regarding the word "all" (*samastā*):
the respective locations, names, modes of worship, and so forth, for these powers of the enclosures (*āvaraṇaśakti*), will be explained in the eighteenth chapter.

Having become pure and having written it down, if one should preserve it free from obstacles or worship it, all accomplishments (siddhi) come into the palm of the hand; for that virtuous person, even the supreme accomplishment is attained. || 59 ||
Consisting of all bliss, the sole sovereign of the entire world, the granter of desires, the dispeller of all diseases, the bestower of auspiciousness, knowledge, and fame—
he is seen as the manifest Kalpavṛkṣa tree, surrounded by hosts of gods and demons.
By means of this, one indeed obtains the merit of bathing at all sacred fords. || 60 ||
[The Promise to Describe the Secret of the Śrīcakra] I shall describe, in due order, the secret of the Sovereign Wheel (cakrarāja).
[The Secret of the Bindu within the Triangle]
In the center, the bindu should be known as Śiva, the agent of creation and dissolution. || 61 ||
The illustrious Tripurasundarī dwells eternally in the center of the bindu;
there she exists as the Great Kāmakalā, whose form consists of the triad of bindus.
[The Secret of the Triangle] The triangle is indeed Tripurā, Bālā, and Tripurasundarī;
Rudra is of the form of the triangle, and because of its triangular nature, Śivā is the Supreme (Parā). 63.
In the three [circles], the fifteenth is constant and the fourteenth is the *samaya*;
there the goddess Ṣaḍaṅgayuvatī is situated, starting from the east.

61-62 | Now he begins to explain the secret of the Śrīcakra with the words "The Secret," and so forth. "In the center" means in the middle of the triangle known as the Bestower of All Siddhis. "Bindu" refers to the white bindu whose essence is Śiva. "In the center of the bindu" means in the center of the white bindu whose essence is Śiva; the meaning is that the Great Kāmakalā, whose essence is the red bindu, namely the venerable Tripurasundarī, shines there. He further qualifies her:

By the words "bindu," etc., it is meant that she consists of the triad of *bindus*: the two aforementioned *bindus* which are the forms of Śiva and Śakti, and the third, the mixed *bindu*, which has become their state of essential union (*samarasībhūta*). The specific details should be consulted in the *Bhūmikā*.
(p. 583) [The Secret of the Eight Spokes]
In the eight corners are the eight Siddhis, for there are indeed eight Bhūtas:
Jṛmbha, Moha, Vaśa, Stambha, Pāśa, Aṅkuśa, Dhanus, and Śara.
The eight deities, beginning with Vaśinī, dwell there eternally.
[The Secret of the Inner Nine-Spoked Wheel] The ten sense organs are situated and reside within bodies;
the ten deities, beginning with the Great God Sarvajña, are likewise established there. 67.
Thus, there are ten vital breaths (prāṇas) at the cardinal points, the intermediate directions, the junctions, and the tips, which constitute the ten digits (kalās).
[The Secret of the Outer Ten-Spoked Wheel] Furthermore, the other ten-spoked wheel has the deities of the ten guardians of the directions as its presiding divinities:
those of the quarters, Vāta, Arka, Pracetas, the two Aśvins, Vahni, Indra, Upendra, Mitra, and Kāla. (69)
But from the Vaikārika [ego] those ten who are proclaimed were born;
there, Sarvasiddhi and the others always remain, being worshipped. (70)
[The Secret of the Fourteen Spokes]:
Likewise, the wheel of the formless has fourteen corners;
there are fourteen scriptures consisting of fourteen limbs, and fourteen worlds. (71)
In the fourteen-spoked wheels, the deities beginning with Saṃkṣobhaṇī reside;
one dharma produces the qualities, while adharma is likewise considered [to produce them]. (72)
[The Secret of the Eight-Petalled Lotus] The eight forms, beginning with Dharma, reside within the eight petals;
these should always be understood by the wise as Anaṅgakusumā and the others. (73)
69. Regarding "mitrakā": Rāghavabhaṭṭa states that Mitra is the third sun. Ka is Prajāpati; according to the *Ekākṣarakoṣa*, "Ka is designated as Prajāpati.
(p. 584) [The Secret of the Sixteen Petals]
In the sixteen-petaled wheels, the sixteen lunar days (tithis) are traditionally taught;
they constantly bestow all prosperity and are preceded by the attraction of desires.
In its threefold state, it exists in the form of the three lines of the moon, the sun, and fire. || 75 ||
Śivarekhā is the morning twilight; Brahmāṇī resides in the Brahma-line.
Aṇimā and the others are proclaimed in sequence as the Brahma-lines. (76)
Likewise, sixty-four crores, as well as the splendors of crores upon crores of Yoginīs and goddesses of the gods, remain stationed, having taken refuge in the wheel.
Its divisions are proclaimed to be the corners and the petals.
[Regarding the different measurements of the yantra: it may be a triangle, or one *tola*, or measured at four finger-breadths (*catur-aṅgula*). || 78 ||
Right there, one should have a very beautiful square mandala drawn,
measuring nine cubits, or two cubits, or likewise even one cubit.

74–77: The *āvaraṇa* (encircling) powers, described by the author with the words beginning "trivṛtta" and ending with "saṃsthitā," will be explained in detail by the authors of the text in the eighteenth chapter on the sequence of worship (*pūjākrama*).
78–80: Now, he states the different measurements of the yantra with the words beginning "trikoṇa" and ending with "yāmalasammatam. Here...

The reading "trikoṇam" (triangle) appears to be erroneous; for it contradicts what will be stated later regarding the "caturasram" (square), the word "vā" (or) would be redundant as it would imply a single alternative, and it contradicts the *Svacchandabhairava-tantrarāja* and other sources. Thus, in the *Svacchandabhairava* as cited in the *Tantrasāra*:
One should fashion a very beautiful yantra, measuring one cubit, upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
However, in the case of constructing it from jewels and such materials, the measurement may be according to one's own desire.
One should draw the yantra on a patch of ground, but on jewels and so forth, according to one's own wish.
Reciting the root mantra while remaining composed is the consensus of the Yāmala. (80)
[The abiding of Mahākāmakalā in the Binducakra]: One should draw Mahākāmakalā in the center of the triangle-cakra;
this supreme cakra has been described, which is difficult to find in the three worlds. (81)
If one should pray for liberation, this great gateway to liberation is proclaimed by the Supreme Self as the supreme reality within the Śrīkrama. 82.
[The Rule of Directions in the Construction of the Śrīcakra] When the mantra-practitioner, facing north, worships the King of Mandalas (cakrarāja),
then that northern direction is indeed declared to be the eastern quarter.
Likewise, the northeast belongs to Īśa; of this there is no doubt. || 83 ||
One *tola*, two *tolas*, three *tolas*, or four *tolas* [of mercury];
having prepared more than this, a man will certainly become subject to penance.
Having filled [the vessel] with blood and menstrual blood, one should worship the *Śrīcakra* upon the ground.
"All obstacles perish and the desired fruit is attained.
Thus it is said. Also, in the thirty-third chapter of the *Tantrarāja*:
"For the consecration, the Śrīcakra should be nine cubits or three cubits [in size]."
In the worship of the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), one should fashion it very beautifully with a measure of one cubit;

however, in the construction of [images] made of gems and the like, the measurement may be according to one's desire. Worship performed on a well-prepared ground is always auspicious, whereas otherwise it is the opposite.

Thus, since these statements show a measurement of three *tolas*, it should be understood that here too the reading "three *tolas*" (*tritola*) alone is more appropriate. Regarding the phrase "the root" (*mūlam*), the connection is that one should draw the yantra while reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
(81) "In the center of the triangular wheel" (*trikoṇacakramadhye*): this means in the *bindu* (dot) in the middle of the triangular wheel.

83. Now, the rule regarding the directions for the construction of the Śrīcakra is set forth. In this regard, according to the statement in the tenth chapter of the Jñānārṇava: "Seated there facing the east, one should draw the King of Cakras."
"Then, seated facing east, one should begin the construction of the Śrīcakra.

By this statement from the fourth chapter of the *Gandharvatantra*, it is taught that the practitioner (*sādhaka*) must face the eastern direction during the creation of the Śrīcakra. Now, [the author] further restricts that very eastern direction with the words beginning "facing north" (*udaṅmukha*).

If the practitioner, facing north, proceeds to construct the *cakra*, then the northern direction itself becomes the eastern direction, and the northeast (*īśāna*) becomes the southeast (*agni*). In this manner, the regulation of directions everywhere is to be understood from subsequent statements. These statements establishing the regulation of directions appear in some places concerning the extraction of the *Śrīcakra*, and in others...
These [rules] are seen to be stated regarding the worship of the illustrious Tripurā; as it is said in the tenth chapter of the Jñānārṇava:
"O Goddess, when the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) raises the wheel while facing the northern direction, then that northern direction is declared to be the eastern direction."
And so forth. Likewise, in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*, this statement serves to establish the rule of direction for the construction of the *cakra*:
"When one, facing north, worships the Goddess... [as stated] in the seventh chapter of the *Gandharvatantra*.

At that time, O Goddess, the northern direction becomes the eastern direction, without a doubt; the northeast becomes the southeast, and likewise the northwest becomes the northeast. At that time, O Maheśvarī, the southern direction should be known as the western direction.

"Rākṣasa [should be] the Vāyukoṇa (northwest), and Āgneya (southeast) should be Rākṣasa"— by such statements, the restriction of directions for worship is established. Thus, by considering the statements from the *Jñānārṇava*, *Gandharva-tantra*, and other sources, the restriction of directions for both the construction (*uddhāra*) and the worship (*pūjana*) of the Śrīcakra follows the aforementioned sequence.
It concludes that [the rite] must be performed; however—

since it was previously shown in the words of Gandharva that "one seated facing east should begin the drawing of the mandala," there is a rule regarding the drawing of the mandala that one must face the east.
Among the divisions of the directions, the northern quarter is the one that bestows the favor of Śivā;
therefore, seated facing that direction, one should always worship Tripurā.

Thus, based on the statement from the seventh chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra* and the rule regarding facing north during worship, it should be understood that while facing east is recommended for the extraction of the *cakra*, facing north is more highly praised for the act of worship itself. Nor should it be argued that the statement beginning with "in the divisions of the directions" allows one to assume only the rule of facing east during worship.
"When the practitioner facing whatever direction should worship Tripurā,
then the East is behind the Goddess and the West is in front of Tripurā"—
since this statement from the *Guptārṇava Tantra* uses the phrase "facing whatever direction" to denote any direction whatsoever, [it follows that...]

When the mantra-practitioner worships the Wheel-King (cakrarāja) in the western direction, then that western quarter becomes the eastern direction; of this there is no doubt. At that time, the wind-corner (vāyukoṇa) becomes the fire-corner (āgneya), and the northeast (īśāna) becomes the southwest (rākṣasa). || 84 ||
When the practitioner facing the southern direction worships the wheel,
then that very direction becomes the east, and the southwest corner becomes like the southeast.
The southeast belongs to Agni, while the northwest is Nirṛti;
this is proclaimed as the doctrine of the Bṛhacchrīkrama Tantra. (86)
When the minister Purandaramukha worships Tripurā,
then the direction behind the Goddess is East and the direction in front of Tripurā is West;
thus the division of the directions has been proclaimed according to the opinion of Guptārṇava.
[The Support for the Installation of the Śrīcakra] Now, the practitioner of mantra should place the Śrīcakra before him upon the lion-throne. || 88 ||

[The prohibition against installing the wheel in lead, etc. The supreme practitioner should never install [the wheel] in lead, in a bell-metal vessel, or in tin; nor should he ever install it on a wooden board, a cloth, or a wall. (89)
If it has been established through greed, delusion, or even ignorance, it will always utterly destroy one's family, wealth, and progeny. (90)

Because the explicit mention of facing north and so forth is found in the words of the root text, such as "When the practitioner of mantra, facing north, should worship the King of Wheels," a contradiction would otherwise arise; therefore, while facing east is recommended for the extraction of the *cakra*,
facing north is more highly praised for the act of worship, as are the other directions.
The essential point is that it is praiseworthy.
(p. 588) [Pīṭhapūjā] One should then perform the worship of the seats (pīṭhapūjā) in successive order, one above the other.
First, one should worship the frog, and then Rudra in the form of the fire of time (Kālāgni).
[He meditated upon] the foundational power (Ādhāraśakti), the Tortoise (Kūrma), likewise Ananta, Varāha, the Earth, the Ocean of Nectar, and beyond that, the Island of Jewels (Ratnadvīpa). || 92 ||
The mountain of gold, the jeweled ground, and the Nandana garden;
likewise, the great grove of various trees and the Kalpa orchard.
One should worship the Santāna grove, the Haricandana grove, the Mandāra grove, and the Pārijāta grove. || 94 ||
And [he saw] the grove of Kadamba trees and the jeweled enclosures, consisting of topaz, rubies, emeralds, and also diamonds. 95.
[He saw] those joined with ninefold walls of jewels: lapis lazuli, sapphire, pearl, emerald, and likewise coral. (96)
Then there is the ruby pavilion and the pavilion with a thousand pillars,
as well as the Amṛtavāpikā and the Ānandavāpikā.
Beyond that, there is the pond of reflection, then the rising of the morning sun, the emergence of moonlight, and even the moat of great erotic passion. 98.
A person should worship the Mahāpadmā forest and the Kalpavṛkṣa tree;
thereafter, the Cintāmaṇi palace with its altar made of jewels. 99.

91. He describes the worship of the *pīṭha* with the passage beginning "the worship of the *pīṭha*" and ending with "one should worship" on page 589: "One should first worship the eastern door, which consists of the Eastern Tradition (*pūrvāmnāya*), in the east;
then likewise [the doors] in the south, the west, and the north, according to their respective traditions. (100)
One should worship the jeweled lion-throne and the white parasol above;
one should then worship Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya starting from the southeast (Agni).
One should worship these previously unmentioned [deities] in the directions starting from the east in sequence:
namely, the Self (Ātman), the Inner Self (Antarātman), the Supreme Self (Paramātman), and the Knowledge-Self (Jñānātman), respectively. 102.
Then, one should visualize a lotus situated in the center of the wheel, with its bulbous root (kanda) having eight petals;
its stalk extends upward from the base and downward from the cover, while the pericarp (karṇikā) has the nature of the [twenty-five] principles (tattvas).
In the mandala, one should worship fire, sun, and moon, as well as rajas, sattva, and tamas;
and here one should worship the principles (tattvas) of knowledge, māyā, kalā, and vidyā.
The practitioner of mantra should worship Gaṇeśa on the left and Vaṭuka on the right;
furthermore, he should worship the seed-syllables consisting of the initial letters of their names within the inner square.
From Īśa to Agni, [he worships] Mitrīśanātha and Muḍḍīśanātha;
then the seat named Jālandhara, and thereafter the Pīṭha of Pūrṇagiri. || 106 ||
Thereafter, the practitioner of mantras should worship on the triangle in this sequence,
and then upon the seat on the board, according to the order starting from the east.

100 | Regarding "pūrva" (the east): the meaning is that one should worship the Eastern Tradition at the eastern gate, and likewise the Southern, Western, and Northern Traditions at the southern, western, and northern gates respectively. By this, the practical application results in such forms as: "Obeisance to the eastern gate consisting of the Eastern Tradition," "Obeisance to the southern gate consisting of the Southern Tradition," and so forth. However, in the *Tantrasāra*, it says:
The application has been stated in such forms as "Salutation to the Eastern Tradition and the Eastern Door" (pūrvāmnāyapūrvadvārāya namaḥ), and so forth.
102. Regarding the term *apūrvān*: this means non-dharma (*adharma*), ignorance (*ajñāna*), lack of dispassion (*avairāgya*), and lack of sovereignty (*anaiśvarya*).
105. Regarding the term *caturasra*: within the square of the Śrīcakra, [the deities are worshipped] in sequence starting from the northeast (*īśāna*) and ending at the southeast (*agnikoṇa*).
The meaning is that one should worship the four seats (pīṭhas), beginning with Jālandhara.
[One should worship] the Lord of the Earth, Brahmā, Amṛteśvara;
Rudra, the sovereign of Viṣṇu’s splendor, and likewise Īśvara, the lord of water. (108)
Having uttered the word for the palace (*prāsāda*) in the middle, one should pronounce the word for the sky (*viyat*);
then, having stated "to the Lord," one should join it with "to the five-faced one" (*pañcavaktrāya*). (109)
One should worship Sadāśiva, who has the great preta as his lotus seat, with the heart-mantra or else with the seat-mantra for all seats. || 110 ||
Having uttered the seed-syllable of the preta and the great station of Sadāśiva, followed by "to the preta seated upon the lotus-throne," this is declared to be the heart-mantra (hṛnmanu). || 111 ||
Upon that, with the very same mantra previously mentioned, one should place the sixfold seat (ṣaḍāsana).
Upon that, the practitioner of mantra should also worship a cushion of flowers;
likewise, he should perform the worship of the forms of Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Pūrṇānanda Paramahaṃsa. || 17 ||
109–110 | Regarding "prāsāda": *hauṃ* is the formula: "Obeisance to Sadāśiva, the Lord of the Sky (*viyat*), who is seated upon the lotus-throne of the great corpse (*mahāpreta-padmāsana*).
111 | Regarding "preta": *hasauḥ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the corpse. Thus, it is: "Obeisance to Sadāśiva, the Great Corpse, who is seated upon the lotus-throne."
The Practice:
The Eighteenth Chapter [The Sequence of Worship from the General Preparation of the Arghya Water to the Final Dismissal].
[The Installation of the General Arghya (therein, on the mandala):
Having constructed a triangle, a circle, and a square enclosure on the left side, or otherwise, one should delineate a square with water. || 1 ||
One should make that square, joined with two triangles;
having placed the support (ādhāra) there— [the installation of the vessel for the conch]— one should worship the fire-mandala.
Worship without a support is proclaimed to be fruitless.
[The varieties of supports:
The support is indeed manifold, being either six-footed or four-footed. (3)

1. Thus, having explained the convention of the *cakras* in the previous section, now, while explaining the convention of worship (*pūjā-saṅketa*), he first describes the procedure for establishing the general *arghya* offering with the words beginning "having fashioned" (*vidhāya*). Regarding "the triangle" (*trikoṇa*): the meaning is that first there is a triangle, outside of that a circle, and outside of that a nine-gated city (a square). Here, the triangle should be made facing downwards because it pertains to the Śakti. As it has been said:
In the *Tārārahasya* and the *Rudrayāmala*:
"Wherever the Mahāvidyā, the Śakti-vidyā, is worshipped,
there a downward-facing triangle is prescribed."
"When a triangle for the deities is to be made, it is proclaimed that it should be [drawn] upwards.
Thus he states another ritual procedure with the words "or else": the meaning is that one should fashion a square with water and, within that, draw two triangles.
Or else, one should perform [the drawing] in a circular shape or as a triangle.
Or one should worship a tripod fashioned from gold or silver.
[Instruction on Mantras:
Whether the seed-syllable is explicitly stated or not, worship preceded by *māyā* (Hrīḥ) and *śrī* (Śrīṃ) should be performed.
When no mantra is specified, one should employ the name-mantra (*nāmamantra*) in all cases. (5)
[The Application of the Sandalwood Clogs Mantra:
One should then impart the mantra known as the Śrīpādukā in its proper sequence at the end. || 6 ||
[The ten digits of fire: Dhūmrā, Nīlavarṇā, Kapilā, Visphuliṅginī,
Jvālā, Haimavatī, Kavyavāhinī, and Havyavāhinī.
Raudrī and Saṅkarṣiṇī are the supreme digits (kalās) of fire, just as these [others] are.

5. It has been stated that one should worship even with three words; now he indicates the mantra for that worship with the words "when the seed-syllables are uttered. *Māyābīja* is *hrīṃ*, and *Śrībīja* is *śrīṃ*. Thus, the practical application (*prayoga*) is: *hrīṃ śrīṃ maṃ vahnimaṇḍalāya daśakalātmane arghyapātrādhārāya namaḥ*. He also taught the application of the *tritārī* by means of joining it with the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable. In the *Tripurārcanarahasya*, however, after the root mantra, one worships the mandala with the formula: "Oṃ, obeisance to the mandala for the general arghya-vessel of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, which consists of ten kalās and is the fire-mandala. Then: "Oṃ, obeisance to the fire-mandala consisting of ten kalās, which serves as the general arghya-vessel for Śrī Mahātripurasundarī."

Thus the sequence for the worship of the vessel for the *arghya* offering has been stated; therein, no mention of the *māyā* and *śrī* seed-syllables (*bīja*) is seen. Regarding the phrase "when the mantra is not stated":

this means the name-mantra, that is, a mantra consisting of the name of the respective deity. Although not specifically mentioned here, it should be understood that the name is preceded by the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*). In the *Brahma-purāṇa*:
"Having meditated with a concentrated mind upon the deity preceded by the *praṇava*,
one should offer flowers and other articles individually, accompanied by a salutation."
Likewise:
"The name of each deity, preceded by the syllable Oṃ and concluded with a salutation (namaskāra), is designated as its mantra. Thus it is said.
6. Regarding "Śrīpādukā": first the name of the deity, then the mantra for the sandals (pādukā) is: "I worship the Śrīpādukā, obeisance.
7. Having thus taught the worship of the fire-maṇḍala with the words beginning "the support there," he teaches the worship of the digits of fire (vahnikalā) in that very same place:
Regarding the passage beginning with "Dhūmrā," it is also stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha* as cited in the *Yoginīhṛdayaṭīkā* (p. 593), concerning another ritual manual (*kalpāntara*):
"Dhūmrārcis, Uṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, and Visphuliṅginī."
One should worship the Fire with these [mantras]: Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, and Havyakavyavahā; or else, one may worship the Fire in sequence with the letters beginning with 'ya' and ending with 'kṣa'.
O Goddess, within the triangle inside the hexagon, the orb of fire endowed with its digits should be invoked from the support (ādhāra), and the one most skilled in mantras should worship it.

Thus it has been stated. Although in this statement, by the phrase "the triangle within the hexagon," the worship of the kalās such as Vahni and the rest is taught specifically for the installation of the *viśeṣārghya* (special offering water) and not at the time of the general *sāmānyārghya* (general offering water)— and this is likewise seen in the *Tripurārcanarahasya*, *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*, *Tantrasāra*, and other texts— nevertheless, in the root text (*mūla*), the opposite is the case.

Since the worship of the ten digits (kalās) beginning with Vahni is taught specifically in the context of the general *arghya* (sāmānyārghya), and because that is not mentioned in the case of the special *arghya* (viśeṣārghya), it appears that this sequence, which is accepted in other scriptures, was adopted by the root authors, the venerable Paramahaṃsas. Regarding the term "dhūmra": the meaning is that there are ten digits of fire, beginning with Dhūmra and ending with Saṅkarṣiṇī.

8 | He states another *kalpa* with the words "dhūmrārciḥ" and so forth. Thus, the meaning is that in this *kalpa*, there are ten digits (*kalā*) beginning with Dhūmrārcis and ending with Kavyavāhana. Here, in the *Tantrasāra* and other works, a difference in the sequence of names and a difference in their essential forms are observed. Regarding the phrase "by these" (*ābhiḥ*): the word "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative *kalpa*. The connection is "by these [digits] beginning with Dhūmra, or by those beginning with Dhūmrārcis. [The repetition of] "by these" (*ābhiḥ*)...

He specifies [the method] with the words "beginning with *ya* and ending with *kṣa*, etc. The meaning is that one should worship by prefixing each of the ten syllables from *ya* to *kṣa* with [the name], ending with *namas*. In this context, the syllables beginning with *ya* should be taken as accompanied by the nasal bindu (*m*).
Thus, it is stated in the sixth chapter of the *Kaulāvalī-nirṇaya*, after mentioning "Dhūmrārcis," and so forth:
Those beginning with "abja" and ending with "indukṣa," joined with the dative case-ending (ṅe) and followed by "namaḥ," are proclaimed as the digits of fire.
By this, it is stated that the letters beginning with *ya* are joined with the *anusvāra*; by the phrase "beginning with *abja*," it is also stated that they are preceded by the *Śrībīja*.

Consequently, according to this author's view, the sequence of practice results in: *Śrīṃ Yaṃ Dhūmrāyai Namaḥ*. However, according to the view of the original author (*mūlakṛt*), whether the seed-syllable is explicitly mentioned or not, worship is preceded by *Māyā* and *Śrī*, in accordance with the previously cited statement: "Worship is preceded by *Māyā* and *Śrī*. Thus, [the mantra is]: *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Yaṃ Dhūmrāyai*.

It appears that the ritual application (*prayoga*) takes the form beginning with "namaḥ" and so forth; however, the author of the *Tantrasāra* has stated the application of the *tritārī* mantra prior to the mantras beginning with "ya".
Furthermore, in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha* cited in the commentary on the *Yoginīhṛdaya* (p.
594), [the essential nature of these kalās is described].
Resembling the young dawn and granting the boons of boons and fearlessness, these [goddesses] are present there.
[Regarding the sequence of worship for the entire fire-mandala:
Having uttered the Vāgbhava syllable, which is the seed-syllable of the belly, one should worship that mandala. (9)
O Maheśvarī, these are the digits (kalās) of Fire, beginning with the letter ‘ya’ and ending with the vowel ‘ṛ’, each corresponding to its own phoneme;
having worshipped these digits according to the rule with their respective letters.
Beginning with their own seed-syllables and ending with the dative case, followed by the word "namaḥ" in the middle of the name—these are declared to be the fire-energies (vahnikalā).
Now listen to the names of the mantras.
Dhūmrārcis, Nīlaraktā, Kapilā, Visphuliṅginī,
Jvālāmālinī, Arciṣmatī, and above those Havyavāhinī;
the eighth is Kavyavāhā, as well as Raudrī and Saṃvāhinī.

In this statement, by the phrase "beginning with its own seed-syllable" (*svabījādya*), the intended meaning is either that [the mantras] begin with the *Śrībīja*, or that they begin with the *Māyā* and *Śrībīja*, or that they are preceded by the *Tritārī* consisting of the *Vāgbhava*, *Māyā*, and *Śrībīja*; such is the summary.
(9) He describes the essential nature of the aforementioned fire-calorific powers (*vahnikalā*) with the word "tender" (*taruṇa*): they possess the color of the newly risen sun.

The meaning is that they grant boons with one hand and fearlessness with the other. It was previously stated, "One should first worship the fire-mandala"; he now teaches the sequence for that worship of the fire-mandala with the words beginning with *udarārṇam*. Having placed the "belly-syllable," which is the *vāgbhava* seed-mantra *aiṃ*, one should worship that mandala, namely the fire-mandala. And thus:

It should be understood that one should worship by uttering either of the two seed-syllables (bīja) according to their etymologies, using the mantra: "Obeisance to the support of the arghya vessel, which consists of the circle of fire (vahnimaṇḍala) and its ten kalās. This is clearly stated in the sixth chapter of the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*:
"Having prepared the maṇḍala as before and having worshipped it by that same path..."

"First, having uttered the mantra ending with the heart [syllable], which consists of Mahākāla with the moon (i) and the fire-mandala (ra) joined with the letter *ṅe*, one should then worship him in the foundation (*ādhāra*).
Thus [it is said]. "Mahākāla" refers to the letter *ma*. Furthermore, regarding this, it is stated in the fourteenth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*:
"Then, having visualized the fire there, one should worship that which consists of the yantra.
Because of this statement, the mention of the term "support-vessel" (ādhāra-pātra) must be performed with the formula: "Obeisance to the support for the arghya vessel.
This is likewise seen in authoritative liturgical manuals such as the *Tripurārcanarahasya*.
p. 595) Having placed the vessel there, one should worship the Sun with its digits right there.
[The twelve solar digits:]
Tapinī, another Tāpinī, Vibudhā, and likewise Bodhinī. || 10 ||
Kaliṇī, Ṣoḍaśī, Vāruṇī, Ākarṣiṇī, Māyā, Viśvāvatī, and Hemaprabhā— these are the digits (kalās) of the Sun.
[In that regard, there is another classification:
Tapinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, Ruci, Suṣumṇā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā.
Or the practitioner should worship with these digits (kalās) using their respective mantras. || 12 ||

10–11 | Now he teaches the worship of the entire solar orb with the words beginning "the vessel" (*pātram*). "In that very [place]" means on one of the previously mentioned six types of pedestals (*ṣaṭpada*) or other supports. He states this explicitly in the sixth chapter of the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*:
"One should place one of these vessels upon the three-footed pedestal."
Thus it is said. Here too, it should be understood that one should draw the maṇḍala as before, worship it, and then worship the solar maṇḍala.
Accordingly, it is stated in that very same work, in the section on the special arghya: "Having prepared the maṇḍala as before, one should worship it according to the previous method."
Having visualized the solar disc there, one should then perform worship.
Thus [it is said]. He describes the twelve solar digits (*kalā*) with the passage beginning "Tāpinī," etc. The twelve digits of the Sun begin with Tāpinī and end with Prabhā.
(12) He states another tradition with the passage beginning "Tāpinī," etc.; in this tradition, there are twelve [digits] beginning with Tāpinī and ending with Kṣamā.

[The Sequence of the Worship of the Kalās] One should sequentially join the letters from *ka* to *ṭha*, endowed with the bindu (*m*), and those from *bhā* to *ḍa*, likewise with the bindu, to the beginning of the *kalās* through their mutual sequential union. (13)
[The nature of the Kalās:
All of them grant boons and fearlessness, and are as dark as the *atasī* flower.
[The sequence for the worship of the solar mandala.]
Or, having joined the forehead with the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja), one should [visualize] the mandala of the sun.

The Solar Kalās. In the sixth chapter of the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*, this very sequence is adopted. "One should worship" means one should worship with [the kalās] beginning with Tapinī and ending with Prabhā, or alternatively, with those beginning with Tapinī and ending with Kṣamā. "With their respective mantras" means with mantras preceded by Māyā, the Śrībīja, and so forth, as previously described.
13. First, he describes the application of the letters with the words beginning with "kādi" and so forth.

The meaning is that one should join the letters from *ka* to *ṭha* (the consonants from *k* to *ṭh*), as well as those from *bha* to *ḍa* (from *bh* to *ḍ*), recited in reverse order, joined with the nasal dot (*bindu*), to the beginning of the aforementioned twelve digits (*kalās*). Thus, having uttered the seed-syllable (*bīja*) according to the previously stated sequence, [one joins] *kaṃ*, *bhaṃ*...

The sequence of ritual application culminates in the form: "Obeisance to Tapinī," "Khaṃ Maṃ, obeisance to Tāpinī," and so forth. This is clearly stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha* as cited in the *Yoginīhṛdayaṭīkā*: "Having placed a conch shell that has been washed with the weapon-mantra (astra) upon [the vessel] in that manner..."
And having invoked the solar disc from one's own heart by means of one's own mantra.

The collection of letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṭha*, and those beginning with *bha* and ending with *ḍha*, should be employed two by two, both in direct and reverse order; immediately thereafter, the *kalās* are to be applied.

Thus it is said. Here too, as in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*, the *Yoginīhṛdaya*, and other texts, differences in the names and differences in the essential forms (*svarūpa*) of the *kalās* are observed, as before.

(14) He states the essential form of these *kalās*: "With the gesture of boon and fearlessness" (*varābhaya*). All [the goddesses] indeed hold the gesture of boon with one hand and [the gesture of fearlessness] with the other.

And they bestow fearlessness. "Resembling the flax flower" means having the same color as the flax flower. It was previously stated that one should worship the Sun with its digits; he now teaches that sequence: "The forehead," etc. "The forehead" is *aṃ*; "the seed of desire" is *klīṃ*.
The meaning is that one should worship the orb of the Sun after first joining one or the other of these two seeds. He describes the sequence of worship:
In the sixth chapter of the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya* (p.
597), regarding the filling of the arghya vessel:
one should fill it with pure water from a sacred site while reciting the root mantra.
[The Instruction on the Worship of the Lunar Kalās]: Having offered fragrance and flowers with the *praṇava*, one performs the worship of the lunar kalās. || 15 ||
[The sixteen digits of the moon:
Amṛtā, Mānasī, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Prītī, Ratī, as well as Śrī, Hrī, Svadhā, Rātri, Jyotsnā, and Haimavatī. || 16 ||
Chāyā is another [form], Pūrṇimā is Vidyā, and Amāvāsyā is the sixteenth;
one should worship Soma with these, either with the former or with the latter, according to the sequence.
Having prepared the maṇḍala as before, one should worship it according to the previous method. Then, having visualized the solar maṇḍala there,
one should worship it with the syllable beginning with a vowel, joined with the bindu and the suffix -ṅe, [forming] *arka-maṇḍalāya*.
"Having recited the mantra ending with *namaḥ* and having worshipped the vessel of offering (*arghyapātra*),

one should worship there the twelve digits (*kalā*) known as those of the Sun. Thus, having recited either the *lalāṭa* or the *kāma* seed-syllable, [one offers] *aṃ* to the solar orb (*arkamaṇḍala*) consisting of the twelve digits.

The ritual application is: "Obeisance to the arghya vessel" (arghyapātrāya namaḥ). 15. Now, he describes the filling of the arghya vessel and so forth with the words beginning with "tīrtha": "one should fill [the arghya vessel]"—this is the ellipsis.
"Uttering the root mantra"—here the causative sense is implied, meaning "causing [it] to be uttered. Then, therein, one should offer sandalwood paste, flowers, and so forth with the *praṇava*.
The meaning is that having set aside the worship of the digit of the moon (*somakalā*), one should perform the worship of the lunar orb (*somamaṇḍala*). As it is stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha*:
"One should throw into that water cardamom, cloves, *kakkola*, and nutmeg, well combined with fragrant flowers and other substances."
"Having drawn the ninefold womb (*navayoni*) as before in the midst of water, one should invoke [the deity] from the purification (*niḥśuddhi*) and worship the lunar disc (*candramaṇḍala*).
(16–17) Now, he teaches the sixteen lunar digits (*somakalā*) and their worship, beginning with the words "Amṛtā" and so forth; these range from Amṛtā to Amāvāsyā.
There are sixteen digits (*kalā*). By means of these aforementioned digits, he introduces another method: "or by others," which means "or by those that are about to be described.
[In this regard, there is another way.]
Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati, Dhṛti, Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, and Aṅgadā. (18)

The digits (kalās) residing in the vowels—Pūrṇā, Pūrṇāmṛtā, and Kāmadāyinī—are known to resemble the young rising sun and to hold the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. [The nature of the lunar digits. 19.
[The Sequence of the Worship of the Kalās]:
One should worship all the kalās even according to the sequence beginning from the west. [The Worship of the Lunar Maṇḍala]
Having joined the syllable *śakti* with the right ear [the letter *ra*], one forms the lunar mandala.
[The Worship of Ānandabhairava and Ānandabhairavī]: One should worship the god Ānandabhairava and also Ānandabhairavī.
Regarding them, he says "Amṛtā" and so forth: in this ritual manual (kalpa), [the goddesses] beginning with Amṛtā and ending with Pūrṇāmṛtā are the bestowers of desires.

The meaning is that one should worship these sixteen *kalās*, which bestow the desired objects. This very ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is set forth in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya* by means of a statement with an identical sequence. "Residing in the vowels" (*svaragāḥ*) means the *kalās* situated within the sixteen vowels beginning with *a*. In this regard, it is stated in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya* that the *kalās* are born from the vowels (*svarajāḥ*).

And it should be understood that one should worship each [deity] by prefixing it with each of the sixteen vowels beginning with *a*. This is clearly stated in the *Svacchandasaṃgraha* as cited in the *Yoginīhṛdayaṭīkā*:
"The sixteen gentle digits (*kalā*) are proclaimed to begin with the first [vowel] and end with the last [consonant]."

Thus, the application of the seed-syllables (*bījayoga*) is as before. And so, having uttered the seed-syllable as previously described, the sequence of ritual application culminates in the form: *aṃ amṛtāyai namaḥ*, *āṃ mānadāyai namaḥ*, and so forth. He states the essential nature of these digits (*kalā*): "youthful," etc.; this is clear. One should worship them in a circular form, proceeding from the westward direction. It is exactly the same in the *Tantrasāra*.

Now he describes the sequence for the worship of the lunar disc (*candramaṇḍala*), beginning with the words "the syllable of power" (*śaktyarṇa*). "The syllable of power" is *sauḥ*; "the right ear" is *uṃ*.

The application of the seed-syllables (*bījayoga*) is as before. Thus, having uttered the aforementioned seed-syllable, the ritual formula is: *uṃ somamaṇḍalāya ṣoḍaśakalātmane arghyapātrāmṛtāya namaḥ* ("Oṃ! Salutation to the lunar disc, whose self consists of sixteen digits, the nectar of the vessel of offering").
21–22. Now, he teaches the worship of Ānandabhairava and Ānandabhairavī there, beginning with the words "Ānanda" and so forth.
(p. 599) [The mantra of Ānandabhairava:
Śiva, Soma, the end of the Mātṛkās, Kāla, Bhū, Varuṇa, and Anala. 21.

Joined with the left ear [the letter *v*], adorned with the wind [the letter *y*] and the crescent moon [the vowel *i*], one should then utter the crest-mantra (śikhā-mantra): "To Ānandabhairava. (22)
Ānandabhairava is Soma; listen to [the mantra of] Ānandabhairavī. Having written the sequence of letters as before, one should remove the moon and lead [the first letter]. (23)
Having joined the left eye with the ear,
the wise one should recite the root mantra or the *tāra* (om) seven times over the *arghya* for the Goddess Sudhā, according to the procedure for recitation.
First Ānandabhairava, then Ānandabhairavī; "one should worship" is to be connected with what precedes.
Regarding that, he states the mantra of Ānandabhairava beginning with "Śiva": *Śiva* is the letter *ha*; *Soma* is the seed-syllable of the Moon, the letter *sa*;
the end of the *Mātṛkā* is the letter *kṣa*; *Kāla* is the letter *ma*; *Bhūḥ* is the seed-syllable of Earth, the letter *la*; and the seed-syllable of Varuṇa is the letter *va*.

*Anala* is the seed-syllable of fire, the letter *ra*; the seed-syllable of wind is the letter *ya*. That seed-syllable of wind is joined with the sixth vowel [ū] via the left ear [the letter *ha*], and likewise adorned with the half-moon, the *anusvāra*. Thus, *ha sa kṣa ma la va ra yūṃ* is obtained. Then follows *ānandabhairavāya*. And then the crest-mantra (*śikhāmantra*) is *vaṣaṭ*. Thus, *ha sa kṣa ma la...* [is completed].
The mantra of Ānandabhairava culminates as follows: *va ra yūṃ ānandabhairavāya vaṣaṭ*.

(23–25) He concludes the mantra of Ānandabhairava with the words "Ānanda... and so forth. In this context, the reading "soma" appears to be a scribal error; "prokta" seems to be the correct reading. Next, he states the mantra of Ānandabhairavī, beginning with "Ānandabhairavīm," etc.

The meaning is that one should write the eight letters beginning with *ha* according to the sequence of Ānandabhairava as before. "Leaving the moon" means bypassing the second letter, *sa*, and one should bring the first letter, *ha*, [there]; the meaning is that one should employ it after the second syllable, *sa*. By this, in the case of *ha sa*, *sa ha* is obtained. Likewise, regarding the ear, [the rule applies] to the aforementioned mantra.
Having joined the fourth vowel with the left eye in the place of the left ear, by this [change] "yūṃ" becomes "yīṃ.
Then [one says] "sudhādevyai. And then, one should join the mantra of the eyes, namely the word "vauṣaṭ"; this is the remainder [of the instruction]. Thus, [the mantra is]:
*ha sa kṣa ma la va ra yīṃ*.
(p. 600) [Conclusion] This is declared to be the general *arghya*;
[the promise to define the specific *arghya*] follows.
Now, the special arghya is described. || 25 ||
[The Preparation of the Śrīpātra] Having received the command of the Great Goddess, one should prepare the Śrīpātra. [The Construction of the Maṇḍala]
One should construct the mandala in such a way that it is situated between oneself and the Śrīcakra. || 26 ||
One should sprinkle with water that triangular [mandala] joined with the vowel *ī*, or a six-cornered one, or a circle within a square enclosure; or else, a circle outside the triangle. || 27 ||

The mantra of Ānandabhairavī culminates in "Sudhādevyai vauṣaṭ. Regarding the word "asya" (of this): it means that one should recite the root mantra or the *tāra* (the syllable Om) seven times over this general *arghya*. He concludes the section on the general *arghya* with the words "sāmānya... (the general...).
Having thus described the procedure for the general *arghya*, he explains the method for establishing the special *arghya* with the words beginning "the special *arghya*" (verses 26–27).
Next, he teaches the location for constructing the mandala suitable for placing the vessels with the word "Self" (*ātman*): [it is] between the Self and the Śrīcakra.

The meaning is that one should construct the maṇḍala on the ground situated between oneself and the deity who is the form of the Śrīcakra, according to the sequence to be described. This has been stated in the sixth chapter of the Kaulāvalīnirṇaya:
"Then, one should draw the cakra on the ground between oneself and the goddess."
Thus [it is said]. He describes the sequence for constructing the mandala with the words "by the letter *ī*": a triangle containing the letter *ī*, conjoined with the letter *ī*.
Also, in the sixth chapter of the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*:
"Having drawn Māyā in the center, one should sprinkle it immediately thereafter."

Thus [it is said]. Even there, by the term *māyā*, the fourth vowel alone is to be understood. And so, one method for constructing the mandala is as follows: a triangle containing the fourth vowel, outside of that a hexagon, outside of that a circle, and outside of that a square in the form of a city-gate (*bhūpura*). He states another method: "with a triangle" (*tryasra*), etc. Alternatively, one should draw a circle outside the aforementioned triangle. And thus, in this method—
The specific detail is that first there is a triangle containing the syllable *ī*, outside of which is a circle, outside of that a hexagon, and outside of that a square.
Thus, two methods for the construction of the mandala are observed elsewhere as well; for example, in the sixth chapter of the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya* (p.
601), regarding the worship beginning with the four seats (*pīṭhas*).
In the square is the supreme seat named Pūrṇaśaila and Uḍḍīyāna; in the six corners are the six seats, Jālandhara and Kāmarūpa.
[Regarding the worship of the hexagon: Alternatively, one may worship the six limbs while reciting their respective mantras.
[Worship of the triangle and so forth:]
And a triangle with three peaks, in the center of which is the Ādhāraśakti.
Then, between the two goddesses of the self, one should draw a wheel upon the ground:
a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, and joined with an enclosure of earth.
Thus [it is said]. This statement establishes the former ritual procedure (*kalpa*). Likewise, in the fourteenth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*:
"The mandala consists of a triangle, a circle, a hexagon, and a square.
This statement establishes the latter ritual procedure. And so, because different ritual procedures are seen according to the division of the tantras...

One should adopt one or the other position according to the tradition of one's own guru; this is the general direction. Regarding the word "that": it means one should sprinkle that maṇḍala with "that water," namely, the water for the general *arghya* offering. This is clearly stated in the sixth chapter of the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*:
"Having drawn the *māyā* [syllable] in the center, one should sprinkle [the maṇḍala] immediately thereafter."
With the root mantra ending in the weapon-mantra (astra) and with the water of the general arghya offering.

Thus [ends verse] 28. Now, he teaches the worship in the previously mentioned maṇḍala according to the sequence beginning with the square, starting with the words "In the square" (caturasre) and so forth.
One should worship the four seats, such as Pūrṇaśaila and the others, in the square. And the worship is performed in the order starting from the east; this has been stated in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*.
In the sixth chapter: In the square [mandala], one should worship Pūrṇaśaila, Uḍḍīyāna, Jālandhara, and Kāmarūpa, according to the sequence starting from the east.

Thus [it is said]. Now, he describes the worship within the six-cornered [figure] inside the defined square—starting with "six": the connection is that one should worship the six seats within the six corners, as follows by the subsequent [text]. And the six seats—the seat of the ocean of nectar (*amṛtārṇavāsana*), the seat of the lotus of the boat (*potāmbujāsana*), the seat of the self (*ātmāsana*), the seat of the wheel (*cakrāsana*), the seat of all mantras (*sarvamantrāsana*), and the seat of the goal and the perfected ones (*sādhyasiddhāsana*)—are described in the *Tripurārcanarahasya*.

These should be understood as being explicitly stated. As for the ritual application (*prayoga*), it takes such forms as uttering the two-syllable mantra *hrīṃ śrīṃ*, or the three-syllable mantra *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*, followed by "Homage to the one seated upon the ocean of nectar" (*amṛtārṇavāsanāya namaḥ*), and so forth.
(29) He states another ritual procedure with the words "the six-limbed" (*ṣaḍaṅga*). He explains this explicitly in the fourteenth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*:

p. 602) [The sequence for placing the vessel for the *arghya* offering upon the mandala: First, one should place the support (*ādhāra*)—which may be triangular, circular, or hexagonal—upon the mandala.
Having sprinkled the support with water while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should establish it on top of the mandala. (30)
[The Worship of the Support]: One should utter the three seed-syllables of Bālā and the *arghya-āsana* of Tripurasundarī;
one should worship the support with the mantra ending in "sādhayāmi namaḥ. || 31 ||
Having worshipped as before while reciting the mantra ending with the *kalā* of Fire, one should say: "To the circle of Fire, whose nature consists of ten *kalās*. (32)

One should worship with the heart-mantra [the deity] at the support of the *arghya* vessel for the sake of the seat; one should worship the six limbs in the six corners and Śivā, the mantra's center, with the individual [syllables].
"One should worship the six limbs by repeating [the mantra] twice within the six triangles.

Thus, the meaning is that one should worship by first reciting the *vāgbhava* syllable-cluster (*kūṭa*), then the *kāmarāja* cluster, then the *śakti* cluster, and once again reciting those same three clusters beginning with *vāgbhava*. This has also been stated by the authors of the *Tantrasāra*:
It has been stated that one should worship the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) in a hexagon by means of the root-mantra (mūlavidyā) repeated twice, following the sequence beginning with Agni.

This is exactly the same in the *Tripurārcanarahasya*. Furthermore, this very intention is understood through the corroboration of the *Jñānārṇava*, the *Tantrasāra*, and other texts regarding the phrase "uttering each respective mantra. He describes the worship of the inner triangle with the word "triangle" (*trikoṇa*); [it is] by three.
"By the *kūṭas* (peaks)" means by the three *kūṭas* taken individually. It is also stated in the fourteenth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*:

"O Supreme Goddess, one should worship there in the triangle with the individual *kūṭas*. Regarding the word "in the center": the meaning is that one should worship Ādhāraśakti in the middle of the triangle.
30. With the heart-mantra, namely *namaḥ*.
31. Now he states the mantra for the worship of the base of the *arghya* vessel: "Bālā," etc. Thus, the resulting mantra is: *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ tripurasundaryarghyāsanaṃ sādhayāmi namaḥ*.

32–33 | "As before" means that one should worship the ten kalās of Fire according to the procedure prescribed for the general *arghya*, and then worship them upon the support (*ādhāra*) with the mantra: "Obeisance to the seat of the *arghya* vessel belonging to the mandala of Fire, which consists of the ten kalās.
[The Determination of the Arghya Vessel] (p. 603)
This vessel—whether made of gold, glass, or silver; produced from pearl shells;

composed of *viśvāmitra* (crystal); golden, dear, and made of rock crystal; copper, which bestows affection; or originating from the auspicious coconut—generates the eight supernatural powers (*aṣṭasiddhi*) and grants all desires.
The skull-bowl (kāpāla) generates the accomplishment of manifest mantras, while the pearl (mauktika) bestows liberation. || 34 ||
A conch shell, a gourd vessel, as well as one produced from a sacred tree, or one made of clay, copper, or even iron; || 35 ||
In ancient times, the wise Viśvāmitra indeed fashioned this vessel;
it is the skull-bowl of Viśvāmitra, the most excellent among all vessels. (36)
Upon seeing a coconut vessel, sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, as well as treachery toward a trusted friend—all such evils are utterly destroyed. (37)
Whoever gives millions of kalpas [of wealth] as well as hundreds of gold pieces to the Lord of Sages when the moon is swallowed by Rāhu; || 38 ||
The fruit of that [offering] is multiplied ten millionfold by means of a coconut vessel for the arghya;
in the absence of such a vessel, one should employ another vessel.
Upon seeing the supreme vessel of offering (arghyapātra), Brahmā and the other deities, as well as all the Yoginīs, always dance with joy; it abundantly bestows spiritual accomplishment (siddhi).
[The distinction of vessels according to the difference in intention:
For the rites of subjugation and attraction, a golden vessel is recommended;
for pacification and nourishment, the wise one should employ a silver vessel. (41)
41. Regarding the difference in results based on the difference in vessels, the *Śivarahasya* cited in the *Haratattvadīdhiti* states:
"May all golden vessels be accepted by me;
having offered the *arghya* with silver, one shall obtain worshipful sons in this world."
One should know that an iron vessel is used for killing and driving away;
for acts of immobilization, a stone vessel; and for causing enmity, one made of iron or clay. (42)
In rites for the destruction of a lineage, a glass vessel is praised;
one should know that a wooden vessel is for the practice of mantra worship. (43)
[The Excellence of Viśvāmitra as a Vessel in All Cases] In all undertakings, O Viśvāmitra, you are to be considered unsurpassed.
[The Variations in Fruit According to the Distinction of Vessels]
The conch is said to bestow knowledge, and the gourd grants all supernatural powers.
The Mahārāja-tantra doctrine, which is extremely difficult to obtain, has been declared:
that vessel, measuring sixteen finger-breadths, bestows all prosperity. (45) [The measurement of the arghya-vessel]
If made of copper, it bestows good fortune; if made of clay, it brings about righteousness;
but if all these are unavailable, one made of earth and fashioned by one's own hand may be used.
One should not place a broken vessel for the *arghya* offering upon the seat;
in all cases, copper is superior to gold as an *arghya* vessel.
"Veneration of the vessels must be performed, for the vessels themselves are indeed supreme;

in the external performance of the fire-sacrifice (homa), nothing is accomplished without the vessel. Thus it is said. Regarding the distinction of vessels according to the difference of qualified practitioners, the Gandharva Tantra states in its twelfth chapter:
"A vessel made of conch, mother-of-pearl, silver, or gold is desired for divine beings;
those made of large conchs are for heroes, and those made of fruit are for forest-dwellers. Thus it is said.
Regarding the excellence of the copper vessel for the *arghya* offering and other rites, he says:
The vessel for worship, the arghya vessel, the support for the food offering (naivedya), and the drinking vessel— all these,
whatever is used here in the worship, should be made of copper.
The gods rejoice in copper; the gods always abide in copper.
Copper is pleasing to the Goddess; therefore, one should employ copper.
A bowl measuring twelve finger-breadths, or even eight finger-breadths, and whatever bowl is smaller than this, is considered an inferior bowl. (46)
[The Examination of Vessels to be Avoided] An excessively large vessel and a minute vessel should be avoided;
the best of practitioners should use one of these for water. 47.
[The sequence for placing the vessel:
Having washed it with the Astra-mantra, one should place it upon the tripod (yantrikā).
(45–47) He states the measurement of the Arghya-vessel with the words beginning with "sixteen" and so forth.
Specifically, it is stated in the sixth chapter of the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*:
"Among these vessels that have been mentioned, one should prepare a single vessel sixteen finger-breadths in width and six finger-breadths in height."
Alternatively, it may be half of that, or even half of that again;
its measurement should be one finger-breadth, or one and a half, or six [finger-breadths].
One should avoid that which is too subtle, too coarse, or has holes; one should not employ a broken vessel. A dream-instruction is highly praised.
Thus it is said. Also in the *Śivarahaśya* as cited in the *Śivārcanacandrikā*:
"A vessel of thirty-six finger-breadths is proclaimed to be the best;
the middling is three parts less than that, and the smallest is twelve finger-breadths."
One should never have an alms-bowl made that is less than eight finger-breadths in size.
One should fashion vessels shaped like lotuses, complete with central cavities, as well as those resembling grapes, blue lotuses, and so forth.
Thus it is said. Likewise, in the *Śyāmārcanacandrikā* cited in the *Haratattvadīdhiti*:
"O Goddess, O Beloved, one should avoid under all circumstances that which is broken, less than eight digits, worn out, cracked, or of a different material."

Then, at the end of the three seed-syllables of Bālā, there is Tripurasundarī. (48)
Immediately after the word "pātram" following the specific *arghya* formula, one should establish the digit (*kalā*) of the Sun with the mantra "sthāpayāmi. (49)

Having worshipped the solar disc and its rays there according to the rule, the wise one should offer oblations to the solar disc and to the twelvefold essence of the rays; for the vessel of the *arghya* offering, the heart-mantra is used. (50)
[The Mandala Ritual: One should then draw a triangle, a circle, and a hexagon within the center of the vessel.
(48–50) Regarding the placement of the *arghya* vessel upon its base, he says: "With the *astra* [mantra]. That is, with the *astra* mantra, namely *phaṭ*. Having washed [the vessel],...

The phrase "with the water for general *arghya*" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. [This refers to] upon the tripod (*yantrikā*) or other previously mentioned supports. Thus it is said in the twelfth chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*:
"In the same manner, with the water for general *arghya* joined with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*)."
Having washed it, O Supreme Goddess, one should then place it within the mandala.
Having thus taught the sequence for placing the support for the arghya vessel within the maṇḍala,

[the text] states that the placement of the arghya vessel itself follows the very same sequence as the placement of the support, beginning with: "O Supreme Goddess, the practitioner should wash the vessel as before," and so forth.

He states the mantra for the installation of the *arghya* vessel with the words "bālā" etc. Thus, the installation mantra is: *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ tripurasundarīviśeṣārghyapātraṃ pratiṣṭhāpayāmi*, as before. The application of the two *tārīs* or the three *tārīs* is everywhere as previously described.

The meaning is "having worshipped. Regarding "the solar orb" (*sūryamaṇḍala*): the meaning is that one should worship the vessel for the *arghya* offering with the mantra: "Obeisance to the solar orb, which consists of twelve digits and serves as the *arghya* vessel" (*oṃ sūryamaṇḍalāya dvādaśakalātmane arghyapātrāya namaḥ*).
[Maṇḍala-worship, p. 607]
One should worship in the triangle using the mantra in its entirety, as well as its individual and combined forms.
[The Procedure for Filling the Vessel]:

Having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) with this mantra—“I fill the vessel upon the base of the arghya of Tripurasundarī, which consists of the three seed-syllables of Bālā”—one should fill the vessel. 52.
Reciting the letters of the Mātṛkā both in direct and reverse order,
one should fill the Śrīpātra with the thought that it is nectar upon nectar.
[Substances for filling the vessel: Water is said to be one hundred times [efficacious]; milk-water is unsurpassed.
Curd is a hundred times more efficacious than milk, and clarified butter (ghṛta) is a hundred times more efficacious than curd. 54.
The merit [of the offering] for the accomplishment of the Goddess’s right-hand path is a hundred times that of clarified butter.

(51) Regarding the phrase "the triangle": the meaning is that one should first draw a triangle in the center of the aforementioned vessel for the *arghya* offering, then a circle outside of that, and then a hexagon outside of that. On this point, it is stated in the sixth chapter of the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*:

"Having prepared the maṇḍala as before, one should worship it according to the previous procedure. Because of this statement, and because the *Tantrasāra* also says "having drawn the yantra as before," and because it is seen likewise in the *Jñānārṇava* and other texts, the underlying intention here is that one should draw the outer square (bhūpura) outside the hexagon. The word "entire" (*samasta*) refers to the mantra consisting of three peaks (*kūṭa*); [the word] "individual" (*vyasta*) refers to each peak separately.
The meaning is: [one should worship] individually with the *vāgbhava*, *kāmarāja*, and *śaktikūṭa* syllables.

(52–53) Now, he describes the sequence for filling the vessel with the words "bālā" and so forth. Thus, the meaning is that one should perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) with the mantra: *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ tripurasundaryarghyapātraṃ saṃpūrayāmi*. Regarding "in direct order" (*anuloma*): from the letter *a* up to the letter *kṣa*, and again...

"Uttering the letters of the Mātṛkā from *kṣa* to *a*, one should contemplate [the vessel] as the supreme nectar by means of the perception of the nectar of nectar"—this is the meaning. The *śrīpātra* is the *arghyapātra*.
(54) Now, he states the substances for filling the vessels and the differences in results according to those substances, beginning with "from water" (*jalāt*). From water...

The meaning is that one should understand the production of results in the sequence stated: milk-water produces a hundredfold result, and from that, curd produces a hundredfold result, and so on. Regarding the phrase "by means of the dakṣiṇā-sādhana," the meaning is: by means of the sādhana in the order of the dakṣiṇā. He states this specifically in the twelfth chapter of the Gandharva-tantra:
[The materials for the *arghya* offering: Dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, red flowers, bilva leaves, and sandalwood. || 55 ||

Having offered various fragrant substances, the nine jewels, and the eight perfumes— [as an offering to the entire lunar mandala]— one should worship the digits of the Moon as before, according to the sequence from east to west.
At the edge of the lunar disc, to the one whose self consists of sixteen digits,
one should offer the *arghya* with the mantra "Obeisance to the nectar of *arghya*," following the leftward sequence.
[The Eight Fragrances:
Sandalwood, agallochum, musk, coraka, saffron, gorocana, jaṭāmāṃsī, and kapi—these are known as the eight fragrances of Śakti. (58)
One should fill [the vessel] with the *mātṛkā* in reverse order, consecrated with the root mantra,
or likewise with flowers and fermented liquors (*āsava*).
Likewise, with the milk of a tawny cow, or even with coconut nectar,
or with fragrant sugarcane juices, or with the three sweets;
One should at times fill that great vessel with various substances;
indeed, the varieties of substances arise according to the distinctions among those qualified [to perform the rite].
"O Supreme Goddess, one should place there *svayambhū* flowers mixed with camphor, agallochum, sandalwood, *rocanā*, and saffron, permeated with musk, along with sugar combined with honey."

55–56. Now, he describes the offering of the *arghya* materials there, beginning with the word "dūrvā. This is clear. Regarding the word "navā" (*nine*): having offered the nine gems (*navaratna*) and the eight fragrances (*gandhāṣṭaka*), one should worship according to the sequence to be described; this is the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*). The nine gems are shown in the fifth chapter (verse 5.93).

The eight perfumes, however, he himself will explain further on. Regarding the word "yajet" (one should worship): it means that one should worship the sixteen lunar digits, beginning with Amṛtā, according to the previously described sequence for the general *arghya* offering. Regarding "soma": the practical application (*prayoga*) is: "Oṃ, obeisance to the lunar orb (*somamaṇḍala*), which consists of sixteen digits and is the nectar of the *arghya*."
58. Previously, it was stated that there are eight fragrant substances (*gandhāṣṭaka*); he now defines those eight fragrances with the verse beginning "sandalwood" (*candana*) and so forth.
*Corā* is black *śaṭhī*; *kapi* is *gāṭhiyālā*, according to the *Tantrasāra*. The remainder is clear. (p.
609) [The sequence for drawing the yantra and other rites in the *Arghyāmṛta*]
Having drawn the yantra with Puṣpa within the space between Pūrva and Soma-amṛta,
one should write the letters beginning with A, Ka, and Tha on the three lines, and write Haṃ Laṃ Kṣaṃ in the center.
In that regard, during the invocation of the image, the mantra-practitioner should worship the triangle with the *trikūṭa* [mantra] in due order;
having covered the vessel with both hands, he should perform the invocation of the *tīrtha*.
[The Ritual Sequence for the Worship of the Five Jewels: One should worship the five jewels in the directions starting from the east and in the center. || 61 ||

The end of *kānta* (the letter *ya*), the Moon (*sa*) and the Sun (*ra*), the radiant (*bha*), the one ending in *dhā* (*na*), joined with the Earth (*la*), and joined with the Moon of the right ear (*śa*)—these are the five jewels in their proper sequence. (62)
[The Five Jewels:
The sky, heaven, the netherworld, the mortal realm, and the world of the Nāgas—this is declared to be the five jewels, which bring great bliss to the Goddess. (63)

59. Regarding "with a flower": within the previous *soma-amṛta* (the nectar of Soma), that is, within the nectar situated in the *arghya* vessel which consists of the digits of Soma (*somakalā*). Furthermore...
The practical meaning is that one should write the three syllables *haṃ*, *laṃ*, and *kṣam* within the aforementioned triangle.
Here, it should be understood that the word *akatha* is the regulator for the letters beginning with *a*, *ka*, and *tha*.

(60) Regarding "the triangle": the aforementioned triangle is [formed] by the three peaks (*trikūṭa*)—namely, the *vāgbhava*, *kāmarāja*, and *śakti* peaks—arranged individually in their proper sequence.
The meaning is that one should worship. "Invocation of the Tīrthas" means by means of the mantra beginning with *oṃ gaṅge ca*, and so forth.
(61) "From the east, etc. means that one should worship the five jewels (*pañcaratna*) in this sequence: four in the four directions starting from the east and one in the center.

62–63 | He states the five jewels (*pañcaratna*) with the words beginning "ending in *kānta*" (*kāntānta*), and so forth. "Ending in *kānta*" refers to the letter *ga*; *soma* is the letter *sa*; *tapana* is the letter *pa*;

"shining" (*bhānta*) is the letter *ma*; and "ending in *dhā*" (*dhānta*) is the letter *na*. This group of five letters is joined with *mahī*, that is, conjoined with the seed-syllable of the earth, the letter *la*;
likewise, it is combined with the right ear, which is the fifth vowel (*ū*), and with the moon, which is the *anusvāra*.
[The Worship of Ānandabhairava] One should worship the god Ānandabhairava as before.

By this, the five seed-syllables *gluṃ*, *sluṃ*, *pluṃ*, *mluṃ*, and *nluṃ* are obtained. The meaning is that one should first join these five jewels (*pañcaratna*) with the [elements] beginning with space (*gagana*) in their respective order. He concludes with the words "the five jewels" and so forth. And thus:
*gluṃ namaḥ to the jewel of space*, *sluṃ namaḥ to the jewel of heaven*, *pluṃ namaḥ to the jewel of the underworld*, *mluṃ*...

"Salutation to the Jewel of Mortals (nluṃ), salutation to the Jewel of Nagas"—such is the sequence of application. It is exactly the same in the *Tripurārcanarahasya*. Thereafter, the excellent practitioner should worship the five jewels (pañcaratna),
which consists of the word "Pañcāntaka" joined with a bindu and endowed with the right ear (the letter *r*).
At the end of "gaganānte," one should extract the mantra ending with "namaḥ";

Having uttered the word "svarga," [one says] "namaḥ ratnebhyaḥ" as well;
and the fifth is "devarāja," joined with the right ear (dakṣa-śrotra).
"Namah" follows "pātālapadaratnebhyaḥ," and this is another mantra;
[then] "mahākālam" joined with the letter "kṣi" (earth) and endowed with the right ear (the letter "r").

Thereafter, one should extract "namo 'tra" from "marttyaratne. Then, having uttered the word for "nāga," one should say "ratnebhyo namaḥ," [the syllables being] the left foot joined with the earth (kṣi), adorned by the right ear (śravaṇa), and the word for "nāga."

Thus [it is said]. However, since we observe the use of singular-numbered terms such as "gaganam" (the sky) and so forth in the root text, and because we observe the use of singular-numbered expressions such as "gaganaratnāya" (to the jewel of the sky) and so forth in the *Tripurārcanarahasya* composed by the author’s own guru, the venerable Brahmānanda, the usage in the *Ṣoḍhā* must indeed be in the singular number.
[This has been] demonstrated. However, the distinction there is that the inclusion of the *martya-ratna* (the mortal jewel) is seen prior to the *pātāla-ratna* (the netherworld jewel).

64. Regarding "Ānanda... and so forth: as before, according to the sequence stated in the previously shown general *arghya* [rite]. Here, the worship of Ānandabhairavī should also be performed as before, since it is seen thus in the *Tripurārcanarahasya*, the *Tantrasāra*, and other such works.

"May the Blessed Lord, the progenitor of all beings and husband of Bhavānī, grant forgiveness for this which is being performed by us.

Furthermore, according to the authoritative definitions of the *Nirukta*, the mantra results as follows: *aiṃ plūṃ jhrauṃ hrūṃ saḥ amṛte amṛtodbhave amṛteśvari amṛtavarṣiṇi amṛtaṃ srāvaya srāvaya svāhā*. Thus it is stated in the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*.
In the sixth chapter (the fifth section), page 612: [The fifth:
Vāgbhava at the end of "vadavada," and "vāgvādini" followed by Vāgbhava.

Then: KṢAUṂ JŪṂ SAṂ AMṚTE 'MṚTODBHAVE 'MṚTEŚVARI.
Having uttered "Amṛtavarṣiṇī," causing the two [syllables] to flow as nectar,
and having recited [the mantra] ending with the wife of fire (svāhā), one should then extract the other [mantra].
Thus [it is said]. Here, because the sixth vowel is seen in conjunction with the *plūm* [syllable], that too has been demonstrated.

(70–71) He states the fifth mantra beginning with "vāgbhava": namely, *aiṃ vadavada vāgvādini e/ klinne kledini kledaya mahākṣobhaṃ kuru kuru klīṃ hrīṃ mokṣaṃ kuru kuru hasauḥ sthauḥ*. This is the mantra.
It concludes here. In this regard, however, a distinction is observed between the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya* and the *Gandharvatantra*; as it says in the sixth chapter of the *Kaulāvalī*:
"The Vāgbhava [bīja], the pair of *Vada*s, and then *Vāgvādini*."
Having uttered the words *vānmanaḥ*, followed by *klinne* and *kledini*.
One should utter *kledaya* twice, followed by *mahāmokṣaṃ* and *kuru* twice.
One should utter the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*), the seed-syllable of power (*śakti-bīja*), *mokṣaṃ*, and *kuru* twice.
Having pronounced the seed-syllable of the preta (*preta-bīja*), one should then say *hasauḥ namas*.

Thus [it is said]. Here, after the word *vāgvādinī*, the words *vānmanaḥ* are added; there is a double repetition of *kledaya*; at the place where *mahākṣobham* occurs, read *mahāmokṣam*; before *hasauḥ*, insert the seed-syllable of the *preta* (*praṃ*); and at the place where *sthauḥ* occurs, read *namaḥ*.
