Likewise, in the twelfth chapter of the *Gandharvatantro*:
The Vāgbhava [syllable], the pair of "vada," and "Vāgvādini"; then the Vāgbhava again;
the Kāma-bīja, followed by saying "Klinna," then "Kledini" and "Kledaya."
Recite "mahākṣobhaṃ" and the pair "kuru," followed by the seed-syllable of desire; then, having uttered the third [syllable] as "mokṣaṃ," one should thereafter say the pair "kuru."
"Furthermore, O Dear One, the mantra for kindling (*sandīpana-manu*) at the end consists of the seed-syllable of *Śakti*.
[The Sequence of Invocation, etc. Having meditated upon Tripurasundarī in the midst of the *arghya* water, one should invoke her."
Then, having performed three claps of the hands, one should likewise perform the veiling.
Having consecrated [the offering] with the *dhenu-mudrā* as nectar, and having performed the binding of the directions with the *sara-mantra*,
the mantra-practitioner should display the mudrās, beginning with the *sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇī* and the others, while demonstrating the nine mudrās. (73)
[The Procedure for the Worship of the Seed-Syllable Union in the Triangle] One should write the Haṃsa-mantra and the syllable of Kāmakalā within the triangle;
there, one should worship the third seed-syllable of the venerable Guru, ending with "namaḥ. (74)
[The Instruction on Displaying the Conch Mudrā] Having displayed the conch mudrā, one should then perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa.
[The Nature of the Conch Mudrā]
Having placed the thumb between the left thumb and forefinger, one should extend all the fingers.
One should touch the right hand with the left thumb;
this is declared by those skilled in the treatises to be the conch mudrā (śaṅkhamudrā).

Thus, in this regard, there is no repetition of the word *kledaya*; this accords with the root text. Furthermore, specific variations are observed, such as the employment of the Kāma-bīja (*klīṃ*) before *klinne* and after the Vāgbhava-bīja (*aiṃ*).
Therefore, since such differences in the nature of the mantra are seen, one should adopt whichever position is appropriate according to the tradition of one's own guru.

"Avaguṇṭhana" means the *avaguṇṭhana-mudrā*; this is the remainder [of the phrase]. And the *avaguṇṭhana-mudrā* has been demonstrated in the commentary on the fifty-seventh verse of the fifteenth chapter.
73. Regarding "dhenvākhyā" (called the cow-seal): having rendered [the water] nectar by means of the *dhenumudrā*, that is to say, having caused the *arghya* water to attain the state of nectar.
The *dhenumudrā* is also demonstrated in the commentary on verse 67 in the *Pañcadaśaprakāśa*. Regarding "dig" (directions):

having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), namely "phaṭ," [one should perform it] with "snaps of the fingers" (*choṭikābhiḥ*); this is the ellipsis. Regarding "mudrās": [this refers to the following].
The connection is that one should display the nine mudrās—beginning with *sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇā*—which will be described in this very section.
(75–76) Regarding the term *śaṅkha*: it refers to the conch-mudrā, whose characteristics will be described later; this also includes the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa*.
According to the sequence that will be explained: therein, he states the definition of the *śaṅkhamudrā*—“between the left thumb and [forefinger],” etc. Regarding “the whole” (*sakala*):
[this is the *sakalīkaraṇamudrā*].
This *sakalīkaraṇa* consists of the six limbs upon the body of the deity.
[In that regard, the distinctions in the number of recitations:
Having concealed [the object] with the mudrā called Mīna, one should recite seven, eight, or ten times. || 77 ||
One should worship with the thought that they are one's chosen deity, offering arghya, incense, and lamps.
[Tarpaṇa: The practitioner of mantra should indeed satisfy them three times with their respective mantras according to the Kaulika tradition. 78.
One should place Ānandabhairava upon the head and the gurus in the heart;
therein is the Kaulikī Mudrā.
The Kaulikī Mudrā is said to be formed by the joining of the middle finger and the thumb. (79)
The connection is that one should touch all the fingers of the right hand with the left thumb; the remainder is clear. It is stated explicitly in the *Tantrasāra*:
"Having grasped [the fingers] with the left thumb by means of a fist made with the right hand..."
Then, having turned the fist palm-upward, one should extend the thumb.
"The left fingers, likewise joined together and extended, should be touched by the right thumb;
this is to be known as the *śaṅkha-mudrā*.
(77) He describes the *sakalīkaraṇa-mudrā*: "on the limbs of the deity," etc. This is clear. It is also [stated] in the *Tantrasāra* regarding the limbs of the deity.

It has been stated that the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) constitutes "the act of making [the deity] complete" (*sakalīkṛti*). In the thirteenth chapter of the *Gandharvatantra*, it is said: "O Dear One, the act of making [the deity] complete is the petition for the state of being fully established.
Furthermore, this act of making [the deity] complete should be performed with the mantras of the six limbs. This is stated in the twelfth chapter of the *Gandharvatantra*:

"One should perform the sakalīkaraṇa with the six limbs as before. Regarding "mīna": this means by the mudrā called Mīna, that is, the Matsya-mudrā (fish-seal). The Tantrasāra describes the Matsya-mudrā:
"One should place the palm of the left hand upon the back of the right hand."
One should properly move the two thumbs; this is the mudrā in the form of a fish.
Thus. "Sevenfold": the meaning is that one should recite seven times, eight times, or ten times.
(78–79). "By the Kaulikī," meaning by the mudrā known by that name. "Ānandabhairava, the Gurus, in the heart"—(p.
615) [the utility of the libation performed with the Kaulikī-mudrā].
The goddess Bhairavī resides in the thumb, and Caṇḍikā is remembered to be in the middle finger;
therefore, the practitioner of mantra should always diligently offer libations with this [sequence].

The connection is as follows: one should satisfy each of the deities stationed there three times with their respective mantras, such as the Ānandabhairava mantra and others. He describes the Kaulikī mudrā with the words "the middle [finger]," etc., which is clear.
(80) He states the reasoning for the satisfaction performed with the Kaulikī mudrā with the words "the thumb," etc.; the goddess Bhairavī is in the thumb, and in the middle [finger]...

And Caṇḍikā is remembered as being in the middle [channel]. Therefore, because of the connection between Bhairavī and Caṇḍikā, one should satisfy [the deities] with this Kaulikī in order to produce the state of nectar (*amṛtatva*) for the substance used in the libation; such is the connection. He himself will later state that this sequence of libation is in accordance with the *Kulārṇava*. However, in the sixth chapter (*ullāsa*) of the *Kulārṇava*, in the section on libation (*tarpaṇa*), [it speaks of] the Kaulikī...
No mudrā is perceived there; however, O Dear One, the thumb is the god Bhairava and the ring finger is Caṇḍikā. By the union of the ring finger and the thumb... [the rest of the verse follows].
Such is the statement found [in the scriptures]. By this, it is stated that the libation (tarpaṇa) is indeed performed with the *tattvamudrā*.
Also, in the *Svatantratantra* as cited in the *Tantrasāra*: "O Pārvatī, by joining the thumb and ring finger of the left hand..."
One should satisfy the beautiful goddess and the oceans along with their vehicles.

One should offer libations three times into the mouth of the goddess using the root mantra (mūlavidyā). [The water] is indicated by the nails through the joining of the thumb and ring finger, and is drawn up.
One should offer a drop of water from the *śrīpātra* to satisfy the Mistress of the Kula. O Goddess, the thumb is Bhairava and the ring finger is Caṇḍikā, O Beloved;
with the right hand joined together, one should thus satisfy the Mistress of the Kula.

Thus [it is said]. Here too, the abiding of Bhairava on the thumb and Caṇḍikā on the ring finger is taught, as well as the libation (*tarpaṇa*) by means of the *tattvamudrā* consisting of the union of the thumb and the ring finger; thus there is no contradiction with the root-text up to the words "therefore, the practitioner of mantra should always perform the libation with this [mudrā] with great effort."

We consider that the statement prescribing the *tarpaṇa* (libation) performed by forming the *kaulikīmudrā*, which consists of the union of the middle finger and the thumb, belongs to another tantra and teaches a different sequence (*krama*). However, we believe that statements such as "by the union of the ring finger and the thumb" and so forth are those spoken in the *Kulārṇava*. In this way, the absence of contradiction is all the more easily established.
p. 616) [Different mudrās for libation according to the difference in desire:
One should perform libation for the rite of subjugation (*vaśyakarman*) by joining the ring finger and the thumb;
one should perform libation for the rite of malevolent sorcery (*abhicāraka*) with the thumb and the forefinger. (81)
The wise one should perform the libation by joining the little finger and the thumb for the purpose of paralyzing;
this is declared to be the method of libation according to the doctrine of the tantra known as the Kulārṇava.
[In this regard, the sequence accepted by other scriptures is as follows:
"Having taken up pure substance, one should satisfy [the deity] with the *tattvamudrā*. Having carefully grasped the purity between the thumb, the ring finger, and the middle finger... (83)
With the left hand and likewise with the right, the wise one should satisfy the Goddess;
thus is described the act of satisfaction, as approved by the conduct of the *samaya*. 84.
[The Procedure for Sprinkling Oneself and the Ritual Implements:
The most excellent practitioner should pour a supreme drop into the general *arghya* water;
with that, he should sprinkle himself as well as the articles of worship. (85)
[The Fruit of Sprinkling] Thus, by mere sprinkling, everything becomes composed of Brahman.
[The Ritual for Satisfying the Deities of the Goddess’s Limbs]
One should satisfy the deities of the limbs with the water of the general arghya offering.

81–82. Now, he states the rule for the fingers regarding the libation (*tarpaṇa*) according to the distinction of desired aims, beginning with the words "the ring finger" (*anāmā*). This is exactly the same in the *Tantrasāra*.
However, in the seventh chapter (*ullāsa*) of the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*, it says:
"One should perform the libation with the thumb and the middle finger for the rite of subjugation (*vaśyakarma*)."
Then, for the rite of immobilization (stambhana), one should offer libations using the union of the little finger and the thumb;
for the rite of malevolent magic (abhicāraka), one should offer libations using the union of the index finger and the thumb.
Thus, a difference in the sequence is observed.

86. "In this way" means according to the sequence previously stated. This sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) must be performed with the *arghya* water alone; for if it were performed with other water, a fault would ensue. As it is said in the twelfth chapter of the *Gandharvatantra*—[the instruction on the worship of Vaṭuka and others]—p.
617: [text follows].
Now, one should perform the offering of bali to the Vaṭukas and others.
[The prohibition against worshipping other deities without first giving bali to the Kṣetrapālas and others:
How can one worship within sacred precincts (kṣetra) without having given [bali] to the Lords of the Fields (kṣetranātha)? || 87 ||
As long as one has not offered [the oblation] to Vaṭuka, how can there be worship?
And without having given [the offering] to Gaṇeśa and the Yoginīs, how can one perform worship? (88)
One should sprinkle oneself with that [liquid], or with the root-mantra, or with the Vāruṇa mantra;
likewise, having sprinkled the articles of worship three times,
everything thus sprinkled with the nectars (amṛtas) becomes composed of Brahman.
"Whatever other substance is given, such as ornaments and the like, one should perform their sprinkling with the seed-syllable of Varuṇa alone. Thus it is said.
Likewise—
"However, that which is mixed with other substances from elsewhere, or [mixed] with things other than those contained in the *arghya* vessel,
the beloved Goddess does not accept it, even if it is offered according to the rules by hundreds of experts.
Thus, in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*, as held in the *Haratattvadīdhiti*.
That which is to be offered should be presented using only the water contained within the arghya vessel;
that which is discarded with other waters is that which has been set aside from what resides in the arghya vessel.

The Goddess does not indeed accept that offering, even if it is given by hundreds of learned ritualists, [if it is considered] "ordinary water for the guest-offering" (*sāmānyārghya*), according to those who know the tradition; this is the *Haratattvadīdhiti*. Furthermore, because the phrase "with the water of the ordinary guest-offering" (*sāmānyārghyasya toyena*) in the root text connects with both [parts], both sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and the satiation of the deities of the limbs (*aṅgadevatātarpaṇa*) are thereby obtained.

This is beyond dispute. However, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) must be performed with the palm facing upwards, according to the statement cited in the *Ekādaśī-tattva*: "Sprinkling is declared to be done with the hand turned upwards. Regarding the word "general" (*sāmānya*): here, by the phrase "one should satisfy," the limb-deities (*aṅgadevatā*) [are indicated].

It should be understood that the worship of those deities who are to be described hereafter must also be performed right here. For this very reason, the authors of the *Tantrasāra* stated that the worship of the auxiliary deities (*aṅgadevatā*) of the goddess Sundarī occurs immediately after the installation of the arghya vessel. Regarding the worship of the retinue, they said: "Having received the command of the Great Goddess immediately after the installation of the arghya vessel, one should then worship the members of the retinue."
Because it will be stated in the root text immediately after the instruction on *tarpaṇa* (p.
618): [The scriptural teaching on the fault of not offering the *bali*:
"If one should worship Tripurā without performing the *bali* offering..."
Indeed, worship is said to be fruitless, and obstacles arise at every step. (89)
[Conclusion] Having understood this, one should diligently perform the offering of the *bali*.
[Herein is the authoritative support from the *Pramāṇika-tantra*]
"In the Śaktiyāmala Tantra, however, it is proclaimed as 'by Śiva'. (90)
[The prohibition against worshiping Sundarī without first performing the worship of Vaṭuka:
As long as one has not offered [oblations] to Vaṭuka, so long one must not [worship] Kuleśvarī.
If [the offering] is given to Sundarī first, the worship shall indeed be fruitless. (91)
[Consensus with another scripture here:
But in the Bṛhacchrīkramatantra, it is proclaimed as "by Śiva. (92)
[The sequence for the worship of Vaṭuka and others; therein, first, the construction of the maṇḍala:

The mantra-practitioner should fashion a maṇḍala consisting of a triangle joined with a circle, either from the northeast to the northwest corner in the cardinal directions, or starting from the east. (93)
Having prepared the ground with the Bhūpura (the outer square), the practitioner, kneeling on the ground,
should draw a triangle, a hexagon, and a square to his left.

93–94. Now, he describes the mandala for the worship of Vaṭuka and the others, beginning with the words "from Īśāna": "From Īśāna up to the Vāyu corner," or "in the four directions starting from the East"—the phrase "of the Śrīcakra" is to be understood as the remainder; the meaning is that one should arrange four mandalas according to the sequence to be described. This is stated explicitly in the fifth chapter of the Jñānārṇava:
O beloved goddess, there is likewise a quartet of mandalas in the northeast, the southeast, the southwest, and the northwest, in due order.
"O Goddess, one should draw a triangle and a void (vyoma) all around the Śrīcakra.
[The mantra for the worship of the mandala: One should utter the Vāgbhava-bīja, the Mahāmāyā, the Kavaca, and the word 'to the mandala'."
This mantra is declared to end with the heart [seed-syllable]; the wise one should worship [the deity] within the maṇḍala.
[The Instruction on the Worship of Vaṭuka:
One should always worship Vaṭuka at the beginning, having meditated upon him with water for the feet and other offerings. 96.
[The Meditation on Vaṭuka: His staff-like arms are exceedingly fierce, holding a vessel of nectar, a mass of matted hair, and a skull, and are intensely wrathful against the most violent ones.
I praise Vaṭukanātha, the blue youth, whose cheeks are adorned with a pair of glorious earrings, and who wears a necklace of great pearls. 97.
[The Mantra for the Vaṭuka-bali:
Having meditated thus, the practitioner of mantra should worship, preceded by the seed-syllable *vāṃ*. [The mantra is:
*ehyehi devīputra*, followed by *vaṭuka* and then *nātha*. (98)
At the end of *kapilā*, at the end of *jaṭābhārabhāsura*, after *trinetrataḥ*,
and at the very end of *sarva*, [recite] *jvālāmukhe* and *vighnān nāśaya nāśaya*.

Thus [it is said]. He describes the nature of the mandala with the words beginning "tri-koṇam" (the triangle) and so forth: first a triangle, outside that a circle, and outside that a city-gate (bhūpura);
such is the sequence of the mandala. He describes the fifth mandala with the words "tri-koṇam":
one should construct a triangle on one's own left side, outside that a hexagon, and outside that a square; this is the connection [of the parts].

95. He states the mantra for the worship of the mandala with the words beginning with "vāgbhavam": *vāgbhava* is *aiṃ*, *mahāmāyā* is *hrīṃ*, and *kavaca* is *huṃ*. Ending with the heart [seed-syllable] and ending with *namaḥ*, it results thus: *aiṃ hrīṃ huṃ maṇḍalāya namaḥ*; this is the mantra for the worship of the mandala.

98–100 | Immediately following the meditations (*dhyāna*), he describes the worship of Vaṭuka with the words "vām" and so forth. Thus, the mantra for worship is: *vāṃ vaṭukāya namaḥ*. This is stated in the *Tantrasāra* (p. 620):
"Accept the offering (*bali*) together with all the ritual services (*upacāra*); [the word] 'pada' is used twice."
One should offer the oblation (bali) to Vaṭuka with the mantra ending in the wife of Vahni (the fire-god).

[The Ritual Procedure for the Vaṭuka Offering: A vessel filled with half water and half cooked rice, combined with jewels, flowers, and other offerings, [is offered] by joining the index finger and thumb, or alternatively, from the little finger and thumb. (101)
Or the practitioner should offer the bali-oblation with the left ring finger and thumb.
[This is the instruction for the worship of the Yoginīs.
Then, having meditated upon the Yoginī, one should worship her in sequence, beginning with the right hand and so forth. 102.

[The Meditation on the Yoginīs]: The Yoginīs, capable of assuming any form at will, possessing all virtuous qualities, with the luster of molten gold, intoxicated, their necks adorned with garlands of human skulls, and wearing red garments as upper cloths;
"The mantra for Vaṭuka and the others, ending with *ne* and concluding with *namaḥ*, is thus declared.

He states the mantra for the offering (*bali*) with the words beginning "Come, come" (*ehyehi*) and ending with "one should present the offering" (*baliṃ haret*). Accordingly: "Come, come, O Son of the Goddess, Vaṭukanātha, radiant with the mass of your tawny matted locks, three-eyed, flame-mouthed! Destroy, destroy all obstacles! [Accept] this offering together with all ritual services..."
The mantra for the offering to Baṭuka concludes as: *baliṃ hṛhṇa gṛhṇa svāhā*. The meaning is that one should offer the oblation (*bali*) with this mantra.
However, in the sixth chapter of the *Kaulāvalī-nirṇaya*, it is stated: "Poison (*viṣa*), Māyā, and Ramā, followed by Devīputra Vaṭukanātha... [The mantra is thus formed].
Having uttered "O Piṅgala,
radiant with matted locks," and "O three-eyed one, accept this offering (bali) and worship," one should then pronounce the name of the great-souled Vaṭuka, ending with the "wife of fire" (svāhā).
"Having offered this oblation (bali), one should then contemplate the Yoginīs.
By this, the variation in the bali-mantras for those respective locations is indicated.
(101-102) He describes the ritual service and the sequence of offering for the Vaṭuka-bali with the words beginning "ardha," etc.; this is clear.

103. He describes the meditation on the Yoginīs with the words "the Yoginīs. They have the luster of molten gold—that is, they are the color of molten gold, which is red. (p. 621) Holding a trident, a noose, a skull-cup, and also a goad, they are smiling and very gracious, bestowing the desired fruit upon their devotees and practitioners; they are beautifully adorned. 103.
[The mantra for the worship of the Yoginī:
Having uttered the seed-syllable *yāṃ*, one should then worship the Yoginī. || 104 ||
[The Yoginī-bali:

Whether above the cosmic egg, or in heaven, in the expanse of the sky, on the surface of the earth, in the partless realm, or in the netherworld; whether in a forest, or in water and wind—wherever they may be situated.

May the goddesses, who have set foot upon the sacred fields, pīṭhas, upapīṭhas, and so forth, and who are ever pleased by incense, lamps, and other offerings—those worshipped by the lords of heroes—protect us always through the rite of the auspicious bali. 105.
At the end of this, the seed-syllable of Vāyu joined with the *mukhavṛtta* [the letter 'i'], then the word for the Yoginīs, the wife of Fire (Svāhā), and the word "Sarvayoginī. (106)
One should perform the offering of the bali-oblation at the end of the armor-mantra (kavaca), the weapon-mantra (astra), and the fire-born wife-mantra (agnijāyā).
[In this regard, there is a rule for the fingers:
it may be done with the right thumb and ring finger, or else with the little finger and the thumb. 107.

*Kapāla* means a human skull-bone; *śṛṇi* means a goad; *aṅkuśa* means a hook. "Holding" (*vidhṛtāḥ*) means bearing [these]. By the mention of "trident" (*śūla*), "noose" (*pāśa*), and so forth, their four-armed nature is also understood by implication. "Being given" (*dīyamānāḥ*) means giving. 104. He states the mantra for the worship of the Yoginīs with the words "yām" etc. Here, although the word *yoginīm* is in the singular, [it refers to] the Yoginīs who can take any form at will (*kāmarūpāḥ*).
Because of the observation of the plural number,

he states the mantra for the worship of the Yoginīs with the words "yām" and so forth. Here, although the singular form "yoginīm" is used, because of the observation of the plural form "yoginyaḥ kāmarūpāḥ," [the plural is intended].
At the end of this, O Maheśānī, one should write the seed-syllable of the Yoginī, followed by "bhyaḥ svāhā"; at the end of all the syllables, one should inscribe the word "yoginī."

Furthermore, based on the observation of the statement in the fifth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*, the formula is simply: "Obeisance to the Yoginīs" (*yoginībhyo namaḥ*). By this, the worship of the Yoginīs is taught through a single, simultaneous utterance of the sentence.
(105–107) He states the mantra for the bali-offering to the Yoginīs with the words beginning "Above" (*ūrdhvam*), etc.; this is clear. [This concludes] up to this point.
[The Worship of the Field Protector (Kṣetrapāla): Having uttered the seed-syllable *kṣāṃ* and meditated upon it, one should worship [the deity] in the field. || 108 ||
[The Meditation on the Field Protector: His hands always uplifted, holding a shimmering skull-cup, a well-fashioned sword, a trident, and a staff, and adorned with a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*).
I take refuge with devotion in the serene Lord of Śrīkṣetra, who resembles a mass of heaped blue collyrium. 109.
[Instruction on the Offering of the Sacrificial Feast to the Field Protector:
Having meditated thus and performed worship, one should carry out the offering of the sacrificial feast (balidāna). || 110 ||
[The sequence for the offering of the bali-oblation:
One should visualize the syllable *kṣa* conjoined with the six long vowels, according to its respective locations and sounds. (111)
Having uttered "gṛhṇa gṛhṇa" followed by the wife of Vahni (svāhā), one should offer the bali-oblation to the station of the Kṣetrapāla, accompanied by incense, lamps, and other offerings.
[Regarding the rule for the fingers there:
Having first formed a left fist, one should then extend the index finger straight;
or, the offering to Kṣetrapāla is considered to be made with the thumb and index finger. 113.

Thus: having first uttered the sequence beginning with "ūrdhvam" and ending with "vīrendravandyāḥ," at its conclusion one should utter the seed-syllable of Vāyu, namely *yam*, joined with the second vowel (*i*) according to the "mouth-circle" (mukhavṛtta) convention; by this, *yām* is obtained.
And so, the mantra for the offering to the Yoginīs is: *ūrdhvam* etc., followed by *yāṃ yoginībhyaḥ svāhā sarvayoginī huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
It concludes [the section]. Regarding the rule for the fingers in the aforementioned offering of *bali*, he says "dakṣa" and so forth; this is clear.
(108) Now, he describes the worship of Kṣetrapāla with the verse beginning "kṣām" and so forth. Accordingly, the mantra for worship is: "Kṣāṃ, obeisance to Kṣetrapāla."
110–113 | Having taught meditation (*dhyāna*), he describes the offering of oblations (*balidāna*) with the words beginning with "evam" (thus). Regarding the word "six":

[The instruction on the worship of Gaṇeśa] || 114 || "The wise one, having meditated upon Gaṇeśa, should worship him with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings. (p. 623) [Instruction on the worship of Gaṇeśa] || 114 ||
[The meditation on Gaṇeśa:
With a noose, a goad, a vessel of nectar, and a trident in his hands,
elephant-faced, with a dark-blue body adorned with various ornaments.
I perpetually bow down to the illustrious Gajānana, who is a constant festival and the cause of the destruction of all obstacles. || 115 ||
[The Procedure for the Worship of Gaṇeśa] Having uttered the seed-syllable *gaṃ*, the wise one should worship Gaṇeśa.
[The Mantra for the Gaṇeśa Offering]
Having uttered the three syllables beginning with *gaṃ*, one should extract [the mantra] joined with the long vowel.
Having uttered "O Gaṇapati," he should not say "the end" (anta), but rather the words "O Bestower of Boons" (varada);
then, having written "all people" (sarvajana), he should say "bring [it] to me" (me vā ānaya). || 117 ||

The syllable *kṣa* joined with the six long vowels beginning with *ā* and ending with *visarga*—namely, *kṣāṃ kṣīṃ kṣūṃ kṣaiṃ kṣauṃ kṣaḥ*—[followed by] "O Kṣetrapāla of this place, accept, accept the *bali* offering together with incense, lamps, and so forth, svāhā! is the mantra for the *kṣetrapāla-bali*. Regarding that, he states the sequence for offering the *bali*: "the left fist," etc., as found in the fifth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*.
"First, having formed the left fist, make the index finger straight;

by this mudrā, O Goddess, the offering to the Kṣetrapāla shall be accomplished. Thus it was said. (114) Now, he instructs on the worship of Gaṇeśa: "One should worship," etc. Having meditated [upon him], one should worship.
The phrase "in the sequence to be described" is the remainder [of the sentence].

(116–118) Regarding the word *gam*: the meaning is that one should worship with the mantra "Gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇeśa. He states the *bali* mantra: "the syllable *gaṃ*"—the meaning is that one should utter three instances of the syllable *gaṃ* joined with the long vowel, that is, joined with the second, fourth, and sixth vowels. Here...
Having uttered "baliṃ gṛhṇayugam" (accept the offering, twice), one should pronounce the wife of Vahni (svāhā).
With this mantra, the practitioner of mantra should offer the oblation to Gaṇeśa. (118)
Having contracted the fingers, the wise one should form them like a staff;
this is proclaimed as the mudrā called Gajatuṇḍā (Elephant-Trunk), belonging to Gaṇeśa.

Although the qualification "joined with a long [vowel]" (*dīrghayuktam*) is not explicitly stated, since there is no authority for abandoning what is first obtained, the inclusion of the second, fourth, and sixth vowels follows by implication. By this, *gāṃ*, *gīṃ*, and *gūṃ* are obtained. This is clearly stated in the fifth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*:
"Having written the triad *gāṃ*, *gīṃ*, *gūṃ*, followed by *gaṇapatiṃ* ending with *nam*, [one should proceed].

Thus, the mantra for the offering to Gaṇeśa results as follows: *gāṃ gīṃ gūṃ gaṇapataye varavarada sarvajanaṃ me vaśamānaya baliṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa svāhā*. However, in the fifth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*:
Having written the triad *gāṃ*, *gīṃ*, and *gūṃ*, one should then write *gaṇapatim* ending with *ne*.
After *vara*, after *varada*, and after *sarva*, one should write *janam*.
Having uttered *me vasaṃ cānaya*, one should write *sarvopapadam*.

Having uttered "cārānte sahitaṃ" and "baliṃ gṛhṇa" as two steps [of the mantra], the mantra joined with the wife of fire (svāhā) should carry the *bali* offering for Gaṇapati. By this, in the aforementioned mantra, the specific qualification for the *bali* is stated as "accompanied by all ritual services (*sarvopacārasahitam*)" following the word "vaśamānaya. This is the distinction.
It is seen.

119. Now, he describes the *gajatuṇḍā* (elephant-trunk) mudrā prescribed for the offering of the *bali* to Gaṇeśa—beginning with the words "having contracted": the meaning is that one should contract the fingers of the left hand.
"Like a staff" means one should make the middle finger like a staff. This very [mudrā]...

"Gaṇeśapriyā" means the *gajatuṇḍa-mudrā*. Thus, it is stated in the fifth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*, after describing the *kṣetrapāla-bali-mudrā* with the words "First, having formed the left fist," [it continues]:
"Likewise, make the middle finger of the fist straight like a staff."
The elephant-trunk great mudrā shall be the offering for Gaṇeśa.
By this, it is clearly stated that forming a fist with the left hand and extending only the middle finger constitutes the *gajatuṇḍa-mudrā*.
(p. 625) [Maṇḍala Worship]
The mantra-practitioner should worship his own left mandala together with its support;
at the end of "vyāpaka," he should say "maṇḍalāya," and at the end of "ai," the word "namaḥ. (120)
[The Offering to All Beings (Sarvabhūtabali):
Having placed the offering right there, the wise practitioner should consecrate it three times with the root mantra and worship all beings with incense, lamps, and other offerings. 121.
[The Bali-mantra: First the syllable *Tāra* (Oṃ), then the goddess Bhuvaneśvarī, followed by the word *sarvavighna* (all obstacles);
then from the heart (*hṛd*), *bhyaḥ* (to), *sarvabhūtebhyaḥ* (all beings), the seed-syllable of sound (*Śabda-bīja*: Phaṭ), and the two *Ṭha*s. (122)
Having uttered this *kalārṇa* at the end of the *tritārā*, one should offer the *bali*;
with the *tattvasaṃjñā* mudrā formed by the thumb and ring finger. (123) [Balimudrā]
[Regarding the other offerings for the deities whose powers have been described: the practitioner of mantra should offer five bali-offerings either in one place or within the pervasive maṇḍala;
standing on the left side, he shall become the remover of all obstacles. 124.

120. Having thus instructed the worship and the *bali* offering for Vaṭuka and the others in the four mandalas in sequence, he now describes the worship of the mandala situated to the left of oneself as previously mentioned: *ai/* At the end of *parā*, the connection is with the word *namaḥ* [for] the pervasive mandala (*vyāpakamaṇḍala*). Thus, *ai/ hrīṃ vyāpakamaṇḍalāya namaḥ* is the mantra for the worship of the mandala.
121. Regarding "the bali": it means on that very same mandala previously described as having three, six, and four corners. "One should worship" means by means of the mantra "Obeisance to all beings.
112–123. He states the bali-mantra with the words beginning with "tāram": *tāra* is the *praṇava* (Oṃ), and *bhuvaneśānī* is *hrīṃ*. Thus, [the mantra is] Oṃ Hrīṃ.

"ai svāhā! [Salutation] to all beings who remove all obstacles"—this is the mantra for the offering to all beings (*sarvabhūtabali*). Regarding the phrase "with the thumb": the connection is that one should present the offering to all beings with the *tattvamudrā*, which consists of the joining of the thumb and the ring finger.
(Verse 124) Previously, when four mandalas were prepared in the four directions of the *śrīcakra*, the four offerings were made on one's own left side.
It has been stated that one should offer a single *bali* in the mandala. Regarding this, he states another ritual procedure: "Or else in one place.
[Again, another ritual procedure: Or rather, one should perform a single *bali* for all beings.
[Again, the six-limbed worship:
Then one should perform the six-limbed [worship] by the very same path previously described. || 125 ||
[The visualization of the form in the heart:

Having uttered the seed-syllable *māyā* (hrīṃ), followed by the seed-syllable of desire (klīṃ), and having projected the essence of the offering (*bali*) into the heart, one should visualize the form. || 126 ||
Regarding the two mudrās prescribed for meditation:
one should meditate while forming the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā, or by joining the hands in the *kacchapa* (tortoise) gesture.
Having meditated in such a way, the practitioner's mind does not become attached to anything else. 127.

The meaning is that, without performing the fourfold [rite], one should simply perform the fivefold bali offering—beginning with Vaṭuka and ending with all the bhūtas—within a pervasive maṇḍala drawn on one's own left side. This is stated explicitly in the fifth chapter of the Jñānārṇava:
"Alternatively, one should draw a single maṇḍala on the left side."
In that very place, one should perform the offering of the bali-oblation for the sake of accomplishing all aims.
Thus [it is said]. He states the fruit of the *bali* prescribed for the left side with the verse beginning "vāma" (125).

Regarding that, he also states another alternative with "athavā" (or else): in this alternative, if one is unable [to perform the full ritual], one may obtain the fruit of the *bali* by means of the *sarvabhūtabali* alone, without performing the fivefold *bali* as previously described.

127. Now, he describes the two mudrās prescribed for the meditation on Tripurā, as well as the praise of the meditation performed with those two previously explained mudrās, beginning with the words "trikhaṇḍā": Regarding that, the *Tantrasāra* describes the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā:
"Having crossed the hands so that the thumbs touch, one should make them equal."
Having placed the two index fingers inside the ring fingers, they should be curved in shape.
O Maheśvarī, one should employ the little finger in its own place;
this is declared to be the "three-part" (trikhaṇḍā) [mudrā] for the practice of meditating upon Tripurā.

Thus; the meaning is that one should meditate upon Tripurā with this mudrā. He states another ritual procedure: "or having bound," which means "or the tortoise-mudrā (kūrmamudrā). He gives the definition of the tortoise-mudrā in the Tantrasāra:
"The little finger of the right hand [should be placed] upon the index finger of the left hand..."
Likewise, one should place the left thumb upon the right index finger.

[The Yoga of Meditation] Having established oneself in the yoga of meditation, by means of the practice of inhalation (*pūraka*), one should join the mind at the root; having constricted the vital breaths from below, [one should hold them]. (128)
One should meditate upon Śivā in the form of a flickering flame at the *mūlādhāra*, having united her with the supreme bliss situated within the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). (129)
Having brought about the state of identity between those two and having rested again and again, one should bring her—
who has become merged in the nectar of the bliss of Śiva, who is of the nature of consciousness, and whose form is pure awareness—
into the station of one's own self and contemplate her as the embodiment of consciousness. (130)
One should raise the right thumb and join the middle and other fingers of the left hand to the back of the right hand.
One should perform [the offering] with the left hand using the *pitṛtīrtha*, namely the middle and ring fingers,
and those two fingers should be turned downwards on the right hand.
One should make the right hand equal to the back of a tortoise on all sides;
this is declared to be the *kūrmamudrā* for the practice of meditating upon the deity.

Thus it is said. Likewise, in the eleventh chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*, it says "yathā" (as follows): the meaning is that for the practitioner who meditates with one of the aforementioned mudrās, the mind does not attach itself elsewhere, but becomes concentrated (*samāhita*) solely upon the object of meditation.
[Verse 128] Regarding "in the root": the meaning is having joined the mind to the *mūlādhāra*. The *Tantrasāra* expresses this very same point:
In the section on the method of yoga:

"At the outset, one should join the mind to the *svādhiṣṭhāna* by means of the practice of inhalation (*pūraka*). Having contracted that *śakti* located between the anus and the genitals, one should awaken it."
Having contracted that *śakti* between the anus and the genitals, and having meditated upon it as possessing incomparable subtlety, one should cause it to expand—this is its explanation.

(Verse 129) Regarding "the *mūlādhāra*": within the four-petaled lotus of the *mūlādhāra*, one should [visualize] the auspicious *Kuṇḍalinī*, whose characteristics have been defined by the etymological analysis (*nirukta*).

The meaning is "one should remember. Regarding "having joined": the meaning is that one has joined that Kuṇḍalinī with the Supreme Śiva, whose nature is supreme bliss, who has entered within the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
130. Regarding "equilibrium" (sāmarasya): and equilibrium is—

The bliss arising from the union of female and male is called *sāmarasya* (equilibrium); this is the definition as previously stated. The meaning is: having accomplished that aforementioned equilibrium between those two, namely Kuṇḍalinī and Paramaśiva.
One should contemplate a great jeweled lion-throne in the center of the pericarp.
That [maṇḍala] of the sixteen accomplishments has sixteen corners and possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns. || 131 ||
In the center of that, the practitioner of mantra should contemplate the most beautiful King of Wheels (cakrarāja);
then, in the middle of the wheel, he should visualize the trident (śakti) as a triangle.
In the center of that, one should contemplate the effulgence, brilliantly radiant and stainless,
resembling the fire of universal dissolution, auspicious, and consisting of all the gods.
It is eternally composed of the splendor of Brahman, consisting of the ascetic power of sages and perfected beings;
it consists of the fruit of all vows and is the very essence of the fruit of all sacrifices.
It consists of all powers and is, moreover, the essence of all sciences;
it has the nature of being the self of all and is likewise composed of all bliss.
Furthermore, one should contemplate the Great Goddess as consisting of all-knowledge and being the self of all beings; for she is indeed the transformation of that radiant energy.
[The Meditation on the Goddess:

Then, one should meditate upon the goddess who resembles a lotus, reddish like the rays of the rising sun, glowing like the hibiscus flower, and possessing the luster of the pomegranate blossom. (137)
"Śiveti" means [the goddess] who has become tremulous with the nectar of bliss flowing from the enjoyment of Paramaśiva; "the place of the self" (ātmasthānam) means the heart. 131.
"One should contemplate" refers to [contemplating her] in the center of the pericarp of the unstruck lotus (anāhatapadma)—this is the ellipsis. The remainder is clear. 132–136.
In the middle of that, in the central region of the aforementioned jewel-throne, is the King of Wheels, the Śrīcakra; in the middle of that...

The realized meaning is that one should contemplate the Śakti in the form of a triangle, and within that, the Radiance (tejas) whose form will be described; and then the Great Goddess Śrīmat Tripurasundarī, who is the transformation of that radiance, according to the sequence of meditation to be described.
(137) Now, intending to state two meditations upon Śrīmat Tripurasundarī, he first describes the first meditation: "Then..."
From the words "lotus-like" (*padmanibhām*) up to "delighted by supreme bliss" (*paramānandananditām*), the meaning is clear and thus is not further explained. (p.
629) She shines with the luster of a ruby, resembling saffron water, and is adorned with a network of tinkling bells from the rubies in her shimmering crown. || 138 ||
Her sprout-like curls were curved and resembled a swarm of black bees; her lotus-face was a circle that appeared as fresh and rosy as the rising sun.
The Supreme Goddess, whose forehead is adorned with a soft fillet curved like the crescent moon, and whose beautiful eyebrows are shaped like the bow of Pinākin.
Her eyes were playfully swinging with waves of bliss and joy,
and her golden earrings shone with a mass of flickering rays.
Her expansive cheeks were like the orb of the moon, surpassing the lunar disc;
her nose was as clearly defined as the measuring line for the architectural constructions of Viśvakarman and others.
Her lips were as red as copper, coral, and the bimba fruit; she was like nectar itself, having surpassed the ocean of the essence of sweetness with the sweetness of her smile. || 143 ||
She possesses two rows of teeth that shine like the seeds of the *bījapura* fruit;
her tongue gleams like the jewels of a jeweled island, and she speaks with pure speech.
The Great Goddess, whose conch-like neck was beautified by the region of her chin endowed with incomparable qualities, possessed arms as graceful as lotus stalks. 145.
Her lotus-like hands are as delicate as the petals of a red lotus,
and the radiance from the nails of her lotus-hands illuminates the expanse of the sky.
Her lofty breasts were adorned with strings of pearl necklaces,
and her waist was beautifully graced by the three folds of skin that encircle it.
Adorned with a navel shaped like an eddy in the river of loveliness, she possessed hips graced by a girdle fashioned from priceless gems. (148)
Her hips, like two rounded globes, were guided by the excellent goad of the line of hair;
her thighs, as delicate as the graceful pillars of a plantain tree, were the mistress of her form. 149.
Adorned with a pair of shanks resembling the plantain tree of loveliness, her two feet with concealed ankles and foreparts surpassed the beauty of tortoises. || 150 ||
Her lotus feet were rubbed by the crest-jewels on the heads of Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
she was adorned with moon-like nails upon her slender, long fingers.
She who causes the continuity of the sun’s rays to fade with her brilliance,
and who possesses a hue like that of the pomegranate flower, surpassing the redness of vermilion and the Sindhu river.
She is clothed in red garments, holding a noose and a goad raised in her hands;
she is seated upon a red lotus and adorned with red ornaments.
She has four arms and three eyes, holds five arrows and a bow,
and her mouth is filled with betel-leaf mixed with camphor.
Her body is ruddy with the intense saffron of great musk;
she is richly endowed with all the attire of the erotic sentiment and adorned with every ornament. (155)
She who generates delight for the world, who causes the world to be enamored, who effects the attraction of the world, and whose form is the cause of the world. || 156 ||
The Goddess who consists of all mantras, beautiful with all auspiciousness, eternally composed of all prosperity, and delighted by supreme bliss. (157)
[The intermediate dhyāna:
Alternatively, one may meditate on the Goddess of auspicious marks in another manner—as having the brilliance of the hibiscus flower and as red as the pomegranate blossom. (158)
Resplendent with a stream of vermilion, resembling the rays of the rising sun, shining like molten gold, and possessing the luster of rubies; 159.
Adorned with an excellent crown and ornaments set with various precious gems, her sprout-like curly locks of hair rest upon the crescent moon on her head. || 160 ||
Her hair was as dark as a yak-tail, curly and stainless,
and her braid was encircled by garlands of jasmine and *mālatī* flowers.
[She is adorned] with hanging clusters of silk cloth joined with various excellent jewels, and a soft fillet upon her forehead curved like the crescent moon of autumn. (162)
In the midst of her hair, she possesses great radiance with waves of vermilion,
and is brilliant with a tilaka made of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron.
She possessed beautiful eyebrows resembling the bow of Kāma, lotus-like eyes,
and was endowed with three eyes whose gaze was radiant with bliss and joy.
Her nose is clearly defined by a thread resembling the full autumnal moon,
and it is adorned at its tip with a great pearl from a king of elephants.
158–193 | Now he describes the intermediate meditative absorption (*dhyānāntara*) with the passage beginning with "Alternatively" and ending with "the supreme practitioner. (p.
632) "She whose cheeks are beautifully rounded has surpassed the orb of nectar;
she is adorned with a facial orb resembling the shimmering full moon. (166)
Her face, with a slight smile, had conquered the ocean of sweetness;
it was adorned with the finest jewel-leaf ornaments shimmering above her ears. || 167 ||
Adorned with ear-ornaments fashioned from jewels of bliss, she shone with golden earrings resplendent with clusters of shimmering gems. || 168 ||
With the luster of her ear-ornaments, she was like a cluster of blossoms upon the surface of her cheeks;
with lips as red as the bandhūka flower, vermilion, and the bimba fruit, she was like nectar itself.
Her two rows of teeth shone like the seeds of a citron fruit,
and her chin was resplendent, endowed with incomparable qualities.
Adorned with neck-ornaments set with various jewels,
her neck was further embellished by clusters of pearls, gems, and coral.
She possesses four creeper-like arms resembling coral vines,
and her lotus-like hands are as delicate and lovely as saffron-red blossoms.
The expanse of the sky was overspread by the moonlight of the nails on her lotus-like hands,
and she was adorned with excellent armlets set with clusters of precious gems.
It was adorned with hanging silk cords inlaid with the nine precious gems,
and it shone at the wrist with the ivory of the lord of serpents and a conch shell.
Adorned with bracelets fashioned from priceless jewels,
she illuminated the quarters of the sky with a gem-studded ring.
She holds in her left hand the noose composed of the elements of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*;
she bears a sugarcane bow that is strung with a row of bees. (176)
In his right hand, he holds a goad adorned with the eight elements;
[he also holds] those produced from the red lotus, the blue lotus, the white water-lily, the jasmine, and the mango sprout.
Beneath that, one should meditate on Tripuresvarī, who bears five arrows upon her shoulders and illuminates the expanse of the sky with the tips of her weapons.
Her breasts were resplendent with a multitude of necklaces of pearls,
and from the region of her back hung clusters of jeweled filigree ornaments.
She possessed rounded, firm, high, and full breasts; her beautiful waist was slender and bent down by the weight of her heavy bosom.
From the lotus of her navel, a creeper-like line of body hair extends toward her breasts;
her body is anointed with fragrant sandalwood and musk. || 181 ||
Adorned with golden jars filled to the brim,
she was graced by a waist beautified with three most charming folds.
Her circular hips were adorned with jingling girdles, and she was draped in a red silk cloth fashioned with golden threads. || 183 ||
Adorned with a fine border of cloth and decorated with excellent, precious gems,
she was endowed with a beautiful girdle fashioned from many jewels.
Her pair of thighs were as delicate as the trunk of a lordly elephant,
and she was endowed with a pair of shanks as beautiful as the graceful pillars of a plantain tree.
Adorned with the splendor of tinkling anklets upon her lotus-feet, which are as red as the morning sun, and her lotus-feet further embellished with pearls, gems, and corals; (186)
She was made manifest by the toes of her feet, which resembled coral sprouts,
and she surpassed the radiance of the moon with the light streaming from the nails of her toes.
She was draped with very tender, radiant garlands upon her lotus-like feet,
while the tips of her garment were illuminated by the crest-jewels of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Mounted upon the body of Kāmarāja, seated upon the lion-throne of Śiva, she is enriched with the splendor of all erotic grace and adorned with every ornament. || 189 ||
Her face was filled with betel-leaf mixed with camphor and other spices, and she captivated the continuous stream of beauty of a thousand autumn moons. (190)

She who had conquered the ocean of sweetness with the pleasantness of her face and her words, and who was beautiful with the casting of glances from her shimmering, dark, and tremulous eyes that kissed her ears. 191.
To the Goddess who generates delight for the world, who is the form of the cause of the universe, who consists of all mantras, and who brings joy to the world. || 192 ||

The best of practitioners should meditate upon her as eternal and consisting of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), resplendent with white umbrellas adorned with various excellent jewels, and surrounded by a circle of millions upon millions of incense burners and lamps. (193)
[The Praise of the Contemplation of the Transformation: One should always contemplate oneself as the Goddess thus transformed.
Then one shall always be possessed by her, and in that manner, one shall always become her very self. 194.
Likewise, being of such a disposition for dramatic representation, of such conduct, and of such purity, one should always become a master of desire and enjoy sensual pleasures. (195)
For if one becomes single-minded through the practice of meditation in this way, then, having attained identity with that, one shall always be liberated while living. (196)
Through constant meditation, he becomes forever free from conceptual construction and always unattached;
liberated from old age and death, he possesses great enjoyments and experiences supreme bliss.
With his command unimpeded everywhere, he may wander through the three worlds;
for him there is neither sin nor merit—he becomes Śiva himself, the manifest God. 198.
Thus perfected through firm practice, one should assume various forms;
through the distinction between gross and subtle, it becomes both visible and invisible. (199)
Form consists of the five elements, even that of the sun and the moon;
likewise, it is the form of Brahmā and the others, as well as of the gods, gandharvas, and rākṣasas. (200)
For indeed, among birds and serpents, [powers] arise by mere will;
or rather, the supernatural accomplishments (siddhis) in the three worlds perish by mere thought alone.
He perceives all beings, his movement being unimpeded everywhere;
likewise, he possesses the powers of killing, expulsion, paralyzing, and bewildering.
Merely by seeing him, the practitioner accomplishes everything through conceptualization alone;
he should offer an oblation to him as if the entire three worlds were his servant. (203)
203 | By performing the offering (*bali*) and worship (*pūjā*), one shall always become equal to Śiva— as the creator, the destroyer, and likewise the protector.
[The invocation into the heart and other parts of the Goddess whose nature has been thus defined.]
In this manner, one should then invoke her from the lotus of the heart by means of the mudrā.
[The Three-Part Mudrā: Having rotated the two hands, one should make the two thumbs equal;
then, one should hold the pair beginning with the little fingers by means of the two index fingers. (205)
Having placed the pair of middle fingers in the center and joined the two little fingers in their own positions, the supreme practitioner should establish them thus. (206)
This *Trikhaṇḍā* is proclaimed for the rite of summoning Tripurā;
with this [Trikhaṇḍā], one should invoke the Goddess, the illustrious *Tripurasundarī*. (207)
[The Bringing Together into the Handful of Flowers]:
Having brought forth the supreme digit (kalā) flowing through the nostril itself, and having gathered it into the handful of flowers while reciting the previously mentioned Bhairavī mantra. (208)
205–206 | Regarding the *trikhaṇḍā-mudrā*, the *Tantrasāra* states:
"Having crossed the hands so that the thumbs touch, one should make them equal;
having placed the two index fingers in a curved shape within the ring fingers."
O Maheśvarī, one should place the little finger in its own position;
this is declared to be the "three-sectioned" (trikhaṇḍā) mudrā for the practice of meditation on Tripurā.
208. Regarding the phrase "by means of the nostril-passage": it means flowing—that is, emerging—by means of the air flowing through the nostrils.

And thus, having meditated upon the Goddess in the lotus of the heart, one should cause her to emerge by means of the air flowing through the nasal aperture, bring her into the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), and then, according to the sequence beginning with "the great lotus," one should establish the Goddess from that handful into the Great Yantra.
However, the joining of the palms (añjali) must not be performed prior to the installation [of the deity]. This is clearly stated in the thirteenth chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*:
"Having then performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should take up a handful of flowers.
One should never invoke the Goddess without a handful of flowers."
Then one should meditate upon the Great Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign, as described:
[The Mantra of Prayer] "O You who abide within the great lotus forest, whose form is the bliss of the Primordial Cause!"
O Mother, who acts for the welfare of all beings, come, come, O Supreme Goddess!
Having uttered, "The installation of the Goddess in the yantra," one should install the Supreme Deity in the great yantra. || 210 ||
[The Invoking Mudrā]: One should lower the raised añjali; this shall be the invoking mudrā.
[The Establishing Mudrā]
But if this [position] were reversed, then it would indeed be the *sthāpanī*. || 211 ||
[The mudrā for summoning presence]:
Two fists with the thumbs pointing upward—this is the *sannidhāpanī* (summoning presence) mudrā.
[The *sannirodhinī* mudrā:]
This same [mudrā], when held between the thumbs and fists, is the Sannirodhinī. || 212 ||

Having realized this within his heart, the practitioner who has conquered his vital breaths should then contemplate the unity of the two forms— the external and the internal— of the Goddess. Then, by means of the *āyu* seed-syllable, he should [visualize] through the nostril.
Having extracted that consciousness, one should place it within the handful of flowers.
Through the emission of the breath through the nostrils, the deity becomes established within the flower.
One should not separate one's hand from it until the Goddess has been fully installed.
"O Maheśvarī, when the hand has been separated from that flower, the Goddess is worshipped by the Gandharvas, yet the fruit is not obtained even by those who perform the worship.
(211) Regarding the word "ūrddhva": it means one should lower the añjali held above, that is, one should bend it downward; but not...

The meaning should be understood as follows: one should turn the añjali-gesture, which faces upward, so that it faces downward; for otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the *sthāpanī-mudrā* to be described later.
Having formed the añjali with both hands, [one places them] upon the root joints of the ring fingers.
One should place the two thumbs [into the palms]; this is known as the āvāhanī mudrā.
This is also clear from the statement in the *Tantrasāra*: "As for 'this one,' it is the opposite, facing downwards. As it is said in the *Tantrasāra*:
"If this [mudrā] should be facing downwards, it is known as the *sthāpanī* (establishing) mudrā. [The nature of invocation (*āvāhana*) follows.]
In the worship of the deity who is already inherently full,
the respectful manifestation [of the deity] before one's presence is here called *āvāhana* (invocation).
[The nature of installation:
The wise have declared that the placing of the Lord within the yantra is "installation" (sthāpana). || 214 ||
Having accepted the worship being offered and [bestowed] grace and so forth—[this is the nature of *sannidhāpana*]—may he be present; that presence of his is what they call *sānnidhya*. (215)
[The nature of complete cessation:
That presence of the All-pervading Lord which extends even unto the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) is designated as "complete cessation" (sannirodha) by men who know the mantras through devotion. 216.
The reality that is extended by bliss, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss— that which pervades all here should be meditated upon as the *avaguṇṭhana* (the veil). 217.
[The Ritual of Totalization] Having performed the ritual of totalization (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with the six mantras, one should then achieve oneness [with them].
[The Ritual of Nectarization]
Together with a woman who is auspicious by nature, one should perform the rite that has the form of nectar.
[The process of perfection: Forbearance toward their offenses should be understood as the act of perfecting them. || 219 ||
[The Installation of the Life-force (Jīvanyāsa): Thereafter, one should perform the installation of the life-force while reciting the previously mentioned mantra.
A wise man [should not sit] even on a seat of *kuśa* grass or upon a lelihana-cobra.
[The *lelihā* mudrā]:
One should make the index, middle, and ring fingers equal and face downward;
having made the little finger straight, one should place the thumb upon the ring finger.
This mudrā is named Lelihānā; it is proclaimed for the rite of infusing life (jīvanyāsa). || 221 ||
[The Nature of Sakalīkaraṇa:
The wise one should assign the six limbs either in the directions beginning with the southeast or upon the respective limbs of the Goddess; this constitutes sakalīkaraṇa. || 222 ||

[The ritual from the three rhythmic claps (tritāla) up to the supreme transformation (paramīkaraṇa): One should perform the three rhythmic claps, the binding of the ten directions, and the veiling; having rendered it nectar-like by means of the [mudrā] called Dhenu, one should perform the supreme transformation.
[The Nature of the Retinue Deities] Having done thus, one should contemplate the retinue as having emerged from the mass of rays issuing outward from that body and becoming firmly established. (224)

"From fire," etc. "In those respective limbs" means in the six limbs, such as the heart and so forth. "One should fashion the six limbs" means by means of the mantras of the six limbs. This is stated in the thirteenth chapter of the Gandharva Tantra:
"O Goddess, the best of practitioners should place the limb-mantras upon the limbs of the deity."
"This mudrā, which consists of pervasion, is called sakalīkaraṇa.

(223) The sequence beginning with the three tālas has already been explained in detail. "One should perform paramīkaraṇa" means by means of the paramīkaraṇa-mudrā. He describes the paramīkaraṇa-mudrā in the Tantrasāra:
With the thumbs interlaced and the other fingers extended,
this is declared by the wise to be the Mahāmudrā for the purpose of supreme transformation.
Thus it is said. Regarding the nature of *paramīkaraṇa* (the act of making supreme), the *Gandharva Tantra*, in its thirteenth chapter, states:
"That which manifests the quality of forbearance toward all kinds of offenses is called *paramīkaraṇa*; here it is defined as a fervent prayer."
224. "Thus" means that the deities who have manifested externally in the form of the *sarīrānmayasvarūpa* (the body-made-of-me) are themselves the retinue (*parivāra*).
[The instruction on the display of the nine mudrās: One should display the nine mudrās according to the method to be described and previously stated.
[In that regard, the mudrā for agitating all is as follows: having placed the two middle fingers together, the two little fingers are blocked by the thumbs. || 225 ||
Having formed the two index fingers like a staff, with the ring fingers above the middle fingers—
this mudrā named Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇī shall agitate the world.
[The Seal for Driving Away All:
When the two middle fingers of this very same seal are made straight, this seal named "Driving Away All" causes [all obstacles] to melt away in an instant. (227)
[The Seal for Attracting All: One should form the middle and index fingers in a pair, bent according to the rule;
this very seal is used for the rite of summoning. || 228 ||
225–226 | Now, he describes in sequence the nine mudrās that are to be displayed during the worship of Tripurā, beginning with the words "to be described" (*vakṣyamāṇa*) and so forth.

Among these, he first states the *sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇī-mudrā* with the words "the middle [finger]" (*madhyamā*) and so forth. Here, the compound *kaniṣṭe’ṅguṣṭharodhite* is an archaic (Vedic) sandhi; it means that the two little fingers (*kaniṣṭe*) are placed upon the middle joint of the middle fingers of both hands and are pressed down by the two thumbs (*aṅguṣṭhābhyām*).

The practical meaning is as follows: having crossed [the hands], one should make the two index fingers straight like a staff and place the two ring fingers upon the two middle fingers. Because this mudrā causes the agitation of the entire world, it is named "Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇī" (The All-Agitating).
As it is stated in the *Tantrasāra*: "Having placed the two middle fingers in the center, with the little fingers pressed by the thumbs,
and having made the two index fingers like staffs above the middle fingers, [one places] the ring fingers upon them."

"And this is the first mudrā, which causes universal agitation. (227) He speaks of the second [mudrā] with the words "of this": if the middle fingers of this mudrā, which causes universal agitation, are straight and not bent, it becomes the mudrā that subdues all. The *Tantrasāra* also says:
"When the two middle fingers of this very mudrā are made straight, it then becomes the supreme [mudrā] that enraptures all.
(228) He states the third [mudrā]: "The middle [fingers]," etc. When both the middle and index fingers of the aforementioned mudrā are curved, it is the "all-attracting" [mudrā].

This is the mudrā. And this mudrā manifests the power to attract the world of practitioners. O Supreme Goddess, with the middle and index fingers, and the little and ring fingers made equal, the two middle fingers take the form of a hook.
[The Mudrā that Brings All Under Control]:
One should worship one's own fingers facing forward by means of the path of rotation;
at the region of the mouths of the two thumbs, the two index fingers are in the shape of hooks.
This mudrā, named Sarvavaśyakarī, is the subduer of all. || 229 ||
[The Sarvonmādinī Mudrā]:
Having placed the two hands facing each other, with the little fingers positioned between the middle fingers, the two ring fingers straight, and the two index fingers outside of them. (230)
Then, the two thumbs, shaped like staffs, should be placed at the base of the nails of the middle fingers;
this is the mudrā named Unmādinī, which causes all women to become moist with passion.
"One should place the thumb upon the little finger and the ring finger;
this is the supreme Ākarṣiṇī mudrā, which attracts the three worlds.
According to this statement found in the *Tantrasāra*, there should be no curvature of the little and ring fingers.
The specific distinction is seen in the placement of the thumbs upon the ring fingers and the little fingers.
(Verse 229) He describes the fourth [mudrā] with the words beginning "parivartana" and so forth. Here, the phrase "the pair of middle and index fingers from before" and so on must be supplied.
Thus, with the two index fingers bent toward each other, the middle fingers are beneath them, and beneath those, the ring fingers are placed in the order of rotation.
Then, in that very same sequence, one should join the little fingers and thumbs firmly together at their tips;

this is what is meant by the statement, "one should worship with one's own fingers facing each other. The meaning of "one should worship" (yajet) is that one should cause them to meet with one another. One should make the two index fingers curved like hooks (*aṅkuśa*), shaped like hooks. However, one should not place the hook-shaped index fingers in the region of the tips of the thumbs.
Regarding the connection, it is clearly stated in the *Tantrasāra* that the thumbs are to be placed upon all the fingers. Thus, the *Tantrasāra* says:
"Having formed the hands into the shape of a casket (*puṭa*), the two index fingers are shaped like hooks (*aṅkuśa*)."
In the sequence of rotation, O Goddess, [place them] in the middle [finger] and those below it;
likewise, in that same sequence, join the little finger and the ring finger. All [fingers] should be pressed firmly from the tips of the thumbs.
"This mudrā, O Supreme One, is considered to be the bringer of all subjugation.

(230–231) Now he describes the fifth: "Facing each other," etc. Having placed the two hands facing one another, one should place the two little fingers (antyaje) between the two middle fingers (madhyamayoḥ), positioned at their middle joints (madhyaparva-saṃsthe). The two ring fingers (anāmike) should be straight (sarale) and unbent.
[The Great Hook Mudrā]:
From this very same mudrā,
the supreme practitioner should join the ring finger and the index finger in succession, in the form of a hook.
This [mudrā] named Mahāṅkuśā accomplishes all purposes and goals. || 232 ||

[The Khecarī Mudrā: Then, having encircled the left [hand] with the right hand and the right [hand] with the left hand by way of wrapping around, [one should join] the little fingers and the ring fingers. (233)
Then, having restrained the two index fingers and kept the middle fingers straight,
the best of practitioners should join them in the form of a vulva.
This mudrā, named Khecarī, is the most excellent of all.

Having formed that [mudrā], one should place the two index fingers outside. Then, one should make the two thumbs straight like staffs, positioned at the nail-base of the middle fingers; the meaning is that one should join the two straight thumbs at the nail-base of the middle fingers.
This is the Unmādinī mudrā, which causes all women to become moistened—that is, it produces arousal.
This mudrā is also described with nearly identical wording in the *Tantrasāra*:
"Having placed the two hands facing each other, with the little fingers positioned between the middle fingers, the two ring fingers straight, and the two index fingers outside of them."
"Then the two thumbs, shaped like staffs, should be placed at the region of the nails of the middle fingers;
this is the mudrā named Unmādinī, which attracts all women.
(232) He speaks of the sixth [mudrā] with the words "of this": of this Unmādinī mudrā, the two ring fingers [are to be arranged] in sequence...
If one joins the two index fingers in the form of a hook, then it becomes the mudrā known as the Great Hook (mahāṅkuśā).
This is clearly stated in the Tantrasāra:
"In this [mudrā], however, the pair of ring fingers should be placed below in the shape of a hook."
One should also employ the two index fingers in that same sequence.
"This is the Mahāṅkuśā mudrā, which accomplishes all purposes and goals.
Regarding the word "asyāḥ" (of this), it refers to the Unmādinī mudrā.
(233–235) Now he describes the seventh [mudrā] with the words beginning with "savyam": the left hand [is placed] upon the right hand...
[The Praise of Khecarīmudrā] Whether self-restrained or unrestrained, pure or even impure; whether walking, standing, sleeping, eating, or engaged in sexual intercourse— (236)
By means of the mudrā, however, when the two middle fingers are joined in the sequence of rotation at the position of the earth, one immediately attains the state of moving through the sky.
And by knowing this very [teaching], one shall become beloved by the Yoginīs. || 238 ||
[Seed-syllable Mudrā]:
Having crossed the two hands and touched them so that they take the shape of a half-moon, the wise one should simultaneously join the pair of index fingers with the pair of thumbs. (239)
One should place the two middle fingers pressed down from below by the little fingers;
likewise, one should join the two ring fingers at the very bottom.

One should join the right hand with the left; then, by way of encircling, one should join the little finger and the ring finger. The meaning is that one should encircle the ring finger of the right hand with the little finger of the left hand, and the ring finger of the left hand with the little finger of the right hand. Regarding "with the two index fingers": likewise, the middle fingers should be straight and unbent according to the previously mentioned method.

Having restrained [the hands] with the two index fingers, one should place them in the shape of a vulva; this is the Khecarī Mudrā. O Great Goddess, having crossed the left arm over the right side and the right arm over the left side, and having turned the hands completely around...
O Goddess, having joined the little fingers and the ring fingers in that same sequence,
both middle fingers are likewise pressed down from above by the two index fingers.
O Maheśānī, one should also make the two thumbs straight;
this is known by the name Khecarī when applied to the Pārthiva-sthāna.
In the statement from the *Tantrasāra*, however, a specific distinction is observed: "the two thumbs should remain straight.
(239–241) He describes the eighth [mudrā] with the words "having turned" (*parivartya*): "O Dear One, having turned the hands, they should be clearly formed in the shape of a half-moon."
Then, one should simultaneously join the pair of the index fingers and the thumbs.
This is declared to be the seed-seal (*bījamudrā*), which sets all accomplishments in motion. || 241 ||
[The *yonimudrā*:
The two middle fingers are curved in shape and placed upon the two index fingers;
likewise, the two ring fingers and the two little fingers are positioned in the middle. 242.
Joining them all together in one place and pressing them with the thumbs—this is declared to be the Yoni-mudrā, the mother of the origin of the three worlds. (243)
[The Promise to Define the Seed-syllables of the Mudrās] I shall explain the seed-syllables of the mudrās in their proper sequence according to the path of the Tantra.
[The Seed-syllables to be Employed in the Ninefold Set of Mudrās]
Having extracted the five arrows, one should then write the seed-syllable of the trident (sūla). || 244 ||
One should place the two middle fingers pressed down below by the little fingers;
likewise, the two ring fingers should be joined at the very bottom in a curved position.
"This is the seed-seal (*bījamudrā*), which quickly increases all accomplishments," so it is said in the *Tantrasāra* (vv.

242–243). Now he describes the ninth, the womb-seal (*yonimudrā*)—beginning with the words "the middle [fingers]": one should place the two middle fingers in a curved shape positioned above the index fingers; likewise, one should place the two little fingers between the ring fingers. Then, all...
Having joined the fingers together and pressed them down with the two thumbs—this is the sequence for binding the *yonimudrā*.
It is called the "Mother of the Origin of the Three Worlds" because the *yoni* is the ground of origin for all things.
Having made the two middle fingers curved and positioned above the two index fingers...
Likewise, the ring fingers and the little fingers should be placed in the middle.
"Having joined all [the fingers] together in one place and pressed them with the thumbs—this is the supreme mudrā, declared to be the Yoni-mudrā. Thus it is said in the *Tantrasāra*.
Regarding the application of these mudrās at the time of worship, he states the same in that very work:
"O Great Goddess, these mudrās of Tripurā have been declared by me;
they should be employed at the time of worship according to the sequence of the twilight rituals. (p.
645) "Śiva, Śakti, [the letters] from *kā* to *pa*, adorned with the *bhaga* (the letter *ha*), the letter *ra*, and the lunar orb (*bindu*)."
The seed-syllable of Sadāśiva is known as Vāgbhava, the ninth.
[Instruction on the libation: Thereafter, one should perform the libation three times with the *tattvamudrā*.
[Instruction on worship with the sixteen offerings:]
One should worship the Supreme Goddess with the sixteen types of offerings.

244–245. Now, he describes in sequence the seed-syllables (*bīja*) to be employed for the mudrās beginning with *Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇī*, which have been previously defined, starting with the words "the five arrows" (*pañcabāṇa*). The seed-syllables of the five arrows have already been shown in the root text and its commentary in verse 343, beginning with "the two letters ending in *tha*. Having extracted the five arrows, they are: *drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ*.

The meaning is: "having extracted the five seed-syllables. And thus, it should be understood that one should employ the aforementioned five seed-syllables in the pentad of mudrās beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇī and ending with Sarvonmādinī. Therefore, having uttered *drām*, one should display the Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇī mudrā; likewise, *drīṃ* for Sarvavidrāvaṇī, *klīṃ* for Sarvākarṣiṇī, *blūṃ* for Sarvavaśyakarī, and *saḥ* [for Sarvonmādinī].
[The mantra] *sarvonmādinī* is *kroṃ*. Thus, having uttered *kroṃ*, one should display the *mahāṅkuśā* mudrā.

Now, he teaches the application of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) for the seventh [mudrā], the *khecarī* mudrā, beginning with the words "Śiva" and so forth. "Śiva" is the letter *ha*; "Śakti" is the letter *sa*;
"Kānta" is the letter *kha*; "Pānta" is the letter *pha*. And that letter *pha* is joined with the "Bhaga," which is the eleventh vowel, the letter *ra*.
"Adorned with the moon (I) and the anusvāra (ṃ)"—by this it is understood that one should utter "Ha Sa Kha Phreṃ" and then display the Khecarī-mudrā.
Regarding the eighth, the Bīja-mudrā, he states the application of the seed-syllable: "Always" (sadā). The seed-syllable of Sadāśiva is "Hsauḥ.
Thus, the meaning is that one should utter "Hsauḥ" and then display the Bīja-mudrā. "Vāgbhava" refers to Aiṃ.

The meaning is that one should display the ninth *yonimudrā*, preceded by the seed-syllable of speech (*vāgbhava*). In the thirteenth chapter of the *Gandharvatantra*, it says: "Then one should display the nine mudrās, each preceded by its own seed-syllable:
*saṃkṣobha*, *drāvaṇa*, *ākarṣa*, *vaśya*, *unmada*, *mahāṅkuśa*," and so forth.
Then follow, in sequence, the nine mudrās known as Khecarī, Bīja, and Yoni;
O Maheśānī, these mudrās have the luster of the Bandhūka flower.
"One should visualize all [the goddesses] holding their respective mudrās, facing Śrīvidyā.

(246) Regarding "and the libation," the definition of the *tattvamudrā* is stated in the thirteenth chapter of the *Gandharva Tantra*: "The joining of the thumb and the ring finger—this is declared to be the *tattvamudrā*."
One should prepare the threefold *arghya* with the three *tattvas*, ending with the *vahnijāyā* (svāhā). || 247 ||
Having applied three seeds each upon the three parts of the root,
the knower of mantras should present the ritual offerings with the Bālā mantra.
[The Sixteen Offerings:
A seat, welcome, water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, honey-mixture, further sipping, bathing, garments, and ornaments. (249)
One should employ these sixteen services in the worship: fragrance, jasmine flowers, lamps, incense, food offerings, and prostrations.
[In that regard, another ritual procedure:
Alternatively, the mantra-practitioner should imagine the water for the feet, the respectful offering, and the water for sipping;
likewise, the bath, the garment, the ornaments, the perfume, the flowers, and the incense. (251)

One should employ the sixteen services in the ritual worship: the lamp, the food offering (naivedya), water for sipping (ācamana), betel leaf (tāmbūla), the hymn of praise (stotra), the libation (tarpaṇa), and the prostration (namaskriyā). || 252 ||
They say the thumb is Śiva, and the ring finger is called Śakti.
"The libation (tarpaṇa), however, should be performed with nectars through their union using the left hand.
Regarding "with ritual services" (upacāraiḥ), he explains the etymological derivation of the word *upacāra* in that same work:
"These [services] are performed for the deity solely out of devotion; they bring about the proximity of the deity to the practitioner."
Because they cause [the dharma] to circulate, for that reason they are called attendants (upacārakas).
"Or they arise from near the feet, or likewise from the end of the *kalā*s.
(249–254) Now, he divides the ritual services (*upacāra*) in order, beginning with "the seat" (*āsana*) and ending with "the fivefold services" (*pañcopacārika*). This is clear.
Regarding that, he states a specific detail concerning the seat in the fourteenth chapter of the *Gandharvatantra*:
One should first offer a seat made of gold, silver, cloth, or fashioned from gems; or else one made of flowers or wood.
[The Ten Offerings]: Water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), the food offering (naivedya), water for sipping (ācamanīyaka),
the honey-mixture (madhuparka), water for sipping again, and then fragrance and flowers.
Incense, lamps, and food offerings are known as the ten modes of service (daśopacāra).
[The Fivefold Offerings: The offerings beginning with fragrance and ending with food constitute the fivefold ritual service.
[Their respective status as superior, middling, and inferior follows this sequence.]
The wise have declared these to be, respectively, the highest, the middling, and the lowest. || 254 ||

[The determination regarding what is not obtained during the ritual services: Whatever among all the ritual services may be difficult to obtain, one should mentally visualize all of that and arrange it by means of scattering flowers. || 255 ||
One should never offer a leaf or a seat here during worship;
rather, one should offer a red woolen blanket to the Goddess according to the prescribed rule.
O Supreme Goddess, O Mother, bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation, please be seated upon this lotus-throne at the foot of Mount Meru.
