O Śivā, he who offers a prescribed seat to the Goddess with this very [mantra] holds both enjoyment and liberation in the palm of his hand and shall become established everywhere.
Thus [it is said]. The nature of other offerings (*upacāra*) as well has been demonstrated right here, for fear of prolixity. He states the five offerings:
"fragrance and so forth. This is clearly stated in the *Nibandhatantra*, in the fifty-fifth chapter:
"Fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, and food-offering—this is the pentad."
One should always offer the fivefold worship during the ritual adoration.
Thus it is said: "Supreme," etc. This means that worship with sixteen services (*upacāra*) is supreme, with ten services is middling, and with five services is inferior.
Regarding the phrase "among the services": in the absence of any particular service, one should even imagine a flower itself as that specific service and offer it to the Goddess.
The meaning is that one should offer it. (p.
648) [The offering of water following each secondary service:
In each instance, one should offer water between the intervals of the secondary services.
[The offering of flowers upon the head of the Goddess:
One should always place the head of the deity adorned with flowers. || 256 ||
[Prohibition against waving the hand above the Goddess:
At the time of worship, one should not wave the hand over the deity.
[Regulation regarding the absence of flowers, etc.]
One should worship the Supreme Goddess even with leaves in the absence of flowers. || 257 ||
But in the absence of leaves, one should worship with grass, shrubs, herbs, and the like;
and in the absence of herbs, one should worship even with their fruits.
One should perform the rite with unbroken grains or water, or in their absence with white mustard seeds;
if even those are unavailable, one should practice mental devotion.
257. Regarding the instruction "one should worship," it means that in the absence of flowers, one should worship with leaves and so forth; however, one must never allow the omission of worship.
If not even one of the aforementioned materials is available, one should perform mental worship; the sense is that by that alone the success of the worship is achieved.
This is clearly stated in the fourteenth chapter of the Gandharvatantra:
In the absence of flowers, one should worship with leaves; if leaves are not available, then with their fruits; or else with unbroken grains or even with water—one should never neglect the worship.
"But even if these are not available, one should resort to mental devotion.
Here, although there is a general injunction regarding leaves—stating that "in the absence of flowers, one should worship with leaves"—it is further specified:
"Among leaves, the bilva leaf and likewise the sprout of the madana tree..."
Likewise, only dūrvā sprouts are prescribed; one should not employ any other leaf.

Thus, based on the statement in the fourteenth chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra* and because of the general prohibition against worship using leaves— expressed by the phrase "one should not worship Śivā with leaves"— it should be understood that in the absence of flowers, worship must be performed using only the aforementioned bilva leaves and so forth, and not with other types of leaves.

[Regarding the priority and posteriority of offerings such as flowers: "The supreme, the intermediate, and likewise the inferior—gold is declared to be the supreme, while that produced from variegated materials is the inferior. (260)
A flower produced from trees or shrubs is proclaimed to be the best;
that consisting of leaves, water, and so forth is the lowest, while that which consists of fruit is middling. (261)
[The Sequence for Offering Flowers:
The mantra-practitioner should offer flowers into the circle with the mudrā called Jñāna.
[The Jñāna-mudrā]
The Jñānamudrā is proclaimed as being formed with the thumb and the index finger. || 262 ||
[The specific rule regarding the offering of flowers and so forth: One should offer a flower or a leaf exactly as it has grown;
however, in the case of offering a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali), this restriction does not apply.
"The fruit shall not be given with the face turned downward; such is the determination of the scripture.
[The Libation: The wise practitioner should offer libations three times as before with the root mantra. (264)
[The ritual from the goddess’s anointing up to the offering of ornaments:
Having led the Goddess to his own left mandala, he should perform the anointing and so forth;
the bathing according to the sequence of mental worship, and the wiping of her body with a cloth. (265)
Having given all the ornaments, one should bring her into the maṇḍala.
[The offering of water for the feet, etc. Having performed the salutation as before, one should present the water for the feet and the other offerings. || 266 ||

265. Regarding the phrase "by means of the sequences of mental worship": the meaning is that one should perform the bathing of the Goddess by means of the procedures for mental adoration and the prescribed sequence of baths as taught in the seventeenth chapter.
[The offering of fragrance and so forth.]

One should satisfy Bhavānī with incense, sandalwood, and incense-sticks, as well as with various lamps and fruits; with milk mixed with sugar, ghee, honey, and fruits, and also with curd and *paramānna* (milk-rice). || 267 ||
[The Procedure for Offering the Food Offering:

Reciting the root mantra of the Goddess followed by her own name and the word "naivedyam" (food offering), and ending with the wife of Agni (svāhā), one should utter "gṛhāṇa" (accept) and thus present the food offering. || 268 ||
[The Specific Rules for the Offering of Sacrifices:
A king should not perform the offering of sacrifices consisting of rams or buffaloes;
nor should the most excellent of Brahmins offer lions, tigers, or human beings. (269)
[The performance of service to please the Goddess with fans and other offerings:
With fans, pure vermilion, bells, chowries, mirrors, canopies, parasols, betel-nut, musk, saffron, and so forth. (270)
With yellow pigment, agallochum, camphor, and likewise with lac-dye,
and with dances, songs, and instrumental music, one should gratify the Supreme Goddess.

268. He describes the sequence for the offering of the food oblation (*naivedya*) with the words beginning "the root-mantra" (*mūlam*), etc. First the root-mantra, then the name of the Goddess herself, then the word "food oblation" (*naivedyam*), and then the two words "accept it" (*gṛhāṇa*) followed by the wife of Fire, *svāhā*.
Thus, the resulting mantra is: "O Śrī Tripurasundarī, accept this food oblation, *svāhā*."

269. He states a specific rule regarding the offering of oblations (*balidāna*) with the words "not a king" (*na rājā*). Although animals are generally prescribed for the offering of oblations, the meaning is that a king should not perform the oblation of a ram or a buffalo, nor should the most excellent Brāhmaṇa perform the oblation of a lion and so forth.
[Tarpaṇa] (p. 651)
Having offered various kinds of substances, one should satisfy the supreme [deity] with [appropriate] reasons.
[This is the instruction for the worship of the retinue deities:
Having received permission from the Great Goddess, one should then worship the members of the retinue. (272)
[Therein, the worship of the six limb-deities:
Just as omniscience is satisfaction, characterized by primordial awakening; so too are these others—autonomous, eternally satisfied, and beginningless in their infinite sequence. (273)
272. Having said "having given," [it is] by means of reasons or causes. Regarding that, he states a specific distinction in the *Gandharvatantra*, in the fifteenth chapter:
"O Goddess, for one who is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), even wine is ordained in the sacred scripture (*āgama*);
that indeed shall be nectar, and that indeed shall be liquor."
A twice-born man should never offer liquor to the Goddess even in times of distress;
if he should offer liquor out of delusion, he falls away from his very status as a Brāhmaṇa.
He alone would be a slayer of a Brahmin; therefore, one should avoid liquor.
When one offers liquor to Mahādevī while free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa), [the merit] of a thousand horse-sacrifices...
"When one possesses conceptual thought, O Goddess, one becomes a partaker of sin; of this there is no doubt.

Now, he introduces the worship of the retinue with the words "having taken," etc. He states the sequence for requesting the command (*ājñā*) in the *Tripurārcanarahasya*: first the root mantra, and then—
O Supreme Goddess, whose nature is consciousness, who delights in the essence of the supreme nectar,
O Tripurā, grant me permission to worship your retinue.
Thus, in the sixteenth chapter of the *Gandharvatantra*: "O Goddess, I worship your hosts of rays according to the ritual rule;
O Mother of the World, command them as you wish."
"Having received the command of the Goddess with palms joined in reverence, the best of practitioners, being satisfied, should perform worship according to the previously stated sequence of yoga.
(273-275). Therein, he first describes the sequence for the worship of the deities of the six limbs, beginning with the words "Just as," and so forth. And thus:
The deities of the six limbs are to be worshipped while reciting their respective mantras. [Their visualization:
They possess rays that are white like snow or crystal, yellow, blue, black, and reddish-brown. (274)

The principal female deities, bearing the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, [occupy] the place of worship in the southeast, southwest, northwest, northeast, and in the center, as well as in the cardinal directions, in due order. (275)
[Again, the libation and the offering of a handful of flowers:
Having again performed the libation, one should recite the root mantra in every respect. || 276 ||
"One should then perform five *añjali*s with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) on the head, chest, the pair of feet, the pair of hands, and sequentially on all the limbs. (277)
[The sequence for joining the seed-syllables at the beginning of the worship of the retinue:

At the beginning of the names of all the attendants, one should join Māyā (the syllable Hrīṃ) or Lakṣmī (the syllable Śrīṃ); or else, one may join Vāk (the syllable Aiṃ), Māyā, and Kamalā (the syllable Śrīṃ), encapsulated by the three. 278.

It follows that one should worship the deities of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgadevatā*) in the following sequence: "Obeisance to the Heart of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, whose power is omniscience" (*sarvajñatāśakti*), "Svāhā to the Head of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, whose power is contentment" (*tṛptiśakti*), and so forth. However, the author of the *Tantrasāra* states that in the phrase "omniscience-power" (*sarvajñatāśakti*), it should be read as "all-knowing power" (*sarvajñāśakti*), and that each mantra should be preceded by the individual seed-syllables of the *Bālā* mantra—*ai*, *klīṃ*, and *sauḥ*—by repeating them twice.
He describes the nature of these limb-deities (aṅgadevatā) in sequence, beginning with "tuṣāra":

the power of omniscience (sarvajñatā-śakti) is snow-white; the power of contentment (tṛpti-śakti) is crystal-colored; the power of primordial awakening (anādibodha-śakti) is dark-blue; the power of sovereignty (svatantra-śakti) is blue; the power of eternal satisfaction (nityatṛpti-śakti) is black; and the infinite power (ananta-śakti) is said to be reddish.

The phrase beginning with "varada" and so forth is common [to all]. He states their positions in sequence with the word "agnī," meaning that one should worship these [deities] according to the sequence starting with Agni.
(276) He describes the offering of five handfuls of flowers with the verse beginning with "mūla" and so forth; thus, first the root-mantra, and then the "sira-" [mantra], etc.
The meaning is that one should offer five handfuls of flowers (puṣpāñjali) in sequence at the beginning, at all the limbs, and at the end.

278. Now, regarding the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇapūjā), he first states the three systems for the application of the seed-syllables (bījayojana) with the words beginning "māyām": "In that manner, one should apply the seed-syllable of Māyā and the seed-syllable of Śrī—namely *hrīṃ* and *śrīṃ*—thus constituting the practice of the two-syllabled mantra."
[pādukāmantraḥ] "I worship the sandals" (pādukāṃ pūjayāmi)—this is the mantra of the sandals preceded by "Śrī.
Having joined it with "namas" at the end, one should worship everything ending with "namas. || 279 ||
[The application of the *pādukā-mantra* even during ritual placement (*nyāsa*):
Even during ritual placement (*nyāsa*), the practitioner of mantra should employ the *pādukā*, for it bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
[In this regard, there is agreement with authoritative scripture:]
"This is declared to be the supreme secret; thus it is agreed upon in the Yāmala. || 280 ||

The sequence is as follows: one should join the three seed-syllables *vāṃ*, *māyāṃ* (which is *ai*), and *kamalām* (which is *hrīṃ* and *śrīṃ*). This is the procedure for the application of the *tritārī*.

Alternatively, "enclosed by the three" is the third ritual method; that is, enclosed by the three seed-syllables *vāṃ*, *māyā*, and *kamalā*. Regarding the definition of "enclosure" (*saṃpuṭa*), the *Tantrasāra* states:

One should utter the mantra at the beginning, followed immediately by the name of the object to be accomplished (sādhya), and then again at the end; this seed-syllable [flanking the name] is known as the "encasement" (saṃpuṭa).

Thus, in this ritual procedure (*kalpa*), the result is that one should first utter *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*, then the name of the deity to be worshipped, and then *śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ* in reverse order. The author of the *Tantrasāra* has also stated that in all cases, the application of the two *tāryās* or the three *tāryās* comes at the beginning.
This is also stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, one should indeed join this pair of seed-syllables consisting of Māyā and Lakṣmī according to the previous sequence, or else the triad, as has been taught.
Thus [it is said]. The author of the *Tantrasāra* states that in the *Kalpasūtra* as well, the application of the *tritārī* (the three stars) occurs at the beginning of every [rite]:
"The *tritārī* is declared to be Vāk, Māyā, and Kamalā.
(279) Now, he states the *pādukā-mantra* to be employed everywhere in the worship of the retinue: "The *pādukā*... Thus: *aiṃ*...
The meaning is that one should worship everything in this sequence: *hrīṃ śrīṃ śrīmahātripurasundarī-śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi namaḥ*.

Regarding the phrase "also in the ritual placement (*nyāsa*)," the meaning is that one should employ the aforementioned *pādukā-mantra* even at the time of performing the ritual placement. In that context, [the mantra is] for the *pādukā*: 280. *hrīṃ śrīṃ śrīmahātripurasundarī-pādukāyai namaḥ*.
The word "namas" is the specific term. To provide scriptural authority for this meaning, he cites the tradition: "It is a secret. (p.
654) [Regarding the number of libations:
The libation should be performed three times, or even once, according to one's own desire.
[Regarding the divisions of sentences at the beginning of the oblation, etc.
One should remember "svāhā" in the case of a homa, and "tarpayāmi" in the case of a libation (tarpaṇa). || 281 ||
[The Arrangement of Vowels in the Worship of the Sixteen Tithinityās]:
Upon the lines of the central triangle, one should write five vowels each in sequence, according to their divisions, starting from its own apex and proceeding in the order of right and left.
One should write the syllable *Aḥ* in the center and likewise worship the Tithinityās.
[Instruction on the worship of Kāmeśvarī and the others:

Having visualized all [the goddesses] beginning with Kāmeśvarī, one should perform their respective mantras from the first lunar day (pratipad) until the full moon, following the sequence of counter-clockwise rotation. (283)
[The meditation on Kāmeśvarī (1): One should visualize Kāmeśvarī as red in color, adorned with red garments, and holding a noose, a goad, a lotus, and a bow. || 284 ||

281. He states the number of libations for the retinue deities with the words "and the libation" (*tarpaṇaṃ ca*). This is clear. In the present context, however, it should be understood that one should perform the libation ending with the words "I offer libation" (*tarpayāmi*).
282–283. Now, intending to describe the worship of the sixteen *Tithinityās* beginning with Kāmeśvarī, [the author first describes] the triangle in the center of the *Śrīcakra*.

He describes the arrangement of the sixteen vowels beginning with *a* and ending with *visarga* by means of the passage beginning with "in the center" (*madhye*) and so forth. The essential meaning is that one should write the five vowels ending with *anusvāra* on the three lines in the order from right to left (i.e., starting from the right), and write the *visarga* in the middle of the triangle. Therein, one should meditate upon the Tithinityās, such as Kāmeśvarī and others, which are to be described later, according to the sequence that will be explained.
The meaning is that one should worship with the mantra of each respective deity. Regarding this, he states the sequence: "on the first lunar day and so forth" (verse 284).

Now, in order, among the fifteen lunar days beginning with the first and ending with the fifteenth, the fifteen *tithinityās*—beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Vicitrā—are to be worshipped sequentially; [this applies] generally to all [of them] on those fifteen lunar days.
[From the *Bhagamālā* (2): Bhagamālā is white in color and adorned with a garland of *bhagas*;
she holds in her hands a noose, a goad, a thread, and a book. || 285 ||
[Of Nityaklinnā (3)]:
Nityaklinnā is white in color, with lotus hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. || 286 ||
One should contemplate Bheruṇḍā, who is red in color, adorned with red ornaments,
holding a severed head and a *veda* (book), and possessing two arms. || 287 ||
One should meditate upon Vahnivāsinī as having a tawny complexion and likewise holding [the mudrā] in her hand;
[of Mahānityeśvarī (6)].
The great eternal Īśvarī, the excellent one, who holds a sword, a shield, and a rosary.
He describes the meditations on the venerable *Śrī Tripurasundarī*, who is to be worshipped, beginning with the words "Kāmeśvarīm" and ending with "sādhakottamaḥ. This is clear.
(Verse 288) Regarding the phrase "Mahānityeśvarīm," the reading in the *Jñānārṇava* is "Vajreśvarī," while in the *Tantrarāja* it is "Mahāvajreśvarī. Here...
Immediately after the meditation on Mahānityeśvarī, the meditation on Tvaritā is thus described as "the very dark one. However—The first eternal goddess is Mahātripurasundarī;
she is likewise known as Kāmeśvarī and Bhagamālinī.
Nityaklinnā, Bheruṇḍā, and likewise Vahnivāsinī; Vajreśvarī, Dūtī, Tvaritā, and Kulasundarī.
Nityā, Nīlapatākā, Vijayā, Sarvamaṅgalā,
and Jvālāmālāvicitrāntā— these fifteen are proclaimed.

Thus, in the statement from the *Kulārṇava* cited in the *Tantrasāra*, the description of Śivadūtī is seen prior to that of Tvaritā. It is exactly the same in the *Tantrarāja-tantra* and likewise in the *Tripurārcanarahasya*. Even in the root text (*mūla*), in the fifteenth chapter (*prakāśa*) during the occasion of the placement (*nyāsa*) of the sixteen Nityās, it says: "One should place this Śivadūtī herself in the heart on the seventh [day]."
*Śivadūtī-nyāsa* (p. 656): *Śivadūtī* (7) [x x x x x x x x x x] |
[Regarding Tvaritā and Kulasundarī (8, 9):
Thus, one should visualize Tvaritā as very dark-complexioned and Kulasundarī as fair-limbed.
[Regarding Nityā (10):]
The Goddess, who possesses the eight siddhis, is situated within the interior of the eight-cornered [mandala]. || 289 ||
[Of Nīlapatākā (11):
One should visualize Nīlapatākā, who is eternal and holds a noose and a goad.
[Of Vijayā (12):]
And Vijayā, Caṇḍarūpā, and likewise Svā, surrounded by Yoginīs. || 290 ||
One should meditate upon Sarvamaṅgalā, who is red in color and holds two lotuses in her hands.
[Jvālāṃśumālinī (14)]
She is garlanded with flames, smoky-colored, three-eyed, and possesses a beautiful white form. || 291 ||
[Of Vicitrā (15)]:
Vicitrā, who is white in color, holding a white lotus, beautiful, with variegated hands, the Great Goddess adorned with all ornaments. || 292 ||
[16] Then, having meditated upon Śrī Sundarī, the best of practitioners should worship her. [The fruit of the daily worship of each individual Nityā, beginning from the first lunar day.]
Whoever indeed worships each one individually shall obtain the fruit of good fortune. || 293 ||

Having thus spoken, [the text] says, "On the eighth day, one should place Tvaritā, consisting of twelve syllables, on the throat. By this, the mention of Tvaritā immediately after Śivadūtī is established. Through this calculation, the number sixteen for the Nityās is also justified; however, if Śivadūtī were not included, there would certainly be a deficiency. Therefore, regarding Śivadūtī in this section on the worship of the sixteen Nityās in the root text:
The meditation is not seen; it appears to have been caused by the negligence of its scribe.
(193) Thus, having described the meditations on the fifteen Nityās beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Vicitrā, [it is stated that Sundarī is to be worshipped on all lunar days]. (p. 657)
In the vowel *aḥ*, one should worship the sixteenth eternal goddess who moves through the fifteen lunar days;
[regarding the difference in sequence according to the division of the fortnights:
in the dark fortnight, one should worship those beginning with Vicitrā and ending with Kāmeśvarī.

He teaches the meditation (*dhyāna*) upon the sixteenth [vowels], the illustrious Tripurasundarī, with the words beginning "Then" (*tataḥ*). Meditation has already been taught previously. The meaning is: "in each one of the aforementioned Nityās.
(Verse 294) He states the place of worship for the beautiful sixteenth [vowel]: "In the vowel *aḥ*. This means that one should write the vowel *aḥ* in the center.

By the previously mentioned statement, "in the middle of the central triangle," the meaning is: in the sixteenth vowel, namely *aḥ*. He specifies the sixteenth [Nityā] with the words "three-fifths" (*tripañca*). Thus, it is stated that one should worship each individual Nityā on the fifteen lunar days beginning with the first (*pratipad*), but one should worship the sixteenth on all lunar days whatsoever. This refers to what was stated regarding the worship of Kāmeśvarī and the others, one by one, on the first lunar day and so forth.

This refers to the subject of the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*). Regarding the specific rule for the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), he says "in the dark [fortnight]" and so forth. Here, the meaning is that one should worship the Nityās, ending with Kāmeśvarī, in this sequence: Vicitrā on the first day (*pratipad*), Jvālā on the second, Āsu-mālinī, and so on.
This is clearly stated in the sixteenth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*:
O Daughter of the Mountain, beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad) and ending with the full moon (paurṇamāsī),
one should worship each Nityā daily and shall attain great good fortune.

"O Maheśānī, during the dark fortnight, one should worship the circle of lunar days (tithi-maṇḍala), beginning with Vicitrā and ending with Kāmeśvarī, O beautiful lady. Thus it is said. Furthermore, the author of the Tantrasāra states that in the great triangle, one should worship the five vowels beginning with *ā* and the five beginning with *ū* in a counter-clockwise direction.

It is clearly stated that one should meditate upon the five [syllables] beginning with *ekāra* and place the *visarga* in their center; then, by moving counter-clockwise among them, one should worship during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) from "Kāme" to "Vicitrānta," and during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) from "Vicitrādi" to "Kāmeśvaryanta.
This is likewise stated in the *Tripurārcanarahasya*: "One should sacrifice," meaning one should meditate according to the aforementioned sequence.

The meaning is that one should worship by reciting the respective mantra according to the method stated in the *Pañcadaśaprakāśīya-tithinityā-nyāsa*, ending with the words "I worship the venerable *pādukā*, obeisance" (*śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi namaḥ*). This is stated in another Tantra cited in the *Tantrasāra*:
"Having first uttered the word 'Śrī', one should then utter the word 'pādukā'."
I worship; after "namas," one should worship the deities of the limbs.

Thus it is said. Here too, the practice should be performed with either two *tārās* or three *tārās*, as this is prescribed generally for the worship of the limb-deities (*aṅgadevatā*). Accordingly: *aiṃ hrīṃ* (or *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*) *aṃ aiṃ krīṃ sauḥ oṃ namaḥ kāmeśvari*. [The substance for the libation (*tarpaṇa*) of the *Nityās*.]
One should satisfy her with honey-based substances with a mind of supreme bliss;
thus, through the sequential application of the phonemes, one should accomplish the worship of Tripureśvarī. (295)
One should perform worship according to one's own capacity and worship the Root Vidyā.
[Receiving the Goddess’s Permission: Placing the Goddess’s command upon my head, I perform the external worship. (296)
[Instruction on the Worship of the Guru] One should worship the three lineages— the divine, the perfected, and the human— within the triple wheel.
[Its conformity with authoritative scripture]
In the Bṛhacchrīkramatantra, however, it is proclaimed as "by Śiva. (297)

[In that regard, there is another ritual procedure: Alternatively, the wise practitioner, having performed the external worship of the Tithinityās, should worship the gurus in three rows according to the sequence of circumambulation along the three lines.

The ritual application (*prayoga*) should be performed in such a form as: "O you who bestow the fruit of desire and love, O you who bring all beings under your control, O you who agitate the entire world, *huṃ huṃ huṃ huṃ* *drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ blūṃ saḥ sauḥ klīṃ ai/* I worship the venerable sandals (*śrīpādukā*) of the eternal digit (*nityākalā*) Kāmeśvarī; obeisance. In this same manner, the mantras for Bhagamālinī and the others are also to be inferred. This applies to the sixteen-fold [deity] Sundarī.

In the worship, however, the procedure is as follows: first, either the *dvitārī* or the *tritārī*; then the sixteen vowels; then the root mantra; then: "I worship the *śrīpādukā* of the *śrīmahātripurasundarī* (Mahā)nityākalā, *namaḥ*.
[295–296] Regarding the phrase "one should satisfy," the remainder is "the *tithinityās*"; this is according to the sequence of the letters.

The meaning is: by means of the conjunction with the sixteen vowels beginning with *a* and ending with the *visarga*. The root-vidyā is Tripurasundarī; the sequence of worship has already been demonstrated previously.

(297) Now, intending to describe the worship of the circle of gurus (*gurumaṇḍala*), he first states the location for the worship of the guru, beginning with the word "trivṛtte" (in a triple circle). In a triple circle...
Outside the sixteen-spoked [mandala], on a triple circle, one should worship the Divine Current (divyaugha), the Siddha Current (siddhaugha), and the Human Current (mānavaugha) in sequence.
This is the established doctrine of the Bṛhacchrīkramatantra.
(298) Regarding this, he states another ritual procedure beginning with the word "tithi": first, the place for the worship of the Tithinityās.
p. 659) [The sequence of the ritual application therein:
One should [worship] the Mother, ending with the word *Ānandanātha* and ending with *Ambā*, in due order. || 298 ||
[The Promise to Describe the Lineage of Gurus] Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the lineage of gurus of the six Ṣoḍaśīs. (299)
[In that regard, there are seven divine currents: The second is named Paraprakāśaka, the second is Paraśiva, the third is Paraśakti, and after that is Kauleśvara. (300)
"Śuklādevī, Pareśāna, Kāmeśvarī, and Ambikā—these are declared to be the Gurus of the Divine Current (divyaugha), known as the seven supreme ones. || 301 ||

The first triangle is named "Bestower of All Siddhis" (*sarvasiddhiprada*); the meaning is that one should worship the Gurus of the Divine Current (*divyaugha*), the Siddha Current (*siddhaugha*), and the Human Current (*mānavaugha*) in sequence upon the three lines of the outer triangle by means of three rows of lines in a clockwise direction—this is the resultant meaning. He states the order of worship with the words "Ānanda," etc.; thus: "I worship the venerable sandals (*śrīpādukā*) of [Name] Ānandanātha."
Thus, in the worship of a male guru, [the formula is used]; in the worship of a female guru, the application is: "I worship the venerable sandals (śrīpādukā) of [Name] Ambā.
This is clearly stated in the Tantrasāra:
"O Parameśvarī, [the names] should be known to end with the word Ānandanātha."
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, those ending in "ambā" are declared to be feminine guru-mantras.

Thus [it is said]. The seed for the conventional usage of terms such as "Śrīpādukā" and so forth was previously demonstrated by the passage beginning with "having first uttered the word Śrī," etc. (vv. 299–301). Now, intending to state the lineage of gurus (*gurupakti*) of the sixteen [vidyās], he first describes the succession of gurus for the Kāmarāja-vidyā and for those vidyās composed of it, beginning with the words "The illuminator of the Supreme" (*paraprakāśaka*), etc. By this [he refers to]: 1. Paraprakāśa, 2. Paraśiva, 3. ...
Paraśakti, Kauleśvara, Śuklādevī, Pareśāna, and Kāmeśvaryambikā—these are the seven divine currents known as the Parā group. As it is stated in the sixteenth chapter of the Jñānārṇava:
"O Goddess, Paraśiva is considered to be the supreme illumination."
O Goddess, Parāśakti is likewise Kauleśvara, O Dear One;
Śuklā, Kuleśānī, Kāmeśvarī, and Ambikā follow in sequence.
These seven teachers, possessing divine forms, are known as the Parā [gurus].

Thus. Here, in the statement from the *Jñānārṇava*, there is the distinction that where [the text] says "kuleśāna," it reads "pareśāna. And in the *Tantrasāra*, where [it says] "kauleśvara," it reads "kauleśvarī.
(p. 660) [The five Siddha lineages.]
The enjoyment-play and the commitment (samaya) are the innate (sahaja), known as the deity;
the successions of the Siddhas called "the higher and lower" [and the seven successions of humans].
Now I shall speak of the multitudes of human beings. || 302 ||
Gagana, Viśvavimala, Madana, Bhuvana, Nīla, Ātmapriya, and [Nirmala]— these seven were the Mānavas. [Conclusion]
This is the lineage of gurus for the vidyā known as Kāmarāja. || 303 ||
302. Now, he describes the lineages of the Siddhas (*siddhaugha*) known as *parāpara*, which follow in sequence, beginning with the word "bhoga" and so forth. Thus: 1. Bhoga, 2.
Krīḍa, 3. Samaya, 4. Sahaja, and 5. Deva—these are the five lineages of the Siddhas known as *parāpara*. As it is said in that very same [text]:

O Dear One, listen: in the lineage of the Siddhas known as Parāpara, there is the Samaya [tradition] called Bhoga-klinna, as well as the one named Veda and the Sahaja; and in the lineage of humans (*mānavaugha*).

Thus, regarding the word *kroḍa*, there is the specific reading *klinna* in the *Jñānārṇava*. Furthermore, there is a difference in the sequence from the root text in the phrase "the innate [state] is the Veda" (*samayaḥ sahajo vedaḥ*), as well as a difference in the reading between the *Jñānārṇava* and the *Tantrasāra* in the word "deity" (*deva*), where the reading is "Veda" (*veda*). Regarding the statement from the *Jñānārṇava* beginning with "enjoyment as previously described" (*niruktabhogetyādi*), there is in some places a variant reading: "the innate [state] is the number of Vedas" (*samayaḥ sahajo vedasaṃkhyakāḥ*).

It is seen there that *bhoga*, *klinna*, *samaya*, and *sahaja*—these four, numbering according to the Vedas—are understood as the "streams of the Siddhas" (*siddhaugha*). Furthermore, in the *Tripurārcanarahasya*, these same four, beginning with *bhoga*, are accepted as the streams of the Siddhas. Regarding the word "deva," since the reading "veda" is observed in the *Jñānārṇava*, the *Tantrasāra*, and other texts, the reading "veda" [is adopted].
Even while considering the possibility of correctness, the reading stated in the original source has not been discarded due to the absence of more powerful evidence.

(303) Now, he states the Siddha-oghas as they follow in sequence, beginning with "Gagana" and so forth. Thus, there are seven other groups known as the Manava-oghas: 1. Gagana, 2. Viśva, 3. Vimala, 4. Madana, 5. Bhuvana, 6. Nīla, and 7. Ātmapriya. Herein...
In the *Jñānārṇava*:
"Gagana, Viśvavimala, Madana, and likewise Bhuvana" (p.
661). [The Sacrifice to One’s Own Guru and Others]
Near the multitude of human beings, the mantra-practitioner should worship his own triad of gurus;
these three are the Parameṣṭhin, the Parama, and one's own Guru.
[The Excellence of the Guru-lineage:
The lineage of the guru, which is most auspicious, should be known as superior to one's own lineage.
[The Excellence of the Mantra-giver:]
The supreme teacher who imparts the mantra should be known as even greater than one's father. || 305 ||
[What is to be done when the name of the Guru is unknown:
If one does not know the name of the Guru, then one should worship with this:
having uttered "Salutation to the Gurus," one should say "Salutation to the Pādukās. || 306 ||
In the *gurvanta* and *paramānta* [mantras], one should likewise say "namas gurubhyaḥ" (salutation to the gurus), and similarly say "namas ācāryebhyaḥ" (salutation to the teachers). || 307 ||
[Conclusion] This is the lineage of gurus for the general teacher and disciples.
[Praise of the Worship of the Lineage of Gurus]
Having worshipped the lineage of gurus, one then becomes Śrī Tripurā herself. || 308 ||
"Līlā is one's own self, then the beloved, and thereafter the humans numbering eight;
these others, O Supreme Goddess, are fixed and imperishable"—
in such statements by certain teachers, both the distinction of names and the number eight are observed.

Furthermore, since the *Tripurārcanarahasya* and the *Tantrasāra* also state that there are exactly eight [mantras] according to the aforementioned sequence, there would be a great contradiction with the statement in the root text (*mūla*) that "human beings consist of seven. Regarding the term "Kāmarāja": it should be understood that the aforementioned lineage of gurus belongs to the *vidyā* known as Kāmarāja, as well as to other *vidyās* composed of it. This is the meaning.

304. Regarding "mānava": the meaning is that one should worship the Guru, the Paramaguru, the Parāparaguru, and the Parameṣṭhiguru in the presence of those who have been explained as the streams of human [lineages].
[The lineage of gurus of Lopāmudrā] (p. 662).
I shall proclaim the lineage of gurus for the vidyā known as Lopāmudrā.
[In that regard, the Divine Current (divyaugha) consists of: Paramādya, Sivānta, Kāmeśvara, and Ambikā; thereafter— || 309 ||
The Divine Current (divyaugha) and the Great Current (mahaugha), and after that, Universal Bliss (sarvānanda);
then the Goddess Prajñā and Prakāśa—these constitute the seven [gurus] in the Divine Current. || 310 ||
The streams of Siddhas (siddhaughāḥ),
Divyacitra, Kaivalyadevyambā, and Mahodaya;
in the stream of Siddhas, there should be this group of four.
Now, the "multitude of men" (mānavaugha) is further explained: || 311 ||
The fourth is the lotus of the Lord who possesses the powers of consciousness and the universe;
the supreme Self is the captivating one, and non-greed is considered the eighth. (312)

309–310 | Having thus described the lineage of gurus (*gurukrama*) for the *Kāmarāja-vidyā*, he states the lineage of gurus for Lopāmudrā and the other *vidyās* composed of those [syllables] with the words beginning "Paramādyaḥ" and so forth. "Paramādyaḥ" refers to Paramaśiva.
And thus: 1. Paramaśiva; 2. Kāmeśvaryambikā; 3. Divyaugha; 4. Mahauṣa; 5. Sarvānanda; 6. [and so on].

Prajñādevī and Prakāśa—thus they conclude as the seven divine currents (*divyaugha*). (311–312) He speaks of the Siddha currents with the words "the divine," etc.: 1. Divya, 2. Citra, 3. Kaivalyadevyambā, and 4.
Mahodaya—these four are the Siddha currents. He speaks of the human currents (*mānavaugha*) with the words "human," etc.; likewise: 1. Cit, 2. Viśva, 3. [and so on].

Īśvara (4), Kamala (5), Manohara (6), Para (7), Svātmā (8), and Alobha—these are the eight [divisions of] the Mānavaugha. However, by the author of the *Tantrasāra*, through the passage "cid-viśva-śakti-īśvara-kamala-paramānanda-manohara-sukhānanda-pratibhāḥ | ete mānavaughāḥ," the variations in nomenclature for the four beginning with Manohara have been demonstrated. [This is stated] in the *Jñānārṇava*.
In the sixteenth chapter, the lineage of gurus for Lopāmudrā is shown as follows:
(p. 663) [The lineage of gurus for other vidyās] For all other vidyās, the gurus are the same in successive order. || 313 ||
Furthermore, there is another method: Parā and the rest constitute the Viśva;
Kāmeśvarī is the third, and Ambikā is the fourth.
O fair-faced one, hear now of the gurus of the lore known as Lopāmudrā:
Paramādyā, Śivādyā, Kāmeśvarī, and Ambikā.
The Divine Current (divyaugha) and the Great Current (mahaugha), then after that All-Bliss (sarvānanda);
thereafter comes the Goddess Prajñā Ambikā, and the seventh shall be the Light (prakāśa).
The divine Parākhya-guru, Lopāmudrā, Prabhāmaya,
Divya, Citra, Kaivalyadevī, Ambā, and Mahodaya.
The Siddhas are to be known as *parāpara*; listen, O beloved, to the *mānavaugha*:
Vidyā, Śakti, Viśva, and the fourth shall be Komala.
The fifth, O beloved, is supreme bliss (parānanda), known as "captivating" (manohara);
the seventh is self-bliss (svātmānanda), and the eighth is called "the manifest" (pratibha).
O Goddess, these are proclaimed as the gurus known as Aparā;
one should subsequently join them in the same manner as before, immediately after the eight.
O lotus-eyed one, the lineage of gurus for the disciples of Dakṣiṇāmūrti is declared to consist of three, or including one's own guru, or ending with nine.

Thus, because the *Niruktajñānārṇava* mentions "Kaivalyadevī Ambā" as the third Guru, and because it is stated that there should be a group of four in the *Siddhaugha*, the number four mentioned in the root text is correctly established. As for the statement in the *Tantrasāra*—"The Divine, the Variegated, Kaivalya, Divyāmbā, and Mahodaya: these are the five *Siddhaughas*"—which asserts that there are five *Siddhaughas*:
We consider that which was set forth [there] to be the result of a scribe’s error, due to its contradiction with the *Jñānārṇavāsrītattvacintāmaṇi*.
Even among the lineages of human gurus (*mānavaugha*), a difference in terminology is observed between them.
(313) "Of others" refers to those composed by Lopāmudrā. They are equal in proximity to the *mānavaugha*.
The meaning is that they are equal to one's own Guru and others as shown in the lineage of the Kāmarāja-vidyā-gurus beginning with the Mantrin.

By this, the meaning is that those who are the common gurus and their sandals (pādukās) which are specified for worship in the lineage of the Kāmarāja-vidyā-gurus, those very same ones are to be employed here in this sequence as well. For this very reason, it is stated in the sixteenth chapter of the Jñānārṇava:
"But the common gurus are indeed equal across all divisions," so it has been said. (p.
664) Liberation, the one called Amṛta, Prakāśa, and Ghorasvāmin;
then the Sadguru, and the Siddhaugha—these follow in sequence from above. || 315 ||
Udbhava, Parama, Sarvajña, and Tattva; likewise Siddha, Govinda, Śaṅkara, and he becomes Mānava. (316)
A man who is devoid of the lineage of gurus is excluded from the assembly;
one should not grant the highest assembly to one who is devoid of the tradition.
If a practitioner performs the ritual sequence without a guru, great misfortune shall befall him; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. || 318 ||
This doctrine of the Dakṣiṇāmūrtitantra has been proclaimed:
[The Instruction on the Worship of the Deity of the Tradition].
Having first worshipped the lineage of gurus, one should then worship the deities of the tradition. (319)
[Regarding the worship according to the Eastern Tradition:
One should worship the Eastern Tradition in the Wheel that Enchants the Three Worlds, which fulfills all desires, and in the Wheel that Agitates All. || 320 ||
One should worship the Dakṣiṇāmnāya within the wheel that bestows all prosperity (*sarvasaubhāgyada*), likewise within the wheel that accomplishes all aims (*sarvārthasādhaka*),
and within the wheel that provides all protection (*sarvarakṣākara*). || 321 ||

320. Having thus described the worship of the lineage of gurus (*gurukrama*), the author, now describing the worship of the deities of the traditions (*amnāyadevatā*), first states the sequence for the worship of the Eastern Tradition (*pūrvāmnāya*) with the verse beginning "trailokya... and so forth.

The meaning is that one should worship the Eastern Tradition within the previously mentioned three wheels—Trailokyamohana and the others—which consist of a square, a sixteen-petaled lotus, and an eight-petaled lotus, and which constitute the Wheel of Emanation (*sṛṣṭicakra*). Thus...
The worship of the Dakṣiṇāmnāya and the others should also be understood as occurring in their respective places within the wheel according to the method to be described [verse 321].

In the fourteen-spoked wheel, which bestows all prosperity; in the outer ten-spoked wheel, which accomplishes all aims; and in the inner ten-spoked wheel, which provides all protection—the meaning is that one should worship the Dakṣiṇāmnāya in this triad.
[The Worship according to the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya):
One should worship the Goddess, the Mistress of the Western Tradition, in the Central Wheel. [The Worship according to the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya):]
One should worship the Goddess, the mistress of the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya), within the eight wheels.
[The worship of the lower tradition (adha-āmnāya): One should worship the lower tradition in the wheel that bestows all accomplishments.
[The worship of the upper tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya):]
In the wheel consisting of all traditions, one should worship the Upper Tradition (Ūrdhvāmnāya).
[The libation: Then, by means of the application of the previously mentioned mantras, one should perform the libation in due order. || 324 ||
[The five pentads; therein, the five Lakṣmīs: “Śrīvidyā, as well as Lakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī, likewise Triśakti, and Sarvasāmrājyalakṣmī—these are proclaimed as the five. (325)

Regarding "the middle wheel": it is because it is clearly stated in the sixteenth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*: "O Goddess, one should worship the Western Tradition within the three middle wheels. And the "three middle wheels" refers to the wheel that removes all diseases (*sarvarogaharacakra*).
The wheel consisting of eight corners bestows all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*); the wheel consisting of three corners consists of universal bliss (*sarvānandamaya*);
and the central point (*madhyabindu*) is the wheel itself. Regarding the phrase "eight wheels":
here, O Goddess, one should worship the Kaubera tradition within these nine wheels.
Thus is the reading in the *Jñānārṇava*.

(323) "Bestower of all accomplishments" (*sarvasiddhiprada*) means in the central triangle (*madhyatrikoṇa*), according to the etymological definition (*nirukta*). Regarding "all" (*sarva*): it means in the wheel consisting of all traditions (*sarvāmnāyamaya*), that is, in the wheel consisting of universal bliss (*sarvānandamaya*) whose essence is the central point (*bindu*). This is also stated by the authors of the *Tantrasāra* regarding the *Vaindava* wheel.
The worship of the *Ūrdhvāmnāya* has been described. The sequence for the worship of the *Adha-āmnāya* is not seen in the *Jñānārṇava* and the *Tantrasāra*;
however, the sequence for the worship of the *Āmnāyas* should be sought in the *Tantrasāra* and other such works.
(325) Now, intending to describe the worship of the *Pañcapañcikā*, he first defines the *Pañcalakṣmī*: "Śrīvidyā," etc.
[The Five Sheaths] Śrīvidyā, Paraṃjyotis, Parā Niṣkalasāmbhavī,
Ajapā, and Mātṛkā— these are proclaimed as the five sheaths. || 326 ||
[The Five Kalpalatās]: "Śrīvidyā and Tvaritā, as well as Pārijāteśvarī, Tripuṭā, and Pañcakāmeśī—these are remembered as the five Kalpalatās. (327)
[The five wish-fulfilling cows]:
“Śrīvidyā at the seat of the dead,” “Sudhā,” “Amṛteśvarī,” and the one renowned as “Annapūrṇā”—these are remembered as the five wish-fulfilling cows. || 328 ||
[The Five Jewels]:
Śrīvidyā, Siddhalakṣmī, Mātaṅgī, Bhuvanēśvarī, and Vārāhī—these are proclaimed and celebrated as the Five Jewels. || 329 ||
“Śrīvidyā, Lakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī, Triśakti, and Sarvasāmrājyā—these are the five Lakṣmīs. Regarding this, it is stated in the sixteenth chapter of the Jñānārṇava:
‘Śrīvidyā, as well as Lakṣmī, and likewise Mahālakṣmī...’”
"Triśakti, Sarvasāmrājyā—these are proclaimed as the five Lakṣmīs. This is the reading.
(326) Regarding "Śrīvidyā": in the Jñānārṇava, however, the description of the five seats (pañcakauśa) is seen prior to the description of the five Lakṣmīs. The remainder is clear.

328. *Kāmadughāḥ* means "wish-fulfilling cows. Thus, in the sixteenth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*, in the passage beginning with "Śrīvidyā," where the reading "pañca kāmadughāḥ smṛtāḥ" (five are remembered as wish-fulfilling cows) is found, the reading "pañcaitāḥ kāmadhenavaḥ" (these five are the wish-fulfilling cows) is observed. However, in the *Tripurārcanarahasya*, the reading "kāmadughā" is employed in the sentence.
[The Place for the Worship of the Five Pentads] (p. 667):
"In the place of worship of Śrīvidyā, in the Greatly Exalted Cakrarāja, in the Great Treasury, she is seated upon a throne adorned by the assembly of Īśvarīs. (330)
[The Sequence of Worship with the Five Pentads]:
Having uttered, "And I worship the sandal (pādukā) which generates all auspiciousness," one should worship it as being enriched by the treasury of supreme light. || 331 ||
By this very procedure, one should worship the Pañcapañcikā.
[Conclusion] Having thus worshipped the entire Śrīvidyā, one should sacrifice around her. 332.
[The libation: One should again perform the libations either three times, once, or as one desires.
[The meditation on the Yoginīs who manifest powers such as atomization (aṇimā):]
Aṇimā and the others are red in color, three-eyed, and adorned with the moon as their crest-ornament. || 333 ||
Holding the gestures of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and a book with her left and right hands,
one should meditate upon the manifest Yoginī within the Trailokyamohana-cakra.

330. Regarding the phrase "in Śrīvidyā": this means in the *baindava-cakra*, which is the locus for the worship of Śrīvidyā; for it is clearly stated in the *Tripurārcanarahasya*: "In the *baindava* [cakra], the locus for the worship of Śrīvidyā, there are the five pentads (*pañcapañcikāḥ*)."

331. He states the sequence for the worship of the *pañcapañcikā* as explained in the *Nirukta*: "All... etc. The specific details, however, should be sought in the sixteenth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*. The phrase "endowed with the treasury of supreme light" (*paraṃjyotiḥkośāḍhyām*) is an epithet of Lakṣmī, meaning "consisting of supreme light. However, according to the reading in the *Jñānārṇava*, "endowed with the treasury and so forth" (*kośādyām*), the meaning is "the five pentads beginning with the five sheaths" (*pañcakośādi-pañcapañcikām*). In that regard:
First, there is the description of the five sheaths (pañcakośas) [in verses 333–334].

Now, he describes the meditation on the Yoginīs who manifest powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth, beginning with the word "aṇimā. The meaning is: in the wheel consisting of three circles outside the sixteen-petaled lotus in the Trailokyamohana [mandala]. This section is clear.
[The Place for the Worship of Aṇimā and the Others] One should worship Aṇimā on the right side of the western gate;
one should thoroughly worship Laghimā at the western [side] of the northern gate. || 335 ||
One should worship Mahimā at the eastern gate and Samarcaya at the northern gate;
and in the region of the southern gate, one should worship the one called Īśitva to the east.

And one attains the perfection known as mastery in the northwest, the perfection of irresistible will in the northeast, the perfection of liberation in the southeast, and the perfection of the fulfillment of desires in the southwest.
Below, there is the attainment of success, and above that, the fulfillment of all desires. [This is the instruction on the meditation upon the eight Bhairavas, beginning with Asitāṅga.
Then, one should meditate at the middle door in the sequence starting from the west.
[The Description of the Eight Bhairavas, beginning with Asitāṅga:
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmattabhairava, Kapālin, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra—these are the eight Bhairavas. (339)
[The Meditation on the Bhairavas] These [Bhairavas] are dark-complexioned, three-eyed, with faces terrifying due to their furrowed brows;
they hold a trident, a staff, a vetāla, a skull-cup, and a small bell.
Held by the hand of the Veda, with elephant hides as their upper garments draped over their shoulders.

338. Regarding the word "in the middle" (*madhye*): here, at this occasion of meditating on the manifest Yoginīs, the instruction for meditating on Bhairavas such as Asitāṅga and the others is for the purpose of worshipping the eight Śaktis beginning with Brāhmī. And he will say: "These [Yoginīs], situated upon the lap of the Bhairavas, should indeed be worshipped together with the Bhairavas" (verse 349). One should meditate [on them] in the four doors of the central square, in the sequence beginning from the west.
The Connection. (p. 669) [The meditation on the eight Śaktis; therein, Brahmāṇī:
Brahmāṇī is yellow in color and adorned with four faces.
With hands granting boons and fearlessness, and holding water-pots and rosaries that gleam. || 341 ||
[Māheśvarī: Māheśvarī is white in color, three-eyed, and holds a trident;
she bears a garland of skulls and an axe, and bestows spiritual accomplishments (siddhi). || 342 ||
Kaumārī, the goddess of maidenhood, is yellow in color and holds a spear and a javelin;
she grants boons and fearlessness with her hands, and she should be meditated upon by the most excellent practitioners. || 343 ||
[Vaiṣṇavyāḥ:
Vaiṣṇavī has a dark complexion, holds a conch, a discus, and a mace;
she bears a lotus in her hand and is adorned with divine ornaments. || 344 ||
[Vārāhyā]:
Vārāhī has a dark complexion and a boar’s face; she is beautiful and holds a plow, a pestle, a sword, and a shield in her arms. (345)
Indrāṇī [of Indrāṇī]: She has a dark complexion and her hands shine with red lotuses. || 346 ||
[Cāmuṇḍā]: Cāmuṇḍā is black in color, and she holds a trident, a hand-drum,
a sword, and a vetāla in her right hands.
He holds aloft a skull-cup, along with a snake, a shield, and a bell. || 347 ||
Mahālakṣmī, however, is yellowish in luster; the Supreme Goddess holds a lotus, a mirror, and a mātuluṅga fruit. (348)
[The specific procedure for the worship of the eight Śaktis as explained]:
These [Śaktis], seated upon the lap of Bhairava, should indeed be worshipped together with the Bhairavas. (349)

One should worship the site of worship, beginning with Mahendra and ending with the [other] directions, either sequentially or, alternatively, in order at the western, northern, eastern, and southern gates. 350.
Together with the vowels in pairs—both even and odd—situated in the directions of wind, Indra, fire, and the Rakshasas;
the mantras of the Bhairavas consist of short syllables, while those of the Mothers take long forms. (351)
[The Worship with Mudrās]:

At the inner gate, one should meditate upon Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇī and the others, positioned toward the west and so forth; they are red in color and hold nooses and goads, while recollecting their respective mantras. (352)
349. Now, he states the specific procedure for the worship of the eight Śaktis, beginning with Brāhmī, who have been etymologically defined: "Bhairava...

The meaning is that these eight Śaktis, beginning with Brāhmī, situated upon the lap of the Bhairavas—namely, seated upon the laps of the eight previously mentioned Bhairavas such as Asitāṅga—are to be worshipped together with those Bhairavas, Asitāṅga and the rest.
350–351 | Now, he specifically defines the place of worship for the eight Śaktis, beginning with the words "mahendrāt" (from Mahendra).

Thus, the meaning is that one should worship them in sequence, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise until the northeast corner. He states another sequence with the words "athavā" (or else):

thus, the meaning is that one should worship them at the four doors starting from the west and ending with the south, as well as at the four corners starting from the northwest and ending with the southwest.

Regarding the term "pair" (*yugma*): the connection is that one should worship together with the odd vowels, such as the first, third, and so on, and with the even vowels, such as the second, fourth, and so on.

He specifies this very division of vowels [with the words] "the short syllables" (*hrasvārṇā*). Thus, the meaning is that in the case of the Bhairava-mantra and others, one should employ the eight short vowels beginning with *a*, while in the case of the Śakti-mantra and others, one should employ the long vowels beginning with *ā*.

Although the status of being a short vowel (*hrasvārṇatva*) is violated in the case of the eleventh and subsequent vowels, there is nonetheless no fault; for the term "short vowels" serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaka*) of each preceding pair of vowels.
352–353. At the inner gate—that is, at the four gates of the inner square—starting from the west [and proceeding clockwise]...
One should worship the three-sectioned [maṇḍala] while uttering the Vāgbhava seed-syllable.
[Regarding the rule for direction in the worship with mudrās:
one should proceed in the sequence starting from the west, as before, in the cardinal and intermediate directions. (353)
[In this regard, the specific detail:
One should worship the *yonimudrā* through the sequential application of upward and downward movement.
[The conclusion.]
May these manifest Yoginīs, residing in the three and four squares, protect [us]. || 354 ||
Then one should worship the wheel named Trailokyamohana;
[this is the nature and worship of Tripurā].
In the first enclosure is the goddess Tripurā, the sovereign of the wheel.
One should visualize her as red, with three eyes, and holding a noose and a goad;
one should worship her in front of the *aṇimā* siddhi while recollecting her mantra.
Having performed the "All-Agitating" [mudrā], one should worship the Buddha. || 356 ||

The meaning is that one should worship the previously shown mudrās, beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇī. "Recalling their respective mantras" means that the ritual application should be performed in the manner previously described by uttering the seed-syllable (bīja), such as: "I worship the *śrīpādukā* of Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇī," and so forth. "In the west, etc. is as before.
The meaning is: "by means of the sequence of worship of the eight powers mentioned previously.

(354) He states the distinction between the *khecarī* and *yoni* mudrās with the words "above and below": the meaning is that one should worship the *khecarī* mudrā at the upper aperture and the *yoni* mudrā below. "Residing in the triangle and square" means situated within the three squares mentioned previously.

355–356 | Regarding "trailokya": one should worship with the formula, *namaḥ trailokyamohanacakrāya*. This is likewise stated in the *Tripurārcanarahasya*. However, in the *Tantrasāra*, the practice is stated as: *namaḥ trailokyamohanacaturasracakrāya*. (395) Regarding "these": thus, the ritual application is as follows: "May these Kula-Kaulika Yoginīs in the Sarvārthasādhaka-cakra—along with their mudrās, siddhis, weapons, vehicles, and retinues—be worshipped with all the ritual offerings."

396–397. Now, while describing the worship of Sarvajñā and the other Nigarbha Yoginīs within the *Sarvarakṣākara-cakra* (the wheel that provides all protection), he states their essential nature: "The Book," etc., and "The West," etc. One should worship these [Yoginīs] starting from the west, moving counter-clockwise.
"One should worship in the lineage-yoni [diagram] by way of reverse order, beginning from the west," it is said.

"By means of the letters from *ma* to *kṣa*" means that, as before, one should worship the ten letters beginning with *ma* and ending with *kṣa*, one by one in sequence, [addressing] the Goddess who consists of all knowledge and who destroys all diseases. (p. 683)
And likewise, she whose nature is the support of all, and who removes all sins. || 398 ||

[One should worship] the Goddess who consists of all bliss, whose very nature is universal protection, and who bestows the fruits of all desires through offerings such as perfumes and other services. (399)
[The worship of the wheel and the worship of the Mistress of the Wheel:
The practitioner of mantra should meditate upon the wheel that provides all protection, and upon the supreme Tripuramālinī, the Mistress of the Śrīcakra, in front of the Abode of All-Knowledge. 400.

One should worship Viṣṇu, the Lord of Jinas, who holds a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows, and possesses the splendor of a white lotus; having displayed the mudrās and so forth, one should manifest the one known as Mahāṅkuśa. || 401 ||
[The Offering of Worship] These Nigarbha Yoginīs are in the Sarvarakṣākara pada;
one should visualize them as being with their mudrās in the maṇḍala, and so forth, as before. || 402 ||
The meaning is that one should worship after having first applied [the mantra]. Thus, the formula takes such forms as: "I worship the *śrīpādukā* of the goddess Sarvajñā, obeisance (*namaḥ*);
I worship the *śrīpādukā* of the goddess Sarvaśakti, obeisance," and so forth. In all cases, the application of either the *dvitārī* or other [mantras] is as previously described.
397–399 | Next, he describes the ten Nigarbha-yoginīs with the passage beginning with *sarvajñām* and ending with *sarvepsitaphalapradām*.
The phrase "one should worship with offerings such as perfumes" (*gandhādyair upacārair yajet*) is to be connected to every [verse].
400–401 | Regarding *sarvarakṣā*: the connection is that "one should worship the wheel. Thus, [the mantra is] *oṃ sarvarakṣākara-antardaśāracakrāya*.
The formula is: "I worship the venerable *pādukā* of the Mistress of the *Tripurāmālinīcakra*, *namaḥ*.

In the *Tantrasāra*, however, following the three *tārās*, the conjunction of the seed-syllables *hrīṃ klīṃ blūṃ* is seen at the beginning. Regarding "the Great": [she is] the seal (*mudrā*) of the Great *Aṅkuśa* of all, possessing the characteristics previously described.
402. Now he describes the sequence for the offering of worship to Mūladevī, beginning with "etā" (these): And thus:
[The conclusion of the *sthiticakra* and the promise to describe the *saṃhāracakra*] "The *sthiticakra* has been fully explained; now I shall describe the *saṃhāra*. (403)
[The Eight Secret Yoginīs beginning with Vāśinī]:
According to the path of the Western Tradition (paścimāmnāya), there are the eight deities beginning with Vāśinī;
[their essential nature].
Resplendent like the newly risen sun, they were adorned with every kind of ornament.
Holding a bow, arrows, a rosary, and a book in their hands,
the practitioner of mantra should worship with the eight groups of letters using the mantras prescribed for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
[The state of these being on eight spokes:
These secret yoginīs reside in the first enclosure. || 405 ||
The ritual application is as follows: "May the Nigarbha Yoginīs in the Sarvarakṣākara-cakra, together with their mudrās, siddhis, weapons, vehicles, and retinues, be worshipped with all offerings.
(403) Regarding the term "sthitīti": it refers to that which consists of this triad—bestowing all prosperity, accomplishing all aims, and providing all protection.

This means the wheel of persistence (*sthiticakra*). He makes a formal declaration to describe the wheel of withdrawal (*saṃhāracakra*), which consists of the three [wheels] to be described hereafter, beginning with the words "the withdrawal" and so forth (verses 404–405).
In that regard, first, within the eight-spoked wheel that removes all diseases, [he describes] the secret yoginīs, Vāsinyā and the others.

While describing the worship, he states their essential nature: "The new sun," etc. As for Vaśinī and the others—the eight Vāgdevīs beginning with Vaśinī—they were indicated in the fifteenth chapter on Nyāsa by the passage beginning, "One should place Vaśinī and the others in these locations. Regarding them, it is stated in the commentary on that [chapter]: Vaśinī, Kāmeśvarī, Modinī, Vimalā, Aruṇā, Jayinī...
All eight known as the *Īśvarīs* of the Kaula tradition have thus been specifically shown. Regarding the phrase "as stated in the *Nyāsa*":

one should worship these very goddesses with the mantras stated in the previously demonstrated *Nyāsa*. By the phrase "with the eight groups" (*vargāṣṭakena*), the meaning is that one should perform worship by applying the eight groups of consonants in sequence before each of the eight [goddesses], beginning with *Vaśinī*. And in this way, having uttered the sixteen vowels beginning with *A*,...
The formula for worship is as follows: "I worship the venerable sandals of Vāgdevatā residing in Varalūṃ; obeisance," and so forth;
however, the application of the three Tārās and other mantras is exactly as before.
(p. 685) [Cakra-worship]
Then, one should worship the wheel named Sarvarogahara (the Remover of All Diseases).
[The Worship of the Mistress of the Wheel:
The wise practitioner should meditate upon Śrī Tripurāsiddhā in front of Vāsinī. (406)
[The essential form of the Mistress of the Wheel:
She is the color of the *javā* flower, holding a noose, a goad, a bow, and an arrow.
[The display of mudrās, etc.]
Having manifested the khecarīmudrā, one should worship Śakti through Māyā.
[The Offering of Worship] These secret yoginīs, who remove all diseases from their feet, should be visualized as being together with their mudrās within the wheel,
and so forth, as previously described. (408)
The wise one should worship the arrows in the four directions starting from the west, located within the eight corners and situated outside the triangle. (409)
[The nature of the arrows:
They have the luster of the young morning sun, are adorned with red garments, enriched by the beauty of red garlands, and possess forms intoxicated with youth. (410)
Adorned with a noose, goad, bow, and five flower-arrows,
followed in sequence by a pair consisting of an arrow, bow, noose, and hook.
406–407 | Regarding "sarvaroga": the formula is *namaḥ sarvarogaharāṣṭāracakrāya*. Regarding "one should meditate":

the formula is *śrītripurāsiddhācakranāyikā-śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi namaḥ*. Although the term *cakranāyikā* is not explicitly mentioned in the root text (*mūla*) here, it has been inserted because its usage is observed everywhere else.

[The Names of the Arrows and the Order of Worship] The best of practitioners should worship Jṛmbhaṇa, Mohana, Vaśa, and Stambhana according to the sequence prescribed for the ritual placement (nyāsa). 412.
[The Worship of the Limb Deities]:
One should worship the limb deities (aṅgadevatā) between the weapon (astra) and the triangle (trikoṇa). || 413 ||
One should worship in the central wheel of the triangle with the root-mantra;
one should sacrifice using it both in its entirety and in its individual parts, according to the distinction between the syllables and the non-syllabic.
One should worship the triangle with the three seed-syllables of Bālā, the three peak-syllables (kūṭa) of Bhairavī, and the three peak-syllables of Sundarī. || 415 ||
One should worship Kāmeśvarī, the power (śakti) of Rudra, in the fire-wheel (agnicakra);
one should worship Vajreśvarī, the power of Viṣṇu, in the sun-wheel (sūryacakra). || 416 ||
One should worship Bhagamālā, the power of Brahmā, in the Soma-cakra;
one should worship the Goddess, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, in the Bindu-cakra. (417)
In Kāma, he was Mitrīśanātha; in Jāla, he was Ṣaṣṭhīśanāthaka;
in Pūrṇa, he was Uḍḍīśanātha; and in Oḍra, he was Caryānātha. || 418 ||
One should worship Kāmeśvarī with the Vāgbhava syllable after meditating upon her as before;
likewise, having meditated upon Cakreśvarī, one should worship her with the Kāmarāja syllable. || 419 ||
One should worship Bhageśī with the *Śaktikūṭa* mantra, meditating as before;
one should lead her into the second enclosure within the wheel that bestows all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhiprada*). || 420 ||
There, one should visualize the Secret Yoginī, who bestows all accomplishments, holding a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows; she is red in color and most beautiful. (421)
Having displayed the seed-syllable mudrā, one should worship the supreme Śakti.
These [are called] "the most secret" (atirahasya); from that word [comes] also "the yoginīs.
In the wheel consisting of all accomplishments, [the words] "ocean" and so forth are as before. 423.

[In the Bindu-cakra: The Worship of Śrī Tripurasundarī] In the supreme Bindu-cakra, which consists of all-bliss, [one should worship] the Supreme Goddess, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman and who is the embodiment of the supreme nectar. || 424 ||
The Goddess who is the sovereign of all wheels, likewise the sovereign of all mantras, the sovereign of all mudrās, and likewise the sovereign of all vidyās. || 425 ||
Furthermore, [one should worship] the Sovereign of all Pīṭhas, the Sovereign of all Vīras,
the Sovereign of all Yogas, and also the Sovereign of all Siddhis.
The supreme Mātṛkā, who effects creation, maintenance, and destruction,
together with her mudrās, weapons, wheels, and vehicles.
[He saw] the Great Goddess, both supreme and non-supreme, who bestows worldly enjoyment and liberation, together with her retinue, her supernatural powers, and the deities. || 428 ||

423. Regarding the word "etā" (these): thus, the ritual application (*prayoga*) is as follows: "May these most secret *yoginīs*, together with their mudrās, siddhis, weapons, vehicles, and retinues, being worshipped with all ritual offerings (*upacāra*), abide within the wheel (*cakra*) consisting of all accomplishments.
(p. 688) [She who is] served even by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and other lords of sages.
Having thus beheld the illustrious Tripurasundarī with the mind alone, [he should worship her]. 429.
The wise one should worship the Śrīpādukā, which is the power (śakti) of the Supreme Brahman and the Self.
[The Worship of the Vaindava-cakra:
One should fully worship the Vaindava-cakra, which consists of universal bliss. || 430 ||
[The Worship of the Mistress of the Cakra:

By means of the invocation mantra, the practitioner of mantra should worship the Mistress of the Bhairavī-cakra before the Goddess with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and other offerings. 431.
Having displayed the *yonimudrā* and other mudrās, one should worship the supreme Śakti;
or else, according to the *Tattvavimarṣiṇīmata*, one should worship her there in that very manner. (432)
A central triangle with an intervening space—this is declared to be the "vision" (darśana).
With "Hauṃ Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya Hauṃ," one should worship Śiva again;
this is the sixfold sequence of vision using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. || 433 ||
[The Offering of Worship to the Root Goddess:

Having uttered "etāḥ parāparā" (these, both supreme and non-supreme), followed by the word "rahasye" (in the secret place), then having extracted the word "yoginyaḥ" (O Yoginīs), and finally from the word "sarvānandamaye" (in that which consists of universal bliss) [one should offer]. 434.
In the Great Wheel and in the Bindu, she is the very nature of the Supreme Brahman;
she is the Power from the state of supreme nectar, the state of the Sovereign of all wheels.
From the word *sarvamantreśvarī*, the term *sarvavidyeśvarī* follows;
then the terms *sarvavīreśvarī* and *sarvapīṭheśvarī*. (436)
434–438 | Now he states the mantra for the offering of worship, beginning with the words "etā" and so forth. Thus:
"These [deities], the Yoginīs of the supreme and the non-supreme secret, reside in the Great Cakra consisting of universal bliss—the Bindu-cakra—which is the very nature of the Supreme Brahman.
From the term "Sovereign of All Yogas" (*sarvayogeśvarī*), the title "Sovereign of All Speech" (*sarvavāgīśvarī*) is derived.
The sovereign of all accomplishments, the mother of the origin of the entire world. || 437 ||
Together with their wheels, oceans, and accomplishments, likewise equipped with weapons, vehicles, and retinues, and accompanied by all great offerings—
at the end of Tripura, she is called Sundarī by means of the supreme and the non-supreme mantra.
The third [form], Parāparā, is at the end; and likewise, having performed the worship, one should offer the oblation to the Goddess, saying: "May they be worshipped. || 439 ||

The supreme nectar-śaktis, sovereigns of all cakras, sovereigns of all mantras, sovereigns of all vidyās, sovereigns of all vīras, sovereigns of all pīṭhas, sovereigns of all yogas, sovereigns of all speech, sovereigns of all siddhis— the mothers who give birth to the entire world,
together with their cakras, mudrās, siddhis, weapons, vehicles, and retinues.

The ritual application (*prayoga*) is as follows: "May they be worshipped with all the services of worship—by means of the supreme (*parā*), the supreme-and-non-supreme (*parāparā*), and the non-supreme (*aparā*) worship dedicated to Mahātripurasundarī.

However, in the *Tantrasāra*, it is stated: "Here, in the Bindu-cakra consisting of universal bliss, [she is] Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme-and-Non-Supreme Power (*parāparaśakti*), the Mistress of all the Cakras, presiding over the Cakra of the Mistress of Consciousness (*saṃvitti*)."

O you who delude the three worlds, who fulfill all desires, who cause universal agitation, who bestow all good fortune, who accomplish all aims, who provide all protection, who remove all diseases, who grant all perfections;

O you who have manifested the entire assembly of the *śrīcakra*, including the manifest, the secret, the more secret, and the most secret traditions of the *kula*; O you who are the innermost secret and the supreme secret of the *kaulinī* womb!
The supreme and secret [goddess] surrounded by the entire assembly of Yoginīs— the venerable Tripurā, Tripureśī, Tripurasundarī, Tripuravāsinī, the venerable Tripurā,
Tripuramālinī, Tripurāsiddhā, and Tripurāmbā;
she whose lotus feet are worshipped by the presiding deities of their respective cakras— the venerable Mahātripurasundarī, the eternal Goddess (Nityādevī).

The Sovereign of all wheels, the Sovereign of all mantras, the Sovereign of all vidyās, the Sovereign of all sacred seats, the Sovereign of all desires, the Sovereign of all principles, the Sovereign of all heroes, the Enchantress of the three worlds, the Mother of the origin of the universe— consisting of all wheels,
together with the Mistress of those wheels, along with their mudrās, siddhis, weapons, vehicles, and retinues.

It is stated that one should offer the special *arghya* water, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and flowers into the left hand of the principal Goddess with the words: "May the venerable Mahātripurasundarī be worshipped and gratified by means of all ritual services (*upacāra*) through the supreme and non-supreme worship.
(p. 690) [One should offer] substances produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*, combined with self-arisen flowers (*svayambhukusuma*).
The practitioner of mantra should worship Sundarī with seven hundred unbroken grains of rice. || 440 ||
[Furthermore, the instruction on worship: Having again offered water for the feet and so forth, one should worship Śrīvidyā as follows.
[Again, the offering of the three arghyas:]
Having again uttered the three principles (tritattva), one should offer the arghya water three times.
[The worship with various offerings:
One should worship with various substances such as perfumes, sandalwood, musk, yellow orpiment, agallochum, saffron, red sandalwood, vermilion, and other diverse materials. 442.
[The invocation mantras for the offering of requisites; therein, the invocation mantra for the water for the feet:
O Goddess, accept this water for the feet, combined with perfumes and flowers and joined with fragrant water, for the sake of accomplishing all desires and aims. (443)
O Goddess of the Suras, accept this *arghya*— provided with *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice, and anointed with fragrant sandalwood— for the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life. 444.
O Śrī Tripurasundarī, accept this water for sipping (ācamanīya), which is well-perfumed and purified with clean silk cloths. 445.
[Of the *madhuparka*:
"Accept this *madhuparka*, a pleasant and most charming mixture of curd, clarified butter, and honey, for the attainment of dharma, kama, and artha. (446)
442. Now, he states in general the recommended offerings for the worship of the Goddess: "Gandha" etc.
(p. 691): [Of the scent:
with moon, sandalwood, musk, gorocana, agallochum, and saffron.
"I prepare a fragrant offering, moistened with fresh pine resin. || 447 ||
With devotion, I prepare this flower— variegated, stainless, beautiful, perfumed with scented waters, fragrant, and in full bloom. 448.

448. He speaks of the offering of flowers, beginning with "variegated" (*vicitram*). "Perfumed" (*vāsitam*) means scented with fragrant waters—that is, made fragrant with sandalwood water. Here, this should be noted: offerings such as perfumes, flowers, and incense that are tainted by defects such as being owned by another or having been smelled by others must be avoided in worship. As it is said in the *Gandharva-tantra*:
In the fourteenth chapter: [One should avoid] those belonging to others, as well as those smelled by them, or those afflicted by their magical rites (kṛtyā),
and likewise flowers, incense, perfumes, and other such offerings.

O Goddess, a man who offers food that has been smelled to the Deity shall fall into hell. O Supreme Sovereign, one should not worship Maheśvarī, the Great Tripurasundarī, with flowers or leaves that have become stale.
All stale leaves, flowers, and fruits are to be avoided,
as are white and red lotuses, water lilies, and blue lotuses.
For these [flowers], one should entertain a suspicion that they have become stale after five days;
for other flowers, however, until there is a change in their fragrance.

Thus, it is stated that for the lotus (*padma*), the water-lily (*kumuda*), and the blue lotus (*utpala*), there is no staleness for up to five days; however, for others, there is no staleness as long as their fragrance persists. Regarding the worship of Tripurā, he specifies the recommended leaves and flowers in that very same [text]:
"The *vakula*, *kesara*, *vajra*, *mālya*, *kunda*, and *śālmala*..."
Karavīra, arka-flower, bandhūka, and likewise lotus.
Mālatī, mallikā, jātī, yūthikā, and likewise mādhavī; tagara, karṇikāra, droṇa, utpala, and campaka.
[The proportions for the sixteen-ingredient incense:
Guggulu, sarala wood, dāru, leaves produced from the Malaya mountains, hrībera, aguru, kuṣṭha, jaggery, sarjarasa, and ghanasāra. (449)
The Aśoka, the Kumuda, the Śephālikā, the Kadambaka,
the Ketakī, the Vanamālā, the Kusumbha, and likewise the Kiṃśuka.
Kahlāra, vakula, as well as lavaṅga and nāgakeśara—
indeed, among all varieties of flowers, these always belong to Tripurā.
These alone are pleasing; one should not worship Śivā with other leaves. Among leaves, however, the bilva leaf as well as the sprout of the madana tree [are acceptable].
Likewise, the durvā sprout is prescribed; one should not employ any other leaf.
Also, the mallikā, mālatī, kunda, droṇa, and the white lotus [are recommended].
"O Great Goddess, during the bright fortnight, one should offer to Tripurā all varieties of flowers, as well as the red lotus and the javā."
O wise one, O Goddess, that which brings delight to the Goddess and bestows the fruit of all desires—
even a flower made of jewels or fashioned from gold and other precious materials—
can never equal a red lotus with a diamond at its center.

Thus, even for flowers that have been prescribed, their offering is forbidden if they are tainted by defects such as having a pungent odor or being contained in an impure vessel; as it is said in that very same [text]:
"That which has a pungent odor, lacks fragrance, or is defiled by worms, hair, and the like..."
[The food] held in an impure vessel by hands, [offered] by those of contemptible character with [garments of] rags.
If one does not offer what has been brought to the Goddess even out of negligence, it causes fault;
likewise with items brought after bathing, those that are stale, those obtained by begging, or those of black color.
One should not worship with buds that have opened by themselves, fallen away by themselves, or dropped to the ground, except for those of the *campaka* and the lotus.

And so forth. In this manner, other authoritative texts (*pramāṇa*) concerning prescribed and prohibited flowers should also be understood from sources such as the *Muṇḍamālā*, the *Yoginītantra*, and the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*.
(p. 693) [One should take] *harītakī*, *nakha*, lac, *jaṭāmāṃsī*, and *śailaja*.
They know the sixteen-ingredient incense to be used in rites for the gods and for the ancestors.
[The measure of other types of incense:
Honey, clarified butter, sugar, sandalwood, agallochum, guggulu, and usīra—these seven alone constitute this incense which is dear to Caṇḍikā. (451)

449–450 | He states the measure of the sixteen-ingredient incense (*ṣoḍaśāṅgadhūpa*) with the verse beginning "guggulu" and so forth. *Sarala* is a specific type of tree. Amarasimha states: "The *pītadru*, *sarala*, and *pūtikāṣṭha* [are synonyms]. *Dāru* is *devadāru*. Amarasimha states: "The seven names—*sakrapādapa*, *paribhadraka*, *bhadradāru*, *drū*, *kilima*, *pītadāru*, and *dāru*, as well as *pūtikāṣṭha*—are synonyms for *devadāru*. Regarding this:
By the word *dāru*, only *devadāru* (deodar) is meant;
*harītakī*, *mustā*, *nakhī*, *māṃsī*, *jatu*, *śailaja*, *devadāru*,
*kuṣṭha*, *guḍa*, and *sarjarasa*— this is declared by the lords of sages to be the ten-ingredient incense (*daśāṅgadhūpa*).

Thus, it is seen in the *Daśāṅgadhūpapramāṇa* within the seventh chapter of the *Kaulāvalīnirṇaya*: "Patra" refers to *tejapatra*. "Malayasambhava" refers to sandalwood (*candana*). *Hrībera* is known as *netravālā*, a specific fragrant substance.
