According to Amara: "Bāla, *hrībera*, *barhiṣṭha*, *udīcya*, and *keśāmbu* are synonyms. *Sarjarasa* is the resin of the *sāla* tree. *Yakṣadhūpa*... [is]... [the incense of the Yakṣas].

According to Amara, *sarjarasa*, *arāla*, and *sarvarasa* are synonyms. *Ghana* refers to *mustā* (cyperus rotundus), commonly known as *muthā*. According to Hemacandra: "The word *ghana* is used for the dense, the firm, firmness, expansion, a mallet, a cloud, a multitude, and *mustā*; it also denotes a type of middle dance and musical instrument.
*Nakha* is a specific fragrant substance; according to Hemacandra: "Furthermore, *nakha* refers to a fragrant substance, while *nakha* [as a noun] also means a fingernail and a type of grass."

*Śailaja*, known as *śilājatu*, is a specific fragrant substance. According to Amara: "Kālānusārya, vṛddhāśman, puṣpa, sīta, and śivā are synonyms for *saileya*. And according to Medinī: "*Saileya* refers to *galaparṇī* and *saindhava*; it is masculine when referring to *śailaja* (bitumen) and a bee, and has other genders when meaning 'equal to stone' (*śilātulya*). The word *siṣṭa* is clear. In the fourteenth chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*:
Patra, musta, nakha, kuṣṭha, jaṭāmāṃsī,
śailaja, sarala, devadāru, jatu, sarja, and sandalwood.
Mixed with cow's ghee, camphor, and a plentitude of sugar,
this sixteen-ingredient great incense bestows delight upon the Sixteenth [Form].
Thus [ends the section].
451. Regarding "madhu": *uśīra* is the root of the *vīraṇa* grass.
(p. 694) [The measure for other types of incense.]
Alternatively, guggulu mixed with aguru, camphor, sandalwood, honey, clarified butter, jaṭāmāṃsī, saileya, and saffron— this incense, blended with these, is dear to Pārvatī. (452)
[The Procedure for Offering Incense:

Having sprinkled the incense vessel with the *astra* mantra and worshipped it with the heart mantra followed by the word "anunā," one should then worship it with the mantra "O Mother of Mantras, victory! Svāhā! accompanied by the sound of "jaya."
Sounding a bell with the left hand, one should present incense and lamps. || 453 ||
[The prayer-mantra for incense: Produced from the essence of trees, rich in fragrance, this is the most excellent scent;
worthy of being smelled by all the gods, may this incense be accepted. || 454 ||
Alternatively, one should incense [the deity] with incenses preceded by the root mantra:
"I manifest this divine incense, produced from fire through the combination of fragrant substances and ghee, which destroys evil tendencies. (455)
This lamp is a great illumination, a magnificent light that dispels the darkness everywhere; it is a radiance both internal and external—please accept this lamp. (456)

453. *Dhūpeti* (one should offer incense). By means of the *astra-mantra*, namely *phaṭ*; by the *hṛdaya-mantra*, namely *namaḥ*—this is the meaning of "by the heart-mantra. Thus, having sprinkled the incense vessel with *phaṭ*, one should worship it with *dhūpāya namaḥ*. Regarding *dhūpeti*: by the phrase "one should present incense and lamps," even for the offering of lamps which will be described later, one should follow the aforementioned sequence: *oṃ jayadhvanimantramātaḥ svāhā*.
It should be understood that one should employ [the rite].
(p. 695) [An alternative procedure therein: Or else, the wise person should offer a lamp in another manner. || 457 ||
[Another mantra of supplication:
I offer this lamp, which blazes incessantly at the tip of a wick saturated with ghee, the bestower of divine vision. (458)
[The rule for offering incense:
A wise person should offer incense either to the left or directly in front. [The prohibition against placing incense on the ground, etc.:]
One should not place the incense on the ground, nor on a seat, nor in a jar. || 459 ||
[The rule regarding the offering of lamps:
The practitioner of mantra should display a ghee lamp on the right and an oil lamp on his own left; he should show a very beautiful row of lamps all around. (460)
[The seven kinds of lamps:
A ghee lamp is first;
then those produced from sesame oil, mustard seed, resinous fruit-extract, or arising from water-lilies.
Lamps made from curd and lamps made from food are proclaimed to be the seven kinds. || 461 ||
[The five kinds of wicks: Those made from silk thread, or those made from thread containing *darbha* grass;
or those born from *śāl* wood, or from the *badarī* tree, or else produced from the interior of a fruit-shell.
The wicks for the purposes of lamps are always remembered as being of five kinds. || 462 ||
[Commended lamp vessels: A vessel made of metal, of wood, of iron, of clay, or born of coconut;
even one produced from the king of grass (palmyra) is praised as a lamp vessel. || 463 ||
In this manner, one should prepare a lamp that brings delight to the eyes.
[The Procedure for Offering Lamps] One should illuminate the incense below, extending the lamp as far as the lotus. || 464 ||
[The prayer-mantra for the offering of garlands:
Through the combination of lotuses, blue lotuses, kahlāra lilies, karavīra flowers, and others, I present these fragrant and sweet-smelling garlands. (465)
With a mind full of supreme bliss, one should give sweet substances as a gift. || 466 ||
[The libation: One should satisfy [the deities] with sweet substances mixed with honey as if they were nectar;
one should satisfy the Supreme Deity with nectar and nectarian substances. 467.
[Instruction on Cooking the Caru]: Thereafter, one should cook the caru of cow’s milk in the consecrated fire.
[The Procedure for Cooking the Caru]
In a new vessel made of copper or other materials, which has been cleansed with a mantra; || 468 ||
464–465 | "Let them shine," etc. "As far as the lotuses" means as far as the [range of the] vision. Regarding the lamp, he states a specific rule in the fourteenth chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*:
"A row of lamps should be prepared; never a single lamp."
"O Supreme Goddess, three lamps or five lamps should be offered;
one should never offer fewer than this to Tripurā.
Thus [it is said]. Regarding "Kamalā," the fruit of offering garlands is stated in the fourteenth chapter of the Gandharva Tantra:
Whatever fruit a man obtains by making a garland from any of these varieties of flowers and offering it to Mahādevī—
even with thousands of mouths, the Lord would not be able to describe that.

Thus, here, by the phrase "of these," the previously shown prescribed flowers are referred to (vv. 468–472). Regarding the word "tataḥ" (then): the ellipsis is "consecrated according to the sequence stated in the eighth chapter. (p. 697) [He should take] rice grains produced from *śāli* rice, consecrated with the root mantra.
Having poured out fifteen handfuls while recollecting the mantra of the weapon, || 469 ||
Having covered the mouth of the vessel and washed it with the *kavaca* mantra,
the lord of practitioners, facing east, should cook the *caru* with the root mantra.
Once the vessel has been heated with clarified butter using the *sruva* ladle, one should perform the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) there. [Regarding the removal of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*):
One should remove that vessel from the fire with the Root Mantra, and set it down with the Armor Mantra (*kavaca*). || 471 ||
In a pavilion strewn with *kuśa* grass over which mantras have been recited, the Guru, according to the prescribed rite, should divide that [caru];
he should then assign one portion to the deity. (472)
One should offer another oblation into the fire, and yet another as the supreme bali;
furthermore, one *caru* is prescribed for the rite of the *ārātrika* lamp-waving as well.
[The Ārātrika, including the preparation of the eight-petaled lotus:
Then, on a surface made of gold, silver, or bell-metal, one should fashion a lotus with eight petals using saffron. (474)
He describes the sequence for cooking the *caru* with the words beginning with "by the *astra*" (*astreṇa*). By the *astra-mantra*, namely *phaṭ*.
The meaning is that one should place fifteen handfuls of rice grown in winter (*haimantika*)—that is, produced from winter grains—into a *caru*-pot made of copper.
Regarding the *astramanu*: likewise, having covered the mouth of the *caru*-pot with *phaṭ*, [one should proceed] with the *kavaca-mantra*, namely the mantra *hūṃ*.

The connection is: "having washed [the vessel], one should cook the *caru*. By the word "with the armor" (*kavacena*), the meaning is that one should cause [the deity] to descend with the syllable *huṃ*.

(472–473) Having thus described the cooking of the *caru* in this sequence, he states its division into four parts, beginning with the words "that" (*tam*) and so forth: having divided that *caru* into four parts, one should offer one to the deity, offer the second as an oblation (*homa*) into the fire, and give the other as a sacrificial offering (*bali*).
The meaning is that one should employ it in the ritual of the *ārātrika* lamp-offering.
(p. 698) [Therein, the division of the cooked rice into nine parts:
"Having prepared the pure cooked rice, one should divide it into nine portions."
And one should contemplate the form of the nine-cornered [mandala] as having the form of a wheel. || 475 ||

[The placing of pure cooked rice upon the eight petals: One should place [the offering] upon the eight-petaled [lotus], adorned with sugar, barley, wheat, and chickpeas, and combined with rice, clarified butter, and sesame seeds. (476)
[The placement in the pericarp of the ninth part, and the display of the nine mudrās:
Having established one in the center, one should display the nine mudrās. [The placement of the nine lamps on the lotus and the worship:]
The knower of mantras should place there nine lamps soaked in ghee.
Having recited the five jewels and the seed-syllable of the preta, one should perform worship;
having worshipped with the root mantra, one should hold [it] with both hands as prescribed.

474–475 | Now he describes the procedure for the *ārātrika* (the waving of lights), beginning with the words "Then, however" (*tatastu*). The meaning is that one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus (*nīraja*) using saffron upon a base or support made from any one of gold or other materials. Then, one should divide the pure rice (*śuddhaudana*) into nine parts. Regarding the number "nine": having taken the eight petals and the pericarp (*karṇikā*), the total count of nine is to be understood.

476–477 | Regarding the placement of the pure rice (*śuddhaudana*) previously mentioned on the eight-petaled lotus (*niruktāṣṭadala*), he says: "With sugar," and so forth. One should place that pure rice, combined with sugar and other ingredients, upon the eight petals of the aforementioned lotus—the "eightfold vessel" (*vasupatra*). As for "one": one portion should be placed in the center, in the pericarp (*karṇikā*). Of the nine portions of the previously mentioned pure rice, the eight portions are to be placed on the eight petals.
The meaning is that one should place the remaining ninth portion upon the pericarp (*karṇikā*). The "nine mudrās" are those previously mentioned, beginning with *Sarvākarṣiṇī* and so forth.
(Verses 477–478) Regarding the placement of the lamps therein, he says "one should place," etc., referring to the nine lamps.

The meaning is: [one should place them] upon the eight petals and the pericarp (karṇikā) according to the sequence of pure rice. Next, he describes the worship of the vessel together with the lamp—starting with "pañcaratnam" (the five jewels). First is the five jewels; then "hsauḥ," which is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the *preta*. The five jewels are the pentad of seed-syllables: *glūṃ slūṃ mlūṃ plūṃ llūṃ*. Before these seeds, one places the two syllables "śrīṃ hrīṃ," and at the end, those same two in reverse order.

The two seed-syllables *hrīṃ* and *śrīṃ* together constitute the nine-syllable mantra of Ratneśī. Although the term "five jewels" (*pañcaratna*) is mentioned here, [it refers to] the whirling of the lamp-vessel (as stated in the Jñānārṇava, p. 699).
Having brought it to the end of the head, the wise one should rotate it nine times with the mantra ending in the root mantra; thereafter, he should perform the lustration (nīrājana).
[The Ārātrika Mantra:
O Goddess Navātmikā, joined with all the lords of the circles, accept this *ārātrika* offering for my spiritual accomplishment! 480.

From the observation of the instruction on the worship of the lamp-vessel with the *Ratneśī* mantra at the beginning [of the ritual], it appears that here too it is called the "five jewels" (*pañcaratna*) precisely with that intention in mind. This is clearly stated in the *Jñānārṇava*, as cited in the *Tantrasāra*:
"Therefore, one should perform the *ārātrika* (the waving of lights) for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals."
O Supreme Goddess, [place it] in a vessel made of gold, silver, or bell-metal.
One should draw a beautiful nine-cornered yantra with saffron;
having prepared a sacrificial oblation (caru) in the form of the moon, one should place it upon the head of Śivā in the center of that.
Having placed one lamp in the center, [he should place] eight lamps in the eight corners,
made of barley, wheat, mung beans, and so forth, mixed with sugar,
filled with ghee, and beautified by chickpeas and *ahita* flowers.
Having consecrated it with mantras, O Great Goddess, [one should then offer] the sovereignty over jewels.
"O lady of excellent complexion, having written the seed-syllable of Śrī and the seed-syllable of Parā,
[place] ga, sa, ma, pa, and la thereafter in the positions of Indra (the east) in sequence, O beloved;
they are joined with the left ear (the vowel *u*) and adorned with the *nāda* and *bindu*."
O beautiful one, these five seed-syllables are the five jewels;
when the first seed-syllable is reversed, this becomes the nine-syllable Ratneśī.

Thus, by placing the two *śrīparā* seed-syllables, *śrīṃ* and *hrīṃ*, at the beginning and at the end—reading them in reverse order as *hrīṃ* and *śrīṃ*—the nine-syllabled *ratneśī* mantra becomes: *śrīṃ hrīṃ glūṃ slūṃ mlūṃ plūṃ llūṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*.

"With the root mantra" means that one should worship with the five jewels (*pañcaratna*), the *preta* seed-syllable, and the root mantra. For this very reason, it has also been stated by the authors of the *Tantrasāra*:
Having uttered the *ratneśī* mantra, it is stated that one should worship with this mantra and the root (*mūla*) mantra.
"Up to the head" is clear. The meaning is: first, having recited the root mantra, one should [worship] with the mantra to be described hereafter.
[The Display of the Mudrās] Having established [the disciple] in the place as described, one should display the *cakramudrā*. || 481 ||
[The Wheel Mudrā]:
Having joined the ring finger and the little finger of the left hand inside the palm of the right hand, one should then place the little finger inside the [right] palm. || 482 ||
The practitioner should place the right thumb upon the left;
through this mutual union, it is proclaimed as the Cakra-mudrā. || 483 ||
[The Offering of Food] Then, having observed the *ārātrika* ceremony, one should present the food offerings (*naivedya*). || 484 ||
[The Vessels for the Food Offering:
A wise person should prepare the food offering (naivedya) in metallic vessels, or on a bed of grass, or on a leaf-cup, or even on one made of sacrificial wood. 485.
But if, O Mahādevī, nothing at all is obtained, [one may use] something fashioned by one's own hand. || 486 ||
[The prohibition against offering water other than that from the arghya vessel:

Whatever is offered with waters other than those contained in the arghya vessel—waters other than those [prescribed]—the Great Goddess does not accept it, even if it is given by hundreds of learned brahmins. 487.
[The food offering:
The food offering consists of pure ghee accompanied by ghee-based side dishes, fish, meat, and mung bean soup well-seasoned with black pepper and other spices. (488)
481. Regarding "the wheel-mudrā" (cakramudrā): it is stated in the *Tantrasāra*:
"O Great Goddess, one should display the wheel-mudrā during the waving of lights (*ārātrika*).
485–486. Regarding "in those made of metal": [this refers to] vessels made of clay in the worship of Māheśī; these are recommended for the worship of Tripurā.
Regarding other vessels for the food offering (*naivedya*), the Gandharva Tantra states in its fifteenth chapter:
"One should present the food offering, which is dear to Tripurā, in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or stone, or else upon a lotus leaf."
(701) "Filled with sugar and cakes, provided with honey, milk, and jaggery, the milk-rice (pāyasa) is endowed with the six flavors and mixed with honey. (486)
Having prepared various kinds of substances and diverse fruits—substances that are pleasing to the mind—the most excellent of practitioners [should proceed]. (490)
[The mandala suitable for its installation, and the worship of the supporting power (ādhāraśakti) therein:
One should draw the mandala on the right, in front, or on the left;
it consists of a triangle, a circle, and the orb of the earth, and the supporting power (ādhāraśakti) is worshipped there. || 491 ||
491. Here, he describes the placement of the food offering (*naivedya*), saying "on the right":
"The food offering [should be placed] on the right, on the left, or in front, but not behind.
This is because the fourteenth chapter of the *Gandharva Tantra* instructs that the food offering is to be placed to the right, the left, or in front of the Goddess.
In this regard, the construction of the mandala is also mentioned here and there; by this, the location for placing the food offering (naivedya) is also established by implication.

Nor should it be argued that, because no specific person is indicated in the phrase "on the right or in front," the placement of the food offering on one's own right side and so forth is what is being taught here.
The lamp should be placed to the right of the Goddess, or in front, but not to the left;
likewise, the incense should be on the left or in front, but not on the right.
One should offer perfume, flowers, and ornaments in the space directly before her.

Immediately following this, based on the observation of the words of the Gandharva previously cited—beginning with "the food offering (naivedya) to the right, to the left," and so forth—it should be understood that the placement of the food offering is for the Goddess alone in her right and other directions, and not for oneself. For this very reason, the authors of the *Tantrasāra* also state:
"The left and right sides belong to the deity alone, and not to the practitioner."
"One should offer incense, lamps, and excellent food before the deity"—thus it is stated because of [the authority of] Darśana. Likewise:
"One should not place unsuitable offerings, such as food and so forth, in front [of the deity]."

Thus, based on the observation of the words of the Gandharvas and because it is improper to place offerings such as *naivedya* to the left or right due to the abundance of substances or the lack of space, they should be placed directly in front. It is implied that if there is available space, they should indeed be placed to the left and right. Regarding the distinction between cooked and uncooked food, the *Tantrasāra* states:
"Cooked food is for the left side of the deity, and raw food is indeed for the right.
Thus, placing [the offerings] in front [of the deity] is contrary to the rule.
[The placement of the *naivedya* and the consecrations such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), etc. (p. 702).
Having placed the food offering (naivedya) there, one should sprinkle it with the weapon-mantra (astramantra),
protect it with the one called the armor-mantra (kavaca), and purify it with the wind-seed syllable (vāyubīja).
Having incinerated [the offering] with the fire-seed syllable (vahni-bīja) and performed the nectar-rite (amṛtīkaraṇa) with the water-seed syllable (vāruṇa),
one should offer the flower for the food-offering (naivedya) and recite one’s own mantra there seven times.
"There is no restriction anywhere regarding the lamp and the food offering (naivedya)"—
this is because of the statement from the *Yāmala* cited in the *Tantrasāra*.
As for that which was stated by the authors of the *Haratattvadīdhiti*:
"White wicks on the right and red wicks on the left;
such is the arrangement of the food offering (naivedya) according to the distinction between cooked and uncooked.
By this statement from the *Yāmala*, cited in the *Tantrasāra*, cooked food is to be placed on the right and raw food on the left.
That which has been propounded—that the "ripe" is on the right and the "unripe" is on the left—is a manifestation of a false interpretation, because it contradicts the statement previously shown.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the division of the ripe and the unripe," since this is a *dvandva* compound consisting of "the unripe" (*apakvam*) and "the ripe" (*pakvam*), the word "ripe" (*pakva*) is placed first due to having fewer syllables.
Thus, there is no contradiction in the meaning that the unripe stands to the south and the ripe stands to the left; all is beyond dispute. And so:
If one sets it aside on the right and places it on the left,
that food becomes unfit for consumption, and the water is like liquor.

This [rule] also does not concern cooked food (*pakvānna*). By the statement "having abandoned the right," the placement on the left—preceded by the abandonment of the right—is prohibited in the case of a single offering (*ekanaivedya*); however, in the case of multiple offerings (*bahunaivedya*), there is no fault even in placing it on the left if a place on the right is unavailable. But there is nothing whatsoever to suggest that the statement "having abandoned the right" has cooked food as its specific subject matter.
There is no such [contradictory] authority; even the authors of the *Tantrasāra* have not stated that this statement refers to cooked food (*pakvānna*).
In the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*, this statement has been explained according to the traditional school (*sāmpradāyika*).

492–493. He describes the sequence for offering the food offering (*naivedya*) with the words beginning "the food offering" (*naivedyam*), etc., using the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), namely the mantra "phaṭ."

With the mantra called *kavaca*, namely *hūṃ*; with the seed-syllable of wind, *yaṃ*; with the seed-syllable of fire, *raṃ*; and with the *vāruṇa* [seed-syllable], *vaṃ*, which is the seed-syllable of Varuṇa. "Having offered a flower" means having honored the food offering (*naivedya*) with a flower. The "mantra" refers to the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*). However, in the *Gandharva-tantra*:

[The manner of offering: O Supreme Goddess, please accept this divine, well-prepared supreme rice-offering contained in a golden vessel, consisting of five types and endowed with the six flavors. 494.

One should offer all the requisites and so forth, ending with the root mantra. [The rule for when an offering is unavailable: If one is unable [to provide them], one should give them mentally; thus, this ritual action must not be omitted. (495)
[The offering of a mouthful to the Goddess and the instruction on displaying the mudrās:
Having mentally offered a mouthful, one should display the five mudrās. || 496 ||
[The mantras of the five mudrās of prāṇa and so forth:

Prāṇa, apāna, as well as vyāna, the one called udāna, and samāna—these are the mudrā-mantras, beginning with the syllable *dhruva* (om), ending in the dative case, and concluding with the wife of Agni (svāhā). (497)
Having observed it to be without covering, one endowed with devotion and faith should purify it with the seed-syllable of air (Yam) and likewise incinerate it with fire (Ram).
One should flood [the vessel] with the Varuṇa-mantra while performing the *svadhāvṛtti* and using the *dhenu-mudrā*;
having protected it with the *astra-mantra*, one should then consecrate it with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*).

At the end of the root deity's own name, one should utter "naivedyam" (the food offering). The mantra for the food offering is said to end with the wife of Agni (svāhā): "gṛhāṇa. Thus the food-offering mantra is proclaimed.
O Goddess, this fourfold food, endowed with the six flavors, has been offered by me with devotion; please accept it.
O Goddess, please eat with compassion these various foods— lickables, suckables, drinks, and other edibles— which have been brought by me with great effort.

Thus, the sequence for the offering of the *naivedya* has been described [verses 496–500]. The passage beginning with “a mouthful” (*culluka*) and so forth is clear. Regarding this, he states the specific detail in the fifteenth chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*: “The water of the celestial river, scented with *jātī*, *lavaṅga*, and *kakola*...”
O beautiful one, having taken this merit-bestowing mouth-perfume, perform the ritual rinsing (ācamana).
p. 704) [Therein, the Prāṇa-mudrā:
Among the elderly, the Prāṇa-mudrā is said to be formed with the thumbs and little fingers.
[The Apāna-mudrā:]
The mudrā of apāna is proclaimed by using the index fingers of the old woman and the middle finger. || 498 ||
The vyāna-mudrā is proclaimed as being formed with the thumb, ring finger, and middle finger.
[The udāna-mudrā]
Excluding the little finger, [the mudrā] with all [the other fingers] is proclaimed as that of udāna. || 499 ||
The *samāna-mudrā* is proclaimed with all the fingers together. [The *grāsa-mudrā*]
In the left hand is the *grāsa-mudrā*, resembling a full-blown blue lotus. || 500 ||
[The offering of water:
One should offer well-scented water in a vessel made of gold, silver, or other precious materials.
[Furthermore, the offering of mouthfuls of water and the offering of betel.]
And again, having offered a mouthful of water, one should present the finest betel leaf.
[The mantra for the offering of betel: Endowed with cardamom, cloves, camphor, and nutmeg,
and rippled with portions of tamāla leaves, camphor, and areca nut.
He should offer betel-leaf that has been well-cleansed and made fragrant. || 502 ||
O Goddess, one should offer five oblations in succession with the root mantra:
to Prāṇa, Apāna, Vyāna, Udāna, and Samāna.
"One should know this essential nature of the five oblations (*āhuti*s).
O Dear One, the five oblations should be performed in sequence using the five fingers themselves.
(501–502) Furthermore, regarding the phrase "again": here follows the method taught in the *Gandharvatantra*:
Having again offered water for sipping (ācamana), one should present mouth-perfume (mukhavāsa).
[The offering of garlands, etc.
A garland, pure water, cool and well-scented—
Then one should offer a fan, a palm-leaf fan, a golden-handled fly-whisk,
and a mirror before the Lord who possesses the splendor of the moon.
One should perform dance, song, and cooling rituals preceded by an abundance of offerings. || 504 ||
[The Offering of a Handful of Flowers and the Libation] Then,
having meditated upon the Supreme Deity as being perfectly serene and adorned with all ornaments,
one should offer three handfuls of flowers and perform the libation. (505)

[The Threefold Nature of Worship] Worship is declared to be threefold: known as the Supreme (parā), designated as the Lower (aparā), and celebrated as the Intermediate (parāparā); this is to be understood by the best of practitioners. (506)

[The characteristics of the supreme and others: The supreme worship is that of the *bindu*; the inferior is that which is external; and the intermediate, which is all-pervasive, is to be understood from the mouth of the Guru. (507)
"Having prepared betel-leaf combined with fragrance and well-scented with camphor and other ingredients, one should offer it after consecrating it with various fragrant substances.
(507-508). Here, the threefold nature of worship and the definitions of the *parā* [levels] and so forth are stated in the two verses beginning with "saparyā."

In that regard as well, it has been stated that [the meaning] must be understood from the mouth of the Guru alone; therefore, a detailed exposition of the "other" (para) and subsequent categories is not necessary here.
However, in the *Tantrasāra*, the fivefold nature of worship (*pūjā*) is described in the *Gautamīya*:
"Worship is said to be fivefold; hear from me their distinctions."
Approaching, receiving, union, self-study, and sacrifice—these are the fivefold modes of worship; I shall describe them to you in due order.
In that context, "approaching" (abhigamana) means the sweeping of the deity’s abode,
as well as its smearing with cow dung and the removal of faded flower offerings.
(p. 706) [Again, breath control and the recollection of Kāmakalā:
Having performed breath control once more, the wise one should recollect Kāmakalā:
her face has the form of a *bindu*, and below that is a pair of breasts. (508)
One should contemplate that [triangle] below it with its apex facing downward;
the bindu at the opening becomes the sun, and both breasts become fire and the moon.
The source (yoni) should be known as the digit within the heart, arisen from the bindu of the mouth; from the nose, the limbs, and the pair of breasts, the two feet arise from the source of the arms.
[Contemplation of the distinctions within the creative power (kalā) of desire of the Self:
In this way, one should always contemplate the Self as having the form of the creative power of desire (kāmakalā). || 511 ||
In the region of the genitals, it has the form of a flame; in the foundation (ādhāra), it has the luster of gold;
situated at the navel, it resembles the orb of the sun and possesses the radiance of the rising sun.
In the heart, it has the form of a flame of fire; above that, the brilliance of the sun;
in the throat, the form of a lamp-flame, resembling a bell of lapis lazuli.

In the *lambikā* [the uvula], the practitioner should contemplate that which has the luster of the moon's orb; between the eyebrows, that which has the brilliance of a jewel; and in the ninth [center], the universal splendor (*viśvatejas*). || 514 ||
Upādāna is the gathering of names, perfumes, flowers, and so forth; likewise, yoga is the contemplation of one's own deity as being identical with one's own self.
Svādhyāya consists of the recitation of mantras preceded by reflection on their meaning,
as well as the chanting of hymns and praises, and likewise the congregational chanting of the names of Hari.
The study of the scriptures concerning reality and so forth is proclaimed as *svādhyāya* (self-study);
while *ijyā* (sacrifice) is indeed the worship of one’s own deity according to the true principle.
"Thus, O observer of noble vows, the fivefold worship has been described to you; it bestows, respectively, the powers of *sārṣṭi*, *sāmīpya*, *sālokya*, *sāyujya*, and *sārūpya*. (p.
707) [Meditation on the Sandals of the Śrī Guru]
Then, one should meditate upon the sandals of the venerable Guru within the thousand-petaled lotus;
she is indeed the power (śakti) of the Kula-kuṇḍalinī.
In the root-tuber (mūlakanda), however, that power has the form of a curved arm.
[The nature of prāṇa:
This wind, which possesses the whirlpools of that [mind's] delusion, is called "prāṇa" by the wise. (515)
When [the breath] is capable, there is a specific movement;
whether it is subtle, unmanifest, and sweet, or throbbing even while one is seated, it proceeds by way of the path of Brahman and enters its own abode. 516.
[Therein, the dissolution of the mind:
One should effect the dissolution of the mind therein even by means of the sequence of coming and going.
[The arising of the mantra-fire:]
By that, the Mantra-crest (mantraśikhā) was born, which illuminates all accomplishments.
[The fruitlessness of a mantra devoid of the *śikhā*:
Just as nothing at all shines forth in a house filled with darkness, so too mantras devoid of the *śikhā* never attain success. (518)
[The secrecy of the *śikhā*]:
"The instruction regarding the *śikhā* has been strictly concealed everywhere by those who know the truth. (519)
[In the absence of this, there is no accomplishment:
Without this, there would be no accomplishment even with hundreds of millions of offerings.
[The futility of mantra-recitation at the time of sleep: At the time of sleep, the recitation of mantras is useless.
However, reciting the mantra during the time of sleep yields results that are devoid of purpose. || 520 ||

514 | Regarding "lambike": the meaning is "on the *lambikā*, that is, on the subtle tongue located above the palate. Regarding "in the ninth," the meaning is "in the ninth wheel (*cakra*), that is, in the thousand-spoked wheel (*sahasrāra*). The detailed analysis of the nine wheels (*navacakraviveka*) is to be found in the *Saubhāgyalakṣmī Upaniṣad*. 515–520 | Regarding "in the root-tuber (*mūlakanda*)," the meaning is "in the *mūlādhāra*."
The wind of the whirling vortex of the power of *kulakuṇḍalinī* residing in the *mūlādhāra* is called *prāṇa*. One should effect the union of the mind there;
from that alone [arise] the characteristics of sleep and waking. (p. 708)
The time of sleep is when the flow is through the left [nostril], and the state of waking is when the flow is through the right.

[Regarding the distinction between sleep and waking in specific mantras: for a mantra of the nature of Fire (Āgneya), it is as described; for a mantra of the nature of the Moon (Saumya), it is the reverse. || 521 ||
One should know the time of awakening for both,
as well as the time of the union of Śiva and Śakti for both.
From the union of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, there occurs the meeting of Śiva and Śakti;
this should be known as the time of awakening, or otherwise, the time of sleep.
[The Dialogue between Hari and Hara on the Praise of the Tripurā-gāyatrī] Now I shall declare the secret dialogue consisting of the words of Hari and Hara,
which took place formerly in the Devadāru forest concerning Brāhmaṇas of exceedingly dull intellect. 523.
Beholding him, the Blessed Viṣṇu went to Śiva and addressed him:
"O God of gods, O Lord of the world, O Mahādeva, O Master of the universe! (524)"
All these birds of evil intellect, excluded from the Vedic way of life and acting according to their own whims, are all twice-born ones in the Devadāru forest.

The "crest of mantra" (*mantraśikhā*) arises. Thus, the established meaning is that in such a manner, without the dissolution of the mind (*manas*) into the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the crest of mantra does not arise;
and if that does not arise, there can be no accomplishment of mantra (*mantrasiddhi*).
[Verse 521–522] Regarding the phrase "at the time of sleep": when the inhalation flows through the left nostril, that is the time of sleep (*svāpakāla*); however, when...

When the breath flows through the right nostril, that is the time for waking; this applies to the recitation of all common mantras. Thus, at the time of beginning the recitation, the flow of air through the right nostril is necessary; otherwise, the recitation is fruitless.
However, for a fire-mantra (āgneya-mantra), the recitation should begin only when the breath flows through the left nostril.
The author indicates this by means of the word "viparyaya" (reversal). Thus,

the intention is that the breath entering through the left nostril and the breath entering through the right nostril for both— the mantra dedicated to Agni and the mantra dedicated to another deity— constitute the time of waking, respectively.
Those who are addicted to sexual intercourse with the wives of others, devoted to the drinking of intoxicants, devoid of self-knowledge, and negligent in the practice of yoga— (526)
O Lord, tell me the means by which their liberation may be attained;
or how might they become qualified for initiation into the knowledge of Brahman? (527)
Having spoken thus, the knower of all things became silent;
then Gāyatrī, who is identical with Brahma and consists of the three cities (Tripurā), was declared to him.
By knowing this very [knowledge],
even one who has committed improper conduct, fallen from grace, or been deprived of the Vedas—
whether a woman, a Śūdra, or an outcast (vrātya)— becomes a Brāhmaṇa as soon as it is known. || 529 ||
[The Discourse on Gāyatrī] Now I shall declare that knowledge, the Gāyatrī, which is ancient than Tripura. (530)

Having extracted the *devīpraṇava*, one should then join [it] with "Tripurasundarī," followed by "ne'ntā vidmahe kāmeśvaryai dhīmahi" and "tannaḥ klinne pracodayāt"; this is to be recited at the beginning of all recitations.
[The eligibility for other recitations after the *gāyatrī* recitation: After reciting the *gāyatrī* twenty-eight times, one becomes eligible for other recitations;
thereafter, one should recite the *brahmavidyā*, as is certain for everyone. (532)

[The Fruits of Reciting the Tripurā Gāyatrī] O twice-born ones, having recited this [mantra], Jamadagnya’s son, my disciple, became liberated while living from terrible sins in the Devadāru forest. 533.

530–532 | Now I shall speak. This is the exposition of the *gāyatrī* of Tripurāsundarī, and that *gāyatrī* is as follows: *hrīṃ tripurasundaryai vidmahe, kāmeśvaryai dhīmahi, tannaḥ klinne pracodayāt*. Thus it is said. (p.
710) Furthermore, Mīnanātha is liberated from the sons of the Mothers (*mātṛputra*). Thus [ends the section].
Jaigīṣavya, Candra, and Vāsava were also liberated.
Likewise, Agastya was liberated from [the sin of] dragging the preceptor’s wife and other such acts by consuming the forbidden food, namely the great asura Vātāpi.
Even Vasiṣṭha was liberated from the sin of approaching a Caṇḍāla woman;
Dattātreya from drinking liquor; and Jvalana from eating all kinds of forbidden food.
In the tantra named Kuloḍḍīśa, it is proclaimed as "Sambhunā. (537)
[The Rule for the Recitation of Gāyatrī] Now,
having performed the recitation of the Gāyatrī while meditating upon the venerable Tripuresvarī,
one should recite the mantra with single-minded focus, abandoning both sluggishness and haste. (538)
One should perform the recitation either one thousand and eight times or one hundred times;
it is traditionally taught that the daily recitation must never be less than thirty times.
"Five hundred and thirty-nine" (*pañca-triṃśad-adhika-śatam*) means one hundred and eight (*aṣṭottara-śatam*). He states the specific details in the seventeenth chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*:
"The best [number] is ten thousand; a thousand is considered middling;
and for Śivā, one should know the lowest to be one hundred and eight."
O Maheśānī, less than this is not prescribed for the rite of recitation;
one should perform the recitation with effort according to the very number, as far as one's capacity allows.
Whatever has been recited without counting will all become fruitless;
since the Rākṣasas seize it, a wise person should count it in every way.
One should not recite the mantra while wearing only a single garment, nor while distracted by many garments;
nor with the hands uncovered, nor even with the head covered.

Nor one whose mind is distracted by anxiety, nor one who is angry, nor one filled with haste; nor one who is unintelligent, nor one whose mind is full of passion, nor one who is diseased, nor one afflicted by hunger.
"Likewise, one should not mutter the mantra while distracted in mind or while prattling;
nor while not seated, nor while lying down, nor while walking, nor while eating.
This is the doctrine proclaimed in the *Mantranirṇaya-tantra*.
[Recitation with the voice, etc. One should recite either aloud, in a whisper, or even mentally. || 540 ||
[The definition of *nigada*: *Nigada* is proclaimed to be the movement of the tongue and the lower lip.
[The definition of *upāṃśu*:]
The mere movement of the tongue is proclaimed as *upāṃśu*.

[The definition of mental recitation: Mental recitation is defined as the contemplation of the syllables of the mantra by means of the mind. [An exposition on the inferior, middling, and superior nature of the types of recitation.]
When recited a hundred thousand times in a whisper, it is equal to [the power of] silent remembrance.
A hundred thousand recitations performed in a whisper is equal to a single mental recitation;
thus it is declared by those who know the mantra that the whispered is inferior, while the mental is superior.

[The prohibition against recitation that is too short or too long: Recitation that is too short is a cause of disease; recitation that is too long is the destruction of austerity. [The manner of recitation.]
One should perform the recitation of the movement of the syllables and the non-syllable like a string of pearls.

540–545 | Regarding "by recitation" (*nigadena*) and so forth: concerning this subject, it is clearly stated in the seventeenth chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*: "O Dear One, the wise practitioner, intent upon the state of being the deity, should begin the recitation (*japa*) either aloud (*nigadena*), in a whisper (*upāṃśunā*), or mentally (*mānasena*)."
O Supreme Goddess, that which is uttered with clear speech without hesitation is called *spaṣṭa*;
that which is indistinct, with a quivering mouth, is proclaimed as *upāṃśu*.
p. 712) [Regarding the specific case of the ten [faults]—the fruitlessness of praise and recitation:
Whoever should remember the hymn with the mind and recite the mantra with the voice, both of these are fruitless for him, like water in a broken vessel. (545)
[Regarding the finger-restriction for recitation: One should rotate the two joints of the ring finger in sequence,
then three joints of the middle finger, ending at the base joint of the index finger.
The rosary is prescribed for the perpetual recitation (nityajāpa), but not for the recitation performed for specific desires (kāmya).
When one recites the series of syllables consisting of phonemes, vowels, and words by means of the intellect,
while keeping them in mind, that is called mental recitation (mānasa-japa).
One should contemplate the mere sound that has arisen on the path of Suṣumṇā,
while contemplating the syllables of the mantra as being strung upon the power of consciousness (cicchakti).
Sustained by the supreme nectar in that very highest heaven,
he reveals the true nature of the Self even without rituals such as worship or fire-offerings.
Having withdrawn the mind from sense objects, with the intellect focused on the meaning of the mantra,
one should recite it neither too quickly nor too slowly, like a string of pearls.
O fair-faced daughter of the mountain, that which is recited a hundred thousand times in a loud voice becomes equal to that which is performed through whispered recitation.
O lotus-eyed one, O lady of excellent complexion, that which is muttered silently to the extent of a hundred thousand is equal to a single [recitation] performed through mental articulation.
In the Tripurātantra, mental recitation (mānasa-japa) is especially praised;
one should either contemplate the hymn with the mind or recite the mantra with the voice.
Both [methods] are fruitless for him, like water in a broken vessel.
(546–548) Regarding "without deceit" (*anāmāyā*): the *Gandharva Tantra*, in its seventeenth chapter, states the rule for finger-recitation (*karajāpa*):
"In the absence of a rosary, the wise one should then recite upon his own fingers."
One should always perform the recitation (japa) with the hand, but never that which is performed for the sake of specific desires (kāmya).
p. 713) [The prohibition against separating the fingers during recitation: One should not separate the fingers; one should slightly contract the palm.
For if there is a separation of the fingers, the recitation flows away through the gaps. (547)
[The fruitlessness of recitation on the tip of a finger:
Whatever is recited on the tip of a finger, whatever is recited while bypassing the *meru*, and whatever is recited at the joints of the fingers—all that shall be fruitless. (548)
Beginning from the middle of the ring finger and proceeding clockwise in sequence,
one should recite [the mantra] over the nine joints up to the base of the index finger.
If a person who possesses the tantra recites [the mantra] with the tip of the index finger and the middle finger, four things will perish for him: life, knowledge, fame, and strength.
One should not cross over the ring-finger joint, making Mount Meru [of the thumb] the limit;
while circumambulating Mount Meru, one should keep the base-joint of the ring finger as the boundary.
"While reciting the mantra with the joints of the fingers, one should not touch the lines [of the palm]. One should not separate the fingers, nor should the palms be slightly contracted.
For when there is a separation between the fingers, the recitation flows away through the gap. Thus it is said.
Regarding the specific excellence of recitation with a rosary, it is said in that very same work:
"Just as there is accomplishment, so too is the rosary an essential limb of the rite of recitation.
For one who recites constantly with a rosary, accomplishment is certain; of this there is no doubt."
This garland composed of letters is declared to be a swift bestower of success,
formed by the letters of the Mātṛkā in both direct and reverse order, together with the bindu.
A rosary made of *sumeruka* seeds should always be used, as it bestows all prosperity;
one should complete it again with groups of eight plus eight [seeds].
The practitioner should perform the recitation after having placed the mantra between [each bead] by color;
in this case, a rosary made of crystal and other such materials bestows success in the recitation.
Having placed the rosary before him, or held it in his right hand,
he should carefully worship the rosary with water at the beginning of the recitation.
p. 714) The sprinkling of the rosary with the chosen mantra is thus proclaimed:
"O *aiṃ*! O garland, O great garland, you whose nature is all-pervading power (*sarva-śakti*), the four aims of life have been entrusted to you; therefore, be the bestower of success upon me."
Having worshipped with camphor, sandalwood, musk, gorocanā, agallochum, and saffron, one should then take up the rosary with the right hand.
Having first uttered the seed-syllable of Gaṇapati, and immediately thereafter [saying],
"O Mālā, perform the removal of obstacles," one should take hold [of it] with this [formula].
One should act in such a way that the rosary does not fall from the hand while reciting;
if it falls from the hand, an obstacle shall arise, and if it is broken, death will occur.
One should protect this with great effort; one should not cause it to wander nor shake it.
One must never reveal the teacher, the yantra, or the mantra.
One should not show the rosary or the mudrā even to one's guru;
for spirits, rākṣasas, vetālas, siddhas, gandharvas, and cāraṇas [would otherwise perceive them].
Since they carry [the mantra] openly, one should always recite it in secret;
the rosary should be held near one's own heart and the right hand.
In the middle portion of the middle finger, having avoided the index finger,
[one joins] with the ring and little fingers from their bent portions.
Having placed the rosary there, taking each individual seed-syllable situated upon it with the tip of the thumb, one should perform [the recitation] with the left hand, without touching it.
One should recite the mantra at each repetition slowly, without moving the lips;
one should not touch the rosary with the index finger, and this is the method for counting by release.
One should perform the ritual rotation while keeping the middle of the ring finger [on the base];
an action performed without the thumb becomes fruitless.
O Goddess, the thumb bestows liberation; the index finger is the slayer of enemies;
the middle finger serves for the attainment of wealth; and the ring finger is for rites of pacification.
It should be known that for attracting the youngest [of sisters] and in the rite of recitation, it bestows success;
however, the seed-beads of the rosary must be recited over, and they must certainly not touch one another.
If one who is reciting the seed-syllable of the preceding deity should touch the seed-syllable of another with his thumb,
that recitation of his becomes fruitless.
[Prāṇāyāma at the commencement and conclusion of recitation:
Having performed prāṇāyāma and having completed the recitation with a concentrated mind, one should again perform prāṇāyāma and offer the recitation itself. (549)
[The Offering of the Recitation] With water and flowers from the *arghya* vessel, [the recitation is offered] into the right hand of the Goddess. || 550 ||
[The Mantra of Dedication] You are the guardian of the most secret of secrets; accept this recitation performed by us.
O Goddess, O Great Sovereign, may accomplishment be mine through your grace. 551.
O Parameśvarī, the garland accompanied by the sound "Kiṭi" may be broken or even severed; having placed the right foot upon the left thigh...
"The mantra-practitioner, having assumed the *vīrāsana* posture and not looking toward the directions,
should contemplate with his intellect the oneness of the Guru, the Deity, and the Mantra.
(550–551) Regarding the *arghya*, there is a specific detail here in the seventeenth chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*:
Having performed the recitation according to the prescribed rule with the mantra and the water of honor (arghya),
one should offer that recitation into the left hand of the Great Goddess.

One should remember that the fruit of the recitation, in the form of radiant energy (*tejorūpa*), has been accepted by Śivā. With the *śrībīja* itself, one should [receive it] from the head down to the feet with both hands;
then, with the *sārasvatabīja*, one should establish it with both hands.
O Dear One, this is the prescribed method for the rosary in the rite of recitation (japa).
O Dear One, the practitioner who prepares the rosary and performs the recitation in this manner, O Goddess, attains his desired goal; for one who acts otherwise, there is a reversal of life-span.
Just as water without a dam flows downward in an instant,
so too does the mantra of practitioners leak away in an instant if it lacks a dam.
Therefore, among all mantras, all castes are twice-born;
the practitioner, during the act of recitation, should establish a boundary on both sides.
In ancient times, Prajāpati extracted the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m* from the three Vedas and fashioned the *praṇava*.
[The offering of blood to the Goddess: Having taken a vessel of blood arising from his own heart, combined with water and rock salt, and mixed with sugar and honey; || 552 ||
Having sprinkled [the offering], the practitioner should offer blood with the Vāgbhava mantra;
the person should give according to his capacity, neither above nor below the navel.
[The duty of performing circumambulation after reciting the hymn: Having offered praise, one should perform circumambulation three, seven, or even nine times.
[The duty of performing prostration with eight limbs:]
The practitioner-mantrin, with a spirit of devotion, should perform the eight-limbed prostration.
"O Great Goddess, for the sake of accomplishing all purposes, one should employ the *praṇava* as a bridge at the beginning of the recitation and at the end of the act of recitation.
(554) Regarding circumambulation after the recitation of the hymn, he says "having praised," etc. On this point, it is stated in the *Gandharva-tantra*:
In the fifteenth chapter:
Endowed with a spirit of devotion, the best of practitioners, praising her with various hymns,
should prostrate before the Supreme Goddess according to the prescribed rite.

Regarding the specific excellence [of this], it is stated in that very same work: "When a salutation is performed by one endowed with devotion, using both prose and verse composed by oneself, it is remembered as the highest form of vocal [worship]."
Whether performed by those versed in the Purāṇas, the Vedas, or the Tantras,
that salutation is always considered a middling salutation, consisting merely of verbal recitation.
"When a salutation to others is performed through both prose and verse,
it should be known as the lowest among all forms of verbal salutation.
The measure for circumambulation is also stated in that very same place:
One should perform the circumambulation as the means for accomplishing the goals of Dharma;
then, extending the right hand while bowing one's head, one should do so again.
Displaying his right side and endowed with devotion and faith,
he who practices the circular form should perform a single circumambulation.
[The Characteristics of the Eight-Limbed Prostration] With the two feet, the two hands, the two knees, the chest, the head, the eyes,
the speech, and the mind— this is declared to be the eight-limbed prostration. (555)
[The eight-limbed prostration by another method: Having prostrated on the ground like a staff with all eight limbs— namely, with the heart, the chin, the face, the nose, and the head.
Either through the ears, through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), or by touching the ground. || 556 ||
That circumambulation is to be known as auspicious, granting satisfaction to the entire multitude of gods;
he who performs one hundred and eight circumambulations of the Goddess [attains this].
Having attained all desires, he shall subsequently obtain liberation.
The sevenfold characteristics of prostration are stated in that very same [text]: "The triangle, the hexagon, the half-moon, the circumambulation,
the staff, the eight-limbed, and the fierce— these are the sevenfold characteristics of bowing."
Having gone from the south to the western direction, and from there to the north-eastern direction,
and then having gone from there again to the south, the salutation is like a triangle.
The salutation known as the triangle bestows pleasure upon Tripurā;
having gone from the southern [corner] to the northwestern, and likewise from the northwestern to the northeastern [corner].
Having gone from there to the south, having abandoned that [direction] and entered the fire,
one should go from the fire to the Rākṣasī direction and then enter the Kauberī direction.
Then, having gone to the south-eastern direction, the salutation is proclaimed;
this salutation known as the "six-cornered" (ṣaṭkoṇa) bestows pleasure upon Durgā.
Having gone from the south to the northwest, and having turned back from there toward the south,
that which is the salutation performed— this is the "Half-moon," which is dear to me.
O Adrijā, one should know that among these salutations,
the Prākṛta form consists of leaving one's own seat and place, going behind [the deity], and then performing the prostration.
Falling upon the ground like a staff is called "daṇḍavat" by the wise;
likewise, having fallen upon the ground like a staff with one's heart [prostrate].
Then, with the chin, the mouth, the nose, and the jaw,
one should again perform a prostration like a staff.
Then, standing on the ground with palms joined in reverence (*añjalipuṭa*), one should bow down.
The practitioner of mantra should bow down to each one individually and prostrate like a staff.
[Prohibition against circumambulating in front of the deity:
"If one performs circumambulation in front while keeping the deity in the middle, his prostration is in vain; moreover, it shall be an offense. (558)
[The prohibition against salutation without joined palms:
"Indeed, he who performs a salutation without having joined his palms is cooked in the hell of great darkness; there is no doubt about this. (559)
[The necessity of touching the ground with the head during prostration:
One should bow with the head while facing another vessel, but one must not touch the ground.
The deities depart from such a person; that [prostration] is declared to be fruitless. (560)
[The Fruit of Prostration like a Staff] As many particles of dust as there are upon the body of a deity when one prostrates,
for that many thousands of years one is honored in the world of Brahmā. || 561 ||
Furthermore, by means of the eyes, the two ears, and indeed the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
that which touches the ground in sequence is declared to be its eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga).
That prostration by which the earth is touched at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) should be known as "Ugra," for it bestows satisfaction upon Viṣṇu.
560. "On another leaf" means on a wall, pillar, or similar surface.

561. Regarding "in prostration": the fruit is the attainment of the world of Brahmā for as many thousands of years as there are particles of dust clinging to the body during a prostration to a deity. This is from the *Gandharvatantra*, in the section praising obeisance.
Gods, humans, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas—
all these great beings are gratified on every side by a single salutation.
Through prostration, one attains the fourfold aims of great prosperity;
for the sake of all accomplishments everywhere, prostration alone is praised.
Having gratified Maheśvarī with circumambulations and prostrations, (p. 719) [verse 562].
[Again, the offering of the mirror and so forth:
Once more, the offering of the mirror, the fly-whisk, the parasol, and the perfumes and other articles. [Again, the display of the mudrās.]
Furthermore, one should display the ninefold mudrā to Mahādevī. || 563 ||
[The Daily Homa]: Thereafter, one should perform the daily homa (nityahoma) which causes delight to Tripurā.
[The Measurement of the Altar]:
To his own right, he should draw a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring one cubit in size.
By bowing, one conquers the worlds; by bowing, the Dharma proceeds.
Through prostration, one obtains long life and unbroken progeny.
The devoted practitioner shall obtain the fourfold aims before long;
salutation is a great sacrifice that always bestows delight in every respect.
Pay homage to the Great Goddess and circumambulate her with devotion;
this is known to be threefold: physical, vocal, and mental.
Salutation should be understood as being of three kinds: superior, inferior, and intermediate;
however, the gods are pleased in every way by physical salutations alone.
Among all forms of salutation, that which is performed with the body is considered the foremost;
it consists of touching the ground with both knees and touching the earth with the head.
That very salutation which is performed by touching the earth with the head while the knees do not touch the ground is known as the bodily [prostration].
The salutation which is performed with the body is the middling one;
when the hands are joined together and the salutation is offered at the head, it is the highest;
that which is done without touching the ground with the knees and the head is called the lowest. Thus it is said.
563 | "Furthermore" (*bhūyo'pi*) means the nine mudrās, namely the group of nine mudrās beginning with *Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇī*. (See pp. 640–570).
By the words "the daily fire-oblation" (*nityahoma*) and so forth, he describes the daily fire-oblation. Therein, he describes the mandala on the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*).
[The Construction of the Mandala] (p. 720)
One should draw a mandala there consisting of a triangle and a hexagon;
in the hexagon one should worship the six limbs, and in the center, one should worship the Goddess. (565)
Regarding the phrase "the triangle": since the specific application for the fire-oblation (*homa*) has not been mentioned here, the procedure for the abbreviated oblation is stated.

On the aforementioned sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*), which has been consecrated by means of inspection and other rites—accordingly, inspection is performed with the root mantra, and striking is considered to be done with the *sara* [mantra].
Sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is declared by that very [mantra], while sprinkling with water (abhyukṣaṇa) is considered to be done with the armor-mantra (varma).
One should draw three lines with their tips pointing eastward and three with their tips pointing northward.

Then, having recited the root mantra and worshipped with "Obeisance to the Pit (Kuṇḍa)," one should worship the six deities— Mukunda, Īśa, Purandara, Brahmā, Vaivasvata, and Indu— placed upon the six stars, using mantras such as "Ai Hrīḥ Srīḥ Ai Klīḥ Sauḥ Obeisance to Mukunda," and so forth, on the eastward-pointing lines and the northward-pointing lines respectively. Then, in the center of the pit (kuṇḍa) or on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), [one should draw] the womb (hṛd-garbha) consisting of a hexagon, a circle, and a triangle.

Having drawn an eight-petalled lotus outside that, and outside that a square provided with four gates, one should offer handfuls of flowers upon it with the *bālā* seed-syllables (*aiḥ klīṃ sauḥ*). Then, having sprinkled all the sacrificial substances with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*), one should worship the sacrificial pedestal (*yāgapīṭha*) of the fire. Likewise, having worshipped the *ādhāraśakti* and others above the pericarp, [one worships] in the four corners starting from the southeast with *oṃ*.

For *dharma*, for *jñāna*, for *vairāgya*, and for *aiśvarya*—in the directions starting from the east; for *adharma*, for *ajñāna*, for *avairāgya*, and for *anaiśvarya*; in the center, for Ananta, for Padma, for the solar orb (*arka-maṇḍala*) consisting of twelve digits with the syllable *aṃ*, for the lunar orb (*soma-maṇḍala*) consisting of sixteen digits with the syllable *u*, and for the fire orb (*vahni-maṇḍala*) consisting of ten digits with the syllable *maṃ*. Then, upon the filaments (*keśara*).

In the center, starting from the east, [one should worship] Pītā, Śvetā, Aruṇā, Kṛṣṇā, Dhūmrā, Tīvrā, Sphuliṅginī, Rucirā, and Jvālinī; [and then] *raṃ* to the fire-seat (*vahnyāsana*). In all cases, one should worship with [mantras] beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
Then, one should worship Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī.
Regarding the fetching of the fire, the Gautamīya states: "One should fetch the fire produced from stone, or that produced from the fire-drill (araṇi),
or that which has come from the house of those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya), or even that found in a forest hermitage."
Indeed, [a gift] obtained from a Brāhmaṇa who maintains no sacred fire yields only half the benefit;
for one born of the Kṣatriya lineage, the sacrificial fire would yield a fourth part of the fruit.
If performed by a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, that act of oblation becomes fruitless;
therefore, one should collect fire with every effort from a mouth of fire.
p. 721) [The abandonment of meat-eating and the installation of the fire:
Having abandoned meat-eating, one should establish the fire there;
having meditated upon the identity of the fire and the deity, one performs the worship of the desired [deity].
Having meditated on the identity of the fire and the deity, one should worship the desired [deity] there.
In another tantra it is said:
"Or else, having brought fire from the house of a twice-born,
the practitioner should gaze upon it while it is consecrated with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*."
Immediately thereafter, one should invoke Agni with the Astra-mantra;
then, using the root mantra ending in "huṃ phaṭ," one should expel the flesh-eating [spirits].

Then, [reciting] *oṃ vahneryogapīṭhāya namaḥ*, and in the four directions *oṃ vāmāyai*, *jyeṣṭhāyai*, *raudryai*, *ambikāyai*, and having worshipped the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) by reciting the root mantra followed by *amukadevatākuṇḍāya namaḥ*, one should bring the fire as prescribed, purify it with the rites of inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*) and so forth, extract the fire from it with the syllable *ram*, and [offer oblations] while reciting the root mantra followed by *huḥ phaṭ* to the goddess Kravyādī.

Having discarded the flesh-eating portions with the word *svāhā*, having protected [the remainder] with the fire-mantra *phaṭ*, having veiled it with *huṃ*, and having rendered it nectar with the *dhenumudrā* and *vaṃ*, one should lift it up with both arms, whirl it three times over the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), and— touching the ground with the knees— deposit it into the womb of the Goddess facing oneself, perceiving it as the seed-syllable of Śiva. Then, *hrīṃ*.

Having worshipped with "Oṃ, obeisance to the form of Fire (Vahnimūrti)," and having joined the consciousness with "Raṃ, obeisance to the consciousness of Fire (Vahnicaitanya)," one should kindle the flame with: "Oṃ Cit-piṅgala, slay, slay! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! O Omniscient One, command, svāhā!
Then: "Oṃ, I revere the blazing fire, Jātavedas, the consumer of oblations."
Golden-hued, stainless, kindled, and facing in all directions.

Thus he should stand in attendance. Then, having assigned a name, saying, "O Agni, you are the deity named so-and-so," he should worship with the *arghya* and other offerings while reciting: "Oṃ, Vaiśvānara, Jātavedas, Lohitākṣa, come here; accomplish all rites, Svāhā! Then, [he should worship] the six limbs of Agni, beginning with: "Oṃ, obeisance to the seven tongues of Agni, Hiraṇyā and the rest; Oṃ, obeisance to the heart, Sahasrārcis," and so forth.

*Namaḥ*, *oṃ agnaye jātavedase*—salutation to the eight forms beginning with this; *oṃ brāhmyādyaṣṭaśaktibhyo namaḥ*, salutation to the eight powers beginning with Brāhmī; outside of that, to the eight treasures beginning with Padma; outside of that, to the world-protectors beginning with Indra; outside of that, to the weapons beginning with the thunderbolt (*vajra*).
Then, having placed two *kuśa* leaves, each a span in length, into the midst of the clarified butter, [one should place] *iḍā* in the left, right, and middle portions.

Having meditated upon Piṅgalā and Suṣumṇā, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*). Taking clarified butter from the right side with the *sruva* ladle, one should offer it to the right eye of the Fire-god with the mantra:
*oṃ agnaye svāhā*. Likewise, taking clarified butter from the left side, one should offer it with the mantra: *oṃ somāya svāhā*.
[This is the purification of the ghee.]
Having poured ghee into the vessel, one should purify it with the root mantra.
Then, the best of practitioners, having performed the *vyāhṛti-homa* for the Goddess, [proceeds].
In the left eye, having taken clarified butter from the middle portion, one should offer it into the forehead-eye of the fire with the mantra: *oṃ agnīṣomābhyāṃ svāhā*.
Again, from the south, having taken clarified butter with *oṃ namaḥ*, one should offer it into the mouth of the fire with *oṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā*.
Then follows the offering of the Great Vyāhṛtis: *oṃ bhūḥ svāhā*, *oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā*, *oṃ svaḥ svāhā*, and *oṃ vaiśvānara*.
One should offer oblations three times with the mantra: "O Jātavedas, bring [the deity] here; O red-eyed one, accomplish all rites, svāhā!

Then, having worshipped the pedestal-deity (pīṭhadevatā) and the root-deity (mūladevatā) within the fire, one should offer twenty-five oblations into its mouth with the root-mantra (mūlamantra). Having meditated upon the oneness of the fire, the deity, and oneself, [one should proceed].

One should offer eleven oblations with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Then, one should offer [oblations] saying, "Svāhā to the limb-deities (*aṅgadevatā*) of the Root Deity," and "Svāhā to the enclosure-deities (*āvaraṇadevatā*). If [the deity] is attached [to the ritual], one should offer one oblation for each individually. Then, having performed the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one should perform the fire-sacrifice (*homa*) with the substances prescribed in one's own ritual manual (*kalpa*). Then, having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra, [one should perform the withdrawal] by means of the *saṃhāramudrā*.

Having brought one’s chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) into the heart, one should dismiss them with the words "forgive me" (kṣamasva); this is the procedure for the abbreviated fire-sacrifice (saṃkṣepahomavidhi).
Furthermore, in the thirty-first chapter of the Gandharvatantra: "The oblation for the Goddess may be performed with kiṃśuka flowers or even with kusumbha blossoms."
Or with *nāgakesara* flowers, or with *madhūka* and red lotuses.
O fair-faced one, a square sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) mixed with *karavīra* flowers, *javā* flowers, and the three sweets bestows all accomplishments.
Having constructed a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) endowed with auspicious characteristics, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the consecrated fire;
or else, O Supreme Goddess, the wise man should prepare a raised altar (sthaṇḍila).

One should perform the daily (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites, but not those performed for specific desires (kāmya). One should practice on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), which is one cubit square and smeared with cow dung.
Likewise, a sand mandala one thumb-joint high,
having drawn the lines there as well, yields fruit when the fire-oblation is performed.
In this manner, from the grains of barley, an *aṅgula* is formed by eight [barley grains] joined together without being too long;
twenty-four such *aṅgulas* constitute a *hasta*.
One should perform the construction of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and other rites using hands of these measurements;
a fire-oblation (homa) performed in a triangular pit brings pleasure to Tripurā.
[The Homage of Ten-thousandths]: One should perform the homa of ten-thousandths with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*. || 567 ||
[The Offering of Vital Oblations, etc.
As for the offering of vital oblations, one should perform six oblations with the root mantra and the six-limbed mantra. || 568 ||
Having drawn three lines from west to east, each measuring one *prādeśa* in length,
which represent the forms of Mukunda, Indu, and Purandara.
Having drawn three lines toward the south immediately thereafter,
the lines shall take the forms of Vaivasvata, Brahmā, and Ananta.
O Goddess, having first drawn a triangle in the center,
one should thereafter fashion a most beautiful hexagon on the outside according to the prescribed rule.

Outside of that, one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus with a beautiful pericarp (*karṇikā*) in a circle, and a square mandala with four gates; having placed a handful of flowers in the center, one should arrange the sacrificial implements, such as the *sruva* ladle and others.

To the left [of the practitioner], one should place the *sruva*, clarified butter (*ājya*), curd, *dūrvā* grass, fuel sticks (*samidh*), the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), the *praṇītā* water vessel, and the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling vessel. Thus.

Having filled the *prokṣaṇī* vessel with imagined water, having purified it three times by pouring it out, having sprinkled those [implements], and having turned them toward oneself, one should consecrate them with the *bālā* mantra. In the same manner, one should wipe them three times with *dūrvā* grasses, from the root to the tip and again from the tip to the root; then, one should spread the *dūrvā* grasses with their tips pointing eastward and northward. Reciting the Root Mantra, one should worship the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) with the words, "Salutation to the sacrificial ground."

Having worshipped Kāmeśvarī and Kāmeśvara in the center of the triangle and meditated upon their union, and having honored them both, one should cause the fire of consciousness (*saṃvidagni*)—which has arisen from the root-mantra and emerged through the door of the eye in the forehead, joined with wind and fire—to descend into her womb with the mantra: *vaiśvānara jātaveda iha āvaha lohitākṣa sarvakarmāṇi sādhaya svāhā*. Then: *oṃ uttiṣṭha puruṣa haripiṅgala*.

Having raised the fire with the mantra, "O red-eyed one, grant me all rites; cause them to be granted, Svāhā! and having meditated upon the fire as held within the womb of Kāmeśvarī while reciting the root mantra followed by "Vauṣaṭ," he should gaze at the fire and protect it with the Astra-mantra. Then, taking the blazing fire, he should circumambulate the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) three times in a clockwise direction.
Having whirled a single blazing fuel stick and reciting "huṃ phaṭ," one should cast the *kravyāda* fire toward the southwest.

Then, touching the ground with both knees and establishing the fire in the center, one should worship the Goddess with the mantra: "Oṃ klīṃ, obeisance to the fire-form of Mahātripurasundarī. Thereafter, by means of that fire flowing from the navel-center through the nostrils, one should unify it with the external fire.

One should sacrifice. Having uttered the root mantra—*aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ āṃ so'haṃ vahnicaitanyāya namaḥ*—and having meditated upon Fire within the womb of Kāmeśvarī, one should place the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) upon His body: *oṃ sahasrārciṣe hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *oṃ svastipūrṇāya śirase svāhā*, *oṃ uttiṣṭha puruṣāya śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *oṃ dhūmavyāpine kavacāya huṃ*, *oṃ...*
To Saptajihvā from the eyes: *vauṣaṭ*; *Oṃ dhanurdharāyāstrāya phaṭ*.
[The fire-offering for the deities of the enclosure:
Thereafter, one should offer one oblation each for the sake of the deities of the enclosure.
[The offering of six oblations with the root mantra:
One should again perform six oblations with the root mantra. || 569 ||

Having thus performed the sacrifice, one should meditate upon [the deity] who has the luster of molten gold, who holds a spear (*śakti*) and a svastika, whose lotus-hands are adorned with the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*), whose body is decorated with divine ornaments, who stands upon a lotus, wears white garments, possesses three eyes, and has his hair tied in a topknot;
then one should worship the seven-tongued [fire-goddesses]: *yūṃ* Lohitā in the northeast, *rūṃ* Raktā in the east, and *lūṃ* in the southeast.

[Nīlā] in the southwest (Nairṛta), [Kṛṣṇā] in the west (Vāruṇa), [Śubhrā] in the south (Yāmya), [Karālī] in the north (Uttara), and [Bahurūpā] in the east (Īśāna). Then, with the mantra "Obeisance to Bhavavahni, who has Kāmeśī as his womb, and to all states of being," one performs for the fire the rites of *garbhādhāna*, *puṃsavana*, *sīmantonnayana*, *jātakarma*, *nāmakaraṇa*, and *annaprāśana*, saying: "I perform such-and-such a rite for such-and-such a fire."

Having completed the rites of tonsure (cūḍā), initiation (upanayana), the offering for the first shaving of the beard (godāna), and marriage, having sprinkled [water], strewn [the sacrificial grass], and donned [the garments], and having meditated again, one should worship the Fire in a triangle with the fire-mantra. Having offered seven oblations into the seven tongues of flame, and having performed three oblations with the three mantras beginning with "Vaiśvānara uttiṣṭha" and "Cit piṅgala," one should assign the six limbs to the six corners and the eight petals— namely, to Agni and Jātavedas.

One should worship the Guardians of the Quarters (Lokapālas) in the earthen chamber with the mantra: "Obeisance to Saptajihva, Havyavāhana, Asrodara, Vaiśvānara, Kaumāratejas, and Devamukha. Having propitiated Brahmā to the south of the Fire, and having placed the vessel of clarified butter (ājyasthālī) in front, one should [visualize] the Śrī Cakrarāja upon the Bahurūpā tongue and the Citkalā situated within it.

Having beheld [the deity] adorned with a multitude of rays, having worshipped and constantly offered oblations, having filled the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the smoke of the pavilion and kindled it with lamps, and having offered fuel-sticks (*samidh*), one should offer whatever is desired. Having presented the ritual offerings (*vali*), [one recites]: "Oṃ bhūr! To Agni, to Pṛthivī, and to Mahat, svāhā! Oṃ bhuvaḥ! To Vāyu, to Antarikṣa, to Divya, and to Mahat, svāhā! Oṃ..."

"Oṃ Svāhā to Svar, Āditya, and the Great Heaven! Oṃ Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ Svāhā to Candramas, the Nakṣatras, and the Great Space! Having performed the Mahāvyāhṛti-homa with these four mantras, thereafter follows the Brahmārpaṇa;
then, having offered fuel-sticks (samidh) and worshipped the Goddess, one should perform the ritual dismissal (visarjana).
The daily fire sacrifice has been proclaimed by me; now hear the fire sacrifice for specific desires.
With jasmine, *mālatī*, and *jātī* flowers mixed with honey—
By offering clusters of flowers filled with ghee, one becomes a master of speech;
likewise, by offering hibiscus flowers or karavīra flowers combined with clarified butter.
[The three oblations:
One should perform the triple oblation with the Praṇava and the mantra "agnaye svāhā. [The dismissal of the Goddess: [The dismissal of the Goddess.]
Then one should dismiss the Goddess; this is known as the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma). || 570 ||
By performing oblations, the practitioner of mantra deludes the inhabitants of the three worlds;
by offering *campaka* and *pāṭala* flowers, one attains unsurpassed prosperity.
An oblation of *varuṇa* lotuses bestows perfect prosperity;
with red lotuses, the world is subjugated; with blue ones, one brings the wicked under control;
and by offering white lotuses, O Dear One, one obtains fortune and sovereignty.
Through oblations of white water-lilies (kahlāra), one attains prosperity and all good fortune;
through oblations of bandhūka flowers, one brings all living beings under one's control.
O fair-faced one, by offering milk, curd, honey, and clarified butter separately,
longevity, strength, health, and prosperity arise for men.
By means of goat’s meat smeared with blood,
one should perform a fire-oblation at night using the three sweets, according to the procedure taught by the Guru.
By performing one hundred thousand oblations with grapes as well as with coconut fruits, a man shall bring another kingdom under his control and become an enjoyer of sensual pleasures; likewise,
kings will come under his sway and he shall attain incomparable prosperity.
By means of *jambū* fruits, all women certainly become submissive;
by means of *śrīphala* fruits one attains incomparable fortune, and likewise by means of its leaves.

O Goddess, by offering pieces of sugarcane one attains happiness, and by its juice kings come under one's control; by the oblation of sesame seeds and clarified butter, one shall accomplish all undertakings.
By means of an oblation of ghee and milk-rice together with sugar, clarified butter, and honey,
the three worlds come under one's control, and one shall obtain wealth and grain.
One should destroy the *upasargas* with well-prepared *vaṭaka* cakes;
and by means of an oblation of camphor, speech becomes submissive to men.
O Goddess, by performing a fire sacrifice with saffron, one shall destroy all sufferings.
By means of a burnt offering of musk, the gods come under one's control; of this there is no doubt.
By means of a burnt offering of sandalwood and agallochum, one may bring all the worlds under one's influence.

p. 726) [Satiating with the shoulder-flesh of the sacrificial offering] Thereafter, one should perform the satiation with the shoulder-flesh (*daṃśāṃsa*) of the sacrificial offering according to the distinctions of caste.
[Instruction on satiating with milk and prohibition of satiating with liquor]
One should perform the satiation with milk, but one must not satisfy [the deity] with liquor.
[The threefold nature of intoxicants:
One should know that the satiating drink is of many kinds, arising from honey, flour, and molasses. (572)
[The substances for the libations of the Brāhmaṇas and others:
A Brāhmaṇa should offer cow’s milk; a Bāhuja (Kṣatriya) should offer cow’s liquor and meat.
