The measure of the substances for the oblations is stated in that very same place:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall declare the measure for the successful performance of the oblation:
one should offer a full hundred flowers, and likewise a hundred sesame seeds."
The parched grain should be the measure of a handful, and the clarified butter should be the measure of one karṣa.
Half a mouthful of honey and milk, along with food in the measure of a single morsel,
may be taken together with whole pieces of sugar and fruits according to one's desire.
The plantain fruit should be divided into four pieces if it is small; otherwise, it should not be cut.
As for the coconut, one should make a large piece that is pleasing to the mind.
At the location of the joints, there should be a stalk of sugarcane that brings satisfaction to the mind;
the entire grape fruit should then be the size of a *guñjā* berry.
It brings delight to the mind of camphor, musk, and other such things.
This measure of oblations has been declared, which brings about all accomplishments.
O beloved, it may be performed with *kiṃśuka* flowers that destroy the multitude of sins,
or with various distinct substances gathered together, O fair-faced one.

"As the wise one should perform the *homa* with whatever materials are available according to his capacity, he will destroy the entire multitude of obstacles; of this there is no doubt. (571–573) Then, regarding "the *homa*": "according to the distinction of caste" refers to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.

The meaning is that one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with substances prescribed for each respective caste, equal in number to the count of the *homa* offerings. Even in that regard, it repeatedly prohibits a Brāhmaṇa from performing the libation with milk rather than with liquor, in order to strengthen the prohibition.
The libation is manifold.
A Vaiśya, however, should give honey; a Śūdra, the juice of flowers and so forth. (573)
[Prohibition against giving liquor to the Goddess:

A Brāhmaṇa should never give liquor to Mahādevī. [Prohibition against a Brāhmaṇa’s giving liquor even if he follows the Vāmācāra path: A Brāhmaṇa should never give liquor to Mahādevī, even if he is a practitioner of the Vāmācāra.
Even a Brāhmaṇa who desires [worldly] pleasures should not consume liquor or meat. || 574 ||

Here, by taking the word *tarpaṇa* in its figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) to mean liquor, he demonstrates its manifold nature with the phrase "arising from honey, flour, and molasses. The threefold nature of *surā* is stated in the eleventh chapter of the *Manusmṛti*:
"Surā should be known as being of three kinds: that made from molasses (*gauḍī*), that made from flour (*paiṣṭī*), and that made from honey (*mādhvī*)."
"Just as one [is not to be drunk], so all [are not to be drunk] by the best of the twice-born.
(574-575) This statement, "one should not give," was spoken in the *Śrīkrama*. Here, corroborating evidence is stated in the first chapter of the *Merutantra*:
"By the Vāma path, it is recommended that one abandon that first letter (the syllable *Om*).
However, a Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor shall go to the Raurava hell;
even a Brāhmaṇa following the Vāma path must not consume wine or meat. Thus it is said.
And in the Rudrayāmala it is said: "By abandoning the Vedas, by drinking liquor, and by consorting with the wife of a Śūdra,
a Brahmin becomes at that very moment more despised even than a Cāṇḍāla."
And in the fourth chapter of the *Kālīkulāmṛta*: "A Brāhmaṇa who gives liquor is indeed deprived of his status as a Brāhmaṇa;
he is called a beast and should practice the ritual of the beasts (*pāśava*)."
And in the *Kālīkulārṇava*:
"Liquor is indeed the impurity of grains; it is called excrement.
Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, and a Vaiśya should not drink liquor."
"Upon merely seeing liquor, one should gaze at the sun;
upon merely smelling it, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma). [Alternative procedure regarding liquor] (p. 728)
Wherever liquor is prescribed, there the best of the twice-born should substitute coconut water for it; if it is in a bronze vessel, he should pour honey into a copper vessel.
In this very manner, one should offer libations to Tripureśvarī;
this is the doctrine proclaimed by the Bṛhacchrīkramatantra.
It is proclaimed in succession for the Satya, Tretā, and Dvāpara ages. || 576 ||
[The *Jñānārṇavamatollekha*:

According to the doctrine of the *Jñānārṇava*, the various types of substances for the practitioner who possesses conceptual thought (*savikalpa*) are now described according to the distinctions of their alphabetical order. (577)
For indeed, there are various substances such as milk, clarified butter, honey, and maireya liquor. || 578 ||

And in the *Kubjikātantra*: "O Bhairavī, having eaten fish and meat, and having touched a *hetu*, one becomes purified by fasting for three nights and [consuming] the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). Thus it is said.
Also in the ninth chapter of the Vārāhītantra:
"O Supreme Goddess, wine, meat, fish, sexual union, and the human offering—these five a Brāhmaṇa should never even think of. And so forth.
Regarding the phrase "in that very [case]": the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi* contains a statement prescribing a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) concerning liquor:
"Wherever one might otherwise consume *āsava*, especially a Brāhmaṇa, one should then give him jaggery and ginger, or release the honey into copper."

577–578 | "By the distinction of the sequence of castes" (*varṇānukramabhedataḥ*) means by the division into Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra. "They are described" (*kathyante*): the sense is that for those who possess conceptual thought (*savikalpa*) and are practitioners (*sādhaka*) of the Brāhmaṇa and other classes, there is, respectively, satiation (*tarpaṇa*) with milk, clarified butter (*ghṛta*), honey, and *maireya* liquor. Regarding the definition of *maireya*, that which is cited from the *Śabdakalpadruma* and spoken by Mādhavācārya is as follows: [text omitted].
The authoritative source states:
"Sīdhu is produced from boiled sugarcane juice; Āsava is produced from both boiled and unboiled [juice];
Maireya is made from Dhātakī flowers combined with jaggery, parched grain, and sour gruel."
p. 729) [Contemplation of the Self in the Form of Kāmakalā]:
Then the lover should contemplate himself in the form of Kāmakalā;
by the very same procedure previously described, he should contemplate the supreme Sundarī. 579.

579. Regarding the term *kāmī*: it means one should contemplate oneself in the form of the *kāmakalā*. The essential nature of *kāmakalā* is described in the thirty-first chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*: "O wise one, listen to its threefold nature, which is hidden in all the tantras."
The gross, the equal, as well as the subtle, and likewise the body of mantra.
And when that earth, whose face is the point of the sky and whose luster is like the moon, the sun, and darkness, shines with the essence of Mount Meru and the heart, then [it is so].
This triple world, consisting of parts, is situated within the depths of the netherworld;
it is for the sake of manifesting this that the purpose is pursued by means of the three seed-syllables of Lalitā.
The reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of those [vowels] is the letter *ī*, which, having become threefold by means of the *bindu*,
is said to possess the three *bindus* that constitute the nature of the fourth state (*turīya*).
When the bindu has moved above the vowel *ī* and the sun has reached the middle,
the breasts become the fire and the moon, and the womb becomes the digit of the heart.
That which consists of her essence resides in the Goddess and likewise in the practitioner;
listen now, O wise one, to that supreme source of great prosperity which arises from it.
One should contemplate the face as consisting of the upper *bindu*, the two breasts as consisting of the two lower *bindus*, and the remaining limbs as consisting of the rest of the letters.
Thus have I described to you the external contemplation of Kāmakalā;
I shall now describe to you once more that very same internal, spiritual contemplation.

O Goddess, one should meditate upon Kuṇḍalinī, who has the form of a flickering flash of lightning extending from the base (mūlādhāra) to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), and whose nature is that very Vidyā.

One should meditate upon that supreme Goddess, who pierces the six cakras, who consists of the three bindus, who is the form of the aesthetic power (kalā) within the heart, and who resides in the center of the lotus.
Thus, she whose form is the aesthetic power of desire (kāmakalā) remains awake within the moving and the unmoving;
she is said to consist of the three Vedas, and there is nothing that exists without her.

This is the Goddess of the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya), who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; such is the clear meaning. O Dear One, Vāgbhava, Parā, Śrī, Hasa, Kha, Pha,

Following the word *yogeśvarī*, this *vidyā* is considered to be Kālikā;

Having meditated upon the illustrious Tripurasundarī together with the wheel (cakra), [verse 599].

Having smelled the flower situated upon the yantra and having formed the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, || 600 ||
[The mantra for dismissal:
Go, go to the supreme abode, your own place, O Supreme Goddess, where Brahmā and the other gods may attain the highest state. 601.

[The Mantra for the Worship of Sevikāsundarī: “Obeisance!
By the command of Śrī Śiva, I offer you food to be licked, sucked, eaten, and drunk, as well as betel, ointments, and the consumption of the remains of the offering (nirmālya). (603)

605. "The triad of bodies" means the triad of root-seeds (*mūlabīja*). The remainder is easy to understand.
(p. 735) [Mental Karma-yoga:
Alternatively, in the mental karma-yoga, however, it is the supreme and imperishable.
One should gradually lead the wheel of powers (śakticakra), which has arisen from the root, back to the root again.
Whatever is cherished within the Self, which is of the nature of consciousness, that indeed is the very root;
one should contemplate that [Self] as dissolved in this very imperishable reality.
In the rite of unification, one should not destroy the flow [of consciousness] within the fire of pure awareness;
rather, with the face turned inward, one should offer as oblation the substance characterized by the notion of "this-ness."
Then, having smelled the flowers and other offerings, one should cast them into the interior space.
This is declared to be the yoga of action (karmayoga), by which there arises steadfastness in that [state]. || 609 ||
Through the practice of this very yoga of action, one becomes a perfected sovereign of yogis. (610)
[Instruction on wearing the remains of offerings and so forth: One should wear the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*) upon the head and apply them as an ointment to all limbs;

606–609 | Alternatively: "In the mental yoga of action" (mānase karmayoge) means "in the yoga of knowledge" (jñānayoge); this is the sense. Therein, having meditated upon the wheel of power (*śakticakra*) at the *mūlādhāra*, one should merge that supreme, immutable reality (*paramamavyayatattva*)—which is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*)—into the Self (*ātman*) situated in the thousand-petaled lotus at the *brahmarandhra*. Then, one should bring that *mūlādhāra* back together with the wheel of power. Again, the wheel of the Self merged with the wheel of power...

One should contemplate [the mind] dissolved into this very immutable reality (*tattva*). When this act of merging has occurred, one should reduce the flow of external objects to ashes in the fire of knowledge; thus, being inward-turned, one should not destroy external objects such as jars therein.
In this way, the eternal reality consisting of knowledge alone becomes manifest within the Self—this is the summary. By this...

The sense is that through the practice of *karmayoga*, one shall attain steadfastness in the Self (*ātmaniṣṭhatā*). (611) He teaches the wearing of *nirmālya* and so forth, beginning with the words "the *nirmālya*. This has been clearly stated in the *Mālinītantra*, as cited in the *Śivārcanacandrikā*:
O Goddess Śivā, having stirred the water for the *arghya* offering— which remains after the previous worship—
with the root mantra a few times, [offer] the eightfold [oblation].
p. 736) [Prostration to the Guru] Thereafter, one should offer three prostrations to the Guru for the sake of attaining the siddhis. || 612 ||
[The Praise of Conch Water]:
The water remaining from the worship of the gods that has entered the interior of a conch shell removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin from those humans upon whose limbs it has fallen. (613)
[The Praise of the Water from the Feet of Śrī Cakra] In the Gaṅgā, Puṣkara, and Narmadā; in the Yamunā, Godāvarī, and Gomatī;
in Gaṅgādvāra, Gayā, Prayāga, Badarī, Vārāṇasī, and the Sindhu;
The water from the feet of the Śrīcakra bestows the fruit of thousands of crores of holy baths in sacred fords such as the Revā, Soṇa, and Sarasvatī within the interior of the vessel of the universe.
[The presentation of the authority of his own statement by way of a specific mode:
Having understood the doctrines of various tantras as well as the doctrine of my venerable Guru, this ritual worship has been proclaimed by the accomplished Pūrṇānanda. (615)
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Worship," in the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Pūrṇānanda Paramahaṃsa.
One should sprinkle oneself with that water while reciting the root mantra;
the practitioner should wear the remains of the offering (nirmālya) upon his head while reciting the root mantra.
"O Goddess, having offered water for the feet, O Beloved, one should distribute the *naivedya*;

In the midst of the immeasurable ocean of jewels, upon an island of shimmering coral, within the interior of a forest of supreme bliss radiating forth,

Upon a wonderful great jeweled pedestal within the interior of the house. || 1 ||

Holding a noose, a goad, a vessel of nectar, and a trident in his hands,

Her lotus-hands are raised in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
her lotus-feet are beautifully adorned by the lotus-posture (padmāsana);
she is Padmā, whose face is like a beautiful lotus—[I bow to] Padmanābha.

May the crystal rosary of Vāgīśvarī, white as the rays of a thousand rising moons and ever-present in the throats of all oceans of speech, rest forever upon my neck.

To the body of the slender-eyed woman, which has the hue of a bandhūka flower, which is reeling with intoxication, and which holds the flower-arrows and bow of the Flower-Arrowed God—

With the splendor of her teeth and the garment of her smile, slightly blossomed and enchanting, she has surpassed the crescent of the newly risen moon;
she is like a painting of musk, the great deity of beauty.
Her forehead-slab was as beautiful as the moon, with its leaf-like hair-ornaments.
Delightful with a pair of beautiful cheeks that are vessels of loveliness, resplendent with hair of incomparable beauty,
and possessing the splendor of cheeks adorned by a pair of divine earrings—
She possesses a splendor like that of the orb of the moon, eclipsed by her own erudition.
Her lower lip, resembling a ripe *khapura* fruit moistened with the juice of beautiful *nāgavallī* leaves and filled with a mass of camphor;
her neck shining with the luster of gems kissed by her necklace.
Her neck, like a conch shell, was doubly beautified by its radiant luster.
Her creeper-like arms were adorned with the pure nectar of playful lotus-stalks bathed in lac-dye, and her hands possessed the delicate,
stainless beauty of the radiant petals of red lotuses.
The playful grace of her hand, with fingers as lovely as young sprouts.
That [hand], fashioned by the diligent efforts of Viśvakarman,
shining with the luster of the nails of a jewel ring,
was seized and bound by someone for some particular reason.
Of those [beings] whose ornaments were the noose, the goad, the arrow, and the bow. || 35 ||
The beauty of a radiant necklace with pearl fruits, closely attached to the great jewel-leader difficult to find in the three worlds;
[he is] a golden pitcher filled with the water of loveliness.
Her full jar-like breasts, which surpass all splendor, are like two perfect water-pots. || 36 ||
Her waist was graced by three folds that radiated a beauty of equanimity and gentleness, exceedingly rare even throughout the three worlds;
it was like a house entered by the depths of her navel, which is the very abode of loveliness.
The glorious and immensely radiant line of nine hairs.
She wore beautiful, variegated red garments with girdles that curved like gold, shimmering with a mass of flickering rays;
she was the Rambhā of love born from the forest of Śrī-Kāma.
Her pair of thighs is more delicate than a pillar-subduing tree. || 38 ||
She who delights with her pair of shanks, whose arrangement is difficult to achieve through the rules of meter and symmetry, whose ankles are hidden by jewels,
and who outshines even the compositions of Vācaspati with her speech—
Whose lotus feet are enchanting, being the very domain of beauty. || 39 ||
[She whose] lotus feet, red with compassion, are gazed upon by the celestial palaces shining upon the crests of Śrī Brahmā, Viṣṇu,
and Śiva; [she who is] exceedingly gracious and full of compassion toward the noble practitioner (sādhaka).
She has bestowed the boon that was both seen and prescribed, and she is gracious with her face turned downward.
To that Supreme Goddess who consists of the enchantment of the three worlds;
to that Supreme Goddess who consists of the cause of the three worlds;
to that Supreme Goddess who consists of the wonder of the three worlds.
I worship Cakreśvarī, the performer of auspicious deeds. || 41 ||
This wheel of the lotus-face of Trailokyamohana is the place where the goddesses who bestow the supernatural powers (*siddhis*) such as *aṇimā* and others are manifest;
[it contains] all the mantras and mudrās of the lineage of the venerable Gurus.
O Supreme Goddess, having worshipped with flowers, I worship you. || 42 ||
Until the fifteenth jewel, beginning with Padmā,
which consists of the sequence of the lunar days (tithis) and is indeed eternal, only certain fortunate ones [know] the fifteen Nityās beginning with Kāmeśvarī.
With mantras, I worship the Supreme One with supreme devotion. || 43 ||
O Mother, you are first praised as Tripurā;
thereafter, as the second Navamatripuresvarī;
as Tripurasundarī in the third; and in the fourth—
O Mother, you alone are the supreme goddess who dwells in Tripura.
In the fifth you are the Blessed Lady Tripurā Parāśrī;
in the sixth you alone are Parā Tripuramālinikā;
in the seventh you are the Blessed Lady Tripurādisiddhā.
And you, O Blessed Lady, are Tripurā by nature in the eighth [day]. || 45 ||
In the full, supreme, and most secret [reality] consisting of the higher and the lower, you alone are the venerable Mahātripurasundarī;
in the most wonderful royal wheel of the venerable Great Self.
Indeed, you are praised by certain virtuous ones as the Goddess.
At first you were ten, eight, ten, sixteen, and eight;
then you became fourteen, ten, and then eight;
afterwards you became four, three, and six.
You are composed of one hundred and seven [verses], yet you are one.

You are the Mistress of Desire (*kāmeśvarī*), the Goddess of the Lotus (*bhagamālinī*), the Ever-Moist (*nityaklinnā*), and Hiraṇḍakā who has ceased from those [states]. You are devoted to the abode of fire (*vahnivāsaniratā*) and the Great Primordial Element (*mahādibhūta*).
And likewise, she is known as Vidyeśvarī and Śivadūtī. || 48 ||
O Mother, you are Parā, Tvaritā, Kulasundarī, Nityā, Nityapara, and Nīlapatākinī;
you are Sarvalokavijayā and Akhilamālikā.
They call her Jvālāmayī and Vicitrakā. || 49 ||
O Mother, having realized this form of yours which consists of both the syllable and the non-syllabic,
those of pure intellect do not count even the illustrious Brahmā,
Viṣṇu, Śiva, Garuḍa, the Sun, Indra, and the Moon.
[He addressed] the leaders of the Yakṣas, Darpaka, the hosts of Īśvara, Vahni, and the foremost [others].
Having worshipped her with all the excellent offerings of the *varaṇa* ceremony, some [sages]—
having untied the knot— bear her, who is the Supreme Goddess (*parameṣṭhinī*),
appearing as the very nature of Māra in the abode of Madana in the form of a lamp.
The virtuous protect it from the very tip of their tongues. || 51 ||
She who resides in the supreme triangle at the center of the lotus-base,
whose crest-jewel is the left [side], who shines like the supreme sprout,
who consists of knowledge, action, and the desired power, and who is the destruction of the destruction of the fetters—
"O Śrī, you alone are the one who possesses the power of the qualities of Brahmā and Viṣṇu. || 52 ||
It is the cause and agent of creation, sustenance, and dissolution; it is known through the Vedānta, unborn, undecaying, and immeasurable.
Their minds were agitated by mutual differences and quarrels.
O Mother, what can those of dull intellect know of your form?
If you alone, O Supreme Goddess, are sung as the hymn; if you alone, O Supreme Goddess, are sung as the singer;
if you alone, O Supreme Goddess, are sung as the object of praise.
Why indeed are you being praised at that time, O Supreme Goddess?
For him who, with undivided mind, daily recites this glorious *Kramastava*, which is like a wish-fulfilling tree of time and a king among hymns,
liberation dwells in the palm of his hand, along with the eight supernatural powers (*siddhis*).
Of what use to him are the minor [goddesses] such as Mātariśvanī, Aṇimā, and the rest? || 55 ||
One who has conceived devotion toward you, O Goddess, shall worship you according to the *Krama* and *Kula* traditions and shall recite this hymn for the attainment of all goals;
therefore, O Goddess, I too [recite it] out of the flavor of devotion to you.
This jewel, which accomplishes the goals of devotees, has been fashioned.

55–56 | Regarding the phrase "yaḥ kalā... and so forth: the author of this hymn has stated that the name of this work is *Kramastava*. In that regard, it is considered likely that the reason for this is that it begins with the description of the Śrīcakra and contains the mention and description of all the deities of the enclosures (*āvaraṇadevatā*) according to the order of worship; for this very reason, the author of the text indicates that same meaning through the phrasing beginning with "one should worship you" (*tvāṃ pūjayet*).
The *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi*:
[The Armor of Tripurasundarī as Spoken in the *Tripurārṇava*]. Now I shall proclaim the armor (*kavaca*) characterized by the *Tripurārṇava*.
For the sake of liberation from all calamities and for the attainment of all prosperity. || 1 ||
For the pacification of afflictions caused by spirits, ghosts, demons, and the like; for the attainment of happiness;
for the destruction of all diseases; and for victory in battle. || 2 ||
In a forest terrifying with thieves, lions, tigers, elephants, and poison; likewise in a mountain thicket or on a path during a famine.
In times of distress caused by afflictions from water, fire, or wind, or other such dangers such as those from constellations,
one who recites the *Nityakavaca* even once overcomes them all.
One who is free from dualities, without rivals, and has conquered the senses lives happily.
Listen, O Goddess, for I shall declare that armor which brings an end to the cycle of existence.
By which I too am likewise a conqueror of gods and asuras in battles;
may Lalitā protect me always, in every way, and at all times. 6.
May Bhagamālā protect me from the east;
may she likewise protect the southern direction and that right side at all times.
May Nityaklinnā always protect me from the northern direction; and likewise, may Vahnivāsinī protect me from the western quarter.
May Mahācakreśvarī always protect the infinite intermediate directions;
may Uḍḍī, thereafter Tvaritā, always protect the left side.
May the others protect the directions, and may Kulasundarī guard me;
may Nityā protect me from above, and Mādhava protect me at all times.
May Nīlā, she who is called the Blue Banner, and Vijayā from all sides,
and Sarvamaṅgalā, always grant me auspicious blessings.
May Jvālāmālinī protect the mind and vital breaths within the body;
may Vicitrā protect [them] from all sides, and may the beautiful Ṣoḍaśī protect [them]. 12.
May the four Gurus, who destroy what is undesirable, protect me for the sake of crossing over the shoreless ocean of cyclic existence. (13)
May the ten renowned Siddhis, who bestow the fruits of what has been ordained and possess inconceivable, great majesty, utterly destroy my obstacles. 14.
May the eight goddesses of speech, whose beautiful forms are auspicious and whose lotus-feet are being worshipped by the multitude of heads of the gods, protect me. 15.
May the sixteen [goddesses], who destroy all obstacles, who consist of the portions of both the eternal and the non-eternal, and who effect the attraction of desires, dispel every hindrance. 16.
May the secret Yoginīs, who dwell in the Sarvāsāpūraka-cakra and are accompanied by Tripureśī, bestow auspiciousness upon me. 17.
May the beloved deities, who cause the stabilization of the world and whose lotus feet are worshipped by the universe, accomplish my great and cherished desire. 18.
May the Yoginīs of great power, who are joined with Tripurasundarī and abide within the wheel that causes universal agitation—being most secret—protect me. (19)
May the fourteen Yoginīs of great attachment protect me—those who are like the rays of the sun to the darkness of the difficult delusion that descends upon the *dūrvā* grass. 20.
In the wheel that bestows all good fortune, may the Yoginīs of the true tradition, together with Tripurāvāsinī, increase my prosperity. 21.
The ten deities, who bestow all accomplishments and whose faces are gladdened by wine, have been saluted; may they accomplish all aims. 22.
May these goddesses, endowed with the glory of Tripura and born of the Kula and Kaula lineages, who abide in the Sarvārthasādhaka-cakra, purify me. 23.
Endowed with all-knowledge and being the causes of all nirvāṇa, may the great goddesses who provide assistance through ten lines protect me. (24)
May the Nigarbha Yoginīs, who are adorned with garlands of Tripuras and abide in the Sarvarakṣākara Cakra, bestow auspiciousness upon me. 25.
May the eight goddesses of speech—who possess both great and small volitions, and who bind one with the desires of their imagination—be ever compassionate toward me. (26)
Endowed with the accomplishments of Tripura and established in the destroyer of all bonds, may the secret Yoginīs in the wheel remove my diseases. (27)
O Mahojambhā, O Mahāstambhā, O Mahāmohā, O Mahāraṇā—may these four mantra-deities be the causes of our welfare. (28)
May these three deities, Kāmeśvarī and the others, who have established their abodes within the six-cornered [mandala] at the front of the wheel on the right and left, protect me. (29)
May the Yoginīs, who bestow all accomplishments and are united with Tripurāmbā within the Cakra, fulfill my heart's desire—these most secret ones. (30)
Among all these goddesses, she is the sovereign and chosen deity,
the youthful Tripurasundarī, who is difficult even for the gods to attain.
May the illustrious Mahātripurasundarī protect [us]—she whom even Brahmā and the other gods do not know in the beginning, the end, or the middle. 32.
May the Yoginīs, who possess the secrets of both the transcendent and the immanent, abide for the sake of joy within this Bindu-cakra, which consists of all bliss and has been established by her.
O Goddess, may Vaṭukeśvara, who knows the ritual of worship according to the samaya and is intent on incantations of enmity,
protect me while standing in the right-hand position on the right side.
May the Yoginīs, who destroy great obstacles, who have made their abode on the left side, and who dwell within the three states of waking, be for our delight. (35)
May the compassionate Kṣetrapāla, who stands before me for the sake of my pleasure, destroy the array of obstacles that cause hindrance. (36)
May the Lord Gaṇeśvara, whose single stride brings about the destruction of intractable afflictions such as epilepsy,
protect me while stationed at the position of the back.
Whoever at any time recites or hears this hymn, all of his afflictions shall perish before long. (38)
That face is the form of poetry; that house is the abode of Lakṣmī;
and that place shall be pure in its very essence where this is recited spontaneously. (39)
A man afflicted by disease is freed from diseases; one who is bound is released from bondage; and one beset by obstacles is liberated from obstacles by reciting this hymn and other such prayers. (40)
This Tripurā, the object of meditation and protection, should be recited with effort;
through her comes the attainment of Lakṣmī, and through her, the destruction of sin. (41)
The auspicious armor (*kavaca*) of the *Tripurārṇava Tantra* is completed.
Now I shall describe another armor, which brings happiness to the [mantras of] the sixteen [Mātṛkās].
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, you who bestow grace upon the worlds!
O Mahādeva, by your favor, many mantras have been heard by me."

O Lord, the various means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), as well as the extraction of the ritual peg (*kīlaka*), and the removal of defects such as curses—these have been heard by me from you, O Master. (2)
The armor (kavaca) of the Goddess Rājarājeśvarī has been indicated by me;
now I wish to hear it—please tell it to me, O Lord.
Īśvara said:
"O Goddess, you have been restrained by me again and again for hundreds of thousands of crores of times; yet, O beloved, due to the nature of women, you ask me once more."
This armor is an absolute secret that bestows the fruits of all desires;
O Goddess of the God of Gods, it brings him pleasure—listen as I recount it.

Of this armor-mantra (*kavaca*) of the sixteen-syllable vidyā of the venerable Mahātripurasundarī, the Queen of the Kings of Queens, Mahādeva is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *prastārapaṅkti* is the meter (*chandas*), the venerable Mahātripurasundarī, the Queen of the Kings of Queens, is the deity (*devatā*),
and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the accomplishment of all aims.
Oṃ! May Bhairavī protect me in the east; may Bālā protect me in the south;
may Mālinī protect me in the west; and may Vāsinī guard me in the north.
May the Great Goddess Mahātripurasundarī protect [me] above;
may the Mistress of Gods, who dwells in the depths of Pātāla, protect [me] below.
May the Vāgbhava protect my foundation; likewise, may the Kāmarāja protect my heart;
may the Ḍāmara, the granter of all desires, protect me eternally on my head.
May the Blessed One, the Great Knowledge, the Supreme Goddess, protect me always at the aperture of Brahmā, in all my limbs, and in all the locations of the bodily openings. 9.
May *ai* and *klī* protect me on the forehead; may *hrīṃ haṃsaḥ* protect the two eyes;
likewise, may *śrīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ* protect the nose, the two ears, and the chin.
May *hasau* protect the throat and *strīṃ* the heart;
may *kalahrīṃ*, *krīṃ*, and *śrīṃ* protect the region of the navel; and may *hūṃ* and *hrīṃ* protect the secret place and the two feet.
O Goddess, may you protect me from all sides; may you protect me at my joints.
Protect me in water, on land, as well as in the sky, in the cardinal directions, and likewise in the royal palace.
Huṃ kṣeṃ māṃ—may Tvaritā protect me; together with hrīṃ and klīṃ, may Manobhavā protect me; haṃsaḥ—may the Great Goddess, the supreme partless deity, protect me. (13)
May Vijayā, Maṅgalā, Dūtī, Kalyāṇī, Bhagamālinī, Jvālā, Mālinī, and Nityā always protect me at all times. 14.
Thus, O Goddess, this armor, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain, has been declared by me out of affection for you; it must be guarded with great effort. (15)
This is the supreme secret, dear one, more hidden than the hidden;
it bestows wealth, fame, long life, and the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (16)
O Goddess, O Śivā, it destroys bad dreams for men, brings together men and women, effects attraction, and causes paralysis and delusion. (17)
He who worships Śivā, the Queen of the Queens of Kings, with the hosts of Yoginīs without knowing this armor-mantra (kavaca), will be devoured by them; of this there is no doubt. 18.
For such a person, there shall never be success in mantra, O Saṃkarī;
in this world, there will be poverty, disease, sorrow, and fear. (19)
Having gone to hell in the next world, one would obtain birth as an animal;
therefore, one who is qualified should always practice this, for from that [practice] one becomes [fit for liberation].
If one recites this most meritorious armor (*kavaca*), which has issued from my own mouth, during the ritual of worship or before [the deity],
having enjoyed auspicious fortunes, pleasures, and delights, [one shall attain liberation].
One attains that state of the Goddess once again at the time of death.
The supreme armor of the Kulārṇava Tantra is hereby completed.
I shall briefly proclaim the hymn of one hundred and eight names of Tripurāsundarī;
it is the supreme secret mantra to be recited, which destroys even the most wondrous calamities. (1)
Śrī is consciousness, Mahāmāyā, Mahāgaurī, Maheśvarī, Mahābuddhi, Mahācaṇḍī, Mahākālī, and Mahākalā. (2)
Great hunger, the great seal, great sleep, the great arising;
great fortune, great enjoyment, great delusion, the great emergence. (3)
Mahājayā, Mahātuṣṭi, Mahālajjā, Mahādhṛti, Mahāghorā, Mahādaṃṣṭrā, Mahākānti, and Mahāsmṛti. || 4 ||
Mahāpadmā, Mahāmedhā, Mahābodhā, Mahātapā, Mahāsvadhā, Mahāsvāhā, Mahābādhā, Mahāsura. || 5 ||
She is the shatterer of great bonds, the destroyer of great fears;
she has great eyes, a great mouth, a great tongue, and great arms.
She is filled with great trees, possessing great shade and great sinlessness;
she has great attachment and great relief, and she delights in the great mountains.
She is composed of the Great Brahma, the mother of great essence and great boons;
she is the slayer of the great Asuras, the mighty Pārvatī, Carcikā, and Śivā.
She is great patience, great delusion, the great mother, most venerable;
she is of noble lineage, greatly fickle, the great illusion, and the one of great fruit.
Mahānīlā, Mahāśīlā, Mahāśubhrā, Mahākalā; Mahācitrā, Mahāsetu, Mahāhetu, and Yaśasvinī. || 10 ||
She is the Great Knowledge, the Great Accomplishment, the Great Truth, and the Great Goal;
she is the Great Goddess, the Great Durgā, and the cutter of great evil dreams.
She is the bestower of great liberation, liberation itself, supremely skillful, most exalted,
the greatly auspicious one, the Great Speech, and the destroyer of great diseases.
The great tree, of great form, the great pestilence, the Great Goddess;
she who brings about great security, the secure one, the bestower of great sovereignty. || 13 ||
She is the great destroyer of poison, the bestower of nectar, and the dispeller of great misfortune;
she is Mahādurgā, the Great Tārā, who dwells upon the great Kailāsa.
She is Mahāsubhadrā, the auspicious one, the most precious, and the great virtuous lady;
she is the eternal Mahāpratyaṅgirā, the bringer of the great dissolution.
She is the great power, the great liberation, and the bestower of great auspiciousness;
whoever recites this with devotion, even if they should be situated in a state of peril.
Standing in the midst of an iron cage, his bondage shall perish;
kings will become his servants, and he will be beloved by all people. || 17 ||
He attains the highest prosperity, and his afflictions shall perish;
he shall conquer his enemies in battle, just as Garuḍa conquers the serpents.
Poison does not affect him, nor do death, fire, or water;
premature death can never happen to him at any time. (19)
Whatever a desirer wishes for, he attains that very thing and not otherwise;
and what is the use of saying more? He stands at the head of all. (20)
"The hundred names proclaimed in the Rudrayāmala Tantra have been recited."
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi* composed by Pūrṇānanda Paramahaṃsa. 19.
The Twentieth Chapter:
[The Description of the Puraścaraṇa of Mantras] Now I shall explain the supreme *puraścaraṇa* of mantras. (1)
[The Necessity of Puraścaraṇa for the Attainment of Mantra-Siddhi] That which, without which a mantra would not be perfected even in hundreds of years—
that is called *puraścaraṇa*, performed by oneself for the sake of attaining success in the mantra. (2)
Just as a body devoid of life is incapable of any action, so too is a mantra proclaimed to be ineffective when it lacks the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa). || 3 ||
[The Necessity of Performing Puraścaraṇa at the Outset] Therefore, at the outset, the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) must be performed by the best of practitioners,
by the mere performance of which the deities come under one's control. || 4 ||
[The Procedure for the Puraścaraṇa: Now, having first fasted and performed his daily obligatory rites, being pure,
that best of mantra-knowers should worship with devotion the twice-born, the gods, and the guru.
1. Now, regarding the definition of *puraścaraṇa*, it is stated in the *Haṃsamaheśvara-tantra*:
"Recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), libation (*tarpaṇa*), sprinkling (*seka*), and the feeding of Brahmins—this fivefold worship in this world is called *puraścaraṇa*."
Also in the *Rāmārcanacandrikā*:
"Success in the worship of the five limbs of the mantra obtained from the Guru according to the rules through [his] grace is prescribed; this is preceded by the *puraścaraṇa*."

3 | Regarding the phrase "devoid of life" (*jīvahīna*): this verse also appears in the twenty-seventh chapter of the *Gandharva-tantra*, where the reading *dehī* is found; and according to the *Puraścaraṇabodhinī*, that term indeed has the meaning of "body."
One should worship Gaṇeśa, the practitioners, and likewise the ancestors;
this applies to all mantras as well as to the vidyās. (6)
Having received the command of the guru, the wise one, with a purified inner self,
should diligently perform the preparatory rites himself or have the guru perform them;
in the absence of the guru, another Brahmin devoted to the welfare of all living beings [should do so].
[Places for the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa):
A sacred field, the bank of a river, a cave, a mountain peak, a region of pilgrimage sites, the confluence of rivers, and a purifying forest. (8)
Various gardens, the foot of a bilva tree, the slope of a mountain, a grove of tulasī, a cow-pen, a bull-less [place], and a temple. (9)

One should perform the recitation (japa) by resorting to any one of these places: at the root of an aśvattha or lakṣmī tree, in a cow-pen, in the midst of water, in a temple, on the shore of the ocean, or in one's own home. 10.
And in the Rudrayāmala: "A mantra indeed bestows fruit only when it is perfected through *puraścaraṇa*;
therefore, one who knows the mantra, desiring success, should perform the *puraskriyā*."
What is the use of fire offerings, what use is recitation, and what use are the elaborate procedures for mantra-installation,
if there is no preliminary service (puraskriyā) of the secret mantras?
"For the honoring of mantras is said to be their primary life-force.

(8–10) Regarding the passage beginning with "a field of merit" and so forth, this very reading also occurs in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*. However, the half-verse beginning with "any one of these" and so forth [is interpreted differently]; in the context of practice (*sādhana*), it simply means: "these places are recommended for practitioners of mantra."
It is not found there.
And the determination of the location is stated in the *Prapañcasārasaṃgraha*:
"Either on the shore of the ocean, or on a mountain peak, or at the confluence of rivers flowing to the sea."
A wise man should recite [the mantra] in a secluded place, in his own excellent house, or in the temple of Viṣṇu.
[p. 763) [Rules for food during the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa):
While eating, one should consume sacrificial food (haviṣya), or food fit for Śakti-worship, or barley-gruel (yāvaka), or milk, or even roots—whatever may be obtained with effort. || 11 ||
[Things to be avoided during *puraścaraṇa*:
One should avoid honey, alkaline substances, salt, and oil; as well as betel-leaf, eating from a bell-metal vessel, and eating during the daytime. (12)
[Actions to be performed after the recitation of the mantra:
Having recited the mantra, one should perform bathing, sipping water, and eating with food and drink;
and one should perform the worship of the deity at the three junctions of the day according to the prescribed rule. (13)
One should not recite the mantra alone at only one of the three junctions of the day.
Also in the Śivagītā: "If one takes refuge at a bilva tree and recites various mantras,
that constitutes the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) in a single day alone."
"But the man who, having constantly constructed a hut made of *vilva* wood, performs recitation (*japa*),
all mantras become perfected through the mere act of recitation alone," and so forth.
Regarding the Gaṅgā, it is said in the *Kuloḍḍīśa*:
"There is no altar nor a seat here, no worship nor likewise a ritual procedure;
having performed the recitation (japa) according to the stated number, one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa) and so forth.
And in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā:
"Japa is recommended in the presence of the sun, a preceptor, the moon, a lamp, water, Brahmins, and cows.
Thus it is stated in the sixteenth chapter of the Nibandha.
For heroes, however, the bank of a great river,
a temple, a solitary linga, a cremation ground, an empty house, and a crossroads [are suitable].
[The Salutation to the Guru] One who dwells constantly in a single village should go and indeed pay homage to the guru.
The guru alone is the supreme Brahman; therefore, one should worship him first. (15)
One should perform the obligatory and occasional duties, associate with the virtuous,
and bathe with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) or with pure myrobalan (amalaka) alone.
[Instruction on Bathing and Libations] When possible, one should bathe at the three junctions of the day; otherwise, twice or even once.
For one who does not bathe, there is no fruit, nor for one who does not offer libations to the ancestors. (17)

One should avoid speaking with women, Śūdras, husbands, outcastes (vratyas), and atheists; one should also avoid speaking what remains uneaten (impure food) and should abandon falsehood and crookedness from afar. 18.
One should avoid listening to singing and instrumental music, watching dances, as well as oil massages, the application of perfumes and ointments, and the wearing of flowers. (19)
He should completely avoid sexual intercourse, conversation about it, and social gatherings concerning it;
at that time, he should not bathe, nor should he touch twice-born men or women.
A person performing the *puraścaraṇa* rite should avoid bathing in hot water, eating food that has not been offered [to the deity],
and should not commit violence against living beings.
[The prohibition against apprehending an entity from anything else: Indeed, apart from fire, no entity whatsoever can be apprehended from other things, even when such a possibility exists.
In the absence [of such a place], having received [the water] from a pure person outside of a sacred bathing site (tīrtha) on a day other than a festival, one should recite the mantra. || 22 ||
p. 765) [Prohibition of Recitation during Specific States]:

One who wears a turban, one wearing a bodice, one from the Ganges region, one with disheveled hair, one who is uncovered, one whose hands lack the *pavitra* ring, one who is impure, or one who is crawling—such a person should never recite [mantras]. (23)
Having uncovered his hands or perhaps covered his head,
or with a mind distracted by anxiety, or angry, bewildered, or filled with haste— (24)

One should not recite [the mantra] with one's lower garment untied, nor while lying down, nor while walking, nor while standing; nor on a street, nor in an inauspicious place, nor in a place of darkness.
[The special instruction regarding recitation:
One should perform the recitation day after day slowly and clearly, neither too fast nor too slow, neither deficient nor excessive. (26)
[The prohibition against skipping days during recitation: The rule of continuity has been proclaimed; one should not let a day pass by.
From the omission of a day, the loss of their accomplishment arises. (27)
[Regarding the duration of the recitation:
Generally, with one-pointed mind, one should perform the recitation until midday.
[Regarding the rule for clothing during recitation:]
One should not recite the mantra while wearing only a single garment, nor while distracted by many garments. || 28 ||
[Regarding the causes for abandoning the recitation while reciting:
Upon seeing, speaking with, or hearing those who have fallen from their caste or those of the lowest castes; upon sneezing, the passing of wind, or yawning, one should abandon the recitation. (29)

25. Regarding the phrase "on a street": a censured location is also mentioned in the sixteenth chapter of the Nibandha: "The practitioner should not dwell on that path by which kings, ministers, powerful men, and influential people travel."

p. 766) [Purification and other rites to be performed before reciting again: Having risen and sipped water, upon reaching that [state], one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with its six limbs. [Having done this, one performs the daily recitation.]
Having performed [the ritual] correctly, one should recite the remainder, or else gaze at the sun and other luminaries.
[The Rule for the Bed during Puraścaraṇa:
One should always sleep on a bed of kuśa grass while wearing clean garments;
one should wash the bed every day and sleep alone, free from fear. (31)

[The Description of the Support for the Worship of the Goddess] One should worship the Goddess as residing in a *liṅga*, and likewise in a book; one should worship Mahāmāyā as residing on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), and in sandals or images. (32)
Then, one should worship a citrine [stone], or even one situated in water, for three days.
[The specific details regarding the sword and other items: the sword should be fifty finger-breadths long, and the trident should have three prongs. || 33 ||
On a stone slab at the mountain peak, as well as in a mountain cave, one should constantly worship the Goddess, endowed with the radiance of devotion. (34)
[The Fruit of Worshipping the Goddess in Specific Locations: Worship performed in Vārāṇasī bestows the full fruit;
it is said to be four times more efficacious in the presence of Puruṣottama. (35)
The worship at Dvāravatī is specifically twice as great as that;
among all sacred fields (kṣetra) and seats (pīṭha), no worship is equal to that of Dvāravatī.
In the Vindhya mountains it is said to be a hundredfold, and it is equal to that in the Gaṅgā;
likewise in Āryāvarta, Madhyadeśa, and Brahmāvarta. (37)
Worship that yields fruit in the Vindhya mountains, as well as at Prayāga and Puṣkara, is said to be four times more effective when performed in the waters of the Karatoyā river. (38)
Therefore, it is said to possess fourfold qualities in the presence of Nandikeśvara;
thereafter, in the womb of Siddheśvarī, it bestows twice that amount of spiritual perfection.
Thereafter, it is said that [the merit] at the pool of the Lauhitya River is fourfold;
equal to that is the merit at Kāmarūpa, everywhere both in water and on land.
Just as Viṣṇu is the most excellent of all, and just as Lakṣmī is the highest of all, so too is the worship of the Goddess esteemed in Kāmarūpa, the abode of the gods. 41.
The sacred field of the Goddess, Kāmarūpa, truly exists as its equal nowhere else;
elsewhere the Goddess is rare, but in Kāmarūpa she is in every house.
Then, "The mandala of Nīlakūṭa is said to be a hundredfold;
even twice that much is said for the Śivaliṅga made of hairaka. (43)
Then: "It is said that [the merit] is a hundredfold in the Kāmākhyā-yoni-maṇḍala for one who has performed the worship of Mahāmāyā in Kāmākhyā even once. (44)
He obtains his desires here in this world and the nature of Śiva in the next;
there is not even one equal to him, nor does any deed remain for him.
This doctrine was spoken by the Lord in the Vāmakeśvaratantras. (45)
[The Procedure for Puraścaraṇa] Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the ritual procedure that should take place here.
[The Installation of the Kīla during the Preparation of the Ground]
Furthermore, one should fashion eight stakes together with the desired [deities]. || 46 ||
46–48 | "And eight stakes" (kīlakān): the ritual for planting the stakes is stated in the *Nibandha* cited in the *Puraścaraṇabodhinī* (p. 768):
"The wise practitioner, having consecrated each [stake] seven or eight times with the root mantra and the weapon mantra (*astramantra*), should draw them into the ground in the eight directions. (47)
[The worship of the lords of the directions upon the stakes:
Having worshipped the eight lords of the directions upon those stakes, starting from the east in due order, with perfumes and other offerings, as well as plantains, sweetmeats, and so forth. (48)
[The offering of bali to the lords of the directions and the worship of the Vāstu deity:
Or else, having given the bali-offering to them, one should worship the Vāstu deity;
thus, when the field has been secured by the mantrin, he is not overcome by obstacles. (49)
[The Worship of the Guardians of the Field and Others:

One should worship the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapāla), Gaṇeśa, Vaṭuka, and likewise the Yoginī with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; thereafter, one should take refuge in the field. || 50 ||
One should drive stakes made from milky trees, consecrated with weapon-mantras,
into the ten directions, and one should worship the Weapon-deity within them.
And when the field has been pinned down, the practitioner is not overcome by obstacles.
Regarding the prohibited places for the ritual implantation of the *kīla*, it is stated in the sixth chapter of the *Kālīkulāmṛta*:
"One should not dig *kīlas* there, whether at a great sacred ford (*mahātīrtha*), in an empty house, or even in a temple; [spiritual power] is accomplished there by mere recitation (*japa*) alone."
The specific detail is given in the *Nibandha*:
"Then, having recited the *Sudarśana* mantra one hundred and eight times,
one should drive those stakes into the ground in sequence at the six directions of the altar."
Oṃ! And those who are creators of obstacles here on earth, in heaven, or in the intermediate space, and those others who have become obstacles to the success of my mantra—[may they depart].
Leaving this field of mine, which has been secured by stakes, may you all withdraw to a great distance;
may there be success for me without obstacles.
"With this [mantra], one should drive in the stakes; in them, one should worship the lords of the worlds. (p.
769) [Drawing the Kūrma-cakra:
"Relying on the center of the field, the wise man should draw the Kūrma-cakra."
One should prepare a pill placed in a lamp that wards off white leprosy.

51. Regarding "the center of the field": the measurement of the tortoise-diagram (*kūrmacakra*) is stated in the *Nibandha* cited in the *Puraścaraṇabodhinī*: "The practitioner of mantra should contemplate the tortoise in whichever village he performs his recitation (*japa*). Having reached the location of the lamp, the rite performed there yields its fruit."
Regarding the location of the lamp, as stated in the *Gautamīya*:
"The location of the lamp is said to be twofold for the practitioner: the front and the back.
Success occurs when the lamp is in its proper place; not otherwise, even by ten million recitations."
In the *Nibandha*: "Having divided the ground into a square, one should draw a grid of nine squares.
Regarding the location for the prohibition of the *kūrmacakra*, it is stated in the *Gautamīya*:
If one performs the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) on a mountain, by the bank of a river, in a sacred forest, or on the shore of a stream,
one need not worry about the tortoise there.
And in the Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā:
"A sacred field, a house, a holy ford, an auspicious temple,
the root of a bilva tree, the ocean, a forest, and likewise a garden."
"O best of Brahmins, one should not contemplate the tortoise-seal (*kūrmamudrā*) in these positions.
Regarding the tortoise-diagram (*kūrmacakra*): "One should write the seven groups [of consonants] in sequence, beginning with the eastern square."
In the central square of the Lakṣmī diagram, one should write the vowels in pairs;
in the directions starting from the east, one should place the initial letter of the village name.
One should know that its face is there, with two hands situated on either side;
the two sides of the chest are the two flanks, and the two feet are the tail;
by this sequence, one should divide even the central part into its respective portions.
Situated in the mouth, one attains success; situated in the hand, one has a short life;
situated in the belly, one is indifferent; situated at the feet, one shall experience suffering.
If the minister is situated in the tail, he is afflicted by imprisonment, eradication, and other such calamities.
This is declared to be the Kūrma-cakra, which bestows success upon practitioners of mantra.
If one performs the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) without knowing the tortoise-diagram (kūrmacakra) within the Piṅgalā,
there is no fruit from that sacrifice; it leads only to total misfortune.

Although the *kūrmacakra* was described by the author Pūrṇānanda in the third chapter of the *Citra*, nevertheless, there exists a specific variation here [in the *Tantrasāra*] as well as in the *Puraścaraṇabodhinī*; therefore, it is mentioned again in the commentary (*ṭippaṇī*).
p. 771) [Thus, the preparation of the ground on the previous day]:
On the day preceding [the commencement], the wise one should perform the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the ground;
[on the day of commencement, the morning rites and so forth].
Then, having risen in the morning and performed his daily obligatory rites, he became pure.
One should make the mandala radiant with powders, incense, lamps, and so forth;
having done so according to the procedure prescribed in the Kalpa, one should worship the Supreme Goddess.
[The manner of sitting and so forth for recitation: Seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana), facing east, refraining from idle chatter,
with the senses purified, and [holding the hands] excluding the threatening gesture (tarjanī).
One should worship her with the beads of the rosary using one's fingers, neither too quickly nor too slowly. || 54 ||
[The number of daily recitations:
One should recite on each subsequent day exactly as many times as one recited on the previous day;
otherwise, it will cause an obstruction to success. 55.
[Instruction on the Recitation of Mantras in the Presence of Śiva’s Image, etc.
"In the presence of Śiva, or of the Sun, of fire, or even of the Guru, or even before a burning lamp, one should commence the rite of recitation. (56)
[The recitation should be performed starting from morning until midday.
One who knows the mantra should recite it starting from morning until the middle of the day.
[The determination of the seat for recitation:]
Now I shall describe the posture by which, it is said, perfection is attained. (57)
57–58 | Now, regarding the seat and so forth: A specific rule concerning the seat is stated in the *Puraścaraṇabodhinī* (p.
772): "Success in knowledge is attained on a seat of *kuśa* grass; one who desires fortune [attains it] on a tiger skin;
the destruction of suffering occurs on a woolen seat; and all perfections are achieved on a blanket. 58 ||
O Goddess of the Gods, in the Haṃsamāheśvara [tradition], a soft woolen blanket, silk, or wooden seat is used as an implement for ritual action; however, a leather seat (carmāsana) is to be accepted.
If one sits upon even a single hair, then everything will perish;
by the mere touch of a hair, the loss of accomplishment occurs.
And thus, the meaning is that one should prepare a seat of hairless skin.
For the sake of attaining specific desires, there is also the woolen blanket; the red woolen blanket is the best.
Knowledge-perfection is attained on a black antelope skin, and liberation on the skin of a tiger.
On a seat of kusha grass, there is accomplishment of mantra; no deliberation is required in this matter.
If the seat is made of earth, there arises suffering; if it is made of wood, there is misfortune;
if it is a bamboo seat, one will be poor; and if it is stone, there is affliction by disease.
On a seat of grass there is loss of fame; on a seat of sprouts, mental confusion;
indeed, a cloth seat causes the loss of recitation, meditation, and austerity.

In this context, the use of a cloth seat alone is prohibited, because it is stated that a cloth seat produces specific results—such as the removal of disease—and because of the Lord’s own statement: "Cloth, deerskin, and kusha grass, in ascending order. Here, the kusha grass mat is at the very bottom, the hide is upon that, and the cloth is upon that.
Then the practitioner, being constant, should always place a kuśa-grass mat at the very bottom;
upon that he should lay an antelope skin, and over those two he should place a cloth covering.

Thus, from the *Tantrārṇava* held by Ratnagarbha: it should be understood that a wooden seat (*dāruja-āsana*) is prohibited when standing alone, but is prescribed when mentioned in conjunction with *kuśa* grass and the like, because of the syntactic unity of the statement, "wooden [seats] are the means for ritual action" (*dāravaṃ karma-sādhanam*). Alternatively, the prohibition of wooden seats refers to wood such as mango (*āmra*), whereas the injunction pertains to [wood] such as *gāmbhāri*. (From the *Tārābhaktisudhārṇava*).
Grass, sprouts, wood, stone, as well as earthenware,
a bamboo seat, and cloth— these are [permissible], but the ground alone is the true seat.
"Thus, O Goddess, one should avoid these eight kinds of seats.
This statement from the *Brahmayāmala* should also be interpreted as having that same intent. Furthermore, in the *Gautamīya*:
"Likewise, the practitioner of mantra [should sit] on a soft seat, covered with a cloth, a deerskin, and kusha grass."
p. 773) "One should prepare either a white or a red garment for one's seat.
[This is the distinction for the ascetic and the student:
the ascetic and the student should always sit upon the skin of a black antelope. (59)
[The measurement of the seat:
One cubit or two cubits in width, and four finger-breadths in height;
one should sit there undisturbed upon either a svastika or a lotus design. 60.

[The Specificity of the Fruits of Seats such as Earth, etc. A seat made of earth brings about the destruction of one's lineage; a seat made of bamboo brings disease; likewise, a wooden seat produces [misfortune], while a stone seat causes great suffering.
The leaf causes suffering, the water causes fear, and the thread causes enmity;
however, the ram, the three-fold seat, and all such items bestow the attainment of liberation and other perfections.

[The specific seat for rites such as *abhicāra*: For *abhicāra*, it is black or red; for all rites such as *vaśya* and so forth, it is likewise; for pacification (*śāntika*), white is prescribed; for all purposes, it is on a multicolored woolen cloth.
In the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
"One initiated into the channels (nāḍī) may sit upon the skin of a black antelope; whether he be a householder, an ascetic, a forest-dweller, a celibate student, or a mendicant."
In the *Tripurāmahārṇava*,

it is stated that one should not sit upon the ground, a fan, or a leaf, and so forth. Regarding the specific seats (*āsana*) for the Kaulikas, however, the *Matsyasūkta* cited in the *Tārābhaktisudhārṇava* states:
"Even while seated on a soft woolen blanket or on other soft seats, or sitting comfortably on a grass mat (viṣṭara), one may accomplish the supreme siddhi. [Description of the Rosary] (p. 774)
Now I shall explain the arrangement of the garland in brief:
the sequence of letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa' is proclaimed as the letter-garland.
[The description of mantra recitation following the pronunciation of each letter with its bindu:
Having pronounced each letter together with its bindu, the wise practitioner should subsequently recite the mantra. [The description of the rosary and its central bead (meru):]
In forward and reverse order, the letter *kṣa* is said to be Meru.
[The Determination of the Specific Fruits of the Rosaries] Now, a rosary made of pearls bestows the four aims of human life;
likewise, it is said that one may practice with a rosary of crystal for the attainment of mastery over speech. 65.
A rosary of red beads leads to liberation and bestows all prosperity;
a coral rosary is for subjugation and grants the fulfillment of all desires and aims;
a rosary of *putrajīva* beads, however, bestows fortune and knowledge.

Through the *mālā* known as *krama*, exceedingly great prosperity (*lakṣmī*) arises; moreover, a garland of red sandalwood brings about subjugation (*vaśya*) and bestows good fortune (*saubhāgya*). (67)
A garland fashioned from gold and silver bestows desired objects; one made from conch shells and gems brings about imperishable fame;
and a garland constructed from all of these together leads to the liberation of men.
[The Determination of the Number of Beads in a Garland] One should fashion a garland for liberation with twenty-five seeds;
for nourishment, with twenty-seven; and for the rite of liberation, with thirty.
With thirty beads plus five preceding ones for the rite of sorcery (*abhicāra*), and that garland which consists of fifty beads is auspicious for all rites. (70)
That [mantra], beginning with four [repetitions], bestows the fruits of all actions;
with one hundred and eight repetitions, it grants all perfections and liberation.
[On the Faults that Obstruct Success in Bell-metal:
In bell-metal alone there are great defects, and practitioners do not achieve success.
[On the Description of the Colors of the Thread:]
"White, red, and likewise black [are used] in rites of pacification and for malevolent magic. (72)
[The Casting of the Thread] The wise one should cast the thread, or else a silk thread.
[The Stringing of Specific Garlands According to the Specific Number of Threads]
The Vaiṣṇava rosary may be made of cotton threads or even of lotus fibers. || 73 ||
A rosary made of wool fibers or even of fruits is declared to be "belonging to Śiva" (saivī).
Having taken up the consecrated rosary, which has been worshipped with sandalwood paste, [one should perform recitation according to the number prescribed in the ritual manual]. (74)
Relying upon this, the wise practitioner should recite for the duration of a *kalpa*;
having completed the recitation according to the full number, it should indeed be ten thousandths of the total count of the recitation. [This is the rule for the number of oblations. 75.

70–71 | Regarding "with thirty": in the rite of *abhicāra* (sorcery), the recitation (*japa*) should be performed with thirty-five [beads]; the meaning is that a rosary (*mālā*) consisting of fifty-four [beads] bestows the fruits of all rites.
75–76 | Regarding "with the complete": likewise, after the recitation of the mantra for the full number of times as prescribed in the respective *kalpa*,...

Having recited the mantra ending in *svāhā*, one should offer oblations in the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) characterized as described in the previous chapter, using either a tenth part or a fourth part of that [total].
Alternatively, while reciting the mantra ending in *svāhā*, one may offer a fourth part of the number of recitations (*japa*).
One should offer oblations in the fire-pit as described, according to the prescribed rules and ritual procedure. || 76 ||
[Another method here:
Alternatively, having performed recitation (japa), one should worship and offer oblations (homa) amounting to one-tenth of that.
[The description of libation (tarpaṇa):]
Then, having worshipped the deity in the water with the shoulder-portion of the oblation, || 77 ||
With the mantra "I satisfy," one should offer libations into the mouth of the deity, visualizing the Goddess standing in the midst of the water together with her retinue and their weapons.
[The rule for substances in the libation: One should perform the libation with all kinds of flowers for the pacification of all calamities;
with clarified butter for the attainment of full longevity; and with honey for the attainment of good fortune. (79)

One should consecrate her who consists of the universe with milk for the attainment of health, with three [measures] for the attainment of sovereignty, with coconut water for the sake of affection, and with cold water for the acquisition of kingship; one should consecrate her with water for the attainment of all goals. (80)
And in the *Sāktānandatarangiṇī*:
"O fair-faced one, having performed the recitation (*japa*) according to the sequence prescribed in one's own ritual manual (*kalpa*),

One should feed Brahmins every day for the sake of pacifying any deficiency or excess.
Alternatively, when everything has been completed, one should then perform the fire-oblation and other rites.

"Alternatively, when the count of one hundred thousand has been completed, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*); or rather, when whatever number of recitations (*japa*) one has performed has been completed, one should perform the fire-oblation."
[The Description of Consecration] Reciting the root mantra at the end of the word "namaḥ," with one-tenth of the libation (*tarpaṇa*),
one should consecrate one's own head with water using the mudrā called the "Vase" (*kumbha*). (81)

worship performed at the three times daily, constant recitation, and likewise the libation (tarpaṇa).
The meal for the Brahmins and this recitation of the *Aṅgiras* [text] constitute the preliminary rite. || 83 ||

[The giving of the teacher’s fee:
One should give a fee to the teacher according to one's means. || 87 ||

a Kṣatriya, however, three times; a Vaiśya, four times; and a Śūdra, five times. (p.

(p. 780) [The Explanation of Nourishment:
If one is afflicted and overcome by shame, one should then become accomplished and nourish [the mantra].
One should apply the three seed-syllables of the *bālā* at the beginning and the end of that [mantra]. (102)
Having written the vidyā with cow's milk and honey, one should hold it in the hand.
[The Description of Drying Up: If this [mantra] has been nourished but has not become perfected, the practitioner of mantra should perform the "drying up" (*soṣaṇa*).
He should place the *vidyā* between the seed-syllable of wind (*vāyubīja*) by means of the *vidarbha* method. 104.
This vidyā should be worn around the neck after being written with excellent ashes. [Regarding the description of burning:
"Even if it has been dried, if it is not yet perfected, it should be burned by means of the fire-seed syllable. (105)
In the rite of burning, one should join each individual syllable of the mantra with the seed-syllable of Agni at the beginning, the end, the middle, and above.
Having written the mantra with the oil of the Brahmavṛkṣa tree, one should wear it on the neck;
then the mantra spoken by Śaṅkara shall become efficacious.
[The Worship of the Guru Following the Puraścaraṇa]: Having thus performed the *puraścaryā*, the wise practitioner should worship the Guru.
[The Concealment of Mantras and so forth].
The wise one should worship the guru and guard the mantra with diligence;
he should not show his rosary or ritual gestures even to the guru. 108.
Devotion must be cultivated toward the mantra-deity and the guru; likewise toward the mantra, the deity, and the guru who knows the mantra.
Devotion toward these three should always be practiced, for that is the primary means of accomplishment. 109.
[The Identity of Mantra and Deity] For the mantra is to be known as the deity, and the deity has the form of the mantra.
One who desires the supreme state must not make a distinction between the two. (110)
[When a mantra is perfected, all perfections are attained:
When a single mantra is correctly perfected, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished here on earth. (111)
[The distinction of results according to the number of recitations, such as one or two hundred thousand:
Now, the greatness of recitation according to the different numbers of hundred-thousands is stated:
By reciting a mere hundred-thousand times, the practitioner of mantra is liberated from great sins. (112)
By two hundred thousand [recitations], even the sins arising from seven lifetimes, including the primary mortal transgressions (mahāpātaka), will be destroyed; of this there is no doubt. (113)
Then, having recited [the mantra] three hundred thousand times, one whose body is composed of mantra and yantra will destroy millions of great sins; of this there is no doubt. (114)
By reciting the mantra four hundred thousand times, the practitioner becomes a great lord of speech;
by five hundred thousand recitations, a person becomes as rich in jewels as Kubera.
By merely reciting it six hundred thousand times, one becomes a great Vidyādhara;
by reciting it seven hundred thousand times, the mantrin becomes one who joins with the Khecarīs. 116.
By reciting the mantra eight hundred thousand times, the practitioner will certainly become worthy of worship by the gods;
he shall become a master of the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*, and kings and women in particular will come under his control. (117)
One should recite the mantra of Tripurasundarī ten million times;
he becomes the very embodiment of Rudra himself—the creator and the destroyer—without a doubt.
[p. 782) [The distinction of locations for the nine-hundred-thousand recitation:
At the location of the genitals, it has the form of a flame; at the foundation (ādhāra), it has the luster of gold.
Residing in the navel, it has the appearance of the solar disc; in the heart, it consists of a flame of light. || 119 ||
Above that, at the throat, is that which consists of the sun; at the uvula, it has the luster of a lamp-flame;
between the eyebrows, it has the brilliance of the lunar orb; and at the center of the brows, it has the radiance of a jewel.
In the ninth [center] is Viśvatejas; with these nine hundred thousand [recitations], the yogi established in these stations should practice the nine hundred thousand.

119–121 | "In the region of the *meḍhra*, etc. This was stated in accordance with the *Navacakraviveka*. "Above that" refers to the *ājñācakra*; "in the *lambikā*" means in the *tālucakra*. The *Navacakraviveka* is found in the *Saubhāgyalakṣmī Upaniṣad*: "Then the gods said to him, 'Please teach us the discernment of the nine wheels (*navacakraviveka*)'. He replied, 'So be it,' and said: 'In the *ādhāra* is the *brahmacakra*, which has three revolutions...'"
There, one should meditate upon the root *deva-śakti* in the form of a triangle (*bhagamaṇḍalākāra*) and in the shape of fire (*pāvakākāra*).

Right there is the seat of Kāmarūpa, which bestows the fruit of all desires. This is the *ādhāra-cakra*. The second is the *svādhiṣṭhāna-cakra*, which has six petals; in its center is a *liṅga* facing westward, resembling a sprout of coral.

One should meditate there; thus, Uḍḍiyāna-pīṭha becomes the bestower of the siddhi of attracting the world. The third is the navel-cakra, which has five whorls and is shaped like a coiled serpent; in its center, one should meditate upon Kuṇḍalinī, who possesses the radiance of ten million rising suns and has a slender waist. Through the power of her capacity, she becomes the bestower of all siddhis. [Then] the Maṇipūraka-cakra...

The heart-cakra has eight petals and faces downward; in its center, one should meditate on the form of a liṅga composed of light. That indeed is the Haṃsa-kalā, beloved by all, which brings all the worlds under one's control. The throat-cakra is four finger-breadths [in extent]; there, on the left is the Iḍā, the lunar channel, and on the right is the Piṅgalā, the solar channel. In the middle of those, one should meditate on the Suṣumṇā as white in color—he who thus...

One becomes a master who has attained the perfection of the Vedas. There, at the *tālucakra*, there is a flow of the stream of nectar; in the cavity of the root-center of the *ghaṇṭā-kāli* and other centers, there is an opening suspended by a royal staff—the tenth door. There, one should meditate on the Void (*śūnya*), and the dissolution of the mind occurs. The seventh is the *bhrū-cakra*, the size of a thumb;
there, one should meditate on the eye of knowledge (*jñānanetra*) in the form of a lamp-flame. That itself is the *pālakada*.
This bestows the perfection of speech (*vāksiddhi*). The eighth is the wheel of command (*ājñācakra*), the wheel of nirvāṇa at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*);

there, one should meditate on that which is other than the "needle-house" (*sūcikāgṛha*), having the form of a smoky crest. Therein lies the sacred seat (*pīṭha*) of Jālandhara, which bestows liberation.
The ninth is the supreme wheel of Brahman, the wheel of space (*ākāśacakra*); there is a sixteen-petaled lotus facing upwards.
In the center of that, within the pericarp (p.

783), [success is attained through nine hundred thousand recitations by means of the division of the nine wheels]; a hundred thousand [recitations] situated in nine locations is called "nine hundred thousand."
Having sequentially pierced the nine locations with the mantra, one pierces Kuṇḍalī.

Having drunk the nectar situated at the point of emission (visarga), one should again enter the foundation (ādhāra). One should thus remember the mantra as it moves from station to station in due order;
even one of meager fortune will certainly attain success—of this there is no doubt.
[The accomplishment of recitation by another method:
Alternatively, upon the foundational lotus, one should visualize the *liṅga* facing west;
it is the supreme self-manifesting (*svayambhū*) expression of the Yoginī in the form of light. 124.
Either in the center of the heart-triangle or in the form of a *bāṇaliṅga*, [one should meditate on it];
but in the center of the triangle at the head, [it faces] north and westward.
Staying there, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, remaining composed in concentration wherever one may be;
then the Blessed Vidyā, the subjugator of the three worlds, [will appear].
[The Description of the Consecration of the Rosary] Now I shall explain the consecration of the rosary, which bestows all accomplishments.

[The censure of mantra recitation with a non-abiding rosary: "Whatever person recites a mantra with non-abiding rosaries, one should know that all of it is fruitless, and Caṇḍikā becomes enraged. (128)
[The construction of the garland-thread: That which is fashioned by a beloved woman is said to bring success quickly.
Three threads should be wound upwards, and three threads should be wound downwards. (129)

One should meditate while visualizing that [triangle] in the center as having the form of three peaks with its apex pointing upwards; therein, at the very seat of Pūrṇagiri, the accomplishment of all desired powers (*icchāsiddhi*) occurs. Thus, although some slight discrepancy is observed here from the system of Pūrṇānanda, nevertheless, since the root source is one and the same, this has been presented as it was.
Having recited the root-mantra over a thread spun by a virtuous woman—whether made of cotton or silk—one should then wash the seed-syllable upon that thread. (130)
[The tying of knots in the garland:
Taking up each individual garland, one should fashion a Brahma-knot; it must not be made without a knot. One is not defiled by touching or not touching [the knots]. || 131 ||

"In the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Saura, Gāṇeśa, and also the Śrīkara [tantras], there is no defect in the absence of a knot at the beginning; one should again perform the seed-syllable ritual (bījakalpa) therein—of this there is no doubt. (132)
[Regarding the absence of defects in those devoid of knots, in the case of the specific goddesses:
Those goddesses who are devoid of knots shall be written down here in their entirety. || 133 ||
One should worship Kālikā and Tvaritā, as well as those beginning with Sakrā, according to the sixfold division; likewise, one should worship the Ācaraṇavāsins and Vārāhī.
[The specific ritual procedure for purifying the rosary:
One should install the *mātṛkā* letters interspersed by means of both direct and reverse order.
[The purification of the rosary with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*):]
One should cast the rosary, consecrated with the *śiva-mantra*, into the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). || 135 ||
[The offering of fragrance and other items to the rosary:
One should rub the rosary with fragrances and other substances using the Sadyojāta mantra, fumigate it with the Aghora mantra, and smear it with the Puruṣa mantra. (136)
One should consecrate each individual [item] one hundred times with the fifth mantra alone; [this is the instruction for the recitation of the mantra].
And one should consecrate Mount Meru with this very fifth mantra. || 137 ||

Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations indeed to Sadyojāta! In every birth, in beginningless birth, salutations indeed to the one who arises from existence! (1) Salutations to Vāmadeva, salutations to Jyeṣṭha, salutations to Rudra.
Salutation to Kāla; salutation to Kālavikaraṇa; salutation to Bala; salutation to Balapramathana; salutation to Sarvabhūtadamana;
salutation to Manomathana. || 139 || (2)
Oṃ, to those who are non-terrible, and to those who are terrible, and to those who are more terrible than the most terrible;
to all those who are everywhere and are everything—to you who possess the forms of Rudra, let there be salutation.
(140) Oṃ, we know that Puruṣa; we meditate upon Mahādeva.
May that Rudra inspire us.
(141) (4) Om! Īśāna is the lord of all knowledge, the lord of all beings;
he is the sovereign of Brahmā and the lord of all knowledge and all beings.
(Brahmā, the sovereign lord, the overlord of Brahmā) "May Śiva be ever mine"— Śivom. (5) [Refutation of the view that there is an absence of mantras regarding the sphere of Śakti]
Thus, purity regarding the sphere of power is not like that [of the five verses];
for that is not intended, since it is recorded in the *Muṇḍamālā*: || 143 ||
[The Installation of the Garland] Then, one should place the consecrated garland in a golden vessel,
or one may place it upon a lotus-shaped base made of nine leaves of the *aśvattha* tree.
[The bathing of the garland with the five nectars, etc.
Having bathed it well with the five nectars and with cool water, the practitioner should then place the seed-syllable upon that great corpse-seat (mahāpretāsana). || 145 ||
There, having worshipped the Goddess thoroughly along with her retinue, one should duly kindle the fire and offer oblations of ghee according to one's ability. (146)
