One should reveal it to a disciple endowed with devotion and to a virtuous son. (62)
One should never reveal [the mantra] even to one's cattle or kinsmen;
[regarding the fruit of giving the mantra to an unworthy recipient: if it is done so, misfortune shall befall him, and the mantras will turn their faces away. || 63 ||
Suffering increases constantly; therefore, one should avoid it with effort.
[The fruit of drawing the King of Mandalas with gorocanā and other substances:
The mantra-practitioner should draw the King of Mandalas using gorocanā and other such materials. (64)

In the midst of that [maṇḍala], one should visualize an excellent image that is exceedingly beautiful and delightful, radiant, conjoined with the Sāman chants, and interwoven with the Kāmarāja mantra. (65)
[The distinction of the fruit according to the distinction of the contemplation:
Even the foremost of practitioners, by contemplating her, shall quickly behold a young woman never seen before—she who is extremely difficult to find, even for thousands of people. 66.
Then the princess, with beautiful limbs, free from fear and shame, being truly deluded by the mantra, will certainly come to the practitioner. 67.
Then, having placed himself in the center of the wheel,
the practitioner should contemplate himself as being ruddy and possessing the brilliance of a thousand rising suns.
The supreme practitioner should also visualize the object of attainment as having become ruddy;
by this sequential yoga, he himself becomes possessed of the form of Kandarpa. (69)
Possessing the beauty and charm of all that is lovely, he brings all the worlds under his sway;
his form is accompanied by mudrās and honored with every kind of offering.
[The specific fruit resulting from writing names on the wheel:
Whoever worships the wheel, having interwoven the name of another, that person shall quickly become like a servant, or even a wealthy man or a king. (71)
The knower of mantras, endowed with the yoni-mudrā, should place the name of whomever he intends to join within the center of the wheel, even if that person has not been seen. 72.
By force, he quickly brings forth a yakṣiṇī,
a princess, a nāga maiden, an apsaras, a khecarī, or a celestial nymph.
[He saw] a Vidyādharī of divine form, the daughter of a ṛṣi and the wife of his enemy, whose orb of hips was quivering with the fever born of passion. (74)
Her inner being pierced by the arrows of desire and her eyes flickering,
he brought about this result through the meditation on the Great Kalā;
indeed, there is no doubt that it arose solely from the yoga of meditating on the Great Kāmakalā.
He would agitate the women of the heavens, the earth, and the depths of the netherworld.

[The description of the subduing tilaka: The practitioner of mantra should take one part of *rocanā* (cow bezoar) and one part of *kuṅkuma* (saffron), and then grind two parts of *candana* (sandalwood) together with them. 76.
One should apply a tilaka mark on one [of the brows] as a means of bringing the three worlds under control;
having empowered it by reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times, one shall bring [the object] under subjection.
Whatever is seen—whether a king, a city, or a village—all that comes under the control of the minister, the supreme practitioner. (78)
[The consecration of betel and other items for the purpose of subjugation:
Betel, incense, water, leaves, flowers, fruit, curd, milk,
ghee, ivory, cloth, and camphor— 79.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times over musk, saffron, cardamom, cloves, and nutmeg leaves, he gives it to whomever he chooses.
He certainly becomes submissive; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Indeed, all women become submissive and turn into servants. (81)
This method of forcible attraction has been explained; it cannot be otherwise.
[The method for attracting women:
The practitioner should draw [the figure] on the ground at a secret location using yellow pigment (rocanā). 82.

Having painted a beautiful and most enchanting image of Sundarī, who is richly adorned with lovely ornaments and fine attire, and who is decorated with all kinds of jewelry, and who is full of joy; (83)
One should join the Great Vidyā of one's birth-name with the forehead, throat, heart, navel, and the circle of the genitals, interlaced at the end with the word *aṅkuśa*.
One should write the syllable of Madana at all the joints of the body;
one should contemplate it at the joints of the body as having the luster of a shimmering pomegranate flower. 85.
Then, facing toward that hope, assuming the form of the Goddess herself and forming the *kṣobhaṇī* mudrā, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.

Having led her into the fire-chamber, which possessed the nature of the digits of the moon and sun, [he beheld] her, whose beautiful limbs were now impaired and who was tormented by the arrows of Māra. (87)
In this way, one may attract a woman even from a distance of a hundred yojanas.
[The Explanation of the Means for Invulnerability:
The wise man should write the entire Mātṛkā on the outside of the wheel,
either on birch bark, a gold leaf, a silver leaf, or even a copper leaf.
He is invulnerable to all living beings, especially to tigers and other such predators.
Likewise, by means of a circle adorned with symbolic signs and joined with *māra*,
and with camphor, saffron, and other substances, one shall attain the status of a favorite of the king. (90)
[The method for subjugation:

Having been purified by this procedure, the knower of mantras should, with yellow orpiment, agallochum, and saffron, draw the king of wheels together with the name of the person to be accomplished. 91.
Whatever is present—whether stationary or moving, the entire circle of living beings—is permeated by its own name. (92)
The supreme practitioner shall certainly bring [all things] under control; of this there is no doubt.
[This is the means for subjugating the three worlds.
The digits of Mahātripurasundarī are remembered as being equal to ten million Kāmas. (93)
In this very manner, having firmly grasped the syllables of the name of the one to be accomplished,
one should cause the wealth to enter by means of the arrows of the Mātṛkā.
One should place it in the middle of gold on the crest or on the left arm;
wherever one wears it, it brings the three worlds under control and makes the entire multitude of great kings into servants. (95)
Kings, swift horses, serpents, greatly wicked and highly fierce beings,
tigers, and rutting lions indeed become submissive to him.
[Causing great agitation:
One who knows the mantra for the beauty of the city's name should, according to the previous procedure, deposit it in the center, at a crossroads, or in the four directions. (97)
A great agitation arises among women, even among great men, and likewise among all living beings, as well as in front of their dwellings. (98)
[The Means for Attaining Equality with Kāma] One should visualize this earth, situated between those two, together with its mountains, forests, and groves,
blazing and adorned by all the lords of kings, clothed in the oceans. (99)
If one should meditate for one month, he will become equal to Kāma himself;
by his very glance, the mantra-practitioner attracts the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving.
[Attaining the capacity to destroy poison and other afflictions by mere sight:
By the mere sight [of this], one destroys poison at that very moment; there is no doubt about this.
It also destroys spirits, ghosts, piśācas, and fevers such as those occurring every fourth day. (101)
By its mere sight, it instantly destroys colic, abdominal tumors, and eye diseases.
[Attainment of the power to attract prosperity: If one should worship this [mantra], which is as beautiful as vermilion, at night... (102)
One should properly attract prosperity from as far as a hundred yojanas;
[this is the subjugation of people situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions].
When one thus worships the Goddess correctly in all the cardinal and intermediate directions, [the result follows]. 103.
There, one quickly brings under control the people situated in the cardinal directions and those in the intermediate directions, along with their sons, cattle, and kinsmen.
[The subjugation of the three worlds:
Having written [the name] on birch bark with yellow pigment (rocanā), agallochum (aguru), and saffron (kuṅkuma), one should place therein a city, a country, a mandala, or even a province. 105.
Having properly worshipped it according to the ritual rules while it is interspersed with the name,
and having placed it within the earth, one shall bring the three worlds under control.
[The specific fruits of wearing it on the neck and other parts:
Alternatively, if one who possesses the mantra wears it on the neck, on the crest-lock, or at the base of the arm, wherever he may be situated, he shall agitate even a great city. 107.
[The result of drawing the wheel with the milk of the Arka tree and other substances:
The juice of the Dhustūra plant combined with the milk of the Arka tree, along with gorocanā,
saffron, lac, musk, and red pigment— 108.
p. 838) With these [mantras], the practitioner should draw this wheel using the name of whomever [he intends].
For that person, [there shall be the removal of] fear of tigers, disease, enemies, portents, elephants, and so forth. 109.
There will certainly be no fear arising from thieves, malevolent planets, possessed persons, ḍākinīs, or śākinīs, nor from the hostile sorcery of others' mantras. (110)
[The fruit of constant wearing of the wheel:
The mantra-practitioner should constantly wear it; he shall destroy untimely death.
[He should meditate on] the Goddess situated in the center of the triangle, who dwells within the essence of the triangle. (111)
On the seventh day, one should cause [the name] joined with [the victim's] name, combined with gorocanā and saffron, to be placed beneath; [the victim] will become a servant like a slave.
[The Stupor of All Debaters]:
Having drawn [the diagram] with yellow substances, one should worship it with yellow substances;
facing the eastern direction, one shall paralyze all debaters. 113.
Even one with a thousand faces becomes mute at that very moment;
yet he who [recites] the name becomes eloquent, while the other becomes like a stone.
[The method for slaying an enemy:
Having drawn a wheel with the juice of the great *nīra* plant, the wise knower of mantras, facing south, should duly inscribe the name [of the victim]. (115)
Having burnt that wheel in fire, one should destroy the host of enemies. [This is the method for causing enmity.
The knower of mantras, having extracted the juice from the dung of buffaloes and horses, [should proceed]. 116.
Having inscribed the name with cow urine and enclosed it as before, and having placed it within a *palāśa* leaf, it shall cause enmity. 117.
[The performance of eradication: Having prepared the center of a *droṇa* crow’s wing with *rocanā*, hanging it thus in the sky causes the eradication of enemies. (118)
[The Rite for Subjugating All:
Having inscribed [the mantra] with mahānīlī and rocanā, using milk, alkali, juice, and so forth, the practitioner should wear it; he shall bring all castes under his control. 119.
[Another method for bringing all under control: By this very procedure, one should place [the object] in the midst of water.
Having bathed well with that water, drinking it brings everyone under control.
Good fortune arises through that water; of this there is no doubt.
[The Method of Agitating]:
Within seven days, the practitioner shall agitate the entire earth or even a city situated in its center; he should visualize it as being garlanded with flames. (121)
[The Method for Subjugating Women:
At night, when ten *daṇḍas* have passed, one should draw the King of Wheels with vermilion and saffron in a bowl that has not been fired by heat. (122)
The wise practitioner should draw an image of the maiden to be won within that [diagram];
above it, he should write the root mantra, and outside of that, he should write the Mātṛkā.
One should worship one's own chosen goddess together with her retinue right there;
[one should offer] one hundred and eight jasmine flowers along with the root-mantra accompanied by the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya).
And from each individual casting, by force, this great pit [arose], triangular and deep red like the moon reflected in rippling water. || 125 ||

Visualizing the [goddess] in the center of the womb of the one to be accomplished (sādhya), resembling the fire of universal dissolution, and having recited [the mantra] a thousand times while meditating, he certainly brings her under his control. (126)
[Another method for subjugating women:
Sitting upon a bed in a secluded, empty house,
one should personally consume betel leaf at night or by day while reciting the name of the person [one wishes to subjugate].
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, he indeed goes to his presence.
[Another method for subjugating a woman: Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should then have her drink water;
having [thus] secured her by means of her very life-breaths, she comes, overwhelmed with passion. 128.

[The method for making her a slave: If one performs a forehead mark (tilaka) after reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, while mixing together moonstone, sandalwood, musk, and red vermilion;
Whomever he sees, that person shall certainly and quickly become his servant. || 129 ||

[Another ritual procedure for subjugating a woman: Having mixed honey and ghee, and having fashioned an effigy out of sugar, one should infuse it with the vital breaths of the target; then, having recited the mantra one hundred and eight times, [one should perform the rite]. (130)
Having approached on Sunday, whoever should consume [it] for seven nights, she, with her limbs trembling, will certainly come into the presence of the practitioner. 131.
[The Stupefying of All Opponents: Facing the eastern direction, one should worship with yellow substances;
having drawn [the deity] in the place of the seat, one shall paralyze all opponents. 132.

[Subjugation of the Entire World by Another Method] Facing north, the wise practitioner should draw with vermilion powder; having worshipped according to the rule, he shall bring the entire world under his control. (133)
[The Enchantment of All Women] Facing westward, one should draw [the diagram] with sandalwood paste;
having worshipped the Vidyā according to the prescribed rite, one shall captivate the minds of all women. 134.
One becomes a beloved minister and can bring others under one's control like a maidservant;
yet, if one faces the direction of Yama and worships the black discus, it causes great loss. (135)
In that case, great loss arises for one who possesses such a name.
[The methods of paralyzing, causing enmity, and so forth:
when applied in the corners of Agni (southeast), Rākṣasa (southwest), Vāyu (northwest), and Śambhu (northeast), || 136 ||
As before, when applied in due order by the best of practitioners, it shall bring about paralyzing, causing hatred, disease, enemies, and eradication. (137)
[The All-Subjugating Rite] A wise person should draw a wheel with yellow pigment (rocanā) and place it in the midst of milk;
it will certainly bring about the subjugation of all, without a doubt. || 138 ||
[The method for causing the eradication of an enemy: Properly placed in the midst of cow urine, it brings about the eradication of the enemy.
[The method for causing enmity:]
But when the king of wheels (cakrarāja) is situated in the tail, it shall cause enmity. || 139 ||
[The Destruction of Enemies] Situated in the midst of a blazing fire, it becomes the destroyer of enemies. (p. 842) [The Attainment of the Power of Moving through the Air]
When one should draw [the design] with vermilion powder on a solitary four-way path. || 140 ||
Starting from the very outside and proceeding toward the center,
the practitioner should inscribe there the Mātṛkā, beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with the letter 'kṣa'.
The practitioner should perform worship at night according to the sequence of the Kula tradition;
he shall become a sky-walker (khecara), of this there is no doubt. || 142 ||

In the same way, one should worship either of the two deities according to the family tradition; having attained the state of being ageless and immortal, the practitioner of mantras becomes happy. (143)
[The Attainment of All Siddhis, such as the Sword, etc.
On a day presided over by a great element, the wise practitioner, with a steady mind, should worship the wheel in the cremation ground according to the prescribed ritual procedure. (144)

The accomplishment of the sword, the accomplishment of the vetāla, the pill and the collyrium, the accomplishment of the sandals and the collyrium, and the mental accomplishment born of the elements. (145)
The practitioner of mantra obtains all of that—the accomplishment of Mahāvīraṇa and the Yakṣiṇī born from a sparrow—there is no need for deliberation in this matter. 146.
[The Method for Destroying All Sins: A wise person should worship the auspicious Goddess with perfumes and flowers;
one whose soul is burdened by great sins shall become a destroyer of sin at that very moment. (147)
With sprouts of śamī and dūrvā grass, or with leaves of the aśvattha tree, or even with lotuses,
a man destroys the impurity created over seven lifetimes within a single month.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the *Śrī-Tattvacintāmaṇi*, composed by the venerable Pūrṇānanda Paramahaṃsa. || 23 ||
The Twenty-fourth Chapter:
[The Determination of the Recitation of Hymns to the Deity]. Now, the determination regarding the recitation of hymns to the deity is being stated.
[The Necessity of Recitation] A mental recitation would not be effective; rather, vocal recitation is praised. (1)
[The Rule for Recitation: "And at the end, one should utter the *praṇava*," so said the Primordial One.
This should be understood to apply everywhere in recitation; otherwise, it would be fruitless.
It should be recited with effort, with a pure mind and undistracted attention. || 2 ||
[The Rule for Placing the Book on a Support] Having placed the book upon a support, the wise one should perform the recitation.
[The Fault in Holding the Book in the Hand]
For by the mere act of placing [the hand] upon it, the fruit would be small. || 3 ||
[The Determination of the Scribe] One should not read that which was written by oneself; rather, one should read what has been written by a skilled scribe.
Furthermore, that which is written by a non-Brāhmaṇa shall also be fruitless. (4)

[The prohibition against reciting praises composed by ordinary people and others: One should not recite a hymn composed by oneself, nor one composed by another; for it has been stated by the sages that in the Kali age, such things are not commendable. || 5 ||
[The recitation of the seers, meters, and so forth must be performed]:
Having assigned the seers, meters, and other elements, the wise practitioner should recite the hymn of praise. || 6 ||

p. 844) [First: Recitation of the Thousand Names] Having first recited the thousand names of whichever deity it may be, the practitioner of mantra should thereafter recite that deity's hymn of praise. (7)
Having obtained an auspicious hymn for the recitation of the *saṃhitā*, one should conclude it;
[one should not pause the recitation in the middle of a chapter].
Having reached the end of a chapter, one should stop, but never in the middle.
But when a pause occurs in the middle, one should recite the beginning of the chapter again.
[The Description of the Ritual for Offering the Sacrificial Feast (Bali)] Now, therefore, the procedure for the offering of the sacrificial feast shall be explained here.
The yak, the black antelope, the fish, the ram, and the boar— || 9 ||
A buffalo, a monkey, a rhinoceros, and a ram—these should be offered first;
one should give two black goats and afterwards offer the great sacrifice (mahābali).
[The description of the six types of goats: White, black, red, tawny, variegated, and pale—these six kinds of goats are declared to be the supreme sacrificial offering for householders. (11)
[Description of the superior, middling, and inferior qualities of the bali offerings:
The white and the black are the two best; the variegated and the pale-white are the middling;
and the red and the tawny are proclaimed as the lowest. || 12 ||
From three months onwards, up to one year,
a black or very white young animal is said to be a praiseworthy sacrificial offering (bali).
That which occurs from six months onwards up to two years is declared the best *bali*; inferior to that is considered the lowest.
[The Sacrificial Animal to be Avoided: If a sacrificial animal that is black in color should have a white tail, the wise man should avoid such a goat from afar. (15)
In this way, a wise man should avoid [the hair] that is white at the tip and black at the end.
If a goat is black in color but white along its backbone, one should recognize it as excellent; however, one should avoid the opposite.
[The exclusion of lame and other defective bulls from the *bali* offering:
A wise man should avoid one that is lame, one-eyed, humpbacked, perforated, afflicted by disease, or lacking horns and teeth. (18)
[The sacrifice of the superior buffalo]:
A white buffalo five years old is proclaimed to be the most excellent. [The sacrifice of the inferior buffalo]:
That very buffalo is black and white; it is the lowest form of the sacrificial offering. || 19 ||

[The excellence of birds in sacrificial offerings: All birds of excellent color are indeed praiseworthy; however, one should avoid those that are less than three months old or those that are deficient. || 20 ||
[The statement regarding the time of satisfaction for the deities according to specific offerings:
Through ten million-colored grains offered by humans, the deities attain satisfaction;
through buffalo testicles, for a thousand years; and through buffaloes, for a hundred autumns.
With goats, [the rite] lasts for twelve years after the first year;
with tortoises, it lasts for ten years or three years, provided the full annual requirement is met.
By means of a boar [the merit lasts] for fifty years, by a yak-tail for half of that;
by means of iguanas for one year, and the blood of the limbs for six months.
Even with milk-rice, the deities attain satisfaction for six months. (24)
[Prohibition of offering women and animals as sacrifices:
One should not offer the flesh of a woman or an animal, especially in offerings to the gods (havya) or the ancestors (kavya). [Description of meat in the context of the fire-oblation (homa):]
One should eat the flesh of a domestic cock, together with its feathers, at midnight.
The shape of a lion, a bilva fruit, a pūga fruit, and a *bukka*— these are the measures for the flesh of a buffalo and a human.
Likewise, the measure of the mouth of the unborn [Viṣṇu] would be equal to that;
and the size of a *dhātakī* fruit is said to be the measure of a lizard. (27)
One should avoid from afar the flesh of an animal with impaired senses, even if it is roasted and free from human contact, provided that the animal itself was not diseased. 28.
[The temporal regulation for the meat-oblation:
One should not offer meat during the day, nor at the two twilights, nor at the conclusion of the ritual.
One should offer it during the Brāhma-muhūrta, or else on the junctions and festival days. (29)
One thousandfold [the merit] may be attained, and it is doubled at midnight;
it is doubled during the Brāhma-muhūrta and fourfold during the twilight (saṃdhyā).
At the junction of the lunar phases (parva-saṃdhi) it is a hundredfold, and at the junction of the lunar days (tithi-saṃdhi) it is one hundred and more.
In rites for specific desires, one may offer meat with the remnants of the preliminary ritual (puraścaraṇa);
however, one should not perform this offering in a pit dug at the birth canal, nor even upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
[The Method for Offering the Bali] Now, having performed the ritual sprinkling, the wise practitioner should offer the bali.
Having himself turned to face the east, he should place the bali facing the north.
Alternatively, this may be reversed: [the deity] adorned with vermilion and other [ornaments] should be sprinkled three times with pure water from the *arghya* vessel using the root mantra. || 33 ||
[The Mantra for Bathing the Animal Sacrifice:
Oṃ Vārāhī, Yamunā, Gaṅgā, Kāratoyā, Sarasvatī, Kāverī,
Candrabhāgā, Sindhu, Bhairava, and the Ocean.
O Maheśānī, manifest your presence here at this daily ablution. || 34 ||
Oṃ, to the destroyer of the bonds of the individual soul, who resides on Mount Hemakūṭa;
to the one who is both transcendent and immanent, the supreme lord, and to the embodied form consisting of the syllable HŪM. || 35 ||
Oṃ. The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet.
Having pervaded the earth on all sides, he transcended it by the measure of ten fingers. || 36 ||
One should also perform a sprinkling with these bilva leaves and water;
one should worship him there three times with desired perfumes and sandalwood.
Then, having gazed at him, the minister himself should recite [the mantra] with palms joined.
[The Mantra for Prostration to the Sacrificial Animal]:
O goat, you have appeared before me in the form of a sacrificial offering through my good fortune;
therefore, I prostrate to you, who possess all forms in the form of a sacrificial victim. (39)
By the gift that pleases Caṇḍikā, the misfortunes of the donor are destroyed;
salutations be to you, O Bala, who are the very form of the offering to Cāmuṇḍā. (40)
"Animals were created by the Self-Existent One himself for the sake of sacrifice;
therefore, I shall cause you to be slain. Thus, in a sacrifice, killing is not killing. (41)
[The recitation of the mantra upon the head of Bali:
One should recite the three mantras three times upon his head with the seed-syllables of Vāc, Māyā, and Kamalā. || 42 ||

Then, having offered the bali-oblation and performed the rites for specific desires, the one of vast intelligence should bring forth a sword before him and worship it with perfumes and other offerings. (43)
[The Sword-like Meditation:
Black, with a trident in hand, having the form of the Night of Doom (Kālarātri), fierce, with a red mouth and eyes, and anointed with fragrant unguents. (44)
Wearing red garments, with a noose in his hand and accompanied by his family, he was drinking blood and devouring heaps of raw flesh. || 45 ||
[The Sword-Worship Mantra:
Having meditated thus, the officiant should worship it with this mantra:
"O tongue of Caṇḍikā, you who bring grace to the world of the gods! (46)
The two *māyās*, the *khaḍga* word, *kāli kāli* at the end of the word, then *vajreśvarī*, and then the word *namaḥ* ending in *ṅe* for *lauhadaṇḍāyai*. (47)
One should write the *kūrca* seed-syllable on the sword with vermilion, sandalwood paste, and so forth;
one should then write the seed-syllable of the Goddess there, and having worshipped it, one should offer salutation. (48)
Having meditated thus, the practitioner should perform a salutation.
[The Mantra for Salutation to the Sword] O sword, the slayer, the blade, with its sharp edge and difficult to approach;
O you who are the womb of glory and victory—homage be to you, O protector of Dharma! (50)
Then, taking up a sword with the thought that it is the tongue of the deity,
he himself should consecrate it with the root mantra and the one that is about to be described.
Poison, the two types of illusion, and the Kali age, by virtue of their terrifying form—[utter] *daṃṣṭre sphe sphe*, and then one should say: "O Phetkāriṇī, devour! (52).
Then, after that, cut the pair "dvitaya" and the pair "chedaya" for all the wicked ones;
afterwards, kill the pair "māraya," and join with "ajaṃ khaḍgena chindhi."
*Kāli kāli*, *kiṃcit-vandvaṃ*, *pibaya rudhiraṃ padaṃ*,
*sphrau sphrau*, *kili-yugaṃ*, *kāli-yugmam*— this is the mantra for consecration (*abhimantraṇa*).
[This is the mantra for fastening the sword to the shoulder of the sacrificial offering (*bali*).]
With the mantra "hūḥ hūḥ phaṭ," one should place the sword upon the shoulder. || 54 ||

[Description of the Characteristics of the Sword] Now I shall describe the characteristics of swords according to the path of the Tantras, by the mere cutting of which the practitioner may attain accomplishment. (55)
[Description of the Characteristics of the Candrahāsa Sword] The Candrahāsa sword is the most excellent of all swords and brings happiness;
it should be made fifty finger-breadths long, or alternatively, three spans (tāla) in length. (56)

[Description of the Sword’s Shape, etc. The sword should be shaped like a *karabīra* fruit, or perhaps like a lotus petal; indeed, the practitioner should pierce it with the stalk of a *kubjaka* flower. (57)

52–54 | Regarding "poison" (*viṣa*): likewise— *oṃ hrīḥ hrīḥ kāli kāli vikaṭarūpadaṃṣṭre spheṃ spheṃ phetkāriṇi khādaya khādaya chedaya chedaya sarvān duṣṭān māraya māraya ajaṃ khaḍgena chindhi chindhi kāli kāli kici kici piba piba rudhiraṃ sphrauḥ sphrauḥ kili kili kāli kāli hūṃ hūṃ*.
The meaning is that one should place the sword upon the shoulder of Bali with the mantra *phaṭ*. (p.
850) [The procedure for sickles and other tools in the cutting of Bali:
For all the great Balis, the sickle is prescribed here.
[The prohibition against cutting with a knife, etc.
One may cut with a small blade or even a razor, but not with a large knife. 58.
One should never split it with an axe or a hatchet; rather,
one should cut it with a sharp sword that has a flawless blade.
One should not cut the thread in the air; rather, one should cut it on level ground that is likewise pure.
It is auspicious to cut it constantly while facing east, and the practitioner himself should face north, using the Netra-bīja mantra.
[The cutting of goats and other sacrificial animals facing east:
And for goats and other sacrificial animals, however, [the cutting is done] with their faces turned in the opposite direction.
[The description of the one who cuts the offering.]
And the authority over those blows is likewise ordained for them alone. || 61 ||
Either he himself, or a brother’s son, or a brother, or even a friend,
or a sapinda relative may perform the cutting, provided his inner heart is pure.

[The statement regarding those who are unsuitable, beginning with enemies: One should not employ an enemy, nor one who is deficient in a limb, nor one who is one-eyed, nor even one who is hunchbacked, on the side of the foe for the task of cutting the sacrificial offering (bali).
60. "Not in the sky": one should not offer the *bali* in an empty place with the mantra "vauṣaṭ" using the seed-syllable of the eye (*netrabīja*).
(p. 851) [The specific results when the head of the *bali* falls in a particular direction:
If it falls in the northwestern quarter, in the southwest, or even in the south...
If the head itself falls, one should predict loss in this matter. || 64 ||
Now hear the fruit regarding all the remaining directions and intermediate points:
if the head falls in the north-eastern direction, one should know it brings all prosperity and should predict a kingdom for kings. || 65 ||
When, after circling, the head indeed falls toward the right, then success is attained at the end of the month; however, if it falls toward the left ear, misfortune shall occur.
Likewise, for kings there is loss in the fire [of battle], but for householders it shall be auspicious. || 67 ||
If the head falls upon either the northeast or the center,
then in a short time, all success will certainly be attained.
If a severed head is seen falling down together with its mouth, one should know that it portends prosperity; for kings, it indicates the acquisition of a kingdom. || 69 ||
Success occurs on the first attempt, while failure is said to occur on the second;
this should be understood regarding householders, whereas for kings, it is the opposite.
[The result of seeing tears in the eyes:
When tears are seen in the eyes, one should then predict loss.
[The result of hearing the sound of teeth grinding:]
Whenever the sound of teeth grinding is heard anywhere, one should know that death is imminent, or one should predict loss in that situation.
67. Regarding the phrase "of the kings": in the southeast corner of the fire-pit (p.
852), the mantra-practitioner himself should offer the head of the sacrificial cake (*baliśiras*) in the direction of the Rākṣasas.
[The placement of the blood vessel: To its right, one should place a blood vessel, ensuring it is not turned upside down. || 72 ||
The best of practitioners should offer oblations for the Mahābalis in the northwest;
he should place the heads of the oblations known as the Aris in front.
Having placed [the material] facing the deity, one should fashion the portions to be cut;
one should know that this alone is excellent, while the opposite is mediocre.
One should place the head at the end of the *kīlaka* so that no shaking occurs.
[The offering of a lamp upon the head of the sacrificial victim:
One should offer a burning lamp, sprinkled with sandalwood paste, upon the head. (75)
With ghee one becomes a sovereign of the whole earth; with oil, one attains supernatural power (siddhi).
Or, one may offer wicks made of thread or wicks made of cloth, and [the desired result] is clearly perceived.
[The measurement of the varttikā]: The measurement of the thumb is six finger-breadths in length;
one should provide it with twenty-one threads made of cotton.
One should prepare that with fragrant substances, such as camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood.
[Prohibition against offering lamps on the heads of crocodiles, etc.
One should not cause a lamp to be offered upon the heads of crocodiles, tortoises, and especially monitor lizards, nor even upon the heads of fish or birds. (79)
[The fruit of lighting a lamp for a long duration:
For as long as the lamp burning above the head continues to burn, for that long one shall dwell in heaven; therefore, one should cause it to be given with effort. (80)
Having meditated on the fragrance arising from the burning of hair, the Goddess becomes pleased;
one should cause the Goddess to increase within that [fragrance], and therefore one should avoid the vessel. || 81 ||
When the lamp is being led away and extinction is reached, one should never offer milk, blood, or clarified butter. 82.
One should offer sugar, unbroken rice, dūrvā grass, and so forth, three hundred times each;
likewise, rock salt, ginger, and the fruit of the plantain tree. (83)
The practitioner should cast [the offering] with sweet substances intended for Śṛta; this is the prescribed method for the presentation of the bali according to the sequence of the Vārāhīsaṃhitā. 84.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the *Śrītattvacintāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Pūrṇānanda Paramahaṃsa. 24.
The Twenty-fifth Chapter:
[The Thousand-Name Hymn of the Auspicious Mahātripurasundarī] Now, the thousand names of the venerable Great Goddess are being told.
On the delightful peak of Kailāsa, adorned with various jewels. || 1 ||
Situated in the midst of wish-fulfilling trees, frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas, standing in the center of a jeweled pavilion, and adorned with various flowers. || 2 ||
Once, while the Blessed One, the Teacher of the World, was seated—bearing a skull-topped staff and a khaṭvāṅga, and having the crescent moon as his crest-ornament— [he was approached]. || 3 ||
The god who holds a trident and a *ḍamaru* drum, who has the great bull as his vehicle,
who wears a mass of matted hair, and whose throat is adorned with the serpent Vāsuki.
The god adorned with supernatural powers, blue-throated and three-eyed,
clad in a tiger skin, resembling pure crystal.
Having bowed his head to the Lord, who resembles a thousand suns, who is adorned by the half-body of the Daughter of the Mountain, and who is the cause and the universal form,
Śikhivāhana spoke to him with palms joined in reverence.
Kārttikeya said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O cause of creation, preservation, and destruction!
You are the refuge of all the gods; you are the refuge of all embodied beings. (7)
You are the refuge of all beings, and you alone are the refuge of the distressed;
you alone are the support of the world, and you alone are the creator of the universe.
(855) You alone are worthy of worship by all; other than you, there is no refuge for me.
What is the supreme secret in the world? What is the one thing that bestows all accomplishments? (9)

What is that one thing which is supreme and most excellent, what is that enjoyment which bestows both heaven and liberation—without pilgrimage sites, without austerity, without sacred knowledge, and without sacrifices? (10)
Without absorption and meditation, by what means could one attain perfection?
From what does creation arise, and in what does dissolution occur? (11)
"O Lord, why is one crossed over from the perilous ocean of saṃsāra?
I desire to hear that; tell me, O Maheśvara. (12)
Śrī Mahādeva said:
"Excellent, excellent! You have asked about the truth, O delighter of Pārvatī.
Thus, my son, I shall explain this most secret matter to you without any doubt."
Sattva, rajas, and tamas, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others—whatever other numerous beings there may be—all originate from Prakṛti. || 14 ||
She alone is the Goddess, the supreme power, Mahātripurasundarī;
she alone gives birth to everything, and she alone protects the entire universe. (15)
She alone withdraws this entire universe of moving and non-moving beings;
she is the support of all creatures and the remover of the affliction of disease.
Desire, action, and likewise knowledge, whose essence consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, exist in a threefold form as power (śakti), bringing about creation, maintenance, and destruction. (17)
He creates by means of the form of Brahmā, he protects by means of the form of Viṣṇu,
and he destroys the world, including all things mobile and immobile, by means of the form of Rudra.
In whose womb the entire world still exists today, in whom it is dissolved at the end, and from whom it is born again. (19)
Having propitiated her, the supreme station in the three worlds was attained;
I shall tell you her thousand names—listen to them. (20)
Oṃ. Of this *Sahasranāmastotra* of the illustrious Mahātripurasundarī,

the venerable Vāmadeva in the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *Gāyatrī* is the meter (*chandas*), and the deity is the illustrious Mahātripurasundarī, who possesses inconceivable power through her manifest, most secret, and transmitted *Kula*, *Kaulika*, *Garbha*, *Rahasya*, *Atirahasya*, and *Parāpararahasya* [forms].

The deity is Ākāśa; the seed-syllable is Māyā-śakti; the *kīlaka* is Kāma-bīja; the power is Buddhi-śakti; the channel is Suṣumṇā; and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of attaining the powers of Sarasvatī-śakti, as well as virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation. || 21 ||
Hrī; Kalyāṇī, Kamalā, Kālī, Karālī, Kāmarūpiṇī;
Kāmākhyā, Kāmadā, Kāmyā, Kamalā, and Kāmacāriṇī. || 22 ||
Kālarātri, Mahārātri, Kaulinī, Kaulyarūpiṇī, Kumārī, Karuṇā, Kīrti, and Kalmāṣanāśinī. || 23 ||
Kātyāyanī, the bearer of the arts, Kaumudī, the beloved of Kamalā;
the giver of fame, the giver of liberation, Medhā, the knower of ethics, and she who is fond of ethics. || 24 ||
Māheśvarī, Mahāmāyā, Mahātejā, Maheśvarī, Mahālolā, Mahājihvā, Mahādaṃṣṭrā, and Mahābhujā. || 25 ||
She is the destroyer of the darkness of great delusion, the illuminator of great liberation, the pacifier of great poverty, and the annihilator of great enemies. || 26 ||
She is the Great Power, the crusher of the great hero Mahiṣāsura;
she is the Great Illusion, possessed of great valor, and the destroyer of great sins. || 27 ||
She is Mahākāmā, the Great Kālī, who removes great sins;
she is the Great Mantra, composed of mantra, and dwells in the Maṇipūraka. || 28 ||
Mental, bestowing honor, worthy of reverence, beyond the range of mind and sight,
she is Gāyatrī, who is led by the Gaṇas and served by the Gaṇas and Gandharvas.
Girijā, Giriśā, Sādhvī, Giristhā, Girisambhavā;
Caṇḍeśvarī, Caṇḍarūpā, Pracaṇḍā, and Caṇḍamālinī. || 30 ||
She who is to be meditated upon, whose art is meditation, Caṇḍikā, who possesses a fierce form;
the mistress of sacrifice, whose form is sacrifice, and who is devoted to the sacrifice of recitation (japa). || 31 ||
She is the mother of sacrifice, the enjoyer of sacrifice, the mistress of sacrifice, and the source of sacrifice;
she is the perfected one, the lover of sacrifice, the accomplishment itself, the embodiment of the limbs of sacrifice, and the binder of sacrifice.
She who loves sacrifice, whose form is sacrifice, the sacrificial one, whose abode is made of sacrifice;
she who supports Jālandhara, the mother of the world, the knower of all births, and the beloved of the universe. || 33 ||
Jitendriyā, Jitakrodhā, Jananī, Janmadāyinī, Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, Gaurī, Gomatī, and Śatadrūkā.
The Ghargharā, the Vedagarbhā, the Devikā born from the hand [of Brahmā], the Sindhu, O Brahmins, the Mandākinī, the Yamunā, and the Sarasvatī; || 35 ||
The Candrabhāgā, Vipāśā, Gaṇḍakī, Vindhyavāsinī, Narmadā, Kadrū, Kāverī, Vetravatī, and Kauṣikī. || 36 ||
The daughter of Mahendra, Ahalyā, Campakāvatī;
Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Māyā, Kāśī, Kāñcī, and Avantikā. (37)
Dvārāvatī, Śikhinī, Mahākilbiṣanāśinī, Padminī, Padmahastā, and Padmakiñjalkavāsinī. || 38 ||
She who has a lotus-face, lotus-eyes, who dwells in a lotus, and is born from a lotus;
she who is the syllable *drīṃ*, who possesses earrings, who is Night, who resides in the heart-lotus, and who has beautiful eyes. (39)
She who is adorned with the syllable *ai*, she who is the goddess Lakṣmī, she who destroys affliction with the syllable *klī*;
she who is beloved by Hari, the mother of Hari, and she who has taken refuge in the eyes of Hari. (40)
Born from the mouth of Hari, she is peaceful; she dwells upon the chest of Hari;
she is Vaiṣṇavī, she has the form of Viṣṇu, and her essential nature is that of Viṣṇu’s Māyā. || 41 ||
The illusory power of Viṣṇu, the large-eyed one, radiant with expansive eyes;
the sovereign of the universe, the soul of the universe, the mistress of the universe, and she whose form is the universe. || 42 ||
She is the soul of the universe, the knowledge of the universe, the destroyer of all bonds;
she inspires confidence, she is the universe itself, the power of the Creator, and the wise one. (43)
Śiveśvarī, worshipped by Śiva, the mistress of Śiva, beloved of Śiva;
the mother of Śiva, named Śivā, the giver of auspiciousness, and whose form is Śiva. || 44 ||
The mistress of existence, she who is to be worshipped by existence, Bhavānī, the sovereign of the world;
the mother of Bhava, accessible through contemplation, and the destroyer of the thorns of worldly existence. || 45 ||
She who loves worldly existence, who delights in worldly existence, who removes the thorns of worldly existence;
she is the supreme refuge, Sāvitrī, Brahmāṇī, and the embodiment of Brahman. || 46 ||
Brahmeśī, Brahmadā, Brāhmī, Brahmāṇī, and Brahmavādinī; she who dwells in the fortress, whose form is the fortress, Durgā, and the destroyer of the suffering of the fortress. || 47 ||
She is easily accessible and difficult to reach; she is the giver, compassion itself, and Gaurī;
she is difficult to overcome; she is the destroyer of evil and difficult to perceive; she is the annihilator of sins committed from afar. || 48 ||
She is the fifth of the fifth, the full one dwelling in the Full Seat (Pūrṇapīṭha);
she abides in the sattva and has the form of sattva; she abides in the kalpa and has the form of the kalpa.
Her limbs are variegated with various jewels, and she is adorned with diverse ornaments;
she is Viśvāmbikā, the Mother of the Universe, who rends asunder the snares of the universe. (50)
She is the creator of the vast, the all-pervading, the universal power, and the unique;
she resembles the hibiscus flower and is as crimson as the pomegranate blossom.
She has four limbs, four arms, and laughs from her four gates;
she is the mistress of all, existing at all times, the all-encompassing one, the omniscient, and the bestower of everything.
She is the Sovereign of All, the First of All, Sarvāṇī, and the Auspiciousness of All;
she is Nalinī, Nandinī, Nandā, and Ānandā, who abides in bliss.
Pervading all beings, she is the destroyer of the burden of worldly existence;
she is noble, abiding in the midst of the Kula, and the instructor of the Kula-dharma. (54)
Richly adorned with every kind of elegant attire, she holds a noose and a goad raised in her hands;
she possesses the brilliance of a thousand suns and a face resembling ten million moons.
She possesses the beauty of ten million Gaṇeśas, she is the crusher of ten million lions,
she blazes like ten million forest fires, and she has the form of ten million Kadrūs.
As deep as ten million oceans, possessing the great strength of ten million winds, as vast as ten million skies, and terrifying as ten million Yamas. || 57 ||
She is as high as ten million Mount Merus, bestowing the supernatural powers of ten million Garuḍas;
she is stainless, without support, devoid of qualities, and free from attributes. (58)
She is the distinguished one, the mother of the universe, known as the All, the nourisher of the universe;
she is the wondrous, the multiform, the one with variegated limbs, she who contains the cause within herself, and the sovereign of battle. || 59 ||
She is the power of will, the power of knowledge, and the power of action; she of pure smiles;
she who is the Veda, who consists of the Veda, who is truth, whose form is the Veda, and who is fond of the Veda.
She is wise through the Vedas, the Great Reality, situated above the five elements; she is Pārvatī, the daughter of Himavat, standing on the further shore, whose form is the further shore. (61)
Jayantī, Bhadrakālī, Ahalyā, Kulanāyikā, Bhūtadhātrī, Bhūteśī, Bhūtasthā, and Bhūtabhāvinī. || 62 ||
The Śakti consists of the Great Family (Mahākulamayi), increasing great prosperity;
she is named Haṃsa, has the form of a swan, resides in the Haṃsa, and possesses the nature of the Haṃsa.
She dwells in the center of the moon, sun, and fire; she resides in the *mūlādhāra*;
she abides in the twelve-petaled lotus; and she dwells within the solar orb.
Residing in the center of the two-petaled leaf and dwelling upon the surface of the forehead are Ḍākinī, Rākiṇī, Lākinī, and likewise Kākinī. (65)
Śākinī and Hākinī, who dwell within the six cakras;
she is creation, maintenance, and destruction, and she brings about the end of creation and maintenance.
She is the beloved of Śrīkaṇṭha, she is Śrīkaṇṭhā, she is known as Nāda, and she is adorned with Bindus;
she is the support of the sixty-four arts and takes refuge in the kalās of the body’s staff.
Māyā, Kālī, Dyuti, Medhā, Svadhā, Puṣṭi, Mahādhṛti, Hiṅgulā, Maṅgalā, Sītā, and Suṣumṇā, who moves through the center. || 68 ||
She is supreme, terrible, with formidable eyes, victorious, and endowed with triumph;
she dwells within the lotus of the heart, fearsome, and roars like Bhairava. 69.
Born from the womb of Menakā, resembling molten gold,
she resides within the seed-syllable of Antakūṭa and dwells in the forest of Trikūṭa.
She is colored yet devoid of color, possessing the form of the fifty letters;
she is the Vidyādharī, the sustainer of the world, the immortal one, and the beloved of the Apsarases.
Dākṣā, Prajāvatī, Dhanyā, the bestower of abundance in wealth and grain;
Īśānī, Bhuvaneśānī, Bhuvanā, and Bhuvaneśvarī. (72)
She whose majesty is infinite and boundless, who is the essence of the world and the source of the world's existence;
whose mind and self consist of inconceivable power, she is thought itself, having the very nature of consciousness.
She is accessible through knowledge, the embodiment of knowledge, the possessor of knowledge, and she who abounds in knowledge;
she is dark-hued, of formidable form, a stream of nectar, and the bearer of nectar.
She is the maker of light, the radiant one, the fear, the one shining with joy,
the follower, the effortless, the patient, the blissful, the difficult to attain, and the essence of the universe.
She who is worshipped by the universe, the hero of the universe, the destroyer of the universe, and the one established in the universe;
she who abides in virtuous conduct, whose form is virtuous conduct, who is virtuous conduct itself, and the bestower of virtuous conduct. || 76 ||
She is awakening, skilled in awakening, the act of awakening, and ever-awakening;
she is the illuminator of knowledge, whose nature is manifold, and who resembles the pale-red hue of lightning.
She is the source of the universe, the great source, the source of karma, and she who speaks kindly;
she is Rohiṇī, the pacifier of disease, and the remover of great maladies. || 77 ||
She is the giver of wealth, she who has the form of Rudra, she who is fierce, and the destroyer of fierce suffering;
she is the progeny, the daughter of Dakṣa, she who is skillful, and the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
She is renowned, filled with glory, born from the womb of Yaśodā;
she is Devakī, the mother of the gods, Rādhikā, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa. (79)
Arundhatī, Śacī, Indrāṇī, Gāndhārī, Gandhamālinī; she who transcends meditation, she who is accessible through meditation, she who is named meditation, and she who sustains meditation. || 80 ||
Lambodarī, Lamboṣṭhī, Jāmbavatī, Jalodarī, Mahodarī, Muktakeśī—she is the bestower of the attainment of liberation, desire, and wealth. 81.
The ascetic one, the destroyer of passion, unstained by the secret jewel;
bodiless yet residing within the body, she is the one who carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra. (82)

Amṛtā is partless (niṣkalā), while Bhadrā is with parts (sakalā); she is dark-brown (kṛṣṇapiṅgalā), the Mistress of the Wheel (cakreśvarī), holding a wheel in her hand, and the destroyer of the wheels of adversaries. || 83 ||
Resembling a ruby, she is like the stainless sky;
she is the knower of taste, situated in the midst of tastes; she abides in fragrance and has the form of fragrance. 84.
She is the very nature of the Supreme Brahman, she whose form is the Supreme Brahman;
she is the very nature of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), she who is called "Sound," yet she is devoid of sound.
She is the supreme success of the increase of supernatural powers, her true fame firmly established;
she is the venerable Śāmbhavī Śakti, beautiful-limbed and the embodiment of ultimate reality.
She is the eternal Mother of Beings and the beloved of the Lord of the Great Elements;
she is the wisdom of the Vedas, the accomplishment of Dharma, the daughter of Dakṣa, and the unconquered Aparājitā.
She kindles desire, she is ever curious about love, skilled in the enjoyment of pleasures, immortal, and lotus-faced. (88)
Compassionate toward her devotees, she is loving-kindness itself; she is affectionate toward those who have come for refuge.
She is the agitator, the deluder, as well as the paralyzer and the yawner. (89)
She is the chariot-bearing army, the banner-bearing host, the triple Veda consisting of all mantras;
she is the wisdom-seal, the great seal, the seal of the world, and the great festival.
She is the thousand-armed power of consciousness (cicchakti), the thousand-eyed, the eternal;
she is Siddhalakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī, Rājalakṣmī, and Sulakṣaṇā. || 91 ||
She whose essence is sacrifice, whose essence is austerity, whose essence is dharma, the sovereign of people;
she who contains the universe in her womb, who is worshipped by the universe, who is named the universe, and who faces in all directions.
She is the one who inspires trust, whose nature consists of hearing and smelling, whose life-breath is the universe, and whose essence is the feet;
she resembles the rising sun and is crowded with manifold rays.
She is preeminent for wearing a mass of matted locks, with withered flesh and extremely terrifying;
she is clothed in a tiger skin and wears rags and bark garments.
Holding a trident and a *ḍamaru* drum in her hands, adorned with garlands of human heads,
she is of exceedingly fierce form, terrible, and like the fire at the end of an aeon.

She who sustains the three worlds, she who is to be accomplished, she who is success itself, she who is affectionate toward practitioners, she who consists of all vidyās, she who is the essence, and she who destroys the host of enemies. (96)
She is fortunate, fair-faced, delightful, eloquent, and adorned with the moon;
she resembles pure crystal and is borne upon a great bull. 97.
She is the Great Queen, mounted upon a buffalo, the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura;
she is the subduer, the lightning-streaked, the self-controlled, compassion itself, the milch-cow, and the one difficult to attain. || 98 ||
Agni-jihvā, most terrible, with a face more horrific than the horrific;
Nārāyaṇī, Nārasiṃhī, she who dwells in the heart of Nṛsiṃha. 99.
She is the Mistress of Yoga, the Embodiment of Yoga, the Mother of Yoga, and the Yoginī;
she moves in the sky and on the earth, she is playful, and she takes refuge in the state of Nirvāṇa. || 100 ||
She is the female nāga, the daughter of the nāgas, the well-born mistress of the nāgas;
she possesses the blazing flames of poison, is fierce, and is adorned with a hundred hoods.
She has a terrifying face and a great face, bearing ten million faces;
she is the one with the great face, known as Dharma, and the bestower of happiness beginning with dharma.
She has a black head, a great head, and a terrible head; she has a beautiful face, consists of all the senses, is established in all things, and is composed of all the senses and the mind.
She bestows victory in all battles, she is intent upon every weapon;
she pacifies all afflictions and grants all desired objects. || 104 ||

She is the source of the arising of all sovereignty, the destroyer of all seizing spirits, the remover of fear, accessible through devotion, and the destroyer of the untimely death of her devotees. || 105 ||
Mātaṅgī, the intoxicated female elephant, adorned with the lineage of Mataṅga;
resembling Gaṇḍamaṇḍita, she is decorated with a necklace of guñjā berries. || 103 ||
She delights in the composition of musical melodies and the playing of the lute;
she dwells in the midst of the ocean of nectar, radiant with a lower lip like coral. 107.
Seated in the center of a jeweled pavilion upon a throne of precious gems,
she rejoices in supreme bliss with a face slightly smiling.
Kumudā, Lalitā, Lolā, Lākṣālalitalocanā, Digvastrā, Devadūtī, and Devadevādhidevatā. (109)
Mounted upon a lion, she dwells on the great mountain; she laughs with a loud, boisterous laugh, she is terrible, and she destroys those with fearsome teeth. || 110 ||
Extremely fierce and red in color, she is adorned with serpent-bracelets;
her high and full breasts are graced by a creeper-like string of pearls. || 111 ||
Her eyes are intoxicated with passion, shaped like the petals of a red lotus;
she is the embodiment of all deities and the destroyer of the asuras. || 112 ||
Khaḍginī, Śūlahastā, Cakriṇī, Akṣamālinī, Śaṅkhinī, Cāpinī, Vāṇī, Vajriṇī, and Raktadantikā. (113)
Standing in the midst of an ocean of bliss, she is adorned with waist-bands;
her limbs shine with various ornaments and are embellished with diverse gems.

She is the source of the wish-fulfilling gem that brings about the bliss of the world, the mine of virtues, bowed to by the three worlds, worthy of worship, and whose form consists of consciousness and bliss. (115)

The Goddess who causes the three worlds to flourish, the destroyer of suffering and evil dreams, the pacifier of the terrible conflagration of fire, and she who is garlanded with the seed-syllables and the deities. 116.
She destroys heaps of great offenses, removes the fear of great thieves, is free from diseases such as passion and the like, and is devoid of old age and death. || 117 ||
Resembling the orb of the moon, born from the ocean of nectar, the Goddess is praised by all the gods and saluted by all the Siddhas. 118.
She is the form of inconceivable power, the great jewel, mantra, and medicinal herb;
she is the auspicious one, the possessor of well-being, the young maiden who dwells on the Malaya mountain. 119.
She is the Sustainer, the Ordainer, the Source of Existence, the Knower of Delight, and the Bestower of Delight;
she is Rudrāṇī, whose form is Rudra, the Fierce One, and the Destroyer of fierce suffering. || 120 ||
She is the knower of all, the knower of Dharma, the knower of flavors, and compassionate toward the wretched;
she is the unstruck sound, the three-eyed one, free from worldly existence, and supreme bliss.
Parā, Ghorā, Karālākṣī, Sumati, Priyabhāṣiṇī, Mahāmbikā, Mantramayī, Mantramātā, and Suputriṇī. || 122 ||
She is Pure Bliss, the Great Auspicious One, who has emerged as the essence of the attributeless;
she is the Sustainer, the Upholder, the Earth, the Supporter, the Nourisher, and the Treasure-Yielder of Wealth.
Abiding between Meru and Mandara, she is steadfast, the beloved of Śaṅkara;
she is the illustrious one, the best among the illustrious, the bestower of fortune, and the manifestor of prosperity.
The bestower of fortune, the ordainer of fortune, the auspicious one, the refuge of the fortunate;
Umāśā, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, Kṛṣṇā, the crooked one, she whose locks are curly. || 125 ||
She has three eyes, she dwells in the three worlds, she is the abode of merit, and she bestows meritorious fame;
she is immortal, her resolve is truth, and she is the one who has set forth toward the beyond. (126)
She is the supreme lord, the highest object of worship, the supreme knowledge, both transcendent and immanent;
she possesses beautiful limbs, has a golden luster, and is saluted by gods and demons alike.
Rudrāṇī, the goddess who bestows nourishment, the giver of honor, beloved of the mind;
she who wears the limbs of Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇā herself, and Kṛṣṇamahodarā. || 128 ||
Śāmbhavī, she whose form is Śambhu, who dwells in Śambhu, who originates from Śambhu;
she whose belly is like the bimba fruit, the mudrā of yoga, the embodiment of yoga, and the Yoginī. || 129 ||
She is Yogamudrā, Yoganidrā, and she is served by millions of yoginīs;
she is Kuṭilā, the daughter of Nandin, and dwells in the seat of Śṛṅgāra. || 130 ||
Kṣemaṅkarī, Sarvarūpā, Divyarūpā, and Divīśvarā;
Dhūmravaktrā, Dhūmrakeśī, and Dhūmravaktāvadhūsarā. || 131 ||
The wielder of the Pināka bow, the Vetālī of Rudra, she who possesses the form of a great Vetāla;
the sister, the fortunate one, the skillful, the knowledge of Viṣṇu, and the Unattached One.
Mantharā, Jaṭharā, Tīvrā, Agnijihvā, Bhayāpahā, Paśughnī, Paśurūpā, Paśuhā, and Paśuvāhinī. || 133 ||
She is the Father, the Satisfied One, the Sustainer, and the destroyer of the bonds of worldly existence;
she is the radiance of the moon, the crescent of the moon, and adorned with the splendor of the moon's light.
Her entire body was marked with saffron, her eyes were like bubbles of nectar;
she was harsh and cruel-hearted, yet her speech was as sweet as the nectar of Akrūra.
Born from the liṅga of space, she flows through the meditation on the worlds;
she is eyeless, thousand-eyed, hundred-eyed, and many-eyed.
Tārā who descends with the staff, the youthful one whose form is radiant, the stream of nectar, the knower of Dharma, and the instructor of the Dharma scriptures. (137)
The Mistress of Existence, she who is to be propitiated through existence, the Sister, the Lady of the Yoni;
the Knowledge of the Yoni, she whose yoni is moist, the Source of the Yoni, and the Bestower of the Yoni. 138.
The Mistress of the Yoni, whose form is the Yoni, whose secret is the Yoni, who brings forth the Yoni;
she whose belly is the Yoni, whose bliss is the Yoni, who begins with the Yoni, and who is garlanded by the Yoni. 139.
Mālinī, Mādhavī, Sādhvī, Madhurūpā, Mahotkaṭā;
Candrikā, Candrimā, Jyotsnā, Viśvacakṣus, and Tamo’pahā. 140.
She is Suprasannā, Mahādūtī, Yamadūtī, and Bhayaṅkarī;
she is Unmādinī, Mahārūpā, Divyarūpā, and Surārcitā. || 141 ||

She who bears fruit for the three worlds, she who is eternal, she who is intoxicated with the pride of perpetual bliss; she whose sole joy is wine, whose eyes are like wine, and who is languid with passion.
Siddheśvarī, the perfected lore, the primordial Siddhā, adored by the Siddhas;
worshipped by the Siddhas, the mother of the Siddhas, she is perfection itself, the bestower of the accomplishment of all goals.
She consists of illusion, yet transcends the qualities; she is the nature of the supreme light.
She is the Supreme Goddess, the one who has gone to the beyond, the further shore, the supreme perfection, and the supreme goal.
She is Vimalā, the Enchantress, the Primordial One, devoted to the drinking of honey-wine;
she is the mother of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and is proficient in all the scriptures. || 145 ||
The Goddess is eternally composed of all the gods, likewise composed of all the scriptures;
she is composed of all sacrifices, and the Sovereign is composed of all dharma.
She is all sacrifices and the great sacrifice; she is the presiding authority over all mantras;
she is the sovereign of all prosperity, and likewise the embodiment of the power of all vidyās.
The goddess who agitates all, the bringer of all auspiciousness;
the goddess who attracts the three worlds, the bringer of delight to all. (148)
The goddess who deludes all, she who causes the paralysis of all, the goddess who makes the three worlds yawn, and likewise she who brings all under her control. (149)
The Goddess who delights the three worlds, whose nature is the intoxication of all, the Goddess who accomplishes all aims, and who liberates from all suffering. || 150 ||
She is the pacifier of all death, the destroyer of all suffering, the mother beautiful in every limb, and the bestower of all prosperity. || 151 ||
She is omniscient and omnipotent, the bestower of the fruit of all sovereignty;
the Goddess consists of all knowledge and is the destroyer of all diseases. 152.
She is the very nature of the support of all, the destroyer of all sins, the Goddess consisting of all bliss, and the embodiment of the protection of all. || 153 ||
She consists of all prosperity, is eternal, bestows the fruits of all desires, pacifies all that is evil, and grants supreme bliss. || 154 ||
She is the abode of the three worlds, she who exists in the three places, the mother of the three, and she who resides in the three levels;
she is the triple knowledge, the triple Veda, Māyā, the three worlds, Tripurā, and the Imperishable. 156.
She who exists in the three states, she who is threefold, Tripurā, she who resides in the triple city;
she who possesses the three abodes, the sovereign of the thirty gods, the multiplier by three, and the dweller in the triple city. || 156 ||
She is the threefold goal, the triple myrobalan, she who dwells in the three states, the triple-formed, the sovereign of the three cities;
she is the threefold one, the queen of the three heavens, and Tripurasundarī with her three [aspects]. (157)
Tripurā Śrī, the mother of the three worlds, the triple city, Tripurabhairavī. Om. 158.
Thus, O son, out of affection for you, I have proclaimed this thousand names of the mantra of Śrī Purasundarī, which is more secret than the secret. (159)
It should be concealed with effort and recited with diligence;
there is no hymn superior to this, and no mantra-repetition superior to this. (160)
There is no merit greater than this, nor is there a goal higher than this:
the hymn known as the Thousand Names, which has issued from my own mouth. (161)
Whoever should recite this with supreme devotion, or listen to it with a concentrated mind—the seeker of liberation shall obtain liberation, and the seeker of heaven shall attain heaven. (162)
One who desires pleasures shall obtain pleasures; one who seeks wealth shall obtain wealth;
one who seeks knowledge shall obtain knowledge; and one who seeks fame shall obtain fame. || 163 ||
One seeking a daughter obtains a daughter; one seeking a son obtains a son.
A pregnant woman shall give birth to a son, and a maiden finds a virtuous husband. (164)
Even a fool obtains the scriptures, and even a thief attains a [better] destination. (165)
On the day of the sun's transit, and especially on the fourteenth, the eighth, the full moon, the new moon, the ninth, and on Tuesdays and Fridays; 166.
One should recite it, or cause it to be recited, or listen to it with a concentrated mind;
it should be guarded with effort and studied with diligence. || 167 ||
He shall be liberated from all sins and become equal to the Lord of Desire;
endowed with fortune, sons, and splendor, he shall be beloved by all women. (168)

The three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile, shall quickly come under his control—just as the gods are when they behold Rudra, or as the immortals are when they behold Viṣṇu. || 169 ||
Just as serpents upon seeing Garuḍa, or elephants upon seeing a lion, or frogs upon seeing a serpent, or mice upon seeing a cat; (170)
But his enemies submit to him simply by looking upon his face; and through his sight, no fear of fire or thieves shall ever arise for him. (171)
There are many sins as massive as Mount Meru or Mandara;
yet [this practice] quickly reduces them to ashes, just as fire offered as an oblation consumes even grass.
By reciting it just once, the destruction of all sins occurs;
and by reciting it ten times, many diseases are destroyed. (173)
By reciting it just one hundred times, one shall attain perfection of speech;
but the man who recites it a thousand times becomes a sky-walker (khecara).
The devoted man who indeed recites it ten thousand times, for him that Mother of the worlds certainly becomes manifest. (175)

If a wise person recites this King of Hymns a full one hundred thousand times, he will be completely liberated from the bonds of worldly existence and become equal to me; of this there is no doubt. (176)

Whatever merit is found in all sacred fords, whatever fruit is found in all sacrifices, whatever dharma is found in all the Vedas, and whatever fruit is found in all acts of giving—(all that is attained here). || 177 ||
Whatever fruit is proclaimed in all the scriptures that have been taught, a person shall obtain that fruit multiplied ten million times by reciting this but once. || 178 ||
Having heard this, he became possessed of great strength, sons, and abundant wealth.
At the end of the body, he will go to the supreme abode which is difficult even for the gods to attain;
there is no doubt that this occurs through the recitation of the King of Hymns. 180.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the *Śrī-Tattvacintāmaṇi* composed by the holy Pūrṇānanda Paramahaṃsa. || 25 ||
The Twenty-sixth Chapter:
[Description of the Consecration of the Great Yantra] Now, the consecration of the great yantra, which bestows all prosperity, is being described. (1)
On an auspicious day, having performed his bath at an auspicious moment and under an auspicious planetary conjunction,
the practitioner of mantra, having completed his daily obligatory rites, should face either the east or the north.
Having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and other preliminary rites, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) as prescribed in the Kalpa.
Then, having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), the pure-souled practitioner [should offer] that which has been purified by the Śiva-mantra.
Having brought together the five products of the cow, one who is composed should place the yantra— which has been fashioned upon a gem such as gold— into it while reciting the syllable *praṇava*.

Having extracted that [substance] and placed it in a vessel made of gold or other materials, the knower of mantras [should worship it] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), with sacred water (tīrtha), and with cool water.
Having bathed [the deity] with the Sahasraśīrṣa mantra preceded by the root mantra, and having lifted up pure water in a metallic vessel, || 6 ||
Having placed [the deity] upon a lion-throne or similar seat, one should anoint it with saffron and other unguents;
thereafter, one should perform the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā) according to the procedure prescribed in one's own ritual manual.
Touching with kuśa grass, one should recite the king of mantras one hundred and eight times.
One should extract the syllable *praṇava* for the King of Mantras; then one should write the word "vidmahe," followed by "mahāmantrāya" and the form "dhīmahi," and then "mahī. (9)
(872) That Yantra is proclaimed as the form of Dayā (Compassion).
Having recited this Gāyatrī of the Yantra, one shall attain divinity. || 10 ||
[Instruction on the Worship of the Desired Deity] Having meditated upon the desired deity, one should invoke it in sequence with the appropriate mudrā;
then, having performed the placement of the vital breath (jīvanyāsa), one should worship the desired deity. (11)
With the sixteen types of ritual services, an extensive array of various riches, and with dances, songs, and instrumental music preceded by the fivefold sounds; (12)
Then one should recite the desired mantra one thousand and eight times;
thereafter, having prepared the fire according to the ritual manual (kalpa) with sacrificial oblations (havis), [one should proceed].

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, he should satisfy the Guru with wealth according to his means, with gold, jewels, and the like, and should also present him with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
[The Instruction on the Symbolic Gestures of the Sixteen Offerings: Now, the characteristics of the sixteen offering gestures (upacāramudrā) are described.
One should extend both hands and place them at the region of the heart. (15)
The fingers should be spread apart, and one should place the two thumbs in the middle;
thus one should display the five-fold mudrā for the placement of the deity's seat.
The fingers should be known as slightly bent, with the hollows of the thumbs closed;
the little finger and the index finger are bent, and the tips of the two hands are joined together. (17)
One should form this mudrā of the seat with the middle and ring fingers;
the right hand, with its fingers slightly bent, should encircle the other thumb.
The Svāgata-svastika mudrā consists of the fingers placed at the base of the middle finger;
it should be employed by the wise one during the ritual of welcoming.
When those two hands are extended, it is proclaimed as the *pādyamudrā*.
When the ring fingers and thumbs are joined and the other three fingers are fully extended, [it is the *arghyamudrā*]. (20)
That is declared by the knowers of Tantra to be the mudrā of the madhuparka;
likewise, the eye-mudrā consists of a clenched fist with the tips of the thumbs pointing downward.
The middle finger and the thumb joined together, with the other three fingers well extended—this is declared to be the Vastra-mudrā, which increases the merit of [offering] garments. || 22 ||
The two little fingers joined together and the three middle fingers extended—
this is declared by those who have mastered the mantras to be the *yajñopavīta* mudrā.
The Madhuparka mudrā is considered to have the fingers joined and turned upward;
the Gandha mudrā is proclaimed as that which is joined by the thumb and the ring finger.

When the middle finger is raised with the palm facing downward and the other [thumb] is joined at the base of the thumb, it is declared to be the Puṣpa-mudrā (Flower Gesture), which increases the merit of offering flowers. || 25 ||
With the thumb joined to the index finger and the other three fingers contracted, this mudrā, when offered as incense, brings satisfaction to the gods. (26)
The *pauṣpikī* mudrā, when turned upward, is called the *dīpa* (lamp) mudrā;
it is formed when the tips of the five fingers are joined and raised, yet the hand faces downward. (27)
This mudrā, bound in three ways, is proclaimed as that of the food offering (naivedya).
With both hands joined back-to-back, one should rotate them with the fingers interlaced;
this is known as the Sphoṭikā, which one should display during prostration.
p. 874) [The Different Varieties of the Mudrās of Incense and the Others] Alternatively, one should display these mudrās with the incense and other offerings in sequence:
the *gandhamudrā* is proclaimed as that in which the little finger and the thumb are joined together. || 29 ||
The thumb and the back [of the hand] are prescribed for incense; the index finger for the lamp; and the middle and ring fingers are proclaimed for the food offering.
Through the joining of the other fingers, five mudrās are proclaimed. || 31 ||
Even when perfumes and other offerings have been presented, one should display these mudrās.
[The Greatness of Mudrās:
Whatever ritual action is performed with a mudrā, that shall yield infinite fruit. || 32 ||
[The Ritual for the Installation of a Deity] Now I shall explain the sequence of the ritual for the installation of a deity:
in a sacred field, at an auspicious time, on a site free from thorns and other defects. (33)
And at the conclusion of the ritual manual for the mantra, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) on the preceding day;
having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) in the evening according to the rules, preceded by the installation of the water-pot (ghaṭasthāpana).
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa and the others, one should fully honor the guardians of the directions;
one should worship the primary deity with offerings according to one's capacity.
One should consecrate it with fragrant oils, perfumes, and so forth, ending with divine substances,
while reciting the mantra beginning with "candreṇa" and preceded by the sound of victory.
Having thus performed the ritual consecration, self-restrained and with senses conquered,
he should rise in the morning, perform his daily rites, and enter the prepared place of sacrifice.
It was crowded with banners and flags, adorned with a divine pavilion, and decorated with canopies, yak-tail whisks, umbrellas, and garlands of flowers. || 38 ||
When the area has been completely filled with auspicious sprouts, vessels, and other such items,
one should draw the Sarvatobhadra mandala upon the altar.
Facing the east and remaining silent, one should make a formal resolve for the attainment of one's desired goal.
Having performed the fivefold purification, he should prepare a water-pot filled with unbroken grains.
Having established [the deity] there in the maṇḍala, one should worship the foundational power (ādhāraśakti);
then the wise one should install the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra) and all [the other elements] therein. 41.
Having performed the initiation according to the procedure prescribed in the Krama, as well as the consecration with the ritual pitcher,
one should then prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), purified by the recitation of Śiva-mantras.
The practitioner, reciting the Praṇava, should thoroughly bathe the image with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), sacrificial ghee, curd, and milk, in that order.
Then, having performed the ritual rubbing with unguents, one should bathe him with water;
having lifted up the water with a cloth, one should clothe him in two fine silk garments (dukūla).
The wise one should lead the deity near the jar that has been set out;
then, having meditated upon her as described, he should invoke her in due order with the appropriate mudrā.
Having placed the hand upon the heart of the deity with the *lelihā-mudrā*,
one should then recite the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā-mantra* ten times,
as well as the *gāyatrī* of the respective deity one hundred and eight times.
Then, according to the procedure prescribed in the Kalpa, one should subsequently worship the deity together with the retinue in the pavilion situated to one's left.
Having placed it upon a pedestal provided with eight petals,
one should indeed give it an anointing with fragrant, divine oil.
The wise one, with devotion, should bathe [the deity] with the nectar from the consecration jars using the *mūla-mantra*, the *pāvamāna* hymns, and the *sahasraśīrṣā*. (49)

One should sprinkle [the deity] with camphor, agallochum, musk, flowers, sandalwood water, and even water from various sacred fords (tīrtha), as well as with waters containing gold and gems, waters of all medicinal herbs, and fragrant waters, while reciting the root mantra.
Then, having lifted up water with a pure silk cloth, the practitioner— || 51 ||
Having clothed her in two silk garments and brought her upon a swing fashioned of gold into the mandala, [he honored her] with dances, songs, and shouts of victory.
One should worship with the sixteen services according to the prescribed ritual. [Instruction on the fire sacrifice:
The mantra-practitioner [should perform it] in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on a consecrated altar (sthaṇḍila), using clarified butter (havis) in the prepared fire.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations and then cooked the sacrificial porridge (caru),
he should perform the fire-oblation with the offering-spoon according to the prescribed ritual procedure.
One who knows the mantras for oblation should offer a sacrificial pap (caru) the size of a mouthful at the base;
having placed a ladle of clarified butter there, he should sacrifice it facing the fire.
Indeed, twenty-five times, one should diligently offer bali oblations with sacrificial porridge (caru) to the deities and the guardians of the directions, starting from the east.
Then, one should offer an oblation of clarified butter to the Āvṛtidevas, or likewise with caru, near the deity. (57)
Having gone there, one should offer five handfuls of flowers along with an umbrella and chowries;
then, being composed, one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
Then, while reciting the Mātṛkā and the root mantra amidst sounds of "Victory! Victory!", one should consecrate the deity with the sprouts placed in the offering jar.
Having gone near the fire-offering (homa), one should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor, consisting of gold weighing one karṣa.

Then the wise man, having first performed [the rites] according to his means, should satisfy the twice-born by giving them half, a quarter, or an eighth part; thereafter, he should receive their blessings.
Thus has been declared the installation of deities, which bestows all prosperity. [The Proclamation of the Fruits of Installation:
Whoever performs the installation of a high-souled deity, || 62 ||
He shall dwell in heaven for two or three thousand years according to the measure of the gods;
thereafter, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā for a hundred thousand times ten thousand years.
Or rather, it may cause delusion for the end of millions of kalpas in the imperishable state.
[The Ritual for the Consecration of a House] Now I shall describe the consecration of a house, preceded by the Vāstu sacrifice,
during the highly meritorious autumn season, in a sacred field, on an auspicious day. (65)
Having given a temple to Durgā according to their respective mantras, and having performed everything previously mentioned preceded by the Vṛddhi-śrāddha rite; || 66 ||
